PREFACE TO REVISED EDITION 

The first edition of this book was published in 1923. Shortly thereafter I removed to Miami, Florida. As I am no longer engaged in the practice of law in Georgia, it might appear that I should not be interested in publishing a revised edition of my Georgia book. However, since the first edition was so graciously received by the members of the Georgia bar and since that edition has been sold out by the publishers, I have decided to publish this revised edition largely as a matter of pride in authorship. The labor has been incredible; the time I could ill afford from my practice, but I take pride in the knowledge that the work has been carefully done.

Sections of the new Code of Georgia Annotated have been cited instead of sections of Park's Annotated Code. Selected decisions of the Supreme Court of Georgia and the Court of Appeals of Georgia have been cited through 185 Georgia Reports, 57 Georgia 

Appeals Reports, and 197 Southeastern Reporter. I have pre served the original text and footnotes wherever possible. The material in this volume could have been used to fill two separate volumes, but, for the convenience of the members of the bar, I have kept it in one volume by increasing the size of the pages approximately fifteen per cent and by keeping the footnotes compact and in small type.

In writing this edition I have observed that a number of statutory changes have been made which were suggested in the first edition. 

While I take no credit for these changes made by the legislature, I feel that it is proper to make additional suggestions which would improve the laws pertaining to wills and administration of estates in Georgia. Accordingly, on pages 14, 21, 131, 132, 140, 142, 153, 159, 165, 199, 312, 323, 510, 529, 538, 542, and 552 of this volume, I have suggested legislative changes. These are suggested with the desire that they may prove helpful. 

I acknowledge with sincere appreciation the splendid assistance given me in the preparation of this edition by Mr. Ralph O. Cullen, by my secretary, Miss Eileen Graham, and by Miss Nina McAdam, (v)

vi 

PREFACE TO REVISED EDITION 

of the Miami Senior High School. Without their assistance the preparation of this volume would have been much more burdensome. 

Miami, Florida, December 1, 1938

D. H. REDFEARN

PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION 

To the legal mind, wills and the administration of estates are perhaps the most fascinating subjects of our jurisprudence. In addition to the special interest of the legal profession in these subjects, mankind generally is much concerned; for all realty and personalty, except that held in perpetuity by the government, or some of its units, or by charitable institutions, changes hands at least once every generation. For this reason, almost every person, sometime during his life, is interested in the settlement of estates, as an heir, devisee, legatee, or creditor, or as the manager of the interests of minor children or of other incapacitated persons. This general interest has resulted in the preparation of many exhaustive treatises on these subjects, by authors in other states. But these excellent works are apt to be confusing as they deal with the laws of all jurisdictions generally. They cover much useful ground for other states, which need not be considered here, as this work is intended primarily for the use of the members of the Georgia Bar and those studying for admission.

As the common law of wills and administration is in force in Georgia, except where changed by statute, the most painstaking effort has been required to solve many problems not yet settled by our statutes and by our courts. Whenever an important question seems not to have been settled in Georgia, I have tried to point the way to its solution by showing decisions of the courts of other states, and, in many instances, the rulings of the English courts on similar questions.

Throughout the preparation of this work, it has been my aim to present succinctly the laws pertaining to wills and the administration of estates, in Georgia, and to outline the procedure and practice for taking cases, pertaining to these subjects, through the Court of Ordinary and to final judgment. I believe that the busy lawyer will be saved much valuable time by having the law in ready reference form like this, rather than in the large, standard works, covering the laws of every state of the Union, and in the decisions of our courts, which at present are scattered through one hundred fifty-three volumes of our Supreme Court Reports and (vii)

viii 

PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION 

twenty-eight volumes of our Court of Appeals Reports. I also believe that students, and others interested, will find this work to be of value to them.

On account of the incredible labor involved, it has required all the time I could spare from my practice for more than six years to prepare this volume. I could not have finished it in this time. if it had not been for many helpful suggestions received from other members of the Bar. I express sincere appreciation to Judge 

Arthur G. Powell and Mr. Marion Smith, of the Atlanta Bar, and to Judge R. C. Bell, of the Court of Appeals, and to Messrs. R. 

H. Ferrell, I. J. Hofmayer, and J. R. Pottle, of the Albany Bar, for their many helpful suggestions. Especially, do I appreciate the invaluable assistance of Mr. Sam S. Bennet, of the firm of Pope & Bennet, of the Albany Bar, who has given his time unsparingly, from a busy practice, to aid me with many of the difficult problems discussed in this volume. 

I also express appreciation to Mrs. Maud Barker Cobb, our efficient State Librarian, and to Miss Ella M. Thornton, our efficient Assistant State Librarian, for the assistance given me in my research work in the State Library. 

Albany, Georgia, February 1, 1923

D. H. REDFEARN

CHAPTER I  § 1. Ancient History. 

2. History of Wills in England. 

3. Feudalism. 

4. Statutes of Wills. 

5. History of Wills in Georgia. 

§ 1.—Ancient History.-Formerly, the opinion was held that the earliest evidences of wills were found in the ancient laws of the Greeks and of the Romans, and in the forty-eighth chapter of Genesis, where Jacob bequeathed to his son Joseph a portion above his brethren.' But this opinion has been revised, in recent years, as a result of information obtained from excavations made in Egypt and elsewhere. A will nearly five thousand years old, similar in form to the modern will, has been found in Egypt. Probably, wills in some form were not unknown in the other ancient nations which rivaled Egypt in the days of her splendor. However, the subject of ancient wills is of interest chiefly to the antiquarian. Other students of the history of wills, in the United States, are concerned primarily with the development of the English will, as most of the states have modeled their statutes of wills on the English Statutes of 1677 and 1837. 

§ 2. History of Wills in England.-Testamentary control in Eng land was probably a gift of the expiring civilization of Rome to the barbarian tribes which overran her vast domains, including England and western Europe, in the fourth and fifth centuries. 

The Romans temporarily occupied England during Caesar's campaigns, 55-54 B.C. About the middle of the first century, A.D., they made their occupancy permanent and continued in control 

1. Blackstone, vol. 2, page 490.

[Ch. 1 until the middle of the fourth century, when they began to withdraw gradually on account of Rome's declining military power. As 

England during these centuries was a Roman province, the Roman law of wills and administration was followed. When the Roman legions were withdrawn, the Anglo-Saxon conquest began, and continued for the next two centuries. Wave after wave of nomadic, barbarian tribes from northern Europe swept into England, and turmoil and strife between the inhabitants and these invaders probably made the permanent and peaceful possession of lands or of chattels impossible. While the original inhabitants were being subjugated, as well as after they had been subjugated, war was continuously waged among various factions of the victorious invaders. 

As a result, few records have survived the wild confusion of this period, but we find that, when England, in the seventh century, began to emerge into authentic history again, far-reaching changes had been taking place; for the fertile grain fields, the excellent highways, the populous cities, and the prosperous villas of the Roman occupation had been abandoned to a great extent or had disappeared, and the inhabitants left there when the Romans withdrew had been amalgamated generally with the invaders. Although we find that the pre-Saxon races had not disappeared completely, they had reverted to a more primordial condition of society.² 

As before stated, the continual warfare between the Anglo-Saxon invaders and the native inhabitants, during this period of conquest and of continuous strife among different factions of the victorious invaders, made the conditions of society such that few men could exercise complete and permanent control over their possessions while living, much less give direction as to their disposition after death. During this period, probably little was known of testamentary disposition.

By the middle of the ninth century the idea of a common king and government had developed, and the inhabitants of the island had made peace sufficiently among themselves to permit the development of the idea of permanent and peaceful possession of lands and of chattels. From this time until the eleventh century, 2. "There are many indications of a very thorough change in the habits and conditions of life and of a very peculiar course of development at this historical juncture." Vinogradoff, The 

Growth of the Manor, page 117. For development in agriculture and for other material progress, see Vinogradoff, The Growth of the Manor, pages 44, 83.

§ 3 

when feudalism became firmly established as a system of land tenure in England, wills both of personal property and of real estate are found. During the centuries of feudalism in England, there were no wills of lands, except in localities where certain customs prevailed, but wills of personalty were allowed. It was during the centuries before feudalism in England that the Church laid the foundation for the great power it was in later centuries to exercise in the control of decedents' estates.

England had been converted to Christianity while it was a Roman province, but during the Anglo-Saxon conquest the power and influence of Christianity largely disappeared in England, along with other evidences of Roman civilization. After conditions had become somewhat settled again, Christianity was firmly re-established in England by missionaries from Rome, the first of whom were Augustine and his band of monks, who arrived in 597 and established a monastery at Canterbury. From this center the conversion of the island was effected gradually. 3 The Church soon began to concern itself with more than the spiritual affairs of men, and so began the accumulation of the wealth which was to make it the richest and most important institution in England in the coming centuries. It taught that the dying man should not only confess his sins but also should make atonement for them by devoting to the relief of the poor and to other pious purposes at least a portion of his wealth. There seems to have been an ancient custom among the Saxons, referred to by Blackstone, of dividing the personal property into three parts: one for the wife, one for the children, and one which the owner could dispose of by will, called "the dead's part." If the owner died without children, one-half belonged to his wife; and if he had neither wife nor children, the whole of his estate was at his disposal by will. It was to the dead's part that the Church looked for the dying man to provide for the pious causes mentioned. The shares of the wife and children were called their "reasonable parts." Through the influence of the Church, this form of division was soon adhered to by the ecclesiastical courts, even though the deceased died intestate. 4

The Church in these early centuries asserted its right to administer only that part of the personal estate of the deceased which he could dispose of by will, except in cases of intestacy. As the centuries passed, the right of the owner to dispose of all his personal assets by will was recognized, and the courts of the Church -the ecclesiastical courts-assumed jurisdiction over the entire personal assets of the deceased.

In these early centuries it was considered a terrible disgrace and an awful sin to die intestate; it was an exception for a man of any means to die without a will. During this time wills were made usually not long before death; they could be made orally, or they could be made by a nod of the head or by other sign of assent.Ⓡ 

As wills were made so easily, and as all men had been taught a religious abhorrence of intestacy, much business was made for the ecclesiastical courts and great profits for the Church; for the cleric who was usually at the bedside of the dying man for his comfort, in his last hours, often by opportune questions obtained a substantial gift for the Church. If no will was made, the ecclesiastical courts, by very early authority from the crown, administered the personal assets anyway, and so well was the interest of the Church. provided for that we find "in 1268 it was necessary for a legatine council to remind the prelates that they were but trustees in this matter and were not to treat the goods of intestates as their own."⁹ 

The right to make a will of personalty was not interrupted by feudalism in England. Such wills, although not made during the last sickness, could be made orally until the Statute of Frauds. 10 

Since this statute, wills of personalty, if not made in the last sickness as nuncupative wills, must be in writing; and since the Wills 

Act of 1837, in England, such wills must also be signed by the testator and attested in the same manner as wills of realty. Nuncupative wills were abolished in England by the Act of 1837, except as to soldiers in actual military service and sailors actually at sea.12 The right to make a will of lands, either orally or in writing, 11

was interrupted about the middle of the eleventh century as a result of feudalism, and was not re-established until the first statute of wills, which was enacted in 1540. For this reason, it will be necessary here to outline briefly the history of feudalism and its effect on the disposition of land by will, before discussing the English statutes of wills. § 3.-Feudalism.-After the breaking up of the Roman Empire in the fifth century, the all-prevailing need in all of Europe was protection. The poor peasants and the small landowners were everywhere subject to attack. The peace and security which Rome had formerly established could no longer be maintained, and the provinces fell into disorder. 13 Roving bands of marauders, highwaymen, robbers, revolted troops, and insurrecting peasants plundered the weak of their possessions on one pretext or another. The natural place for the individual to look for protection under such circumstances was to the government. But the government, on account of the continual strife, was unable even to protect itself. 

Consequently, those in need of protection had to seek it elsewhere. 

Feudalism in Europe was the natural outcome of these peculiar conditions.14

Feudalism in England, as a system of land tenure and of society, was largely a result of the Norman Conquest in 1066, when England was overrun again by invaders from the continent. This invasion resulted in a complete change of the system of land tenure in England and ultimately made it impossible, for several centuries, for the owner of lands to dispose of the same by will.15 This 

13. George Burton Adams, Civilization During the Middle Ages, page 198. 

14. "This historical feudal system came into existence in the eighth and ninth centuries, owing to the political disorders of the time, and the inability of the central governmenteven of so strong a government as Charlemagne's to do its necessary work without some such help. It is itself a crude and barbarous form of government in which the political organization is based on the tenure of land; that is, the public duties and obligations which ordinarily the citizen owes to the state, are turned into private personal services which he owes to his lord in return for land which he has received from him. The state no longer depends on its citizens, as citizens, for the fulfillment of public duties, but it depends upon a certain few to perform specified duties, which they owe as vassals of the king, and these in turn depend upon their vassals for services, which will enable them to meet their own obligations toward the king." change of land tenure was not made suddenly as a result of the Conquest; it was a gradual growth which spread with feudalism over England.16

In the beginning of feudalism, small landowners brought their lands into the feudal relation by surrendering them to rich landowners who were able to furnish protection. Large landowners, who needed an army of vassals to fight for them against barbarian invaders and against their rivals, divided their lands into numerous fiefs among men who lacked estates and who were willing and able to fight.17 In one of these ways, the wealthy landowners built up around them territories which they controlled and defended. When the small landowner surrendered his land to the lord and became his vassal, he parted with the title but received the promise of protection; and, when the great landowner granted a tract of land to a vassal, he gave with it the promise of protection but retained the title. The vassal and his heirs after him had the right to use the land, but in return for this use certain services had to be rendered to the lord; such as, accompanying him to war, guarding his castle, attending his court, and assisting in paying his ransom if he were captured.18 Land thus granted was known as the fief. The fief usually meant land, though it might be a privilege like the right to 16. The system of feudalism had made some progress in England prior to the Norman Conquest. By the oath exacted by William at the Salisbury gemote in 1086, feudalism was halted as a system of government but was kept as a system of land tenure. "The conqueror introduced great principle which made feudalism in England very different from what it was in other European countries. 

In other countries a man's allegiance was satisfactorily fulfilled by giving it under all circumstances to his immediate lord. In England William's law required that loyalty to the king should take precedence of all other allegiance, even of a man's fealty to his feudal lord. At the ceremony of the Salisbury oath, imposed by William in the last year of his reign, in the words of the old chronicle, 'All the land-holding men of all England, one whosesoever men they were, knelt to him and became his men, and swore solemn oaths to him that they would be faithful to him before all other men.' Nevertheless this ideal was but poorly carried out. When the great barons rose in rebellion their tenants marched with them against the king; and more than once subtenants were excused for rebellion because they had risen in obedience to the command of the lord to whom they owed direct allegiance." Cheyney, A Short History of England, page 138. See also Gardiner's Students History of England, page 113.

hold an office, operate a mill, or enjoy the use of any desirable thing. 19

The lord himself might need protection; so he would bind himself and his land to someone else, who in turn might be bound to another, and thus on to the king, of whom all land, under the feudal theory, was held and who, himself, under his claim of divine right, was said to hold all the land from God.20 Thus no man, under the theory of feudalism, might be said to be free, and no one could dispose of his land freely. The title, with certain privileges, descended to the "heir" of the lord; and the use of the land, with certain obligations, belonged to the vassals from generation to generation. In the beginning of feudalism, the fief was precarious in that it was held practically at the will of the lord, but in the course of a century it became inheritable. and there heard causes under the presidency of the grand justiciary of the realm (this is the origin of the appellate jurisdiction of the House of

20. "The feudal system, with all its tyranny and all its faults and shortcomings, was based upon the requirements of mutual help and service, and was maintained by obligations of honour and fealty. Regular subordination, mutual obligation, social unity, were the pillars of the fabric. The whole state was one: the king representing the unity of the nation. The great barons held their estates of him, the minor nobles of the great barons, the gentry of these vassals, the poorer freemen of the gentry, the serfs themselves were not without rights and protectors as well as duties and service. Each gradation, and every man in each, owed service, fixed definite service, to the next above him, and expected and received protection and security in return. Each was bound by fealty to his immediate superior, and the oath of one implies the pledged honour and troth of the other. Doubt-

[Ch. 1 

Thus, under the theory of feudalism, a will of lands could not be made, because it would be contrary to feudal tenure.21 However, it can be demonstrated that parts of England never came under the complete control of the feudal system, 22 and consequently wills of land controlled by local customs as before the Conquest are found in these localities.23

The feudal system, thus founded on the knightly idea of protection to the weak, continued in existence until the latter half of the fourteenth century, when it gradually fell into disuse. Its disappearance in England is attributable largely to the increased demand for labor and the consequent increase of wages due to the ravages of the Hundred Years' War and to the "black death," now supposed to have been the bubonic plague, from which nearly half of the population of England died in the years 1348 and 1349. 

Then, too, feudalism itself had degenerated into a means of legalized plunder, which was probably worse than the unlawful indignities suffered by the poor in the earlier centuries, when they had to beg the large landowners for protection. 

The obligations of feudalism grew to be more burdensome and multiplied in number as the years passed. After the death of the vassal, before his successor, his heir, was allowed to control the fief, the lord claimed a fine, called "relief," for the privilege of succession. When the land was held by knight-service and the heir was a minor, the lord was his guardian and claimed all the income from the estate without having to account for his guardianship when his ward became of age.24 In addition to this exaction, the less there were many hardships, more in theory perhaps than in reality." If the tenant died leaving as his heiress a daughter under fourteen years of age, her condition was even worse, for, in addition to the rights mentioned, the lord had the right to control her marriage;25 and he usually delivered her to the highest bidder unless she bought the right of her marriage by the payment of a heavy fine. Thus, the descendants of the poor freemen who had begged the rich landowners for protection in the earlier centuries were now in serious need of protection from legalized robbery by the descendants of the rich landowners, who in their need or greed for wealth had devised these many burdens attached to the fief.27 

During the development of the feudal system, the Church continued to add to its land holdings. The monasteries had owned and controlled great tracts of land prior to the beginning of feudalism, 28 but it was during the development of this system that their landed estates became so vast. It seems that whenever possible the poor freemen preferred to grant their land to the monasteries for protection rather than to the rich landowners. Probably this was due to the fact that the terms of service exacted of a vassal by the Church were less burdensome and to the fact that the monks not only promised him protection but also assured him that they

would intercede for his happiness after death.29 As the ravages of the Hundred Years' War and the bubonic plague greatly decreased the number of tenants in England and also made heavier the burdens of taxation, the wealthy landowners naturally became more envious of the vast estates of the monasteries. As long as these lands were retained by the monasteries, the rich overlords naturally received no revenue from them. As the monasteries never died, and as they could have no children, the overlords were deprived of vast sums of wealth, in the form of "reliefs," "wardships," and other feudal fines and obligations, which they would have received had their vassals been in possession of these lands.30 

This situation led to the extension of the Statute of Mortmain³1 of 1279, by which Parliament had prohibited gifts of land to the Church, thus accentuating the struggle between Church and State. 

As a result of this struggle, a new system of land tenure was evolved gradually. The mortmain statutes were designed to prevent ecclesiastical as well as temporal corporations from holding land. The ecclesiastics, in order to defeat the purpose of the mortmain statutes, invented the doctrine of uses.32 As the feudal system fell into disuse, this new system of land tenure was used very generally, and for more than two centuries land was disposed of for almost every conceivable "use" the shrewd lawyers of that age could imagine.

Under this system, the owner simply conveyed the legal title to his land to some person or corporation for the benefit of some named usee; the usee could be such owner himself. The usee then held the equitable title and could convey it, either orally or in writing, publicly or secretly, by deed or by will.33 Under this system of uses, wills of land could be made, as the use was not considered as land, though it was the only valuable feature of it. Church secured the use and enjoyment of large quantities of land in this manner contrary to the mortmain statutes. The equitable courts upheld such transfers, as the clergy were generally the judges of these courts.34

Parliament struck back at the Church in 1535, in the reign of Henry the Eighth, by enacting the famous Statute of Uses,35 which annexed the legal title and the possession to the use, thus making the use the very land itself and consequently not devisable. This statute was enacted in hostility to all trust estates and was especially designed to defeat the contrivances by which land was dedicated to ecclesiastical establishments in defiance of the various statutes of mortmain.36 § 4. [Ch. 1 qualified.42 As wills of personal property were governed by the ecclesiastical law, these statutes did not make any change in such wills.43

Under these statutes, married women, minors, idiots, and lunatics were incapacitated to make wills. It was necessary that a will of lands under these statutes should be in writing, but it was not necessary to have witnesses to it. Simple notes in the handwriting of the testator, or even in the handwriting of another person, constituted a sufficient will when the testator intended such writing to be his will.44 The testator could show his intention by making known the contents of such paper and declaring the same to be his will. Under such a loose system of making a will, it was natural that frauds and forgeries would abound. This condition finally led to the enactment of one of the most famous statutes ever passed by the English Parliament, the Statute of Frauds, which is primarily a wills act.45 This statute was enacted in 1677, the twenty-ninth year of the reign of Charles the Second. It was designed chiefly for the purpose of preventing the frauds, forgeries, and perjuries resulting from the first wills acts of 1540 and 1542; it provided for the manner in which wills of realty and of personalty should be executed. By the nineteenth, twentieth, twenty-first, and twentysecond sections of this statute, certain restrictions are placed on nuncupative wills and the repeal or alteration of written wills of personal property.46

By the fifth section of this statute, it is provided that all devises and bequests of lands and tenements shall be in writing, signed by the testator, "or by some other person in his presence, and by his express directions, and shall be attested and subscribed in the presence of the said devisor by three or four credible witnesses." This section opened many questions with which the courts have since puzzled themselves. It took more than two centuries to settle such questions as the following, if, indeed, they are absolutely settled yet: What is it that is attested? What is meant by "in the presence of the testator"? Was it necessary for all the witnesses to

The sixth section of the Statute of Frauds indicates the solemnities necessary for revoking a will. Under this section, in order that a will may be revoked, it must be done by "some other will or codicil in writing, or other writing declaring the same, or by burning, cancelling, tearing or obliterating the same by the testator himself, or in his presence and by his directions and consent.' 

Many interesting decisions dealing with these methods of revocation indicate the long and tedious way over which our present law on the subject of revocation has advanced to attain even its present status.48 Besides the other provisions of the Statute of Frauds as to wills, the fifth section provided that a will must be attested by three or four credible witnesses. The courts again had trouble in determining who are credible witnesses. So strict did the courts become in their interpretation as to who were credible witnesses that a gift in a will to a subscribing witness, even though for a trifling amount to a servant called in to witness the will, was held to invalidate the entire instrument.49

To remedy this condition, an act50 was passed in 1752, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of George II, which made such witnesses competent but declared the legacy or devise to such witness void. It also declared that creditors of the testator should be considered competent witnesses. By the tenth section of this act, its provisions are extended to the "British Colonies or Plantations in America." (Rather interesting plantations, these great American states are now!)

History of Wills in Georgia. In Georgia, the basis of our law of wills is the Statute of Frauds as interpreted by the English courts and by our own courts. By the Act of 1784,53 this state adopted the laws in force in England prior to May 14, 1776, so far as suited to our conditions and form of government.54 

As our state was settled after the enactment of the Statute of Frauds, it has always been necessary in Georgia for wills, other than nuncupative wills, to be in writing and signed and attested, if land is devised, according to the requirements of that statute. CHAPTER II GENERAL PRINCIPLES § 6. Definition of a Will. 

7.

Definitions. 

§ 6. Definition of a Will.-A will is the legal expression of a person's wishes as to the disposition of his property after his death.' As the word property is defined by our Code² to mean either realty or personalty, it is seen from the foregoing definition of a will that our Code does not distinguish a will from a testament. By the common law "will" referred to the disposition of real estate; "testament" to the disposition of personal property, and "last will and testament" to the disposition of both realty and personalty. Our supreme court in a very early decision said that "a will is a disposition of real and personal property to take effect after the death of the testator."4 Thus the word "will" has a definite meaning in Georgia law; it is synonymous with "testament" and "last will and testament." 3 § 7. A nuncupative will is one spoken in extremis, during the last sickness, before the requisite number of witnesses, and reduced to writing within the time prescribed by law. In addition to the customary written will, joint wills and mutual wills are recognized in Georgia. In some states holographic wills are recognized and so are mystic wills, but they are not known in Georgia. A joint will is an ordinary written will signed by two or more testators, and if used at all should be used to dispose of joint property. Upon the death of either of the makers, the will may be probated as the will of the one deceased; then, upon the death of the other, it may be probated again as his will. 9. A mystic will is a form of will introduced in Louisiana by the French and Spanish settlers; it is based on the civil law rather than on the English law of wills. It consists of a written testamentary disposition of property, signed by the testator and then sealed in an envelope in the presence of a notary and three witnesses. The testator then acknowledges or declares in the presence of the notary and the witnesses that the envelope contains his will. The testator, notary, and witnesses then sign a superscription on the envelope which must recite that the testator presented the envelope to the notary, closed and sealed, with the declaration that it contained his last will or that he closed and sealed it in their presence after making such declaration. The ordinary written will, signed by the testator and attested by three witnesses, is the one most commonly used; it forms the chief topic of discussion in this volume. § 8.-Nature of Wills.-In the early stages of civilization no man had power over his property longer than he kept it in his possession; and, when death overtook him, there were no special laws under which it was distributed. His family had no recognized right to his property, natural or legal; it, therefore, usually belonged to the first who was powerful enough to take and retain it by force against the claims of all other persons. After civilization had advanced to the point where it was recognized that a man had more than a mere usufruct or right of occupancy in property acquired by him, the question very naturally arose as to whether his desires relative to such property should be respected after his death, or whether his estate should once more belong in common to his tribe, organization, state, or society. As the owner held his property, not as a result of a natural right, but as a result of the rules or laws of his tribe or state, it was conceived that, by authority from the same source, he could be given the right to dispose of it at death as he saw fit. Wills are, therefore, the creation of the statutes or laws of civilized peoples rather than the result of natural, inherent rights.12 13 No one has any inherent right to testate or intestate estates unless that right is authorized by existing law. Such right may be regulated without infringing on the private rights of any person' whenever the legislative authorities of the state consider it neces- The right to such estate does not vest until the death of the testate or intestate, and consequently is affected by change of statute in the meantime.14 A will takes effect instantly upon the death of sary.

Character of Wills.-As no right under a will vests until the death of the testator, a will is said to be an ambulatory instrument;¹7 it is entirely inoperative during the lifetime of the testator. At his death it becomes operative, and it is to be construed in accordance with the intentions of the testator in so far as they are legal.18 This intention is to be sought for by looking to the whole will and not to detached parts of it;19 the intention of the testator may be ascertained not only from the instrument itself but from extrinsic evidence.20

The true test to determine whether an instrument is a deed or a will is whether it is to take effect immediately or to take effect after the death of the maker. If it is to take effect after the death of the maker and is revocable, it is a will; if it is to take effect immediately, or if it conveys a present estate, with right of possession postponed, it is a deed, and delivery must be proved.27 If from this test it is determined that an instrument is testamentary, in order to be valid it must be executed in the manner prescribed by statute for the execution of wills. Where the words are doubtful, the court will incline to that construction which supports the instrument; there need be no consideration to support a will, but there must be to make a deed valid.28 So little attention is paid in Georgia to the form of a will that an instrument may have effect in part as a deed and in part as a will, even as to the same property.29 But for such instrument to take effect as a will it must be attested by three witnesses and be otherwise properly executed. tion of the original is not required as in the case of ancient deeds. § 11. Property Which May Be Devised.-The common-law rule of seisina facit stipitem³ is not in force in Georgia,32 and, therefore, it is unnecessary for a testator to have actual seizin of property in order to dispose of the same by will; nor is it necessary for an intestate to have actual seizin in order that his heirs may inherit according to the rules of inheritance in force in Georgia. Any estate, real or personal, held by any title, legal or equitable, with or without actual seizin, will descend to the heirs of the owner, and conversely such owner may dispose of such estate and title by will if he so desires.33 From the foregoing, it is seen that a person may dispose of all his property by will, whether it is real estate or personal property, or a right in the same. This right may be corporeal or incorporeal, or it may be a future, executory, or contingent interest,34 provided such interest is not merely a life estate in the testator. This was the rule in Georgia until the adoption of our first Code, which went into effect on the first day of January, 1863.38 This Code changed the common law to the extent that all property, real or personal, acquired subsequently to the making of a will, shall pass under it, if its provisions were sufficiently broad to embrace such property.39 

The general rule in Georgia now is that a will speaks from the death of the testator,40 and that all property, real or personal, acquired after the making of the will is transmissible under general expressions in the will showing such to be the intention of the testa- Consequently, a testator may assume to pass after-acquired property at the time his will is drawn, if he so desires. As indicated by Code section 113-811, a will does not necessarily have to dispose of after-acquired property. By the use of plain language, a testator may limit the property disposed of in his will to that existing at the time such will is made. Where the language of the testator refers to a state of affairs existing at the time of the execution of the will which is to determine the division of his thenexisting property, the courts would construe his will not to pass after-acquired property. § 13.-Same-Undevised Property.-When a will has been so worded that it does not pass after-acquired property, or when a testator fails to include in his will part of his estate in existence at the time the will is made, such property is not affected by the will; it passes to the heirs at law by inheritance, and, since the Act of 1828, the executor is required to administer the same42 and to hold the proceeds for distribution according to the laws of this state.

The usual requisites to the validity of a contract are necessary to make valid a contract to make a will, such as capacity of the parties to contract, legal consideration,58 certainty,59 acceptance, performance by complaining party, 60 and good faith.61 A contract to make a will need not be express; it may be implied from the circumstances, as where the duties performed are so burdensome or unpleasant as to warrant the conclusion that compensation was intended.62 Such circumstances may exist where one has nursed an afflicted person through such a period of time or through such a trying affliction as to indicate that compensation should be given, even though love and affection prompted such tender ministration.63

As a person has a right to contract to make a will, there is no reason why he could not make a valid contract not to make a will. 

Such a contract would be enforceable against the estate of the promisor if he violated it.

If a person contracts to devise certain property but disposes of it to an innocent third party, the promisee's remedy would be a suit for damages for the breach of the contract.64 If the contract is in writing, it would be admissible in evidence as proof of the making of such contract. After a will has been executed in accordance with a contract to make a will or devise, it can not be changed by a codicil at a later date so as to defeat the contract.65

It must be executed with the same formalities 67 as a will, and, when admitted to probate, forms part of the will.68 A codicil is effective even though it is not attached to the will, provided it unequivocally identifies the will and is duly executed and probated.69 It is good practice to attach the codicil to the will at the time it is made. A codicil is part of the will after probate and differs from it only in that a will is an instrument which is usually intended to revoke all previous wills, whereas a codicil recognizes the existence of a previous will and simply attempts to add to such will, take from it, or alter its provisions.70 It is usually better to redraft the whole will than to depend on a codicil, but where this is impracticable by reason of the length of the will or the condition of the testator, a codicil should be used, provided that care is exercised in seeing that it does not so conflict with the will as to be a prolific source of litigation. Other occasions may arise where a codicil could be used to advantage, as where a will is void because it is improperly attested. Such a will could be made valid by a codicil.71 Also, where it is desired to make a simple change in a will, like changing a life estate to an absolute estate or vice versa, a codicil could be

§ 17.-Why a Will Should Be Made.-There are many valid rea sons why a person should make a will, but the chief one is that a will gives the testator the power to determine how his property shall be distributed, rather than leaving such distribution to be determined by the laws of intestate succession. Any man who has an estate of sufficient value to be of interest to him during his life should leave a will, as it is impossible for him to know when the inevitable hour73 will arrive or who will be his heirs at law at the time of his death. Even if a man owes no debts and desires that his estate be distributed according to the laws of descent and distribution, it is better to leave a will stating such to be his desire,74 as he can thus dispense with many of the annoying formalities and much of the expense connected with the administration of estates. 

As the owner is much better acquainted with the condition of his assets, a will is almost a necessity where the owner has an estate of considerable magnitude which is heavily indebted. By a will the owner can give many valuable directions for the marshalling of his assets for the payment of debts and legacies. 

No person should wait until his last hours to make his will, when bodily pain and the fear of death may prevent a just disposition. It is a regrettable fact that testators oftentimes postpone making their wills until their hours are few in number and the hand of death is upon them, when they hurriedly try to dispose of the accumulations of a lifetime. This may be due to indifference, superstition, false economy, or procrastination; but, whatever the cause, the results are usually the same-litigation among the heirs, wastage of assets, and the promotion of family quarrels. If a will is to be made, the testator should employ a competent person to draft it rather than depend on his own efforts. If there is anything

§ 19.-History.-As shown in the first chapter of this volume, feudalism so changed the system of land tenure in England that no will of real estate could be made, either orally or in writing, for several centuries; the right to make oral or written testaments of personalty was not destroyed by feudalism. Wills of land were permitted again by the first statute of wills,' provided such wills were in writing. The right to make oral testaments of personalty was not affected by this statute. So many frauds and forgeries were perpetrated as a result of this situation and as a result of the imperfections of this first statute of wills that Parliament enacted the famous Statute of Frauds,3 the nineteenth section of which made all nuncupative or oral wills invalid unless made during the last sickness of the deceased and in accordance with the requirements of that section.4

As will be noticed from the foregoing, a nuncupative will, under the English statutes, could dispose of personal property only. As the Statute of Frauds was adopted in Georgia, in 1784,5 as our law of wills, the provisions of that statute, as to nuncupative wills, as modified by the codifiers of our first Code, are applicable in 

Georgia now. Sections 113-502 and 113-503 of our present Code? 

of Georgia state our law as to the making of nuncupative wills. By comparison of Code section 113-5028 with the nineteenth section of the Statute of Frauds, it will be seen that this Code section is almost a verbatim copy of the nineteenth section of that statute. Our codifiers added to the powers conferred by this section of the Statute of Frauds in that they specified that "all property, real and personal, may pass by nuncupative wills properly made and proved."10

Therefore, in Georgia real or personal property, or both, may be transmitted by a nuncupative will; this is not true under the Statute of Frauds or under the statutes of most of the states of the Union. § 20.-Definitions.-The word nuncupative means oral, according to Webster's Dictionary. This is the accepted meaning under the Code of Georgia as well as under the English Statute of 

Frauds. A nuncupative will in Georgia is one spoken in extremis, during the last sickness, before at least three competent witnesses whom the testator desires to bear witness that such spoken words are his will. The substance of the words spoken by the testator must be reduced to writing within thirty days from the speaking of the same. This instrument then becomes a valid will if probated within six months from the death of the testator.11

From this definition as well as from Code section 113-502,12 it is seen that a nuncupative will is not a favorite of the law.¹³ It is well that oral wills are thus made difficult to execute properly; for there is too much room for mistake, fraud, and perjury where a

§ 21.-Requisites to Validity of Nuncupative Will.-"No nuncupa tive will shall be good unless proved by the oaths of at least three competent witnesses who were present at the making thereof; nor unless it shall be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the same, bade the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; nor unless such nuncupative will was made in the time of the last sickness of the deceased, and in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he had been resident for the space of 10 days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person was surprised or taken sick, being away from his own home, and died before he returned to the place of his dwelling."15 In addition to the requirements mentioned in this Code section, a nuncupative will must be reduced to writing within thirty days after it is spoken by the testator;' otherwise it is invalid. It should be reduced to writing, dated by one of the witnesses or by someone at the request of the witnesses, and it should name the date on which it was spoken, and the witnesses should all agree as to its terms.17 It is good practice to have the witnesses sign an affidavit stating that the will has been correctly reduced to writing; this affidavit should be attached to the will. It is not essential to the validity of the will that such affidavit be executed,18 yet it would be of value when the will was presented for probate in that it would incline the witnesses to remember the will as written; the will would be invalid unless it was proved substantially as written. .16

After a nuncupative will has been reduced to writing, it is still not a valid instrument unless it is probated within six months, not from the date it is spoken, but from the date of the death of the testator.19 When admitted to probate, it becomes a valid instrument, and all future procedure as to it is the same as that applicable to written wills. 20 It must be presented for probate within six months from the date of the death of the testator, but the fact that

§ 22.-Intention of Testator to Make Nuncupative Will.-When a nuncupative will is presented for probate, it may be attacked on any of the grounds on which a written will may be contested; such as lack of testamentary capacity on the part of the testator, undue influence, fraud, or mistake.22 In addition to the grounds on which a written will may be attacked, a nuncupative will is subject to attack on the ground that the testator had no intention of making a nuncupative will when the words were spoken.23 It is necessary that the testator intend that his spoken words be considered his oral will and that he ask the witnesses to bear witness that such spoken words are his will.24 A person, in his last sickness, may talk very freely of his financial affairs and express wishes as to the disposition of his assets, but such declarations do not constitute a nuncupative will unless intended as such and unless the other legal requirements as to nuncupative wills are met.

A written will signed by the testator but otherwise improperly executed can not be set up as a nuncupative will;25 it must be intended as a nuncupative will and not as a written will. Nor can a will be established as a nuncupative will where the testator, even in his last sickness, gave instructions for the preparation of his written will, and where the same was not prepared in time for him to sign before his death or where he was otherwise prevented from executing it.26 The rule that the testator must intend his declarations as a nuncupative will at the time of the speaking of the same is invariable in Georgia.27

 § 23. Nuncupative Will Must Be Reduced to Writing.-As our 

Code28 provides that a nuncupative will must be reduced to writing within thirty days after it is spoken, it is evident that some interested person should see that this duty is performed in order not to defeat the intentions of the testator. If it is not reduced to writing, the testator's attempt to make a will is void. If it is reduced to writing before the testator dies, it should be executed by him as a written will if his condition is such as to allow it; for, if the testator after speaking such will should have the time, opportunity, and means at hand to reduce it to writing as a proper written will, but should fail to do so, then such attempt to make a nuncupative will would be void.29 It is a question of fact as to whether a proper written will could have been made under the circumstances after the speaking of the oral will.30 The fact that the testator might have made a valid written will during the last sickness, prior to the speaking of the oral will, can not be considered.31 

§ 24. "In Time of His Last Sickness."-What may be termed the last sickness is dependent on each particular case,32 and is naturally a question of fact to be determined by the court of ordinary in the first instance or by a jury on appeal. It is possible for a person to make a nuncupative will and then lapse into a state of unconsciousness and remain so for weeks, or in such a weakened condition that it would not be advisable to attempt to have the will executed as a written will. § 25.-Witnesses to Nuncupative Wills.-In Georgia three witnesses are required to all wills whether written or oral, and these witnesses must be competent at the time the will is made. All three of the witnesses must hear the nuncupative will spoken, and the testator must bid the witnesses, or one of them,34 to bear witness that such spoken words constitute his will. It is not necessary for the testator to request all the witnesses to bear witness that he is speaking his will; it is sufficient if the request is made of one or more of the witnesses if all three hear the will.35 Such request need not be in any particular form of words or in the language of the statute. All that is required is that the testator make it known to the witnesses, or at least to one of them, that he wishes to speak his will and desires that it be witnessed. The testator's request need not be an oral request; he may by acts, signs, or gestures36 bid the witnesses to bear witness that he is going to speak his will.

In England, prior to the Wills Act of 1752,37 a will was invalid if either of the attesting witnesses was a legatee or devisee under the will, but this act changed the law by declaring the witness competent but the devise or legacy to such witness void. This is the rule in Georgia now as to written wills,38 but not the rule as to nuncupative wills.39 Since the Evidence Act of 1866, a witness to a nuncupative will is not incompetent because he is a legatee or devisee under the will,40 nor is the legacy or devise to such witness void. § 26.-Form of Nuncupative Will.-As in written wills, no particular form of words is necessary41 to the validity of a nuncupative will. Any words by which the testator makes it known that he is making his will intentionally are sufficient to make a will valid if the same is otherwise legal.42 However, the words used must indicate that the testator has made up his mind finally as to what disposition he desires to make of his assets. The testator's wishes must be sufficiently clear as to leave no doubt as to what are his intentions. It is not necessary to the validity of an oral or a written will for the testator to name an executor.43 § 27.-Probate of Nuncupative Will.-After a nuncupative will has been spoken, it should be reduced to writing as soon as possible while its contents are fresh in the minds of the witnesses; it must be reduced to writing within thirty days after it is spoken.44 Then, after the death of the testator, it should be immediately probated, although our Code45 allows six months in which to present it for probate after the death of the testator. This has led to the custom of the witnesses' signing an affidavit, at the time the will is reduced to writing, that it is correct.47 This is a good custom, as it may serve to keep the witnesses from forgetting, but it is by no means necessary.48 The "oaths" of three or more competent witnesses refers to their oaths on probate before the court of ordinary and not to their oaths at the time the will is reduced to writing. Where there are many witnesses who hear the will spoken, it may be proved by any three of them, notwithstanding the fact that it might have been reduced to writing and verified by witnesses other than those offering it for probate. If all the witnesses can not agree as to what the declarations of the testator were, the will may be probated anyway if any three of them agree and if the will is reduced to writing and offered for probate as required by law. This would involve a question of fact which would have to be determined by the court of ordinary in the first instance, and by a jury on appeal. 

If there were only three witnesses present when a nuncupative will was spoken, and if one of them should die before it was offered for probate, the will could not be proved, as there would not be three competent witnesses by the oaths of whom it could be proved before the court of ordinary. This indicates the importance of offering a nuncupative will for probate as soon as possible. Where a nuncupative will is offered for probate and an appeal is entered to the judgment of the court of ordinary, or where a new trial is granted, the substance of the testimony of any witness at the former trial could be proved by other witnesses or by the official record, if it should appear that such witness was dead or had removed from the state of Georgia and was residing in another state.49 

Upon all applications for probate of nuncupative wills, the same notice must be given to the heirs at law as is required on the probate of written wills in solemn form.50 The judgment probating a nuncupative will is not binding on the heirs not legally served with notice of the application for probate, especially if they are

In proving a nuncupative will, a strict compliance with the law should be shown, and the provisions of our Code should be construed strictly with reference thereto.53 Any person who has enough assets to be of concern to him in his dying hours and who hastily tries to make an oral will while the fear of death is upon him should not expect much leniency from the law, especially when he has owned such assets for many years and has neglected to have a written will deliberately prepared and solemnly executed. However, occasions may arise where it would be a hardship not to have the privilege of making a nuncupative will, but such occasions should be the result of necessity and not of choice.54

However, for a nuncupative codicil to be valid, all the requirements as to making nuncupative wills would have to be met. An unsigned will or a defectively executed will can be made valid by a written codicil,57 but such wills could not be made valid by a nuncupative codicil, as no will can be proved as a nuncupative will unless it was intended58 by the testator as a nuncupative will at the time it was spoken. This would be true even in a case where the testator had given instructions for the drafting of his will, and the same had been promptly drafted but not presented to him until he was too weak to sign it. In such a case, the testator would have to speak the will as a nuncupative will before the requisite number of competent witnesses; for a written will can not be set up as a nuncupative will, nor could it be made valid by a nuncupative codicil, as it had not been spoken as a nuncupative will.

Yet, a will might be set up as a nuncupative will if the testator had bidden a sufficient number of competent witnesses to bear witness that he was speaking his nuncupative will and had then requested that it be reduced to writing in order that it might be executed as a written will, provided he was in a condition to do so after it had been written. Such a state of circumstances would create a conditional nuncupative will, but it is hardly conceivable that such a state of circumstances will ever arise. If a written will has been prepared according to the wishes of the testator, or if the testator desires to republish a written will, he could not even in extremis declare to the requisite number of competent witnesses that the contents of such written will were intended as his nuncupative will, because, under such circumstances, he would have the opportunity of signing the will and having it properly witnessed. 

For a nuncupative will to be valid, it must appear that the testator had not the means and opportunity of reducing it to writing and executing it as a written will.59

§ 29.-Revocation of Nuncupative Will.-After a nuncupative will has been spoken by the testator, if he so desires and if he still retains testamentary capacity, he can revoke it, but such revocation would have to be made in the presence of three or more competent witnesses. As to whether such a will was revoked by such an attempt would be a question of fact. A written will could not be expressly revoked by a nuncupative will, as such revocation must be made by a written instrument executed with the same formality as the written will itself.60 A testator may impliedly revoke a written will by executing a later written will, inconsistent with the former.61 Whether a later nuncupative will would operate impliedly to revoke a written will is a question which is settled in the negative by the twenty-second section of the Statute of Frauds.62 It will be noticed that this section of the Statute of 

Frauds refers only to personalty. This is due to the fact that land in England, after the Norman Conquest and the introduction of feudalism, was never subject again to disposition by nuncupative will. Therefore, this section could refer only to personal property.63 The fact that our Code has extended the scope of nuncupative wills so as to allow the disposition of realty by such wills does not alter this section of the Statute of Frauds as to the method of revocation of written wills. Consequently, a written will, in Georgia, disposing of realty or personalty or both, can not be revoked by a nuncupative will. It would appear without reference to this section of the Statute of Frauds that there could be an implied revocation of a written will by a nuncupative will in Georgia, as the last will executed is recognized as the one expressing the testator's intentions. However, as the laws of Georgia as to wills are based on the Statute of Frauds, a nuncupative will in this state could neither impliedly nor expressly revoke a previously written will

§ 30.-Characteristics of Nuncupative Wills in Georgia.-In most of the states of the Union nuncupative wills may dispose of personal property only; the value of such property which may be disposed of by nuncupative will is also limited in most of the states.66 In 

Georgia a nuncupative will may transmit realty or personalty or both, regardless of the value.67

§ 31.-Who May Make a Will.-No person has an inherent right to make a will,' but the best interests of civilized society require that this right be authorized by law.2 This right may at any time be regulated by the state or power granting it without infringing on the private rights of any person.3 Consequently, certain qualifications of the right to make a will have been established both as to the person and as to the mental capacity of the testator. At common law, aliens, minors, idiots, married women,4 persons de non sane memorie,5 and many classes of criminals were disqualified.

By statute in Georgia, every person is entitled to make a will unless he is laboring under some legal disability. In Georgia, no person is an alien except a subject of a foreign government who has not been naturalized under the laws of the United States;16 a citizen of a state or territory of the United

Since the adoption of our first Code,21 an infant fourteen years of age, whether male or female, may make a valid will of realty or of personalty.22 An infant under the age of fourteen is considered wanting in the discretion necessary to make a will; consequently, a will made by such infant is invalid, unless re-executed or republished by him while possessing 15. In computing the legal age of a person, whether for determining the date of majority or the earliest date on which he could make a will, the day of birth should be included. Therefore, as fractions of a day are not counted, the will of an infant, born during any hour of September 5, 1920, would be valid although executed during any hour of September 4, 1934.23 § 34.-Criminals.-Under common law, conviction of certain felonies attainted the inheritable blood.24 In addition to this method of corrupting the blood, Parliament by legislative act, called a bill of attainder, could pronounce judgment of treason or felony upon one who had not been convicted in the courts and thus corrupt the blood of such person. When the inheritable blood of a person had been attainted by conviction in the courts or by legislative enactment, he could not convey title by descent or devise. However, this is of little interest to us now, except historically, as our state constitution25 and the Constitution of the United States26 forbid the enactment of bills of attainder and the corruption of blood.27 Forfeiture of estate and corruption of blood may exist under the Constitution of the United States in cases of treason,28 but even then it does not extend beyond the life of the person attainted. Under the Code of Georgia,29 conviction of crime in no case deprives a person of the power of making a will. Consequently, a convict in 

Georgia can make a will whether he is serving his sentence or awaiting the death penalty.

The same common-law rule is applicable in computing the date on which an infant acquires testamentary capacity.

§ 35.-Persons Deaf, Dumb, and Blind.-A person deaf, dumb,30 and blind may make a will provided he has knowledge of the contents of such will.31 Where all three of these afflictions exist at the same time, a person thus afflicted may make a valid will, but the rules for determining the validity of such a will are more strict than in cases where the testator is suffering only from deafness, or from being dumb or blind. When the testator is deaf, dumb, and blind, for his will to be valid, the interpreter and the scrivener must both be attesting witnesses, and both should be examined when the will is presented for probate.32 If these witnesses are dead or not within the jurisdiction of the court when the will is presented for probate, if knowledge of contents and proper execution could be established by persons other than these witnesses, the will should be admitted to record.33 The interpreter must be a competent witness or the will is invalid because of the lack of a sufficient num-

A careful practitioner when called on to prepare the will of a person deaf, dumb, and blind should write it in his own handwriting. 

§ 36. Married Women.-At common law a married woman could not make a testamentary disposition of her personal property35 without the consent, express or implied, of her husband, nor could she make a valid devise of her realty36 unless the instrument by which the same was conveyed to her or settled to her use reserved to her this power.3 37 

34. Persons incapable of being sworn are not competent. 

House (1849), 6 Ga. 324.

Potts v. 

35. "The incapacity of married women to make wills has its root in our common-law principle of coverture, by which husband and wife were treated as one person in such a sense that the woman took her place under the cover or protection of her lord; her rights not less than her obligations becoming suspended, for the better harmony and peace of the marriage state, while the husband exercised an undisputed sway as head of his household. By the fundamental terms of their nuptial union, the husband remained capable of making his own will, though the wife if surviving could claim her dower, or lifethirds interest, in his real estate. But the wife, on the other hand, parted with all control over her own property while coverture lasted, presented her spouse outright or conditionally with the whole of her personal property, and conferred upon him the usufruct during marriage of her real estate, which was enlarged, if a child was born alive, to a right by curtesy lasting for his whole lifetime. With the property brought into the marriage state thus parcelled out by the common law, and a surviving husband entitled, moreover, to administer upon the estate of his deceased wife for his own benefit and recover her outstanding personal property to his own use and enjoyment, it is not strange that the female spouse was under the disability of making her own will."

Schouler on Wills, Executors and Ad ministrators, 5th ed., sec. 45.

In Georgia a complete change was made in the common law by the Act of 1866, commonly known as "the married woman's act,"38 and by our constitution of 1868. As a result of this change, an entirely new rule of property was introduced, and women in Georgia, since 1866, with reference to their property, remain as effectually separated from men after marriage as before marriage. 

Married women in Georgia, with or without the consent of their husbands, may make testamentary dispositions as freely as men.39 "The husband has as little interest in, or control over, his wife's property as she has in or over his, indeed less, for she is entitled to be supported out of his, and when necessary is recognized by the law as his agent to charge it with her support; whereas, his power and control over her property, rests, in all cases, upon her voluntary consent."40 The wife also retains her right to dower41 and to year's support in her husband's property, whereas the husband has no curtesy or other right in the wife's property, except as an heir. 

§ 37.-Mental Capacity.-The preceding sections of this chapter have been devoted to a discussion of the persons who may make a will; the remaining sections will consider the mental capacity necessary to valid testamentary disposition by such persons. We thus enter the broad field of mental phenomena, into which psychologists and trained medical experts have delved for many years. From such expert investigations many interesting theories concerning the various states of the human mind have been advanced. It has been established that sanity and insanity shade into each other to such an extent that it is difficult to say where the one ends and the other begins. It has been said that a mind evenly balanced in all its faculties is rather an exception; indeed, the theory has been ad-

However, the law of wills is not concerned with these nice distinctions as to the states of the human mind. Generally, any person is recognized as possessing sufficient mental capacity to make a will who is capable of distinguishing right from wrong and who has sufficient intelligence to understand his ordinary business and to know and understand what disposition he is making of his property at the time he makes his will.42 § 38.-Idiocy. An idiot is a person who has been without understanding since his birth and who is, therefore, presumed to be wanting in that mental capacity necessary to the execution of a valid will.43 The mind of such person is wholly deficient in perceptive and reflective faculties; it has little power to remember past transactions and none to plan for future conduct; it is passive and wanting in discretion and judgment. Such mind is incapable of making an understanding disposition of property to take effect after death. 

Our courts always have been liberal in determining testamentary capacity. But our supreme court went dangerously far in the famous case of Potts v. House44 by holding that a "mere glimmering of reason"45 was sufficient to establish mental capacity to make

It is unnecessary for the mind of the testator to be perfect as a very low standard of mental capacity is sufficient, but certainly the mind of a testator should be in a condition to understand what disposition is being made rather than in a mental haze through which an occasional glimmer of reason penetrates. § 39.-Imbecility.-Imbecility and idiocy are practically synonymous, but in medical jurisprudence imbecility may be regarded as a slightly higher form of mental capacity than idiocy in that imbecility may originate from causes other than prenatal influences, whereas idiocy is a lack of mentality resulting from prenatal conditions and dating from birth. Imbecility is an extreme weakness of body or mind or both, and it may result from old age or from other causes. The test to be applied as to the effect of imbecility on testamentary capacity is whether or not the testator has sufficient rational judgment and desire to make an understanding disposition of his property, and this is a question of fact. Imbecility, of itself, is not sufficient to destroy testamentary capacity unless it deprives the testator of his reason and memory to such an extent that he does not understand what he is doing when he executes his will.47 

In cases of doubt, the reasonableness or unreasonableness of the terms of the will should have weight in determining whether the testator possessed testamentary capacity at the time he executed his will.48

§ 40.-Insanity.-Insanity is the term commonly used to describe all forms of mental derangement whether existing from birth or from subsequent affliction. However, strictly speaking, an insane person is of a higher order of intelligence than an idiot, in that such person once possessed a mind, which may return upon the removal of the cause of insanity, whereas an idiot was never endowed with the faculties of a mind. Yet, so long as the mind is unsound, regardless of the cause or the term which may be applied to describe such mental condition, a will which is the offspring of such unsound mind is invalid.49 An insane person, during a lucid interval, may make a valid will.50 It is sufficient if he understands what he is doing even though he has less mental capacity than is required to make a contract.51 However, it should not be taken for granted that the presence of ability to contract conclusively establishes testamentary capacity, as it requires more mental ability to make and understand some wills than it does some contracts, and vice versa. of the will itself should be considered as evidence of the testator's ability or lack of ability to execute the will. § 41-Monomania and Insane Delusions.-Monomania means partial insanity.53 The monomaniac is subject to hallucinations and insane delusions as to one or a few subjects and yet is perfectly rational as to others; he believes in the reality of events which have never occurred and in things which do not exist, and he is incapable of being permanently reasoned out of his erroneous conceptions.54

Monomania is a diseased condition of the mind55 and is distinguished from ill will, bad judgment, animosity, prejudice, erroneous conclusions from facts, illogical views, and other conditions of mind which can be co-existent with sanity. The will of a monomaniac is invalid if it is the result of his delusions and hallucinations.56 However, monomania does not invalidate a will unless such will results from, or is connected with, the monomania.57 

Consequently a will which is not the result of mental perversion is valid, although made by a monomaniac.

§ 42.-Illiteracy, Immorality, and Superstitions.--Illiteracy does not deprive a person of testamentary capacity.58 But, usually, when an illiterate person makes a will, more proof is required to show that he knew and understood the contents and the terms of his will than is required where the testator is well educated. An illiterate person may sign his will by making a mark, or he may direct someone else to sign his name in his presence, and such signing is valid without his making a mark.5 59 Immorality does not deprive a person of testamentary capacity in Georgia.60 Immorality may result simply from wickedness; it may be co-existent with perfect sanity and, unfortunately, with mental ability of the highest quality. Such an immoral person has testamentary capacity of equal dignity in law with the most moral and upright citizen. However, when immorality leads to such a depraved condition of mind as to establish insanity, monomania, or other perverted mental condition, the testamentary capacity of such immoral person is limited by the rules governing such mental conditions.61

Superstitions, like other abnormal conditions of mind, do not deprive a person of testamentary capacity unless they render him incapable of making an intelligent disposition of his property. If the superstition amounts to monomania, and if the will is the result of such monomania, it is invalid.62 

§ 43.-Delirium, Drunkenness, and the Use of Drugs.-Delirium is a temporary dethronement of reason and may be due to a sudden mental shock or to a fevered condition of the body or to the slow ravages of some chronic disease. Whatever may be the cause of a delirious condition, a will made by a testator while he is delirious and out of his mind is absolutely invalid. If it can be proved that the will was made during a lucid interval, it is valid even though.

The same rule applies to drunkenness. During a drunken debauch, the reasoning faculties of a testator may be so blurred that he could not make an understanding disposition of his property. 

But, when the effect of the drunkenness has been sufficiently overcome for the testator to know and understand what he is about, he may make a valid will, although he immediately begins another period of drunkenness. What is said here of alcoholic drinks applies as well to the use of drugs. It is a question of fact, in each particular case, as to whether drunkenness or the use of drugs has deprived a testator of his testamentary capacity at the time of the execution of his will.

Reasonableness and Unreasonableness.-Under our law any person of sound mind may make any testamentary disposition of his property which is not inconsistent with the laws or contrary to the policies of our state. 68 This freedom in making a will permits a testator to make an unreasonable or an unjust disposition of his property; yet, so long as he possesses testamentary capacity and makes his will freely and voluntarily, it is valid.69 The unreasonableness of the terms of a will can not be considered in determining its validity except in connection with some legal attack on the will, as for fraud, undue influence, or lack of testamentary capacity.70
