§ 47.-Proof of Mental Capacity.-Soundness or unsoundness of mind is a question of fact. In many jurisdictions it has been held that every man is presumed to be sane until the contrary has been proved, and consequently the burden of proving the testator's lack of testamentary capacity is on the person alleging it.74 In other jurisdictions it has been held that there is no presumption of testamentary capacity, and consequently the burden of proving the same is on the propounder of the will.75 In Georgia our supreme court adheres to the latter rule, although in an obiter dictum, in the case of Jackson and Moye v. Jackson et al. (1861), 32 Ga. 338, it was said that "presumption is always in favor of mental capacity to make a will." In the case of Evans v. Arnold (1874), 52 Ga. 169, our supreme court held that the burden of proof is on the propounder to show all the facts necessary to make a good will, and this includes not only the fact of execution, but also that the will is the free act of a man competent under the law to make a will.76 

73. "A ground of a caveat alleging that, 'from advancing age and longprotracted intemperance, dissipations and excesses,' a testator 'had become so weak of intellect and will power as to be mentally incapacitated to execute a will, and that as a result thereof he made an unnatural and unreasonable disposition' of his property by disinheriting his sole heir at law and bestowing it upon strangers, is not open to demurrer on the ground that the allegations therein ‘are vague and indefinite and fail to set out facts sufficient to show that [the testator] was wanting in testamentary capacity.' 

Wherein a will of this nature is unnatural and unreasonable need not be set forth in a caveat, but it is not improper to therein allege in detail the reasons why the will should be so regarded." Bohler v. Hicks (1904), 120 Ga. 800 (4), 48 S. E. 306.

Caveators may allege and prove, on the issue of fraud, undue influence or lack of testamentary capacity, the unreasonableness of the will towards one who does not even join in the caveat or otherwise contest the will. Pergason v. Etcherson (1893), 91 Ga. 785, 787, 18 S. E. 29. "What is an unnatural will, because of inequality among members of the testator's family, is a question of fact, not of law." Thompson v. § 48.-Same-Opinions of Witnesses. When there is an issue as to the testamentary capacity of the testator, the opinions as to the sanity of the testator may be given in evidence by physicians and by the witnesses who attested the will without their first stating the facts upon which they base such opinions.84 The opinions of physicians are admissible, whether founded on symptoms or circumstances coming within their own observation or from the testimony of others.85 The law recognizes the testimony of physicians as expert testimony, as they are presumed to be better acquainted with the mental and physical afflictions of mankind than the average person. The reason the opinions of the subscribing witnesses are admissible without a previous statement as to the facts on which such opinions are founded is that they necessarily saw the testator at the time his will was executed and are, therefore, presumed to undue influence exerted over him in the matter, nor as evidence that he had revoked the will, but simply for the purpose of showing the state of his mind when the paper purporting to be his will was executed, and whether or not he then had sufficient mental capacity to make a will, or was then in such a mental condition as to be easily and unduly influenced by another." Credille v. Credille (1905), 123 Ga. 673 (3), 51 S. E. 628; Purser v. McNair (1922), 153 Ga. 405, 112

60. Person May Make Will Against His Will. 

61. Pleading. § 49.-Generally.-The acts of every rational being are determined by the influences with which he has been surrounded and with which he comes in daily contact. Hence, any will is the result of influence growing out of the testator's experiences in life. When a competent testator acts freely and voluntarily, his will is valid, although it may be the offspring of an impious mind, narrowed by prejudices,' peculiar beliefs, or wrong ideals resulting from the influences with which he has been surrounded. The law regards influence as undue only when it constrains or coerces a person into doing that which his best judgment tells him not to do and deprives him of his free agency and substitutes the will of another person for his own.2 

1. "A testator may have his preferences, dislikes and animosities towards his heirs, and may be guided by them in the disposition of his estate; still, if he is competent in mind, and makes a will freely and voluntarily, these conditions of mind will not per se destroy his testamentary capacity. And though prejudices may be unfounded, still if they are not used to coerce and control his will or impose a fraud upon him, they will not avoid his will." Carter v. 

Dixon (1882), 69 Ga. 82 (6); Bohler v.

§ 50.-Undue Influence Defined.-Influence, to be undue so as to invalidate a will, must amount to fear, overpersuasion, force, or coercion to the extent of destroying the free agency and will power of the testator and must be operative on the mind of the testator at the time the will is executed. In such a case the will speaks not the wishes of the testator but those of the person exercising the undue influence. A will procured through fraud is invalid, but fraud and undue influence are not identical. Fraud defeats the true wishes of the testator by deception, while undue influence subjugates his will and coerces him into acting contrary to his desires.5 Fraud is practiced through misrepresentations and deceit; while undue influence may sometimes savor of deceit, yet it may be exerted without any actual fraud's being perpetrated on the testator and without any misrepresentation's being made to him. 

68 C. J. 743; Thompson v. Davitte (1877), 59 Ga. 473; Davis v. Frederick (1923), 155 Ga. 809, 118 S. E. 206, 211; 

Brown v. Kendrick (1926), 163 Ga. 

149, 135 S. E. 721, 730. "Sir J. P. Wilde, in summing up, gave the following direction to the jury on the question of undue influence: To make a good will a man must be a free agent. But all influences are not unlawful. Persuasion, appeals to the affections or ties of kindred, to a sentiment of gratitude for past services, or pity for future destitution, or the like-these are all legitimate, and may be fairly pressed on a testator. On the other hand, pressure of whatever character, whether acting on the fears or the hopes, if so exerted as to overpower the volition without convincing the judgment, is a species of restraint under which no valid will can be made. 

Importunity or threats, such as the testator has not the courage to resist, moral command asserted and yielded to for the sake of peace and quiet, or of escaping from distress of mind or social discomfort, these, if carried to a degree in which the free play of the testator's judgment, discretion or wishes, is overborne, will constitute undue influence, though no force is either used or threatened. In a word, a testator may be led but not driven; and his will must be the offspring of his own volition, and not the record of someone else's." Hall V. Hall 

(1868), L. R. 1 P. & D. 481.

UNDUE INFLUENCE § 51.-Undue Influence-Burden of Proof.-When a will is pre sented for probate, the burden of proving the testamentary capacity of the testator and the due execution of the will is on the propounder. When such proof has been made, the burden shifts to the contestant.8 A person who attacks a will on the ground that it was procured by undue influence necessarily admits, so far as this issue is concerned, that the will is otherwise valid. If the will were not otherwise valid, there would be no will to have been procured by undue influence. However, the burden is on the propounder to prove the existence of the will and to prove that at the time of its execution the testator apparently had sufficient mental capacity to make it and that, in making it, he acted freely and voluntarily. The burden then shifts to the caveator to prove the undue influence alleged in the caveat. 

§ 52.-Proof-Admissibility of Evidence.-A very wide range of testimony is permissible on the issue of undue influence. This is due to the fact that undue influence seldom can be shown except by circumstantial evidence. It results from the circumstances and surroundings of the testator and his associations with the person or persons exercising the undue influence. For this reason it is proper, on this issue, to consider the testator's dealings and associations with the beneficiaries; his habits, motives, 10 feelings; his strength or weakness of character; his confidential family,12 social, and business relations; 13 the reasonableness or unreasonableness of the will;14 11

§ 53. Inadmissible Evidence.-Although a wide range of evi dence is allowed on the question of undue influence, there are necessarily some limitations. The evidence must be relevant and must tend to prove the issues made. The opinion of a witness is not admissible unless he testifies to relevant facts on which his opinion is based.18 Proof of undue influence could not be made by evidence alone that the opportunity for undue influence existed. 

Nor should evidence be admitted which merely shows a possibility or suspicion of undue influence.19 Evidence that one person had the power to influence another unduly would be inadmissible to prove undue influence, unless it was proved also that this power was exercised and that the will resulted from the exercise of such power. Undue influence can not be proved by declarations of the testator alone, but such declarations may be admitted to prove that undue influence, otherwise established, did have effect on the mind of the testator.20

As a general rule, the declarations and admissions of a beneficiary under a will are not admissible so as to affect the rights of other legatees or devisees. § 56.-Confidential Relations.-Confidential relations are pre sumed to exist between parent and child, guardian and ward, attorney and client, husband and wife, nurse and patient, and between others where one is presumed to exert the power of leadership and the other to impose confidence and trust.

In some states the mere existence of a confidential relation between the testator and the beneficiary raises the presumption that the will was procured through undue influence.33 In Georgia the existence of undue influence is not presumed merely from confidential relations between the testator and the beneficiary,34 but the existence of confidential relations is a circumstance which may be considered on this issue. If it is proved that a beneficiary who is charged with undue influence occupied a confidential relation towards the testator and was active in procuring the execution of the will, a presumption of undue influence will arise, and the burden of proving the will to be valid is shifted to the propounder of the will.

This presumption is one of fact and not of law.35 Consequently, this presumption may be rebutted by any evidence which shows that the testator acted freely and voluntarily in making his will and not under the coercion or the constraint of the person charged with the undue influence.36

[Ch. 5 

If the testator occupied a confidential relation towards one or more of the beneficiaries in the will and if undue influence is an issue, the mental and physical condition of the testator at the time the will was executed is of great consequence. Proof of a sound mind and body does not preclude the possibility of undue influence; nor does proof of a weak mind and feeble body alone establish undue influence; yet it is well known that a person in feeble health or with a weak mind is more susceptible to improper influences than one of robust health and of strong mind. 

§ 57.-Same-Husband and Wife.-As the law permits a testator to make any disposition of his property which he may desire and which is not inconsistent with the laws or contrary to the policy of the state,37 it naturally allows full play to his affections. He is rather expected to remember more liberally those who occupy relations towards him where love and affection are presumed to exist. 

The relation of a husband to his wife with whom he has lived many years is such that undue influence is difficult to conceive even where the greatest persuasion and importunity have been exercised. However, the manner and motive of the influence in such a case may be investigated where undue influence is an issue. When a testator makes a liberal provision for a young wife to the total or partial exclusion of his children by a former wife, a charge of undue influence is more likely to be meritorious than in a case where a first wife is charged with undue influence. But the mere fact that the second wife is made a large beneficiary or the sole beneficiary to the exclusion of the children of the former marriage does not raise the presumption of undue influence ;38 this fact may be considered in determining whether or not undue influence has been exercised.

§ 60.-Person May Make Will Against His Will.-A will to be valid must be made by a competent testator who has the freedom of choice.49 If his ability to express his own wishes and desires is destroyed by fraud or undue influence, his testamentary freedom is destroyed, and his will is invalid. He may thus be forced to make a will against his will, but it can be avoided as it does not express his wishes, but expresses the wishes of another. If the testator is not deprived of his testamentary freedom by undue influence or otherwise, and acts freely and voluntarily, he may make a valid will against his will, if the word will is used in the sense of desire. A person may force desire to bend to duty in a testamentary act as well as in any other act.50 He may not desire to perform an act, yet a sense of duty may compel him to perform it. § 61.-Pleading.-When a will is presented for probate, any interested person may enter a caveat to such probate on the ground of undue influence. General allegations of undue influence in such contest present no issue to be determined.52 The facts relied on to constitute the undue influence must be specifically averred. No particular form of caveat is required.53 Any statement is sufficient which sets forth the nature of the case and avers the facts relied on to prove the alleged undue influence. 74. Attestation. § 62.-History.-When Georgia became an independent state, the 

English law of wills was adopted as the law of this state. The 

Statute of Frauds was in force in England at that time, and by that statute it was not necessary for wills of personalty to be executed with the same formalities as wills of realty.' That part of the 

Statute of Frauds pertaining to wills was superseded in England by the Wills Act of 1837. Since 1837 it has been necessary in England to execute wills of personalty with the same formalities as wills of realty.2 In Georgia the distinction made by the Statute of Frauds between the execution of wills disposing of personalty and that of wills devising realty continued in force until the Act of 1852. By this act a will disposing of personalty must be executed with the same formalities as a will disposing of realty.³ 

§ 63.-Signature of Testator.-"All wills (except nuncupative wills) disposing of realty or personalty shall be in writing, signed by the party making the same or by some other person in his presence and by his express direction, and shall be attested and subscribed in the presence of the testator by three or more competent witnesses."4 

1. See pages 12 and 14 of chapter 1. 

2. See page 14 of chapter 1. 

3. Acts 1852, page 104. 

4. Code 113-301.

§ 63] 

This section of the Code is almost a verbatim copy of the fifth paragraph of the Statute of Frauds; it differs from the Statute of 

Frauds in that it includes both personalty and realty while the Statute of Frauds refers only to realty.5 Thus, in Georgia the first formality to be observed in the execution of any will is for the testator to sign it."

The English courts in construing the Statute of Frauds held that it was not necessary for the testator to sign the will at the end thereof. It was a good signing regardless of whether the testator's signature occurred at the top, bottom, or margin,7 provided such signing was done with testamentary intent. Our Code does not require that the testator subscribe the will; it stipulates that he must sign it; so, according to the requirements of our Code and in compliance with the decisions of the English courts construing the Statute of Frauds, signing by the testator on any part of the will, animo testandi, would be held to be a sufficient signing by him.10 

Our supreme court has held that a will was valid even though signed by the testator below the attestation clause.11 This decision.

And this is the first ground of error assigned. Our Code, section 2379, speaking of the formalities of the execution of a will, says, it should be in writing, signed by the party making the same, and by some other person in his presence, and by his express directions, and shall be attested and subscribed in the presence of the testator, by three or more competent witnesses. is undoubtedly correct as our law now stands, and it can be said with equal force that a will signed animo testandi by the testator at the top of the page or on the margin would be valid, if otherwise and shall be attested and subscribed in the presence of said devisor by three or four credible witnesses.' The

Code only changes the phraseology of a word or two, and with these we have the whole law, directing the manner of executing and attesting wills. They shall be signed by the party. "Now, looking at this will, we find it was signed by the party, and the place of signing after the attestation clause does not change the fact or invalidate the execution. We take the whole instrument and the signature of 

Daniel Huff in connection therewith, and find that the formalities, as well as the legalities of the execution, have been complied with. He has signed the will as his will, with three witnesses to the fact, who also signed, attesting and subscribing their names. 

If we go into the most minute details of the law on this subject, we find nothing that contravenes this position. 

A will written on one side of a sheet, with the signature of the testator and witnesses, held, was a signing at the 'foot or end,' under the statute: Jermyn v. Hervey, 1 English Law and Equity

In Jonele v. Under our law, no place is designated and no attestation clause is prescribed. 

A will signed without attestation clause is good: 2 R. I., 88; 3 Bradford

Armstrong, 29 Alabama, 538. 'Although testator's name is not written by himself, nor subscribed to the will, yet, if it be written in the beginning of the will by another, in his presence, and under his direction, and if it be acknowledged by him to the attesting witnesses,' it is good. "No rule has been rigidly laid down on this subject, and we find, even under the English Statutes, a more technical definition than our own by specifying the end of the will, that the rules have been uniformly to hold a substantial compliance sufficient. In notes to page 

282, Redfield on Wills, Part 1st, where the will fills two sides of a sheet of paper, leaving no room on the second page for the signatures, which were written along the side of the will on the third page, this was held sufficient.

And we might multiply authorities, but enough has been glanced at to sustain the judgment of this court in the case before us, that there was no error in the charge of the court. It is good practice to have the testator sign not only at the end of the will but also on the margin of each. sheet12 for the purpose of identification in the event the sheets become separated. In England, since the Statute of 1837, and by statute in some of our states, a will must be signed at the end; so the careful practitioner in Georgia will see that a will executed under his instructions is signed at the end, just before the attestation clause. 

§ 64.-Testator Must Sign First.-As our Code¹³ requires all wills except nuncupative wills to be in writing and signed by the testator, an instrument which has been prepared under the direction of the testator and which is in every way satisfactory to him is not his will until his signature has been affixed thereto and properly attested. The signatures of the witnesses are primarily an attestation of the signature of the testator or the factum of the signing by the testator.14 Therefore, unless he signs first there is nothing for them to attest except an anticipated signing by the testator, a future event which may or may not occur. Such future event could not be attested by them, whether it occurred the next moment or the next year.15 If the testator acknowledges to the witnesses that he has signed the will, this acknowledgment carries with it the rebuttable implication that he has signed it before presenting it to them, even though they do not see his signature. 16 Our Code does not

As stated above, an instrument is not the will of the testator until his signature has been affixed. However, it is unnecessary that the testator actually sign his name himself. He may direct someone else in his presence to sign his name for him, and that is sufficient without his making a mark. When someone else signs the testator's name for him, such signing must be done by his direction and in his presence.19 Our law makes a peculiar difference as to the signature of a witness, as his signature is not valid when he has directed someone else to sign his name unless he does make his mark.20 If the testator directs someone to sign his name for him, such direction should be given in the presence of the attesting witnesses, unless the testator acknowledges such signing to be his signature when he presents the will to the witnesses for attestation. 

However, it is not imperative that such direction be given in the presence of the attesting witnesses nor that the testator acknowledge to the witnesses that he gave such express direction for the signing of his name, as such direction could be proved on probate by other competent witnesses, if such witnesses could be found.21

§ 65.-Acknowledgment of Signature by Testator.-The testator may affix his signature to his will before seeing the witnesses and then acknowledge it in their presence at the time he presents it to them for their signatures.22 If the testator has signed his will or has caused someone else to sign it for him before he comes into the presence of the witnesses, he must acknowledge his signature to the witnesses after he comes into their presence, or his will is invalid.23 

Our law does not require a testator to use any particular form of words in acknowledging his signature. Any conduct or expressions by the testator which convey to the witnesses the idea that the testator is acknowledging his signature to his will are sufficient. 

This is true even though the witnesses do not see the signature,24 if it can be proved on probate that his signature was affixed to the will before the witnesses signed. The acknowledgment of his signature by the testator carries with it the implication that he has signed his will.25

§ 66.-Testamentary Intent.-A will must be signed by the testator animo testandi.26 If the testator intends to execute a certain instrument as his will but by mistake executes the wrong one, the paper thus executed is not his will. An innocent mistake of this character would be most likely to occur in a case where two or more illiterate testators were executing their wills at the same time and place and each signed the wrong will; such a mistake might also occur where some interested person, with ulterior motive, substituted for all or a part of an instrument, unknown to the testator, something different from that intended by him to be his will. It is possible for testamentary intent to arise after the execution of an instrument which the testator does not intend as his will, as where a testator executed a will as a sample for someone else to use, or where fraud has been practiced on him. Such a non-testamentary act could at any time be converted into a testamentary act by the proper execution of a codicil adopting such an instrument as the will of the testator, 27 provided the testator was not lacking in testamentary capacity at the time of the execution of the codicil. § 67.-Alterations, Interlineations, and Additions.-When a will has been properly executed, the law presumes that it expresses the intentions of the testator; it can not be reformed in equity, nor is parol evidence admissible to change the meaning from that clearly expressed by the testator.28 However, as it is an ambulatory inthe instrument is his will carries an implication that he has signed it, and that the signatures of the attesting witnesses, with an attesting clause reciting that the paper was signed and sealed by the testator and attested by them, carries the probative force that the will has been regularly executed. 

If in fact the instrument had not been signed by the testator or by some other person in his presence and by his express direction before it was attested by the witnesses, it would not be a will, because a testamentary paper does not become a will until it is signed, and the witnessing of an unsigned paper would not suffice." Shewmake v. Shewmake (1915), 144 Ga. 

801, 821, 87 S. E. 1046; Moore v. Walton (1924), 158 Ga. 408, 123 S. E. 812.

Therefore, one who is careful in drafting a testamentary instrument will never allow it to be signed and attested where interlineations, erasures, additions, or other changes appear on the face of it, unless they are adopted in a subsequent item of the will or in the attestation clause. It is much the safer plan to rewrite the whole will. When this is impossible or impracticable on account of the condition of the testator, then such changes or alterations can be validated against the presumption of law-that they were made after the execution and that they are invalid-by mentioning them in a subsequent item of the will or in the attestation clause, or by republishing the will in its altered form by a codicil, or by having the testator sign a notation in the margin adopting such changes and having this signing and notation attested in the same manner as wills are attested.

A testator, after signing his will and having it attested, might lay it aside for a time, perhaps years, and then become dissatisfied with some of its provisions. He then might undertake to make changes by interlineations, alterations, or additions without saying anything about it to anyone. Such changes are absolutely invalid unless a codicil is made to the will reciting these changes, and this codicil to be valid must be executed with all the formalities of a will. In other words, a testator could make such changes only by signing a note or codicil to the will and having this attested by three or more witnesses. There is a possible exception to this rule: where a testator has cut out part of his will or otherwise defaced it, and the missing parts can not be established by parol or other extrinsic evidence, and the remaining parts form an intelligible testamentary scheme, the will may be probated as to the remainder, although the testator's acts of alteration were not attested.  § 68. Incorporation by Reference.- Incorporation by reference is a doctrine which has been subject to much judicial discussion in England and in many of the American states.39 As our law of wills in Georgia is founded primarily on the Statute of Frauds, we may infer that this statute and the English decisions thereunder establish the basis of our law in Georgia on this question. Incorporation by reference means the right of the testator to include in his will other papers not themselves signed and attested. For illustration, if a testator in an item of his will gave certain realty or personalty to persons named in a writing sealed in an envelope and deposited in a certain bank vault, the question would immediately arise as to whether this was a valid disposition or whether it failed and this particular property went to the residuum of the estate. It seems to be an established rule that an extrinsic document can not be incorporated in a will by reference to it unless it is in existence before the execution of the will and unless the description of it in the will is so clear, explicit, and unambiguous as to leave the identity of such document free from doubt.40

It is readily seen that a paper not in existence at the time the will was executed could not be incorporated, because it was to be the result of a future act, and a future act could not be signed or attested at the time the will was made. It is equally clear that a paper not properly described could not be incorporated by reference thereto, as to do so would leave too much room for fraud and forgery. 

The burden of proof as to the identity of the paper alleged to have been incorporated is on the person claiming that it was so incorporated. Parol evidence is admissible to show that such paper was in existence at the time the will was executed, and also to identify it where the reference to it in the will is sufficiently clear to permit an identification of it.41 But when the reference in the

§ 70.-Foreign Wills.-The states of the Union have the power to regulate the manner in which real estate within their respective boundaries may be acquired and transferred, the tenure, or method, under which it may be held, the rules of its descent, and the testamentary powers which the owners thereof may exercise over the same.61 As each state is regarded as an independent unit, to allow the lands within its borders to be controlled by the laws of other states would hardly accord with its dignity and independence.62

[Ch. 6 

However, a state may provide by statute as to what effect it will give to the statutes of other states, respecting the title to lands. 

In most states only two witnesses are required to a will; in Georgia three witnesses are necessary. Therefore, if a resident of another state which requires only two witnesses to a will owns realty in Georgia and dies leaving his will executed according to the laws of the state of his residence, he will be considered as having died intestate so far as his lands in Georgia are concerned.63 The justice of this rule lies in the fact that it prevents the introduction of confusion into land titles in Georgia, which naturally should be kept as uniform as possible. To allow the laws of any foreign state to determine the method of transmission of realty in Georgia would necessarily result in much confusion. Public policy,64 which thus requires devises of realty to be controlled by the laws of the state in which the realty is located, does not apply to personal property.

A foreign will65 executed according to the laws of the state in which the testator resides is a valid disposition of personalty located in Georgia, whether such will is executed according to our laws or not.66 The reason for this rule is that the law of the testator's domicile governs regardless of the fact that the personalty may be located in another state.67 By reason of these different rules as to realty and personalty, it is possible for a non-resident to execute a will which is valid as to his personalty and invalid as to his realty located in Georgia. 68 will and testament is in writing and subscribed by the testator."  § 71.-Duplicate Wills and Copies.-When a will has been prop erly executed, it is an ambulatory instrument, revocable at any time by the testator during his life, so long as he retains testamentary capacity. For this reason, the testator has complete control over the instrument during his life, and he usually retains possession of it until death. It is customary for the testator to retain his will after it has been executed and to place it with his other important papers, where it usually remains until search has been made for it after his death. A careless testator may lose his will, or disappointed relatives may hide or destroy it subsequently to his death. 

Under such circumstances, the desire of the testator to leave a will has been defeated unless a copy of the same can be established for probate.69 .69 In order to prevent such a disaster, the testator should execute his will in duplicate and leave the duplicate with some friend. If this is done, care should be taken to see that the duplicate is an exact copy of the will.70 This duplicate could be probated in lieu of the lost or destroyed will;71 the subscribing witnesses or others72 could prove the execution and could identify such the testator's residence at the time of his death; but as to a devise of real estate the lex loci rei sitae governs. 

If, therefore, a will bequeathing personalty is executed according to the laws of the state where the testator resided, it is a sufficient bequest to such personalty, although it may not conform to the laws of the state where the personal property happens to be actually located at the time of the death of the testator. On the other hand, if such a will undertakes to devise lands in another state, the law of the state where the lands are located must be strictly followed in the execution of the will; otherwise it is no testament at all as to such realty. . . "We therefore think that the will in question, being attested by only two witnesses, is inoperative so far as it undertakes to devise lands in this state; but inasmuch as the will bequeaths personal property and has been executed according to the laws of the state of the residence of the testatrix, we think it should have been admitted to probate as a muniment of title to such personalty; and the court therefore did not err in overruling the demurrer to the petition." Knight v. 

Wheedon (1898), 104 Ga. 310, 312, 30 

S. E. 794.

§ 73.—Form, Seal, Revenue Stamp, Date, Bad Grammar.-No par ticular form of words is necessary to the validity of a will, if it expresses the intention of the testator and if it is executed according to the formalities required by law. It is also true that no formal words are necessary to create a valid will, like "give," "devise," and "bequeath." A will may be written in shorthand or in any language which can be translated into English,77 and it may be written with pencil,78 ink, or typewriter. Although it is customary to use the word "sealed" in the attestation clause or to affix the letters "L. S." to the testator's signature, it is unnecessary to do so, as a will is valid without a seal in Georgia.79 

A revenue stamp is not necessary to the validity of a will even though required by statute.80

A date should always be inserted in a will and in the attestation clause, and these dates should correspond, but a date is not necessary to the validity of a will, and even a wrong date does not invalidate it, as parol evidence is admissible to prove when it was executed.81

§ 75.-Generally.-After a testator has signed his will, it is not a valid instrument, under Georgia law, until it has been attested by at least three competent witnesses;' most of the states of the Union require only two witnesses.2 The reason three witnesses are necessary in Georgia is that our law of wills follows the Statute of Frauds, enacted in England in 1677, and adopted by our general assembly as the basis of our law of wills in 1784, just after the Revolutionary War.4 Under this statute wills of personalty did not require attestation, and this rule was recognized as our law until the Act of 1852. This act required wills of personalty to be attested by three witnesses in the same manner as wills of realty. 

The provision of the fifth section of the Statute of Frauds, as to the attestation of wills of realty by three or more competent witnesses, has been followed as our law of attestation of wills of realty since Georgia became a state and has been substantially adopted in our Code.7 

§ 76.-Purpose of Attestation.-The purpose of requiring wit nesses to attest a will is to safeguard the testator's intentions.

If

no witnesses were required, so many frauds and forgeries would be perpetrated that doubt would be cast on all instruments presented for probate, even though no contest arose. The distribution of estates is the most prolific cause of family disputes, and if it were not required that wills be witnessed, family feuds and the wrangling of heirs would be vastly multiplied. The first wills act ever passed in England did not require wills or testaments to be witnessed. Frauds and forgeries "did so abound" that they resulted in the enactment of the famous Statute of Frauds, under which witnesses to wills were required. Therefore, the attestation of wills is the result of human experience over a long period of years. 

Under our present plan of probate, a will can not be presented to the court until after the death of the testator. For this reason, the possibility of proving the will and carrying out the intentions of the testator is far greater, where there are attesting witnesses, than it would be if no witnesses were required to the will. Consequently, the purpose of attestation is to safeguard the wishes of the testator and to minimize frauds and forgeries. § 77.-Attestation Clause.-An attestation clause to a will in 

Georgia is not necessary to the validity of the will. If the testator signs his will and then has it attested by three competent witnesses, this is sufficient, provided all the formalities for the execution of wills in Georgia were observed. § 79.-Interest as Affecting Competency.-An attesting witness who receives an interest under a will as a legatee or devisee is a competent witness, but the legacy or devise to him is void.35 

Under the Statute of Frauds36 a will was invalid if one or more of the witnesses received a legacy or devise under the will, unless there were a sufficient number of attesting witnesses without counting those interested. Consequently, a small legacy or devise to a witness called in to attest the will or the gift of some trifling amount to a faithful servant who happened to be called on to witness the will invalidated the entire instrument.37 To remedy this unjust condition an act was passed in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of George II, 1752,38 which made such witnesses competent to attest the will but declared the legacies or devises to them void.39

As the compensation allowed executors is fixed by statute and is not a gift under the will, and as our statute45 names only attesting devisees and legatees and not executors as those whose gifts under the will are void, an executor is entitled to his statutory compensation even though he is an attesting witness. The same rule would probably apply where a legacy or devise had been given to the executor in lieu of the compensation allowed by law.

The interest necessary to prevent a subscribing witness who is also a legatee or devisee from receiving the benefit intended for him. must be a direct and certain interest. If the attesting witness is a member of a church or society which is named as a beneficiary in the will, the legacy or devise to such church or society is not void by reason of the fact that one of its members was a witness to the will.

The same is true of a citizen of a county to which a gift is made by will for the benefit of the poor or for other charitable purposes. In such instances the witness is benefited indirectly by the reduction of his dues or taxes, but his precise interest can not be ascertained under the will by reason of the indirectness and uncertainty of such interest and, therefore, such legacy or devise does not lapse into the estate. Such an interest in the gift is not void; it does not render the witness incompetent; it simply affects his credibility as a witness.47 § 80.-Attestation by Illiterate Person.-"A witness may attest by his mark, provided he can swear to the same; but one witness may not subscribe the name of another, even in his presence and by his direction."48 This Code section makes a peculiar difference between the signing by the testator and by a witness; for it is a valid signing by the testator for him to direct someone in his presence to sign his name, and he need not make his marķ, but a similar signing by a witness would not be sufficient; a witness must make his mark when someone else signs his name for him, or his attestation is invalid.49 If the witness, on account of illiteracy or other reason, is unable to sign his name, it is proper for him to direct someone else to sign his name for him, but in order for such signing to be valid he must make his mark. To give such a meaning to these words would result in defeating a will where an illiterate witness had died or become blind prior to probate or failed to remember. 

The cautious practitioner, when possible, always should secure the services of attesting witnesses who are able to sign their names, as a safeguard to the validity of the will. 

§ 81.-Witness Can Not Acknowledge Signature.-In order that a will may be valid in Georgia, the testator must sign his name thereto first, and then the witnesses must attest it. Under our Code a witness can not acknowledge his signature; consequently, where the witnesses sign first and then the testator signs immediately as part of the same transaction and then the witnesses acknowledge their signatures, the provisions of the law have not been met and the will is invalid.54 The witnesses must subscribe their names as witnesses after the will has been signed by the testator, 55 or by someone for him, in his presence and by his direction.56

English law of wills was adopted as our law of wills by our adopting act of 1784,59 witnesses to wills of personalty in Georgia were unnecessary until our Act of 185260 required that wills of personalty be executed with the same formalities as wills of realty. 

This act, like the Statute of Frauds, specified that the witnesses should sign "in the presence" of the testator. The fifth section of the Statute of Frauds and our Act of 1852 were codified in our first Code of 1863 and in all our subsequent Codes,61 and this rule that witnesses must sign "in the presence" of the testator has never been varied. The question which naturally arises is what is meant by the words "in the presence" of the testator? From a careful examination of the history of the attestation of wills it is seen that the courts of England, as well as our own courts, have given this question much consideration during the last two centuries in their efforts to interpret the meaning of these words. Are the witnesses compelled to attest in the same room with the testator in order to be in his presence ?62 May they attest in an adjoining house or in an adjoining room in a position where he can see them and yet still be in his presence ?63 Are the witnesses in the presence of the testator if he sits outside of a building in his automobile and looks through the window into the room and sees the witnesses sign ?64

The meaning of the words "in the presence of the testator" was considered by the English courts for the first time in 1687, about ten years after the enactment of the Statute of Frauds. It was held in this case67 that "the statute required attesting in his presence, to prevent obtruding another will in the place of the true one.68 It is enough if the testator might see, it is not necessary that he should actually see them signing; for at that rate if a man should but turn his back, or look off, it would vitiate the will. Here the signing was in the view of the testator; he might have seen it, and that is enough. So if the testator being sick should be in bed and the curtain drawn."69

The witnesses may attest in the presence of the testator without being in the same room or house with him if the situation and circumstances of the testator and the witnesses are such that the testator in his actual location might have seen the attestation.70 If it is necessary for the testator to change his situation, not position, in order to see the witnesses sign and if there is no evidence that he did so change, it is not an attestation in his presence and the will is void, even though the attestation occurred in the same room with him. It is not necessary that the testator actually see the witnesses sign, but his position and circumstances must be such that he might have seen without a change of situation in order for it to be considered that the witnesses actually signed in his presence; of course, if it is proved that he did change his situation and did see the attestation or could have seen it from his new location, the attestation would be "in his presence."72

The presumption of law is that a will has not been attested in the presence of the testator if he signs it in the presence of the witnesses and then retires to an adjoining room while the witnesses attest it; or, if the testator signs the will in the presence of the witnesses and they then take the will to attest it into an adjoining room or to a place in the same room where the testator can not see them without changing his situation, the presumption of law is that it is not attested in his presence.73 This presumption would

If the testator later recovered, the witnesses could not then acknowledge their signatures to him and remedy the improper attestation, as a witness can not acknowledge his signature and thus validate it.76 Under such circumstances, the witnesses would have to attest the will again, in the presence of the testator (not trace their signatures) after the testator had acknowledged his signature. The better plan would be to require the testator to sign his will again and observe all the formalities of execution.

The reason for this rule is quite apparent, as the purpose of attestation is primarily to assure the testator that the identical instrument which he executes will be propounded as his will, and this assurance is sufficiently given if all the witnesses sign in his presence and not in the presence of each other. However, it is much the safer plan to require the witnesses to sign in the presence of each other and in the presence of the testator, after the testator has signed his name in the presence of the witnesses.86 Such procedure, accompanied by a request by the testator to the witnesses to attest his will, serves to impress the execution of the will upon the minds of the witnesses and makes probate more certain.

99. Revocavit Vel Non. § 85.-History of Revocation.-In the seventeenth verse of the ninth chapter of St. Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews is found this statement: "A testament is of force after men are dead; otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth." This correct statement of the law has never been changed by legislative enactment or by any court, and wills are still regarded as ambulatory in their nature and revocable at any time by the testator before his death so long as he retains testamentary capacity. Prior to the 

Norman Conquest in 1066, oral and written wills of realty or testaments of personalty could be made in England and could be revoked either by written or by parol declarations. After the Conquest and the establishment of feudalism, wills of realty were not allowed,' but oral and written testaments of personalty were permitted2 with full right of revocation in the testator. Wills of realty were allowed again in 1540, under the first wills act, provided they were in writing. The right of revocation was not 3 

1. See chapter 1, page 8, showing that wills of realty were permitted by local customs in some localities even after feudalism. 

2. See chapter 3, page 34. 

3. See chapter 1, page 11.

§ 85] 

117 

interfered with by this statute; consequently, a written will could be revoked by an oral will or by oral declarations.4 This condition led to so many frauds and forgeries that it was one of the primary causes of the enactment of the Statute of Frauds.5 Under the sixth section of the Statute of Frauds wills of realty could not be revoked except by the observance of the formalities required by that section. Under this statute testaments of personalty, other than nuncupative wills, must be in writing, but they need not be signed by the testator or attested. Such testaments of personalty could not be revoked orally or by written declarations unless such declarations were proved by three witnesses. 

By our adopting act of 1784 the English law of wills prior to May 14, 1776, was adopted as our law of wills so far as suited to our conditions and form of government. Thus, the English law as to the revocation of wills was accepted as the basis of our law of revocation. By an act¹º of our legislature in 1851 wills of personalty were required to be revoked in the same manner as devises of realty under the Statute of Frauds. Since this act, wills of personalty are executed and revoked in the same manner, in Georgia, as wills of realty. § 86.-Methods of Revocation.-In Georgia revocation may be either express or implied.14 An express revocation may be made by a subsequent will or codicil or other writing, properly executed, in which the former will is expressly revoked, or it may be made by any destruction or obliteration of the will, or a duplicate of it, done by the testator, or by someone acting under his direction, with intention to revoke, while he retains testamentary capacity.15

To this classification may be added these two methods of revocation: first, the implied revocation which takes place by the alienation or loss of the property by the testator subsequently to the making of his will;23 second, the implied revocation of a will by a change in statute which by operation of law invalidates it.24 All of these methods of revocation will be discussed in the following sections of this chapter. 

§ 87.-Revocation by Subsequent Writing.-The usual form for the beginning of a will in Georgia is this: "I, John Doe, being of sound and disposing mind and memory, do make this my last will and testament, hereby revoking and annulling all others by me heretofore made." When such revoking words are used in a validly executed will, whether in the beginning or in any item of the will, they amount to an express revocation of all former wills executed by the testator,25 and this revocation becomes operative immediately. If this latter will is revoked in any manner, the former will is not revived.26.A will may be revoked expressly by a later codicil, whether attached to it or not, if the codicil sufficiently identifies the will.27 A will may also be expressly revoked by a written instru-

§ 88.-Implied Revocation by Subsequent Inconsistent Will.—If a testator makes his will and then at a later date executes another written will, the last will executed is the one the law accepts as expressing his intentions. Even if the last will does not expressly revoke all previous wills, it impliedly revokes all with which it is inconsistent, but this revocation extends only so far as the inconsistency exists.35 Therefore, a testator may leave several valid wills if he has executed several but has not expressly revoked any and none of them is wholly inconsistent with the others. In such case, each will would have to dispose of property not included in the other wills. From this doctrine of implied revocation, in Georgia, arises the fact that a testator may dispose of different parts of his estate by different wills, or he may leave a separate will to each devisee or legatee, provided that the testamentary scheme of each will is not inconsistent with the other wills. For an implied revocation to be effectual in any case, the will containing the implied revocation must ultimately take effect. If it fails for any reason, the former will remains valid without any act on the part of the testator or anyone else unless the testator has otherwise revoked

 § 89.-Revocation by Obliteration or Destruction.-The Statute of 

Frauds provides that a will may be revoked "by burning, cancelling, tearing or obliterating the same"41 by the testator or by someone else in his presence acting under his directions. Our Code42 provides that "an express revocation may be effected by any destruction or obliteration of the original will or a duplicate, done by the testator or by his direction with an intention to revoke; such intention will be presumed from the obliteration or cancelling of a material portion of the will." It will be noticed that our Code section, as quoted, has made this method of revocation broader than apparently was allowed by the Statute of Frauds. This results from the fact that our codifiers were following not only the Statute of Frauds but also the judicial interpretations of this subject, by the English courts43 and by our own courts, previous to this codification. As a result our Code section on this method of revocation is broader than the Statute of Frauds. 

Whether a will has been revoked by destruction or obliteration is always a question of fact, and the intention of the testator is the controlling factor which determines whether any revocation has taken place or not.44 There can be no revocation, destruction, or obliteration unless there is some act done, nor will any act of destruction or obliteration, however great, amount to a revocation unless done by the testator or by someone acting under his directions45 

41. Section VI of Statute of Frauds.

43. "We regard it as a settled doctrine of the interpretation of statutes, that when an English statute is enacted in this state, if it had received a judicial interpretation in England prior to its enactment here, it is to be taken that the language is used in our statutes in the sense given to it by the adjudications in England, unless there is some other sense impressed upon it by attendant provisions of the statute thus enacted. But if it had received no such interpretation, it stands for interpretation here the same as if it had been first enacted here. Adjudications in England, made since such enactment here, have not the force of authority, as to the sense of the language as used in our law. 

As resting on reasons that commend themselves to our approbation, all adjudications upon the subject may aid in giving to terms used a just sense and effect, having reference to the subject-matter of, and to the purposes designed to be served by, the statute in question." Perkes (1820), King's Bench, reported 3 B. & Ald. 489, that it was a question for the jury to determine whether the act of cancellation was complete before the intention of the testator changed. 

In this case it appears that "the testator, being moved with a sudden impulse of passion against one of the devisees under his will, conceived the intention of cancelling it, and of accomplishing that object by tearing. Having torn it twice through, but before he had completed his purpose, his arms were arrested by a bystander and his anger mitigated by the submission of the party who had provoked him; he then proceeded no farther, and after having fitted the pieces together, and found that no material word had been obliterated, he said, 'It is well it is no worse.' Now if the cancellation had been once complete, nothing that took place afterwards could set up the will. But it was a question for the jury to determine whether the act of cancellation was complete." As the testator had not destroyed any material portion of the will, in this case, and as he changed his intention relative to revoking it, the will was allowed to stand even though the intention to revoke had gone so far as to result in tearing the will into four parts, in which condition it remained until presented for probate. 

By express provision of our statute in Georgia,48 a presumption of revocation arises where either the will or a duplicate of it has been cancelled, obliterated, or destroyed in a material part, and the burden of proving that there was no intention to revoke is on the propounder of the will. Just how far this cancellation or obliteration must extend before this presumption will arise is not settled definitely,49 but for such revocation to take place the cancellation or obliteration, whether established by such presumption or by extrinsic evidence, must affect some material part of the will.50 Our

Code and, whether correct or incorrect, it varied the common-law rule that intention alone could not revoke a will. It established a dangerous doctrine; for, if a will can be revoked by intention combined with an act done to some other paper, then by the same logic a will could be executed simply by the testator's intending to do so but failing through fraud or by mistake in signing some other paper. Certainly, a will could not be executed in such manner, as it must be signed by the testator and attested by three or more competent witnesses. Our Code53 now provides that a will may be revoked by the destruction or the obliteration of a material part of the will if done by the testator, or by his direction, to the original will or to a duplicate, with intention to revoke. Pryor v. Coggin was decided in 1855 prior to the adoption of our first Code. The rule established by this decision seems to have been superseded by our Code, and the common-law doctrine re-established.

§ 92.-Revocation in Presence of Testator.-A testator may re voke his will by cancelling a material part or by obliterating or destroying the original will, or a duplicate, if his acts are done with. an intention to revoke; these acts he may do himself, or he may direct someone else to do them. The plain wording of our Code72 is that the acts of revocation may be done "by his direction," and it is not required that they be done "in his presence." This is an unsafe rule that permits a revocation to take place by a cancellation, obliteration, or destruction of a will by some person not in the presence of the testator; it leaves too much room for fraud. It would safeguard wills more to require that if they are revoked by acts of destruction or obliteration, such acts be done with an intention to revoke by the testator, or by his direction and in his presence. Under the plain wording of our Code section, a person interested in seeing that a will is declared invalid might destroy it, unknown to the testator, and then claim after the testator's death, when the issue of revocavit vel non was raised, that he was authorized to destroy it. To refute this contention might be a difficult and uncertain undertaking. Of course, if our statute required that such acts be done in the presence of the testator, the same condition might arise; for the person who destroyed or obliterated the will might claim that he did so by the direction of the testator and in his presence when, as a matter of fact, such a claim might be false. But it would be easier to overcome such fraudulent at-

"An express revocation may be effected by any destruction or obliteration of the original will or a duplicate, done by the testator or by his direction with an intention to revoke; such intention will be presumed from the obliteration or cancelling of a material portion of the will; but if the part cancelled is immaterial, such as the seal, no such presumption shall arise."

tempt to revoke a will if the statute required such acts to be done in the presence of the testator; for the person claiming to have acted by direction of the testator would have to account for the testator at the time he claimed to have acted, and it might be possible to prove that the testator was not present at the place and time specified. Thus, the requirement that such acts be done in the presence of the testator would be an additional safeguard for the protection of wills.73

In many states of the Union, such acts of revocation must be done in the presence of the testator as well as by his direction.74 

The Statute of Frauds,75 which is the basis of our law of wills in Georgia, required that such acts of revocation be done in the presence of the testator as well as by his directions. This rule was changed by the adoption of our Code.76 It is probable that this section of our Code77 will never be construed to mean that such acts must be done in the presence of the testator, because such construction would be contrary to the plain wording of the statute. 

This Code section should be changed by legislative enactment so that in the future no will could be revoked except by the obliteration or destruction of the original will, or a duplicate of the same, or a material part of such original will or duplicate; and such acts of destruction or obliteration should be done with intention to revoke by the testator, or by someone else, in his conscious presence, acting under his directions.

he is of sound mind and no fraud or undue influence is practiced on him.78 The same is true when the testator destroys or obliterates his will with the intention of revoking it. But, if the testator destroys his valid will with the intention of making a new one and he is overtaken by insanity, death, or other calamity before making the new will, or if he makes it and it is invalid, the question arises as to whether his old will has been revoked. If he destroyed the old will or otherwise revoked it merely intending to make a new one some time in the future but neglected to do so, there can be no question as to the completeness of the revocation,79 as the revocation would not be dependent upon the making of the new will. As we have seen,so there must be a joint operation of act and intention in order to revoke a will; the intent must not be conditional. For illustration, if a testator executes a new will, not expressly revoking former wills, and then as part of the same transaction destroys his old will for the purpose of making the new one effective, the revocation of the old will is so related to the making of the new will as to be dependent upon it. Then, if the new will is invalid for any reason, the old will, though destroyed, will be given effect if its contents can be ascertained legally. 

The doctrine under which a will, presumed to be revoked, could thus be established, is known as conditional or dependent relative revocation. This doctrine has been the subject of much judicial discussion by the English and the American courts. It is generally conceded that the case which originated this doctrine is that of 

Onions v. Tyrer (1717), reported 2 Vern. 742. In this case the testator executed a new will in which he revoked a former will; he then gave his former will to his wife and directed her to cancel it, and she did so by tearing it. The last will was improperly attested; so it was invalid and consequently did not revoke the former will. The question then arose as to whether the tearing of the first will was a sufficient act of revocation. It was held that it was not sufficient, as the testator ordered the revocation by tearing "upon a supposition that he had made a later will at the same time." The tearing of the old will and the execution of the new

During the passing of the two centuries since this decision was rendered, the courts have dealt in many interesting discussions concerning this doctrine.82 It is now properly confined in very narrow limits. "Under the operation of this doctrine it has been held that if a testator cancel or destroy a will, with a present intention to make a new will as a substitute for the old, and the new will is not made, or if made fails of effect for some reason, it will be presumed that the testator preferred the old will to an intestacy, and this testament will be given effect. 

We believe this doctrine to be sound, when properly understood and properly qualified. It is a doctrine of presumed intention, and has grown up as a result of an effort which courts always make to arrive at the real intention of the testator. Some of the cases appear to go to extreme lengths in the application of this doctrine, and seem to defeat the very intention at which they were seeking to arrive. 

The doctrine, as we understand it and are willing to apply it, is this: The mere fact that the testator intended to make a new will, or made one which failed of effect, will not alone, 

in every case, prevent a cancellation or obliteration of a will from operating as a revocation. If it is clear that the cancellation and the making of the new will were parts of one scheme, and the revocation of the old will was so related to the making of the new as to be dependent upon it, then if the new will be not made, or if made is invalid, the old will, though cancelled, should be given effect, if its contents can be ascertained in any legal way. 

But if the old will is once revoked, if the act of revocation is completed, as if the will be totally destroyed by burning and the like, or if any other act is done which evidences an unmistakable intention to revoke, though the will be not totally destroyed, the fact that the testator intended to make a new will, or made one which can not take effect, counts for nothing. In other words, evidence that the testator intended to make or did actually make a new will, which was inoperative, may throw light on the question of intention to revoke the old one, but it can never revive a will once completely revoked." But suppose the testator, as a part of the same testamentary scheme, destroyed or cancelled the old will, thus intending to make the new will effective and not intending his acts simply as a revocation of the old will; then, if the new one were to fail, the rebuttable presumption would be that the testator did not desire intestacy, and the old destroyed or cancelled will could be established under the doctrine of dependent relative revocation. Since marriage of the testator after making his will revokes it, unless such event is contemplated in the will, the question naturally arises as to whether the granting of a divorce subsequently to the making of a will would revoke it. It is well settled in some jurisdictions that the granting of a divorce alone does not revoke a will.104 In other jurisdictions, it has been held that the granting of a divorce is such a change of circumstances as impliedly to revoke a will, when the decree of divorce determines the property rights of the parties or where the property rights are settled between the parties before, or at the time, the decree was granted.¹ 105 In Georgia this question appears not to have been settled until 1929, when our supreme court held that a divorce and property settlement would not impliedly revoke a will.106 

In 1784 the common law of England of force prior to May 14, 1776, except where modified by statute or not suited to local conditions, was adopted as the law of Georgia. Therefore, as there is no statute in Georgia making divorce and property settlement an implied revocation of a will, it is necessary to look to the common law for the solution of this problem, but this will give no aid, as divorce as known in Georgia did not exist under the common law.107 As our Code provides only two circumstances or conditions the change of which will impliedly revoke a will, viz., “In all cases, the marriage of the testator or the birth of a child to him, 104. § 95.-Revocation by Alienation or Loss of Property. If a testa tor conveys all the property which he has bequeathed or devised, this amounts to a revocation of his will, and it may be pleaded in bar to the probate of the will.109 The whole will may be revoked, or any legacy or devise mentioned in it may be adeemed, by alienation. At common law, the alienation by the testator of bequeathed or devised property operated as a revocation of the bequest or devise even though he again acquired the same before his death; the common law required that the interest which the testator had when he made the will should continue to be the same interest and remain unaltered until his death. 110 This rule of the common law has been changed by statute in Georgia so that now, if a testator disposes of devised property and reacquires it before his death, it is subject to the will as though it had not been sold and reacquired.111

Involuntary alienation of property previously devised also operates to revoke the will as to the property thus alienated unless the same is reacquired by the testator. Such alienation may result from bankrupt, judicial, or tax sale, or from eminent domain proceedings. 113

For voluntary or involuntary alienation to operate as a revocation, such alienation must be valid. A defective conveyance would not amount to a revocation.114

If a legacy mentioned in a will is lost or destroyed, that part of the will referring to it is revoked. If a lost legacy should be found, the will would become operative again as to it. § 96.-Revocation by Change of Statute.-A will is an ambulatory instrument during the life of the testator and does not become operative until his death.115 As a result, it is affected by a change of statute occurring at any time between the date of its execution and the date of the death of the testator.116 A statute enacted during the life of the testator which changes the method of the execution of wills would revoke a will executed only in accordance with the law as it existed before the enactment of such statute.117 

However, such revocation is only an implied revocation; for, if the invalidating statute itself is repealed before the death of the testator, the will is valid.118 Thus, our courts have established the rule that a change of statute prior to the death of the testator affects an instrument which has been executed by him as his will prior to the enactment of such statute. This rule probably has its inception in the theory that an instrument executed by a testator is not his will until it has been made operative by his death. In many other states119 it has been held that the validity of a will is deter-

Nevertheless, their wills would be invalidated if a statute were to be enacted changing the method of the execution of a will so that our present method would not comply with it. If we ever have a statute of wills enacted in Georgia, it should provide that no will then in existence shall be revoked or in any manner invalidated by reason of such new statute. § 97.-Partial Revocation.-If a testator, after making his will, conveys part of the property of which the will disposes, this amounts to a revocation pro tanto unless he later acquires the specific property of which he has thus disposed.120 While a testator may thus partially revoke his will, he can not revoke parts of it by cancelling, obliterating, or destroying such parts, if the obliterated or destroyed parts can be ascertained by any legal investigation. 121 If such obliteration or destruction of material parts of a will is done with the intention of revoking the entire will, this will amount to a total revocation. 122 But where the obliteration or destruction of such material parts is done with the intention of revoking only such parts, this is not a revocation of the will or v. CHAPTER IX REPUBLICATION OF WILLS § 100. Definitions and General Principles.

§ 100.-Definitions and General Principles.-The republication of a will is an act from which it can be concluded that a revoked will has been revived. In this sense, the revival of a will is synonymous with the republication of a will.' There are two steps necessary before a will can be republished; it must have been executed as a will, and it must have been revoked. When a testator executes a will, it is not necessary that he publish the contents thereof to the witnesses or to others.3 Likewise, when a testator republishes his will, it is not necessary that he make the contents known; if he observes the same formalities as required for the execution of a will, that is sufficient.4 The effect of a republication is to make the will operative in the same manner as if executed at the time of such republication. In other words, it makes the will speak as of that date unless a contrary intent is manifest in the republication to restrain such operation and give it a less extensive effect.5 will which has been expressly revoked by a subsequent will is not revived by the revocation of the subsequent will. For such former will to become operative again, it must be republished. The same is true where a will has been revoked by marriage or birth of issue.7

REPUBLICATION OF WILLS § 101.-Methods of Republication.-At common law, prior to the 

Statute of Frauds, a revoked will of realty or personalty could be republished by an informal writing or by the oral declarations of the testator showing an intent to revive. By statute in Georgia⁹ a will may be republished (1) by a codicil; (2) by any writing executed with the required formalities for the execution of a will; (3) by a republication of the same paper in the presence of three witnesses, who shall subscribe as additional attesting witnesses; (4) by a parol republication in the presence of the original witnesses to the will. These methods of republication will be discussed in the succeeding sections of this chapter. § 102.-Republication by a Codicil.-When a will has once been unconditionally revoked, it is simply a nullity and is considered in law as no longer expressing the intentions of the testator. If the testator should desire to make such revoked will valid again, it would be necessary for him to republish it. The careful testator would not be satisfied with a mere republication of such will; he would make and properly execute an entirely new will expressing his wishes. However, if for any reason it was desirable to validate the old will, this could be done by one of the methods of republication provided by our Code. 10 The usual method of republication is by a codicil.

The Code section referred to indicates that the codicil to be operative should be annexed to the will." However, our supreme court has held that it is sufficient if the codicil unequivocally identifies the will without being attached to it.12 The codicil itself must be signed by the testator and attested by three witnesses and must be otherwise executed with the same formalities as are required by law in the execution of wills. 13

Alterations made in a will are presumed to be invalid,14 but this presumption may be overcome by the adoption of such alterations in a codicil or by the republication of the will in its altered form by a codicil.15 It may be proved by extrinsic evidence that such alterations were made prior to the republication of the will by the codicil.16 The best method of proving that such alterations were made prior to the execution of the codicil is for the codicil itself so to state. If a will has been altered or changed in any manner and the testator republishes it in its altered form by a codicil, he should see, by way of precaution, that the codicil definitely refers to and adopts such alterations or changes. A codicil executed as a result of mistake, 17 fraud, or undue influence is not operative.

§ 104.-Republication in the Presence of Other Witnesses.-It may happen that the testator is satisfied with his will which has been revoked. In such a case he may republish it, however long it may have been revoked, by presenting it to three competent witnesses, acknowledging his signature to them, and then having them sign in his presence as witnesses to his will.21 It would be unnecessary for him to sign such will again, as his former signature would be sufficient if he acknowledged it to the witnesses at the time of republication. These new witnesses may attest the will without the formality of an attestation clause.22 

While this method of republication is legal under our Code, it is unsafe unless a new attestation clause is used which recites the fact of such acknowledgment and republication. If the witnesses were all dead, and if there was no new attestation clause containing the proper recitals, 23 it would be very difficult to prove a republication under this method. If a codicil is used to republish a will, it must be signed by the testator, as well as by the witnesses.24 A codicil is not valid unless it is signed by the testator. If a will is republished by the testator's acknowledging his old signature to new witnesses, it is unnecessary, under our statute, for him to sign the will again unless he has made changes or alterations in the will.

§ 105.-Parol Republication in the Presence of the Original Wit nesses.-Contrary to the rule in other states, 25 in Georgia a will may be republished by parol declarations made by the testator to the original witnesses.26 It is apparent, however, that for such republication to be valid, the will must remain unchanged from the time of the original execution; for, to allow a will which had been altered or changed in any manner to be republished by parol declarations would be to recognize the oral execution of wills, and oral execution is not allowed in Georgia, except in the case of nuncupative wills.27

This method of republication should never be used, even though allowed by statute, except in extremis; for it is very unsafe. If considerable time elapses after such republication before the death of the testator and the presentation of the will for probate, the witnesses may all fail to remember such republication, or they may perjure themselves, or they may die. Then, if no other evidence28 could be adduced to prove such republication in the presence of the original witnesses, the republication would fail, and the will would become invalid; there would be no presumption that such parol republication was made. § 106.-Re-execution of Wills.-If a will has been executed under undue influence, it may be validated by republication or re-execution by the testator while he is not under undue influence. Likewise, a will executed by a testator laboring under any disability which invalidates the will may be made valid by a republication or re-execution of the will by the testator when such disability has been removed. In all such cases, as well as in cases of defective execution or of revocation in any manner, it is best not to depend on a republication of the will. The old will should be re-executed

§ 107.-History.-In each county of the various states of the 

Union there is some tribunal of probate and administration. This tribunal is called the probate court in most states. In New York it is named the surrogate's court; in Pennsylvania, the orphans' court; in New Jersey, the prerogative court. In Georgia it is styled the court of ordinary. This name is derived from the old ecclesiastical courts of England.' The ordinary, under the ecclesi-
