Since that act, the person having authority to preside over a probate court in Georgia is known as the ordinary. One is elected in each county of the state. Some leading thinkers in Georgia contend that, in the interest of efficiency, this court should be abolished and one court established in each county. with jurisdiction over all criminal and civil matters, including probate and administration. § 108.-Purpose and Necessity of Probate.-A will breaks the descent of property from the testator to his next of kin. It may be considered, therefore, as a conveyance; yet, before it becomes operative as such, it must be proved or probated after the death of the testator. The purpose of probate, then, is to establish the will as the identical instrument intended by the testator to be his will. The law very properly does not recognize an instrument as a will until it has been proved before the court of ordinary.⁹

At common law it was unnecessary to probate a will of real estate. 10 Such a will operated as a conveyance to the devisee, who was thereby entitled to take possession. If a contest as to the validity of the will arose between a devisee and an heir at law, the one not in possession usually tested the validity of the will by means of an ejectment suit against the other. On the trial of this action, evidence as to the testamentary capacity of the testator, fraud, undue influence, the formalities of execution, and other questions as to the validity of the whole will or the particular devise in question was admissible. The decision in such action was conclusive between the parties as to that action and upon any person subsequently acquiring title from either of the parties to that action, but the decision had no effect on others not parties to the suit, nor did it establish the validity of the will except as to that particular action. 

The validity of the will could be attacked by others who were interested in a contest resulting from it. Thus, at common law, a will" might be declared valid in one action and invalid in another."

 § 109.-Place of Probate and Who May Propound. The will of a citizen of the state of Georgia must be probated in the county of his domicile at the time of his death.18 The domicile of a person is the place where he resides with intention to remain, or to claim that place as his home indefinitely.19 The domicile of a wife is that of her husband;20 the domicile of a minor is that of his father or other person having legal authority over him.21 If a person dies while temporarily absent from the county of his domicile, the court of ordinary of such county does not lose jurisdiction of his estate.22 

18. Code 113-603. "The residence of the testator at. the time of his death gives jurisdiction to the ordinary of that county to probate his will. A legatee can not have it probated in another county merely because the property devised is in the latter county and all of the parties in interest reside there." Godwin v. Godwin (1907), 129 Ga. 67 (3), 58 S. E. 652; Thomas v. Morrisett (1886), 76 Ga. 384. 

19. Code 79-401, 79-402. Domicile embraces the fact of residence and the intention to remain. Code 79-406. "There must be a concurrence of actual residence and of intention to remain, to acquire a domicile. Residence and domicile are not synonymous and convertible terms. In order to change his domicile a person must actually remove to another place with a present intention of remaining there as his place of domicile, or, having removed to the new place, avow his intention of remaining there as his place of domicile; but such avowal may be proved by express declaration or acts equivalent thereto. The instruction of the court on the subject of change of domicile was misleading." Worsham v. Ligon (1915), 144 

Ga. 707 (2), 87 S. E. 1025; Avery v. 

Bower (1930), 170 Ga. 202, 152 S. E. 

239; Mayo v. Ivan Allen-Marshall Co. (1935), 51 Ga. App. 250, 180 S. E. 20. 

20. "The domicile of а married woman shall be that of her husband, except in two cases: 1. Of voluntary separation and living apart. 2. Of a pending application for divorce. In either case her domicile shall be determined as if she were a feme sole." 

Code 79-403. 

21. Code 79-407. The domicile of a person having been established by the courts of another state is conclusive in this state. Thomas v. Morrisett (1886), 76 Ga. 384, 13 A. L. R. 501n. "The domicile of every minor shall be that of his father, if alive, unless such father shall have voluntarily relinquished his parental authority to some other person. In such event the domicile of the minor shall be that of the person to whom parental authority has been relinquished, or, his master, if an apprentice, or his employer; if neither master nor employer, then the place of his own choice; if the father shall be dead, then the domicile of the minor shall be that of his guardian, if he has one in this State; if no guardian, then of his mother, if alive; if no mother, then of his employer; if no employer, then of his own choice. The domicile of an illegitimate child shall be that of his mother." Code 79-404.

As a general rule, after a testator has made his will, he keeps it in his own possession, custody, and control until his death. It then falls into the hands of those who investigate his business affairs. A person thus coming into the possession of a will should deliver it at once to the executor if practicable.23 The executor should then present the will for probate to the ordinary having jurisdiction, or renounce the executorship; if a renunciation is made, it is final.24 The ordinary may issue process for contempt and fine and imprison any person in possession of a will who refuses to file the same with the ordinary.25 The right to offer a will for probate belongs to the executor, if one is named in the will. In the event the executor is dead or non-resident,26 or if none is named, or if named he refuses to act, any person interested27 may offer the will for probate.28

Under such circumstances, it is the duty of the ordinary to grant administration with the will annexed under the same rules as prescribed for the granting of administration generally.29 

It is thus seen that any citizen of Georgia, if not laboring under any disability of law, may be appointed executor of an estate. The preference is given first to the executor named in the will.30 If the he remained at such hospital a few days or many years.

A form of preliminary probate is allowed where the testator dies in Georgia out of the county of his residence and the witnesses or one of them49 resides in the county where he died.50 Under such circumstances, the court of ordinary of the county where the testator died may probate the will in common form. The original will, together with a certified copy of such probate, should then be transmitted to the ordinary of the county of the testator's domicile, where it will be received and probated in common form without further proof than the introduction in evidence of the certified copy of the probate. This preliminary probate is convenient in such cases in that it saves taking the depositions of a witness to the will as would be necessary in the event the will was first probated in the county of the testator's residence.51 If the will, after having thus been probated in common form, should be presented for probate in solemn form, a certified copy of this preliminary probate in the county where the testator died would not be admissible, as probate in solemn form must be made in the county of the testator's domicile, according to the requirements of our Code. 52

§ 112.-Proof of Death.-Preliminary to the valid probate of a will, it is necessary to prove the death of the testator. Such proof may be made by any person cognizant of the fact. The jurisdiction of the court of ordinary to probate a will or to administer an estate is dependent upon the fact of death.56 The will of a living person can not be probated nor can his estate be administered, and any attempt to do so is violative of the Fourteenth Amendment of the Constitution of the United States, which provides that no person can be deprived of his property without due process of law.57 

In Georgia a presumption of death arises when a person has been absent and unheard of for a period of seven years.58 Acting on kin of a decedent." Jennings et al. v.

The purchaser at a sale under such an administration would receive no valid title as against such person if he should be living.59 However, such an order would be good until set aside, but it could be attacked directly or collaterally by such living person or his heirs or by any interested person whose rights had been affected. 

§ 113.-Probate in Common Form.-Probate in common form60 

and probate per testes-in solemn form-are the two methods recognized at common law for probating a will. The common law, or to speak more correctly, the English ecclesiastical law, as to the probate of wills, was followed in Georgia until the Act of 1845.61 

This act, as codified, 62 changes the common law as to probate in common form in two important respects: first, at common law there was no definite time fixed at the expiration of which probate in common form became conclusive; second, at common law probate in common form was made on the oath of the executor.63 

Under our Code, probate in common form becomes conclusive upon all parties after the expiration of seven years from the time of probate except minor heirs at law, who may require proof in solemn form and interpose a caveat at any time within four years after arrival at age.64

In probating a will in common form, the propounder need not give notice to anyone. The probate may be taken by the ordinary at any time during vacation, but the order admitting the will to record and granting letters testamentary can be granted only at a regular term of the court of ordinary.67 There can be no caveat to the probate of a will in common form, and an appeal can not be made to the superior court from the judgment of the ordinary years from the time of such probate, except minor heirs at law who require proof in solemn form and interpose a caveat within four years after arrival at age. This form of probate differs from probate in common form in three important respects: first, notice must be given to the heirs at law of the testator; second, all the witnesses to the will in life and of sound mind and within the jurisdiction of the court must be used as witnesses in proving the will; and, third, the judgment of probate is conclusive immediately upon all the heirs notified.74 If a witness is dead or non compos mentis, his signature and the formalities of the execution of the will may be proved by anyone familiar with these facts. If a witness is a nonresident of the state of Georgia and beyond the limits of the state at the time of probate, the same rule applies as to proving his signature and proving the will as though he were dead. If a witness is a resident of the state but not of the county where the will has been offered for probate, he can not be required to attend the probate court, but his depositions 75 must be taken76 by one of the

§ 116.-Contract Not to Offer Will for Probate.-Every person having possession of the will of a deceased person must file it with the ordinary of the county having jurisdiction. The ordinary may fine and imprison any person who fails or refuses to comply with this provision of the law.95 For this reason, a contract between those interested in a will, or between the heirs at law and such interested persons, not to offer the will for probate is not enforceable for the purpose of preventing such probate.96 While it would not be a bar to the probate of the will, the terms of a valid contract of this character could be enforced in a court of equity against all legatees and devisees sui juris who signed it. Minors and other persons under legal disability would not be bound by such contract, but they could ratify it upon the removal of the disability.97 The

§ 117.-Collateral Attack on Order of Probate.-As the court of ordinary has exclusive jurisdiction over the probate of wills, 100 its judgments are conclusive on the issues involved on probate. However, for the protection of those whose rights have been adversely affected by a judgment of the ordinary, an appeal is allowed to the superior court.101 Unless an appeal is taken, the judgment of the ordinary either for or against probate is conclusive, and is not subject to collateral attack in any other proceeding in the court of ordinary or in any other court. 102 An exception to this rule occurs notes due by each of them were not to constitute a part of the estate, one of the distributees being the administrator, in a subsequent suit between them, such an agreement would be binding, and the other party could not claim that the notes were a part of the estate; but that, if the converse of the proposition were true, and they were to make such a division of the estate, and the notes of the respective parties were to be included, then it would be the duty of the jury to carry out the agreement." Cutliff v. Boyd (1884), 72 Ga. 302 (5).

§ 120. Probate of Foreign Wills.—A foreign will is one executed by a person whose domicile is not in the state of Georgia but in some other state or country.122 If real estate is devised, such foreign will can not be probated in the state of Georgia as to such real estate unless it is executed with the formalities required by our statutes.123 The validity of a will, as a conveyance of real estate in Georgia, is determined by our laws, regardless of the fact that its validity may have been established by probate in another state. It is good as to personalty and may be probated in this state, whether executed according to our laws or not, if it is executed according to the laws of the state of the testator's domicile.124 A foreign will may be probated in any county in this state in which there are assets belonging to the estate of the deceased, but the ordinary first taking jurisdiction will retain it.125 Such

§ 121] 185 CAVEAT as our Code already provided that a properly certified copy of such will, the probate thereof, and the order admitting the same to record are admissible in evidence.137 Thus, under our law a foreign will disposing of realty, in order to be a good muniment of title in Georgia and admissible in evidence without first being probated here, must be executed according to our laws, probated in the state of the testator's residence, and recorded in Georgia in the deed records in the office of the clerk of the superior court in the county where the land is situated, and then when offered in evidence must have presented with it a properly certified exemplification of the record admitting it to probate. This exemplification should contain a copy of all the record leading up to and including the order to probate. The same rules apply to foreign wills of personalty except that they need not be executed according to the laws of Georgia, but must be executed according to the laws of the state of the testator's domicile and except that they need not be recorded in the office of the clerk of the superior court, as required of foreign wills of realty.

Our statutes, in thus providing for the admission in evidence of foreign wills without probate in Georgia, do not prevent them from being probated in Georgia also.

§ 128. Jurisdiction. As explained in the chapter on Probate,' 

the only issue which can be considered when a will is presented for probate is devisavit vel non-will or no will, testacy or intestacyand, when an appeal is taken to the superior court on the judgment of the ordinary probating or refusing to probate the will, the only questions which can be adjudicated by that court are those which were considered or which might have been considered by the court of ordinary.2 In probate proceedings, questions of construction are left for the consideration of the proper court under pleadings presented for that purpose.

It becomes necessary, therefore, to determine which courts have jurisdiction to construe wills. In some jurisdictions it has been held that the probate court, after it has admitted the will to probate, has the first opportunity to construe its terms,³ and from the decision of such probate court an appeal usually lies to a court of

§ 129.—Same—Superior Courts.-In Georgia equity jurisdiction is vested in the superior courts. As equity has exclusive jurisdiction over petitions for the construction of wills, it follows that petitions for construction must be filed in the superior courts. 

The petition for construction should be filed by the executor in the superior court of some county in the state where one or more of the interested parties reside. § 130.-Same-Federal Courts. In the chapter on Probate, it was shown that the federal courts have no jurisdiction over the probate of wills. [Ch. 11 times happen that our superior courts and city or county courts may be called on to construe an instrument before it may be admitted to probate in order to determine whether or not it is a will. 

This occurs where an instrument, testamentary in character, has been treated as a deed and has been withheld from probate for that reason, or for some other reason, and then is introduced in evidence as a muniment of title to realty or personalty. It then becomes necessary for the court to determine whether the instrument offered in evidence is a deed or a will. In such cases the court does not attempt to construe the terms of the instrument or to establish the rights of the parties named therein further than to determine whether the instrument is a deed or a will. If it is a deed, it is admissible in evidence, provided it is relevant; if it is a will, it is not admissible in evidence, as a will can not be admitted in evidence until it has been probated in the proper court, the court of ordinary.20 In order to determine whether the instrument is a will or a deed, the court seeks the intention of the testator by considering the whole instrument "read in the light of surrounding circumstances."21 This expression, as used in the Code, necessarily admits parol and other extrinsic evidence in the consideration of this question, but evidence that the instrument is a will is opinionative and is not admissible for the additional reason that the question of will or no will is one for the probate court to consider.22 

In considering instruments of the kind now under discussion, our courts are inclined to apply the rule of ut res valeat,23-the courts lean towards that construction which will give the instrument efaction when they with the life-tenant brought the suit could not proceed therein on a cause of action accruing to them on the death of the life-tenant during its pendency." Weaver v. 

McCullar (1921), 150 Ga. 820 (2), 105

20. See section 10, footnote 24, chapter 2. 

21. "No particular form of words is necessary to constitute a will. In all cases to determine whether an instrument is testamentary in character or not, the test is the intention of the maker to be gathered from the whole instrument, read in the light of the surrounding circumstances. If such intention is to convey a present estate, though the possession is postponed until after his death, the instrument is a deed; if the intention is to convey an interest accruing and having effect only after his death, it is a will." Code 113-102.

24. "From the great wealth of authorities thus gathered and analyzed the general agreement of courts may be stated. (1) An instrument which is in the form of a deed to take effect on the death of the maker, where there are no other indicia to prove the intention of the grantor, and the instrument can be held valid either as a deed or as a will, the court will construe the instrument so as to prevent its becoming inoperative. (2) 

Whether such an instrument is to be construed as a deed or a will depends upon the intention of the grantor as to the passing of a present irrevocable interest, or whether no interest should pass until after the death of the grantor, and whether the grantor until then should have the right to revoke the instrument. (3) The intention of the maker of the instrument is to be ascertained from the whole construed together. (4) Looking to extraneous facts, the delivery of the instrument is some evidence that the same shall operate as a deed, although its terms provide that possession is postponed until after the death of the maker." § 132.—Pleadings-Parties.-The pleadings in a case filed for the construction of a will should be in the same form as in other cases in the superior court.29 The bill in equity is verified and filed by the person desiring the construction against those whose interest it is desired to bind; it must be filed after the validity of the will has been determined by the probate court. A copy of the will should be attached, and the parts to be construed should be specified.30

§ 133.-General Principles Governing Construction.-As the form of a will is immaterial and as the language used in one will is always different from the language of all other wills, it is impossible to make a set of rules by which all cases which may arise may be determined. As wills usually spring from the better part of human nature, the courts always endeavor to carry out the intentions of the testator. Adjudicated cases are generally of little help in deciding upon the intention of a testator in a particular case, for the reasons that no two wills are in exactly the same language, that the character and outlook on life of each testator colors his ideas and intentions, and that the surrounding circumstances are necessarily different in each case.37 Still, there are some general rules of construction which are followed by the courts in the construction of wills.38 

36. Foster v. Hardee (1910), 135 Ga. 

591, 69 S. E. 1110. 

37. "In the construction of wills, the intention of the testator should be the first and great object of inquiry. And this is to be sought for by looking to the whole will, and not to detached parts of it." Cook v. Weaver (1852), 12 Ga. 47 (1). "Every court must determine for itself, what the intention of the testator is in the particular case before it, and that intention should be carried into effect, provided it be not unlawful." Cook v. Weaver (1852), 12 Ga. 47 (2). "Precedents, or adjudged cases, are of but little authority, and of dangerous application, in deciding upon the intention of a testator; the construction depends so much on each case, upon the character of the testator, the terms he employs, and all the surrounding circumstances." Fourth. Fifth.-The will of a non-resident which conveys realty in this state is to be construed as to such realty in accordance with the laws of Georgia, and the courts of this state are not bound by the construction of the courts of another state concerning realty devised in this state.47 That part of a will disposing of personal property in Georgia, executed by a non-resident, should be construed under the laws of the state of the testator's domicile.48

Eighth. In construing the terms of a will, the court will not lay too minute a stress on the precise meaning of the words used in the will.55 The presumption is that words, even technical words, are used in accordance with their generally accepted meanings, unless a contrary intent is manifestly implied in the context.56 When this contrary intent appears from the will itself, words used by the testator will be construed to mean what he intended them to mean rather than what they usually mean. This may result in giving words a meaning that they do not ordinarily or properly possess, but the intention of the testator must prevail.

"Not only may the rules of grammar be entirely disregarded in order to carry into effect the manifest intention of the testator, but even well-defined technical terms of the law will be given an unusual meaning, or will be held to be meaningless, when it is clear from the provisions of the will that the testator did not use them in their technical sense, or when, to carry out his intention, it is necessary to entirely disregard such technical terms. If, however, the will uses words which have a wellsettled, definite meaning in the law, and there is nothing in the will itself to indicate that it was the intention of the testator that such words should be given any other meaning than that which the law gives them, then it is to be presumed that it was the intention of the testator that the words should be construed in that sense in which the law would ordinarily construe them." Tenth. A general intention of a testator, as gathered from his entire will, must prevail over a particular intention gathered from part of the will.59 It would be unjust to allow a general intention, gathered from the whole will, to be defeated by an inaccuracy or an inconsistent expression of a particular intention.60

Twelfth. Intestacies are not favored in construing wills. If the terms of a will are such as to permit two constructions, one of which results in intestacy and the other of which leads to a valid testamentary disposition, the construction is preferred which will prevent intestacy.63 

Thirteenth. The law presumes the testator had a legal intention in view in making his will until the contrary appears.64 When it has been determined that the testator's intentions are illegal, the courts can not remake the will or arbitrarily give it some other meaning which it may be supposed the testator would have adopted if he had known that his intentions could not be carried out.65 

Fourteenth.-An heir can not be disinherited except by express devise or necessary implication, and the implication, to effect such disruption in the descent of property, must amount to such a strong probability that a contrary intention can not be presumed.66 The law prefers the natural channel of descent to the creation of estates by implication. 67

This rule is in harmony with the English authorities prior to the American Revolution but contrary to the later English cases and contrary to the rule in some of the states of the Union. To illustrate this rule: 

Suppose a man devises a certain tract of land to his wife "for and during her natural life, and after her death to be sold; and the proceeds to be equally divided between my surviving children and the children of any of my deceased children."69 Do the words of survivorship refer to his death or that of his wife? No contrary intent appearing in the will, the supreme court construed these words of survivorship to refer to the death of the testator, with the result that the children had a vested remainder interest in the estate immediately upon the death of the testator.

An express direction in a will to keep the estate together for a period of time implies the power to borrow money to meet the necessary expenses of so doing, even though no mention is made of such necessity in the will.73 If the power is expressly given in the will to the executor or his successor to borrow money, or otherwise create indebtedness against the estate, there would be no question as to his power to do so and thus to bind the estate.

The foregoing are some of the general rules of construction; they are by no means exhaustive, but they serve to illustrate the cardinal rule of construction that the intention of the testator governs, if legal. No necessity would ever arise for construing wills if the intentions of the testators were always legal and unmistakable; but, so long as the imperfections of the human mind continue, the necessity for the construction of intentions will exist. 

§ 134.-Words and Phrases Construed.-The meaning of words used in a will is to be sought from the context of the will rather than from their customary usage or from their adjudicated meaning in other cases. The courts may construe a word to have an entirely different meaning in one will from that which it was construed to have in another will. This liberal and just rule results from the efforts of the courts to give effect to the intentions of the testator in every case. Words often have different meanings, and two testators, using the same word, may use it correctly in different senses. Then, too, words are often used by the uneducated in senses different from the accepted meanings. Yet, in all cases, the courts will ignore the usual meaning of words, if necessary, in construing wills and follow those meanings intended by the testators. 

If no contrary intent appears from the will, words and phrases are presumed to have been used in their ordinary and accepted meanings.78 The following words and phrases are chosen as illustrative of the foregoing statements: "Lend" will be construed to mean "give" unless the context requires its restricted meaning.7 79 An unconditional gift of the entire "income" of property or "interest" accruing from a fund will be construed as a gift of the property or fund unless the provisions of the will require a more limited meaning.80

"Per capita" and "per stirpes" have a definite meaning in law and are presumed always to be used in their technical sense unless a contrary intention appears in the context of the will. "Per capita" means "by the head," or share and share alike, according to the number of individuals. "Per stirpes" means "by the roots" or "stocks," or by representation. It denotes that method of distribution where a class or group of individuals or distributees take the share which their "stock" (deceased ancestor) would have been able to take in a per capita distribution.  § 136.-Effect of Change of Statute on Validity of Will.-A will conveys no interest until the death of the testator, and it is affected by a change of statute in the meantime. 105 Therefore, a will executed only in the manner prescribed by existing law at the time of its execution is not a valid will if the law of execution has been changed by statute between the date of the execution of the will and the death of the testator. At the death of the testator, the will takes effect immediately, however long the probate may be postponed. If, for any reason, a will is not probated at once upon the death of the testator, and if while it is being withheld a change of statute is made affecting the execution or the construction of the will, such change in statute would have no effect on the validity of the will, as the will takes effect according to the law existing at the time of the death of the testator.106 If a will is valid under the law as it exists at the time of the execution and if a statute is enacted which makes the will invalid, it is nevertheless a good will, provided such statute is repealed or becomes obsolete before the death of the testator and provided the testator has not revoked such will. 107 Thus, a will may become invalid by a change of "A devise of 'all of one's estate,' or of a certain 'plantation,' described as being in a given county, is not void for uncertainty, and extrinsic evidence is admissible to show that a particular tract constituted a component part of the land intended to be embraced within such general descriptive terms."

There is a distinction which the Georgia statutes draw between the invalidation of a will during the life of the testator by a change of statute and by a change in the status or condition of the testator himself. As just stated above, a will invalidated during the life of the testator by a change in statute may become valid by the repeal of that statute, yet a will invalidated by law by reason of a change in the status of the testator does not again become valid by reason of the testator's return to his former status. 108 Thus, a will becomes invalid upon the marriage of the testator or upon the birth of a child to him unless such events have been contemplated in the will,109 and it does not automatically become valid again by the restoration of the testator to his former status by reason of the death of such wife or child.110 

The will remains invalid unless it is republished or re-executed by the testator.111 

§ 137.-Will Following Rules of Inheritance.-A testator may by will leave his property to be distributed according to the rules of inheritance in Georgia, and such will is valid, even though he names no person in his will as a legatee or devisee.112 The court of ordinary has jurisdiction to admit such will to probate, regardless of the fact that, had no will been made, the statutes of distribution would have allowed the same persons to take the property anyway. A will of this character is usually made where the testator desires to save his heirs the expense and the annoying formalities of an administration; for by his will, the testator can relieve his executor from making an inventory of the estate or making returns to the court, and can allow him to make sales, public or private, for cash or credit, with or without notice, and without an order from any court.113 An administration of an estate under such a

"Whether a will is to be regarded as contingent turns upon the point whether the contingency is referred to merely as the occasion of or reason for making the will at the time it is made, or is referred to as the reason for making the particular disposition of property which is provided for, and is intended to specify the condition upon which the will is to become operative."118 In the latter case the will is contingent; if the condition or contingency is simply the reason for making the will, then the will is not contingent and is a valid instrument, regardless of whether the particular event referred to happened or not. Distribution. § 142.-Legatees and Devisees.-As it is necessary for the testator to have testamentary capacity before he can make a valid will, it becomes interesting to inquire as to what capacity a person who is the object of the testator's bounty must possess in order to enjoy the benefits provided for him in the will.

A beneficiary named in a will is incapacitated to take a benefit designed by the testator to be used for illegal or immoral purposes, as such bequest or devise is void. Under the Statute of Frauds a will was invalid if a legatee or devisee named therein was an attesting witness. This provision of the statute was based on the idea that the temptation to commit perjury might exist when the witnesses were called on to prove the will if they were interested in the provisions of the will. This statute was later modified in 1752,9 so that the will was valid but the bequest or devise to the witness was void. This latter rule was adopted in our state and is now a Code section. 10 A void will may be made valid by a codicil or by other method of republication,¹¹ and a void legacy or devise may likewise be made valid.

 § 144.-Kinds of Legacies and Devises.-Under our Code legacies are divided into two classes, general and specific.31 Our law also recognizes demonstrative and residuary legacies. A specific legacy is a gift by will of property which is particularly designated and which is to be satisfied only by the receipt of the particular property described.32 "My goldheaded cane, the gift of my grandfather to me," or "my ten shares of stock in the City National Bank of

Albany" are illustrations of specific legacies. A general legacy or devise is one which does not direct the delivery of any particular property; it is not limited to any particular asset and may be satisfied out of any property of the same general character belonging to the estate of the testator and not otherwise disposed of in the will.33 A gift of money is a general legacy, even though the will specifies that it is to be paid out of a particular fund.34 If this particular fund is not in existence at the death of the testator, the gift will be paid out of the general assets of the estate in the same manner as other general legacies are paid. A specific legacy of money may be made if the entire fund or part of it is given with that intention, as the intention of the testator would govern.35

Specific legacies are not favored under our law, and when there is doubt as to the testator's intentions, a legacy will be construed to

However, the specific legacy possesses certain advantages in that the income, interest, rent, or hire from such legacy commences at the death of the testator38 and in that such legacy does not abate with general legacies for the payment of the debts of the estate and the expenses of administration.39

A demonstrative legacy is one which designates the fund or property from which it is to be satisfied but is nevertheless an unconditional gift to the legatee of the amount or value specified. That it names a particular fund or other property from which it is to be satisfied is considered to be demonstrative of a convenient mode of payment; if that mode fails, the legacy is to be satisfied out of the general assets of the estate.40 A demonstrative legacy differs from a general legacy in that it does not, in the first instance, abate upon insufficiency of assets to pay the debts of the estate and the expenses of administration; it differs from a specific legacy in that there is recourse for its payment from the general assets of the estate in the event of ademption in part or in whole.41 

A residuary legacy is a general legacy into which fall all the assets of the estate42 after the satisfaction of all other legacies and the payment of all debts of the estate and all costs of administration. It is customary for the testator to make provision for the "rest" or "residue" of his estate in the form of a residuary bequest or devise. The presumption is that the testator intended that all the legacies provided for in his will would be paid in full and that he contemplated that his estate would be sufficient to meet this requirement. However, his good intentions are no protection for his legatees from the just claims of his creditors or from the lawful charges resulting from the setting in motion of the machinery of the courts. The first assets of the estate to be applied to the payment of debts and costs are those charged by the testator with this particular indebtedness; next, the assets found in the residuary clause of the will are applied; and, if there is no residuary clause, then the undevised estate is applied. If these assets are insufficient, or if there is no residuary clause or undevised estate, then general legacies must abate pro rata to make up the deficiency.51 If the general legacies are insufficient to meet these requirements, then specific and demonstrative legacies abate in the same manner.52

§ 147-Lapse.-A lapsed legacy or devise is one, unrevoked by the testator, which was good at the time the will was made but which fails to take effect because of the death without issue or other incapacity of the beneficiary in the lifetime of the testators or before the time for the estate to vest. A void legacy is one which was void at the time the will was made or which later became void by a change of statute or by a change of the status of the testator;82 the same rules of distribution apply to void and to lapsed legacies.83 

A legacy to a person dead at the time the will was made is void, unless such legatee leaves children, or descendants of children, who are living at the time of the death of the testator84 or at the time fixed by the will for the vesting of the estate. If a legatee or devisee dies after the will is made and before the death of the of his intent in case of a sale or the like, the law declares what it deems is his legal intent; or, in other words, provides what shall be the result in such case. This excludes the idea that in every case what the law deems to be the intent has no force, and that the courts will go afield hunting for an intent expressed in parol or to be gathered from conduct or acts of the testator after the making of the will.

LEGACIES AND Devises devise is made to the members of a class, as to the children of "A," only those receive the benefit of such bequest or devise who are born before the event which fixes the time for the vesting of the estate and who live until such event takes place. The law fixes the death of the testator as the event which vests the legacies or devises, but the testator, by his will, may provide that some other event must happen before a legacy or devise shall vest. If one member of a class dies before the estate vests, the others of the class who survive take the entire interest to the exclusion of the heirs or issue of the one who died.90 This rule of survivorship applies to bequests or devises to a class instead of the rule as to lapsed legacies; for as long as a member of the class exists the legacy can not lapse.91 The rule as to survivorship, or as to lapsed legacies, does not apply if the testator has expressed a different intention in the will.

§ 148.-Income from Legacies and Devises.-When a testator dies, it is obviously impossible for a distribution to be made immediately. 

His will must first be probated, creditors ascertained and satisfied, and, where necessary, his will construed; then comes the distribution according to the terms of the will, after the payment of inheritance taxes and costs. The question then arises as to what becomes of the income, rent, hire, or interest from the general and specific legacies or devises while the estate is in the process of administration. 

The income from specific legacies or devises, after the death of the testator, whether in the nature of interest, rent, hire, or other form of profit, is part of the legacy or devise although the time of enjoyment or vesting of such legacy or devise may be postponed by the terms of the will.99 This income, increase, or profit is to be calculated from the date of the death of the testator.100 

As a devise of land is necessarily specific unless a contrary intention appears in the will, rents accruing during the year in which the testator died follow the land and belong to the devisees thereof.101 

When the will does not fix a definite time for the payment of a general legacy, it is payable at the end of the first year after the date of the death of the testator, and it usually bears interest from the date it is payable.102

A general legacy to be paid at a future time or upon a future event bears no interest until such time or event."

§ 149.-Taxation of Legacies and Devises.-Before the executor assents to any legacy or devise and delivers or conveys it, he should see that all the obligations against the estate have been paid. As we have heretofore seen, these obligations must be paid out of the residuum unless the will provides otherwise; if the residuum is not sufficient, then the legacies abate proportionately according to the rules of abatement. 103 These obligations consist of costs, taxes, year's support, and other claims against the estate, all of which are to be paid in the order of priority named by our Code. 104 Unless the will provides otherwise, the estate tax must be paid out of the assets of the estate rather than by the beneficiaries out of their respective shares. 105. State, county, and municipal taxes should be borne by the residuum on general legacies for the first year, as the income from general legacies for the first year after the testator's death goes to the residuum, but specific legacies and devises should be responsible for their own taxes from the date of the death of the testator. Devises are taxed according to the laws in force at the place where the land is located; legacies are taxed before distribution according to the rules of law in force at the place of the testator's domicile. 106 § 150.-Assent of Executor.-Upon the death of the owner of realty intestate, the title to the realty vests immediately in the heirs If the testator fixes by his will the date on which a general legacy is to be paid, it bears interest from that date.

§ 152.—Election.—Election is an equitable doctrine in relation to wills which is recognized by our Code: 126 It means the choice between one of two rights or claims, to each one of which the legatee or devisee choosing has an equal right, but both of which he can not enjoy on account of an expressed intention on the part of the testator that he should not enjoy both. 127 If a legatee or devisee has a claim adverse to the will, he must either relinquish his rights to the property thus adversely claimed, or he must relinquish his rights under the will. "He must accept the will as a whole, or not at all; that is, if he claims under the will, he must recognize the testator's right to dispose of the property, although he, the beneficiary, in fact owned it."128 A person can not take a beneficial interest under a will and at the same time set up some legal right which will defeat the full operation of some other part of the will; he must take under the will or against it. 

Election most frequently arises in cases where dower rights are involved. If the testator names his wife as a devisee, 129 she is

This our statute has wisely prohibited. § 155.-Devises to a Class.-A bequest or a devise may be made to several persons either as individuals or as a class;153 if the gift is to them as individuals, each one takes only the definite interest intended for him, regardless of whether the others survive the testator or not, and the rights of each individual to his interest in the bequest or devise are the same as in a case where the entire interest is given to one legatee or devisee. If the gift is to them as a class, they take interests proportional to the number surviving at the time the estate vests. If an unconditional devise or bequest is made to an individual and such individual dies before the death of the testator and leaves issue surviving, such issue takes in lieu of the deceased. 154 But, if the bequest or devise is to a class and a member of the class dies before the death of the testator or before the time fixed for the vesting of the estate, his issue does not take his interest; it goes to the surviving members of the class, 155 unless the testator has provided that the issue shall take.

A gift to a class to take effect immediately, at the death of the testator, includes only those who are living at that time, 156 and the amount of their interest is determined by the number in existence at that time. Where the quantity each is to take is specified, the only uncertainty is as to the number who are to take at the designated time.164

§ 157.—Definitions.—By estate is meant "the quantity of interest which an owner has in property, ," whether real or personal. This quantity of interest may signify either absolute or limited ownership; it describes the circumstances in which the owner is placed with reference to his things, real or personal. At common law this quantity of interest was divided into freehold estates and estates of less than freehold. Freehold estates were divided into estates of inheritance and estates not of inheritance. Those of inheritance were further divided into fee-simple estates and limited estates; one species of the latter was an estate tail. Those not of 

1. Code 85-104. The word "property" includes realty and personalty. Code 

102-103; Lamar v. Sheffield (1881), 66 

Ga. 710; DeVaughn v. McLeroy (1889), 82 Ga. 687, 694, 10 S. E. 211. Strictly speaking, the word "property" means the quantity of interest an owner may have in things real or personal, but custom and our Code have so changed this meaning that the word "property" now is used to signify the things themselves, whether real or personal, instead of the interest in them.

Bouvier's Law Dictionary defines estate to be the degree, quantity, nature, and extent of interest which a person has in his real property. Our 

Code makes it applicable to both realty and personalty. Code 85-104.

[Ch. 13 

inheritance were estates for life only, whether expressly created by the acts of the parties or by operation of law, as in the case of an estate in curtesy or in dower. Estates less than freehold were classed as estates for years, estates at will, and estates by sufferance.2 With reference to the time of their enjoyment, estates at common law were further classified as estates in possession, which include all those mentioned above, and estates in expectancy, as remainders, reversions, and executory interests.³ 

Under the Code of Georgia not all of these common-law estates are recognized. Only those recognized by our Code, together with their many modifications, will be considered in this chapter. 

§ 158.—Fee-Simple Estates.-An absolute or fee-simple estate is one in which the owner is entitled to the entire property, with unconditional power of disposition during his life.4 Upon the death of the owner intestate, a fee-simple estate descends to his heirs according to the rules of descent and distribution.5 

At common law the word "heirs" was necessary to the creation of an absolute or fee-simple estate. If land was conveyed to a person forever or to him and his assigns forever, only a life estate vested. This technical rule of the common law has been abolished in Georgia, so that now every conveyance is construed to pass a fee-simple estate, whether the word "heirs" or its equivalent is used or not, unless the instrument specifies a less than absolute estate.

As heretofore shown,29 at common law freehold estates of inheritance were classed as fee-simple estates and limited estates, or inheritances limited. Limited estates were further classified as qualified or base fees and fees tail, commonly called estates tail. 

Qualified or base fees were such as passed the fee-simple title but subject to be divested upon the happening of some contingency, as where the fee was given to "A" and, upon his dying without children living at the time of his death, then to "B." An estate tail is one which descends to some particular lineal heirs, exclusive of others, of the person to whom the estate is granted; it contemplates 

27. Mattox v. Wescott (1908), 156 

Ala. 492, 47 So. 170; Peters v. Pilcher (1924), 211 Ala. 548, 100 So. 902. 

28. "Estates tail are prohibited and abolished and the law shall not presume or imply such an estate. Gifts or grants to one and the heirs of his body, or his heirs male or heirs female, or his heirs by a particular person, or his children, or his issue, shall convey an absolute fee. Limitations which, by the English rules of construction, would create an estate tail by implication, shall give a life estate to the first taker, with remainder over in fee to his children and their descendants, as above provided; and if none is living at the time of his death, remainder over in fee to the beneficiaries intended by the maker of the instrument." Code 85-505; Cole v. Ogg (1935), 180 Ga. 343, 179 S. E. 116. 

29. See section 157 of this chapter.

[Ch. 13 

an indefinite failure of issue with reversion to the original grantor. 

Thus, if an estate were granted to a man and the heirs of his body, or the heirs male or female of his body, such issue continued to take the estate from generation to generation until some future date, however remote, when there was a failure of such lineal heirs. Whenever such failure occurred, the estate reverted to the original donor, or to his heirs, and did not vest in the collateral kindred of the person to whom it had been granted in tail. An estate tail thus contemplated the fettering of land to a grantee and the designated heirs of his body without the power of alienation. 

After the introduction of feudalism into England,30 and prior to the year 1285, estates thus limited were known as conditional fees. Thus an estate granted to a person and the heirs of his body was presumed by the courts to have terminated when the condition of having issue of his body had been fulfilled. Immediately upon the birth of such issue he could alienate his land and thus forever bar the right of the original donor to the reversion, even though it were immediately repurchased by the holder of the original conditional fee. If he failed to alienate it and his issue died, the rights of the original donor to such reversion were not affected by the birth of such issue.31 As the holders of such conditional fees were careful always to alien the land, as soon as they had issue, and thus cut off the entail, or the reversionary rights of the original donor, the feudal barons became dissatisfied. They wanted the privilege of entailing the land, as they held most of it and desired to keep the right to it in their families for social, political, and financial reasons. In order to prevent the destruction of these conditional fees by alienation, the nobility procured in the year 1285 the enactment by Parliament of the Statute of Westminster the Second,32 commonly called the statute "de donis."33

This statute prevented the alienation of a conditional fee by the grantee even though he complied with the condition by having issue. 

After this statute, such an alienation would not affect the right of the original donor, or his heirs, to the reversion which would return, whenever there was a failure of issue in the grantee and the particular heirs of his body to whom such estate was limited, how-

This cumbersome method of overthrowing estates tail finally evolved into their general statutory destruction, thus causing the American colonies to suffer little from their evil effects. 

As the word "heirs" was necessary to the creation of a fee-simple estate by deed, so was the word "body," or other word of procreation,37 necessary to the creation of an estate tail.38 Where such words of procreation were used, an express estate tail was created. 

Under our Code, the only words which would create an express estate tail are the following: "Gifts or grants to one and the heirs of his body, or his heirs male or heirs female, or his heirs by a particular person, or his children, or his issue."39 Such gifts or grants now convey the absolute fee, as estates tail are abolished in Georgia.40 As these words are exhaustive of the common-law words of procreation which would create an express estate tail, it becomes interesting to determine when the English rules of con-

Under the statute "de donis," the English courts had little difficulty in determining that an estate tail was created if the grant or devise contained the necessary words of procreation. As a grant or devise to "A" and his heirs or issue was a fee-simple estate, the courts would not infer that it was the intention of the grantor or testator to create such an estate, as his mention of "B" was unnecessary if it were not intended that "B" should have some rights in the estate. The second meaning or use of this word is the sense in which it is used in this Code section as to estates tail.48

For this reason, the Rule in Wild's Case is followed in Georgia, so that if a grant or devise is made to a person and his "children," and such person has no children at the time such instrument takes effect,49 an express estate tail is created which by operation of law is converted into a fee-simple estate. 50 Therefore, a devise to a person and his "children" places the fee-simple title in such person if there are no childrens¹ in being at the death of the testator, and a deed from such person will pass an absolute title even though children are later born to him. The Rule in Wild's Case is applicable where the word "children" is coupled immediately in the grant or devise with the name of the ancestor, as a gift or grant to "A" and his children. It has no application where an estate is given expressly to one for life with remainder to his children; in such case, the ancestor has an estate for life and his children a remainder as purchasers.53

Georgia, all these expressions, when coupled directly with the name of the grantee or devisee, now convey a fee-simple estate to the grantee or devisee. made to Edward Shelley for life, then after several intermediate estates for years "to the use of the heirs, males of the body of the said Edward Shelley, lawfully begotten, and of the heirs, males of the body of such heirs, males, lawfully begotten." It is thus seen that an attempt was made to create a perpetuity in the heirs, males, lawfully begotten, of Edward Shelley, from generation to generation indefinitely. In deciding this case, the court established the celebrated rule in English law known as the Rule in Shelley's Case. 

This rule is to the effect that whenever a freehold estate57 is granted or devised to a person for life with remainder, either mediately or immediately,58 to his heirs or the heirs of his body, the word "heirs" is a word of limitation and not of purchase.59

Such a limitation of an estate was valid if the remainder was limited to some person other than the heirs of the first taker; but, when the remainder was limited to the heirs of the first taker or the heirs of his body, a fee simple or a fee tail vested in him. For illustration, if an estate was conveyed to "A" with remainder to his heirs, an absolute, fee-simple title vested in "A"; if it were to "A" and the heirs of his body, "A" would take an estate tail.60 Such words being considered words of limitation and not words of purchase, the heirs of the first taker took by descent only. The distinction between purchase and descent is this: An heir who takes by descent has no rights in his ancestor's estate until the death of such ancestor; a person who takes by purchase takes an independent estate of his own by virtue of the first grant or devise through which the first taker acquired his interest. Therefore, an ancestor may alien. or encumber the estate to the detriment of the heir, whereas a person who takes by purchase takes his estate free from the alienation, encumbrance, or other acts of the intermediate holders.61

The establishment of the Rule in Shelley's Case is attributed by some writers to the aversion the common law had to the inheritance' being held in abeyance and to the desire to facilitate the alienation of land and to throw it into the track of commerce one generation sooner, by vesting the inheritance in the ancestor, thereby giving him the power of disposition.62 By others its foundation is attributed to feudal policy.63 

The Rule in Shelley's Case is noticed here, because an understanding of it is essential to a knowledge of some of the problems of estates with which this chapter is dealing. This rule has been abolished in England by statute, and it is no longer of force in Georgia, as the reverse of its doctrine has been established by our Code.64 Under our Code, in limitations over, words which were words of limitation have been made words of purchase and declared to have the same meaning as the word "children." Therefore, in Georgia, a conveyance to "A" of a life estate with remainder to his "heirs," "issue," "heirs of his body," "children,' or others named by words of similar import would create an estate for life in "A" with remainder to his children in being at the time the grant or devise took effect.65

The passage of the first wills act, enacted by Parliament in 1540, created the possibility for such estates to be established by means of executory devises. 

Such devises were not the result of any statute but were the result of the inventive genius of the feudal lawyers who persuaded the courts70 to recognize such devises and thus brought into existence a form of estate tail which could not be barred by a common recovery. Thus, estates tail in their most pernicious form were again fastened on English lands.

Executory devises were estates which violated the rules of common law conveyancing inter vivos and which could be created only by will.71 Such estates as those mentioned above, which could not be created at common law by conveyances inter vivos, may now be created in Georgia by deed or by will.72 When they are created

285 § 165.-Perpetuities.-In the preceding section of this chapter it was said that executory devises 78 were the invention of the feudal lawyers, who thus created a most pernicious form of estate tail, as an estate tail after which an executory devise was limited could not be barred by a common recovery.79 A devise to "A," and, upon his dying without issue, then to "B," at common law, was held to mean an indefinite failure of issue, thus creating an estate tail by implications in "A" with an executory devise in "B." It is generally conceded that the courts, in order to unfetter lands from this public evil, for which Parliament would not provide legislative remedy, finally invented or recognized the rule against perpetuities.81

The rule against perpetuities is to the effect that a future estate, whether created as an executory devise or as a contingent remainder, must vest, if at all, during the period comprised within a life or lives in being, and twenty-one years and the usual period of gestation thereafter.82 Therefore, limitations of an estate under the rule against perpetuities may extend over any number of lives in being at the time the limitations commence, and twenty-one years and the usual period of gestation thereafter. A limitation beyond that period the law terms a perpetuity and forbids its creation. 

When an attempt is made to create a perpetuity, the law gives effect to the limitations not too remote, declaring the others void, thereby vesting the fee in the last person within the legal limitations.83

The rule against perpetuities, as finally established by the common-law courts, is the rule recognized now in Georgia by the following Code section: "Limitations of estates may extend through any number of lives in being at the time when the limitations commence, and 21 years, and the usual period of gestation added thereafter. A limitation beyond that period the law terms a perpetuity, and forbids its creation. When an attempt is made to create a perpetuity, the law gives effect to the limitations not too remote, declaring the others void, and thereby vests the fee in the last taker under legal limitations."84

After the rule against perpetuities was recognized at common law, no executory devise was valid which violated this rule. The effect of this rule, in connection with the common-law presumption that "dying without issue" and equivalent phrases referred to an indefinite failure of issue, was to make many executory devises. void.85 In order not to defeat the rights of the executory devisee, the courts, whenever the context of the will would permit, held that it was the intention of the testator to refer to a definite failure of issue-failure of issue at the death of the first taker. Much confusion was thus created and continued in England until Parliament, in 1837,86 settled this question by providing that such phrases as "dying without issue" refer to the death of the first taker. Our legislature in 185487 followed Parliament by enacting a similar statute, which is now a part of our Code.88 Thus, executory devises which were formerly void for remoteness are now valid, as the words formerly importing an indefinite failure of issue, and thus violative of the rule against perpetuities, have been made by statute

The rule against perpetuities creates a positive limit beyond which limitations over can not exist; that is, the vesting of future interest can not be postponed beyond the period of time allowed by law. As shown in section one hundred seventy-one of this chapter, the rights of a reversioner are the same as those of a vested remainderman in fee. As vested remainders are not subject to the rule against perpetuities, it follows that the rule against perpetuities does not apply to reversions. The logical deduction from this conclusion is that a grantor or a testator may create a vested estate for any number of years, and such estate will not be destroyed by the rule against perpetuities. For illustration, a testator or a grantor may create a present estate to endure for any number of years, either more or less than one thousand years, provided such estate is followed by a reversion to the maker of the instrument, or to his heirs, or by a vested remainder in fee. The rule against perpetuities applies to a succession of future estates, for a period longer than that allowed by the rule, each of which is to be enjoyed after the previous estate has been determined or exhausted. For illustration, an estate for life to "A" with remainder to "B," with remainder to "B's" children, with remainder to their children, and so on indefinitely, would violate the rule against perpetuities, and the law would give effect to the limitations over not too remote, declaring the others void, and thereby would vest the fee in the last taker under the legal limitations. It is immaterial how many estates for life are created for persons in being, as each life tenant after the first takes a vested remainder. It is the limitation of the estate over to future persons not in being with which the rule against perpetuities is concerned, for no future interest in property can be created which can not vest in lives in being at the time the estate commences, or within twenty-one years and the usual period of gestation thereafter.91

[Ch. 13 

The rule against perpetuities does not apply to vested estates or vested interests. As stated above, it applies only to remote future and contingent estates and interests, legal or equitable. If the vesting of the interest is postponed or the power of alienation is suspended for a longer period than that allowed by the rule, it is unlawful, and the devise or grant is void. The limitation must be so made that the estate or interest not only may, but must necessarily, vest within the prescribed period; and, if by any possibility the vesting of the estate or interest may be postponed beyond this period, the limitation is void, as the rule concerns itself with the vesting or commencing of estates and not with their termination. 

The standard for measuring the period of time for the postponement of the vesting of future estates or interests is the life or lives of the beneficiaries then in existence, and twenty-one years and the usual period of gestation thereafter. If the testator or grantor elects to shorten this standard of measurement by not using the time of the life or lives in being and uses only an absolute period of years, such absolute period can not exceed twenty-one years.92 

The rule against perpetuities is one of the most beneficent provisions of our law relative to estates. Nothing could interfere more with commerce in lands than for the title to be encumbered with an indefinite succession.

Remainders are either vested or contingent. A vested remainder is one limited to a certain person at a certain time or to such person upon the happening of a necessary event; a present estate passes to be enjoyed in the future.98 A contingent remainder is one so limited that either the person who is to enjoy the estate is at present uncertain, or the event upon which the future estate is to vest may or may not happen.99 It is the uncertainty of the right of future enjoyment which makes a remainder contingent.

"A contingent remainder is one which is limited to take effect on an event or condition which may never happen or be performed, or which may not happen or be performed until after the determination of the preceding particular estate." Griswold and Griswold v. Greer (1855), 18 Ga. 545, 549. "When a future time for the payment of a legacy, is defined by the will, the legacy will be vested or contingent, according as upon construing the will, it appears whether the testator meant to annex the time to the payment of the legacy or to the gift of it." (2 Wms. on Ex'ors. 1051). "In ascertaining the intention of the testator in this respect, the Courts of equity have established the following rules of construction: "1st. That a bequest to a person, payable, or to be paid at or when he shall attain twenty-one years of age, or at the end of any other certain determinate period or term, confers on him a vested interest immediately at

the right to the future enjoyment which makes a remainder contingent. Whether the contingency results from the uncertainty of the person who is to take or the uncertainty of the event which is to vest it, the remainder is defeated unless the contingency happens on or before the termination of the precedent estate.117 For illustration, if a devise is made to "A" for life with remainder in fee the testator's death, as debitum in presenti solvendum ad futuro: For the words payable or to be paid, are supposed to disannex the time from the gift to the legacy, so as to leave the gift immediate in the same manner in respect to its vesting, as if the bequest stood singly and contained no mention of time. (Ib. 1052.) "2ndly. That if the words payable or to be paid, are omitted, and the legacies are given at twenty-one, or if, when, in case, or provided, the legatees attain twenty or any other future, definite period or term, these expressions annex the time to the substance of the legacy and make the legatee's right to it, depend on his being alive at the time fixed for its payment. Consequently, if the legatee happens to die before that period arrives, his personal representative will not be entitled to the legacy. (Ib.)"

Bowman Ex'or. and Trustee v. Long 

(1857), 23 Ga. 242, 246. "Where real estate is granted to a person when or as soon as he shall attain a given age, or when an event shall happen which may never occur at all, or at, or upon, or from and after his attaining such age, or the happening of such event, and there are no other words indicative of an intent to confer a vested interest, and nothing in the form of a limitation itself to indicate an intent merely to delay the vesting in possession or enjoyment, and no disposition of the intermediate income, the interest of the grantee will be contingent until he attains the age specified, or the event described has happened. If futurity is annexed to the substance of the gift, the vesting is suspended; but if it appears to relate to an intent merely to delay vesting in possession or enjoyment of the grant, the grant vests instanter." 128 to that effect, but such remainders could be raised in a will by implication. This seems to be the rule in Georgia now.126 According to Blackstone, 127 such remainders were not allowed at common law among more than two devisees. The contrary was later established, and Lord Mansfield laid down the rule in the case of 

Perry et al. v. White (1778), Cowp. 777, 4 T. R. 710, that whenever cross remainders are to be raised between two and no more, the presumption is in favor of cross remainders; where among more than two, the presumption is against them; but the intention of the testator may defeat the presumption in either case. From the common-law principles, it may be deduced that the rule in Georgia is that, in a will, there may be cross remainders by implication amongst any number of persons where the words of the will indicate this to be the intention of the testator. For illustration, if a testator devises certain land to his two sons for their natural lives, and then to their children, if they shall have any, and further provides that, if both of said sons die without children, then the title to such land shall vest in another person, the sons take as tenants in common for life with cross remainders for life necessarily implied between them. Upon the death of one without issue, the title to the land vests in the surviving son for life with remainder in fee to his children. If both sons die without leaving any children, then the title would vest in the third person designated by the testator to take the same. Such an estate is called a cross remainder, because each of the devisees has reciprocally a remainder in the share of the other. the same land between two or more

Cross remainders may be created either by deed or by will, but when created in a deed they must be expressly created, whereas cross remainders may be created in a will by implication. § 170.-Acceleration and Destruction of Remainders.-As there are two vestings of a vested remainder, one in interest and the other in possession, 129 the vesting in possession may be accelerated by a forfeiture of the precedent estate¹30 or by a renunciation by the tenant of all his rights in the precedent estate. A vested remainder may be accelerated also by the death of the life tenant or tenant for years prior to the time the instrument creating the remainder takes effect. For illustration, since a will does not take effect until the death of the testator, if a life estate with vested remainder is created by will and if the life tenant dies before the death of the testator, the remainder vests in interest and in possession at the death of the testator.131

At common law a particular estate, that is, an estate precedent to the remainder, was necessary in order to sustain a remainder. 

If, for any reason, the particular estate was destroyed, the remainder was defeated. Under our Code no particular estate is necessary to sustain a remainder, and consequently the defeat of the particular estate does not destroy the remainder.132 At common law, in order to preserve a contingent remainder, it was necessary to appoint a trustee to hold the same, but under our Code a trust is not necessary. 133 § 171.-Estates in Reversion.-A reversion is the return of an estate to the grantor or his heirs after the grant is over, or the return of a residue to the estate of the testator when only a particular interest has been devised with no valid provision as to the disposition of the remainder. A reversion is created by operation.

The condition in the grant or devise is intended to vest, enlarge, or defeat the estate granted or devised. When a condition is annexed to an estate, no legal disability, except being non compos mentis, will relieve the person to whom the estate is granted or devised from complying with the condition.137

The entire will may be conditional, or a particular legacy or devise may have a condition attached to it.138 If a will is made in view of an impending peril, as undertaking a dangerous journey, 139 engaging in a battle, or having a serious operation performed, it may be conditional upon the testator's surviving such peril. In order that it may be conditional, the will itself must so provide, as parol evidence would not be admissible to prove that the testator intended the instrument as a conditional will; to admit parol evidence for that purpose would be attempting to revoke a written will by parol evidence, and this is not permissible. For illustration, a gift to "A" to become operative only when he reaches the age of twentyone is contingent upon his reaching that age, 145 and is void if he dies before the age of twenty-one. If a condition precedent becomes impossible to perform, or if the condition is illegal, or contrary to public policy, the estate will not arise, even though there is no fault on the part of the devisee or legatee, as reasons why the condition did not happen will not serve to vest the title.146 When the condition has been fulfilled, the title vests immediately. 147

§ 173.-Generally. It is not the object of this chapter to give a discussion in detail of the subject of trusts and trustees. Such discussion would require more space than can be afforded in this volume. The subject of trusts and trustees is one of the great branches of our law with which is interwoven to some extent testamentary disposition and the administration of estates. The purpose of this chapter is to discuss generally the law of this subject in relation to testamentary disposition and to point out the principles which will aid the scrivener or practitioner in creating a valid testamentary trust whenever the occasion arises. § 174.—History of Trusts.-During the latter part of the thirteenth century, the ecclesiastics introduced into England the system of conveying land to "uses" for the purpose of evading the statutes of mortmain. In the course of time, this method of conveyancing was 

1. A history of the struggle between 

Church and State with reference to the statutes of mortmain and the methods devised by the ecclesiastics to evade

§ 174] 307 

TRUST ESTATES 

employed generally, not only by ecclesiastics, but also by laymen in their transactions pertaining to land, thus depriving the king and the lords of feudal dues to which they were entitled under the feudal system.2 Under this system of holding land to uses, the legal title was vested in one person on the trust or confidence that he would permit some other person or corporation, as the equitable owner, to have the possession, use, and enjoyment of the land, as well as the income therefrom. Thus, a double ownership of lands was permitted. Two titles and estates existed in the same land,4 one the legal estate cognizable in the courts of law and the other, the equitable estate, enforceable only in courts of chancery.5 

To remedy these inconveniences, Parliament enacted many statutes which tended to make the usee the real owner of the land. 

Finally, this idea was carried into effect by the Statute of Uses.7 

This statute enacts that "when any person shall be seised of lands, &c., to the use, confidence, or trust of any other person or body politic, the person or corporation entitled to the use in fee-simple, fee-tail, for life, or years, or otherwise, shall from thenceforth stand and be seised or possessed of the land, &c., of and in the like estates as they have in the use, trust, or confidence; and that the estate of the person so seised to uses shall be deemed to be in him or them that have the use, in such quality, manner, form, and condition, as they had before in the use."8

The effect of the Statute of Uses was to unite the use and the possession, thereby making the usee the owner of both the legal and the equitable estates. The "use" and the land thus became convertible terms.⁹ The Statute of Uses does not abolish "the these statutes is given in section 192 of chapter 15 on Charitable Trusts.
