conveyance to uses, but only annihilates the intervening estate, and turns the interest of the cestui que use into a legal instead of an equitable estate. A use, a trust, and a confidence is one and the same thing, and if an estate is conveyed to one person for the use of, or upon, a trust for another, and nothing more is said, the statute immediately transfers the legal estate to the use, and no trust is created, although express words of trust are used."10 

The Statute of Uses did not forbid the creation of uses or declare them illegal. It merely provided that, when a use was created, the legal estate was immediately merged into the equitable estate; this was an attempt to abolish the jurisdiction of the equity courts and restore the jurisdiction over landed estates to the common-law courts.

Under modern conditions, a conveyance of title is ordinarily made by a deed executed according to law and recorded in the public records of the county where the land is situated. In early times, when few people could read and write and there were no public registers for deeds, title to land was conveyed by livery of seizin. Such livery of seizin was made usually on the land itself by the delivery of a leaf or a twig from a tree on the land or a handful of the soil, by a public ceremony. "In the early periods of English jurisprudence, the want of public registers, the ignorance of forms, and general incapacity of the common people to read or write, were supplied by solemnities, ceremonies, and notoriety in their transactions, and particularly in the transfer of real estate. 

Lands were aliened by making livery of seisin in public before witnesses, a custom in imitation of the ancient feudal investiture. 

The two essential elements of a conveyance of a freehold interest in it were, first, a formal delivery of possession, called livery of seisin; and, second, words accompanying such delivery indicating the nature and extent of the grantee's interest and the service to be rendered for it. This mode of conveying land was termed a feoffment. The grantor was the feoffor, the grantee the feoffee."11

Under such transfers of title by livery of seizin it was not necessary to embody in a deed the words of transfer, as the livery of seizin was sufficient. However, deeds of transfer were in common use, not for the purpose of conveying the title, as title was conveyed 

10. Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 298. 

11. Thompson on Real Property, vol. 

3, sec. 2650, page 792.

§ 174] 309 

TRUST ESTATES 

by the livery of seizin, but for the purpose of preserving the conditions and terms of the transfer.

The Statute of Uses had the effect of creating a new method of transferring title unknown to the common law at that time, for, when a conveyance of title was made to one person for the use of another, the Statute of Uses immediately transferred the legal estate to the usee, thus vesting the legal and the equitable title in the usee, without livery of seizin or other act or ceremony. "The statute of uses at the time when it was passed had an immense effect upon the tenures of the realm. Many interests in land which had been merely equitable, and cognizable only according to the rules of equity, became at once legal interests, cognizable in courts of common law. Many persons who were seized of estates to uses, and who only could sue or be sued at law in relation. to the same, ceased at once to have any title either at law or equity. 

Although it is probable that it was the intent of the statute to convert all uses or trusts into legal estates, yet the convenience to the subject of being able to keep the legal title to an estate in one person, while the beneficial interest should be in another, was too great to be given up altogether, and courts of equity were astute in finding reasons to withdraw a conveyance from the operation of the statute."12 The construction placed on the Statute of Uses by the chancery courts prevented it from executing all uses or trusts their creation as was evidently the intention of Parliament. 

The strict construction placed upon the statute caused a distinction to be drawn between such uses as were executed by the statute and such as were not executed. Chancery took jurisdiction of the latter, and they are now known as trusts. Under the Statute of Uses dry or passive trusts were executed as there were no duties to be performed by the trustee. Prior to the Statute of Uses, uses or trusts were perhaps known only in their simplest form, as where one person held the legal title for the benefit of another without any active duty to perform. As the Statute of Uses destroyed all such upon 

12. Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 300. "The strict construction which was given to this statute by the judges of its time, and the inconvenience and injustice which thereby fol lowed, led, after a lapse of time, through the interposition of the court of chancery, and the ingenuity and learning of lawyers, to the establishment of a regular and enlightened system of trusts. In this way uses were partially revived under the name of trusts." 26 R. C. L. 1172.

[Ch. 14 

uses or trusts, it had an immense effect at the time. However, it was soon established by the courts that there were three methods of creating a use which would prevent it from being executed by the Statute of Uses.13 

The first of these methods was by the limitation of a use upon a use. The statute executed the first use but did not destroy the second.14 The first use was void anyway, as it had been settled prior to the Statute of Uses that a use raised upon a use was void.15 

The second method of creating a use which was not executed by the statute was the granting of a term of years to one person for the use of another. The reason assigned for the survival of a use of this kind was that the Statute of Uses executed the legal titles of estates of which the grantee was seized and that no person could be seized of a term of years.16 The third method of creating a use which was not executed by the statute was to provide some active duty for the trustee to perform. Wherever a trustee had imposed upon him any duties which made it necessary for him to hold the legal title in order to perform such duties, the trust was classed as an active trust and was not executed by the statute.17

15. "Thus, if A. enfeoffed B. to the use of C., in trust for D., the statute immediately transferred the legal estate to C., and extinguished all interest in B., but it did not touch or affect the use or trust for D. It had been settled before the statute, as a rule of property, that a use could not be raised upon a use. At law such use raised upon a use was simply void. And at law it was held that the statute extended only to execute the first use by transferring the legal estate from B. to C., and that all its powers were exhausted in that act, and thus C. held a legal title in trust or for the use of D., which the statute did not execute. And although C. was bound in equity and good conscience to give to D. the use and enjoyment of the estate, there was no remedy for D. at law, and he could only proceed as before the statute by subpoena in chancery to compel C. to perform the trust." Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 6. 

16. Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 6; 28 R. C. L. 1175.

"Therefore if any agency, duty, or power be imposed on the trustee, as by a limitation to a trustee and his heirs to pay the rents, or to convey the estate, or if any control is to be exercised, or duty performed by the trustee in applying the rents to a person's maintenance, or in making repairs, or to preserve contingent remainders, or to raise a sum of money, or to dispose of the estate by sale,-

TRUST ESTATES 

The Georgia Code did not adopt this construction of the Statute of Uses. The result is that the trend of our law as to trusts is contrary to that in the other states of the Union. Our Code does not recognize that active duties to perform on the part of the trustee will preserve a trust; it bases the idea of a trust rather on the idea of disability on the part of the beneficiary." 

The Statute of Uses was not intended to apply to personal property; it was designed to prevent the creation of trusts in land.¹9 

The use of the word "seize" in the Statute of Uses prevents it from operating on personal property, as the word "seized" is applicable only to freehold estates.20 Nevertheless, our supreme court is committed to the view that the Statute of Uses, as enforced in in all these, and in other and like cases, the operation of the statute is excluded, and the trusts or uses remain mere equitable estates. So if the trustee is to exercise any discretion in the management of the estate, in the investment of the proceeds or the principal, or in the application of the income; (as if he has the duty of paying over the rents and profits to the beneficiary; or if the time and manner of turning over the principal to the beneficiary are discretionary with the trustee, although he may have no discretion to hold it indefinitely;) or if the purpose of the trust is to protect the estate for a given time, or until the death of some one, or until division, or until a request for a conveyance is made. So if an estate is given upon a trust to sell or mortgage for the payment of debts, legacies or annuities, or to purchase other lands to be settled to certain uses; and this construction will not be affected by a power given to one of the cestuis que trust to control the sale of part of the estate, nor by the fact that the direction for the payment of debts and legacies, out of the proceeds of the sale of the land, is only in aid of the personal property." Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 305; 

Potter v. Couch (1891), 141 U. S. 296, 11 Sup. Ct. 1005, 35 L. ed. 721; Eldred v. Meek (1899), 183 Ill. 26, 55 N. 

E. 536; Snelling v. Lamar (1890), 32 

S. C. 72, 10 S. E. 825. "Three principal reasons or rules of construction were laid down, whereby conveyances were excepted from such operation: first, where a use was limited upon a use; second, where a copyhold or leasehold estate, or per. sonal property, was limited to uses; third, where such powers or duties were imposed with the estate upon a donee to uses that it was necessary that he should continue to hold the legal title in order to perform his duty or execute the power. In all of these three instances, courts both of law and equity held that the statute did not execute the use, but that such use remained, as it was before the statute, a mere equitable interest to be administered in a court of equity. These uses, which the statute did not execute, were called trusts." Perry on 

Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 300.

Georgia, applies to trusts created in realty, or in personalty, or in both.21 § 175.-Definition and Nature of Trusts.-A trust is an equitable obligation, either express or implied, resting on a person by reason of a confidence reposed in him to apply and deal with property conveyed to him for the benefit of some other person or persons; the trustee himself may be included as one of the beneficiaries.22 

The person to whom the realty or personalty is conveyed in trust holds the legal title for the benefit of the person or persons named as the beneficiaries; he is called the trustee. The draftsman of a trust instrument should see that the instrument conveys an estate to a designated person as trustee for the benefit of a named beneficiary or beneficiaries. The failure to designate a trustee is immaterial, as equity will appoint one,23 but this is a privilege which the grantor or testator should exercise. There is an apparent conflict between the Statute of Uses and our rule that a life estate may be created in money or its equivalent, like negotiable securities and bearer bonds. See chapter 13, section 159, as to creation of life estates in money. Under this rule the life tenant must give bond in order to take possession of such property. If he fails to give bond, then the executor of the will in which the life estate was created would be required to hold such property in trust for the benefit of the life tenant and the remainderman. If the life tenant and the remainderman were both sui juris, we would have the anomalous situation of a trust of a character which appears to be prohibited by our Code. This theoretical difficulty grows out of the fact that the Statute of 

Uses was not intended to apply to personal property, but in Georgia it has been so applied. This inconsistency should perhaps yield to the practical necessity of protecting the rights of the remainderman in such an instance. The better plan would be for the legislature to establish the rule followed in other states to the effect that active duties on the part of the trustee to perform permit the creation of a trust for any person, whether sui juris or not, for any length of time, provided the rule against perpetuities is not violated.

§ 178.-Same-Contingent and Shifting Trusts.-Express trusts, under our Code,35 may be contingent and shifting.36 A contingent trust is one the activity or operation of which depends upon the happening of a future event. For illustration, if a testator creates a trust estate for the benefit of the children of his unmarried daughter,37 who may be born after the testator's death, 38 such trust is contingent for its operation upon the future existence of such children. A contingent trust of this character would be shifting in that it would operate in favor of each child as it was born, thereby shifting or changing as new beneficiaries came into existence.

Charitable Trusts.-The subject of charities and charitable trusts is discussed in a separate chapter of this volume.64 

§ 185.-Persons by Whom Trusts May Be Created.-Any person who is competent to make a will may create a trust. As a general rule, any person65 who is competent to enter into a contract has the power to convey or transfer the title to his real or personal property and the power to create a trust. When a trust is created, the legal title passes from the owner to the trustee for the benefit of the beneficiaries of the trust. No person can create a trust in property in which he has no title or interest.66 

§ 186.—Persons for Whom Trusts May Be Created.—As explained in section 174 of this chapter, the Statute of Uses67 was enacted in hostility to all uses or trusts. However, both the law and equity courts in England soon established the rule that, where there was any active duty on the part of the trustee to perform, the trust was not executed by the statute.68 This is the general rule followed in the other states of the Union. In Georgia the Statute of Uses as established by our Code does not recognize active duties on the part of the trustee to perform as a criterion for determining whether or not a trust exists. Our Code provides that certain disabilities on the part of the beneficiary must exist before a trust can be created or recognized. The idea is disability on the part of the beneficiary rather than active duties to perform on the part of the trustee.

For illustration, in Georgia, trusts, with the exception of charitable trusts, can be created only for the following classes of persons: minors,69 spendthrifts, persons non compos mentis, and life

The law in Georgia as to trusts should be modified by our legislature so as to permit trusts to be valid whenever there are active duties prescribed for the trustee. As the law now stands, trusts can be created only for certain beneficiaries as specified above, whereas it is the desire of many Georgians to create trusts for other relatives or friends. The law as to the execution of trusts created for persons sui juris immediately executes such trusts in Georgia. This has resulted in many wealthy Georgians' moving their assets out of the state in order to create trusts in states with more liberal provisions as to active trusts. Those of modest circumstances can not afford such a move and must suffer the disadvantages of the present law.

§ 187.-Same-Living Trusts.-The expression "living trusts" is one now in common usage. In other states this expression is often used to designate any trust by which a person sets aside a fund for his wife, children, or some other relative or friend, or even for himself, and where he provides in the trust instrument active duties for the trustee to perform. As heretofore explained,88 in cases of trust created by will, the trust does not take effect until the death of the testator. It then becomes operative but subject to be defeated by adjudication by the probate court that the will is invalid, or by the necessary use of the trust property for the payment of the debts of the testator in the administration of his estate. When these two emergencies have been survived, the trust property is ready for delivery to the trustee named by the testator, and the executor should assent to such legacy or devise in trust as soon as is consistent with a just administration of the estate of the testator.89 This is true even where the same person has been named in the will as executor and as trustee, as the trust property always should be separated from the general estate as soon as possible.91 When the trust property has been delivered to the trustee, his administration of it has be- 90

It is important that the trust instrument set out particularly the powers and duties of the trustee, but this is unnecessary so far as the validity of the trust is concerned. Equity, ever watchful of trust estates, is always ready to prevent the destruction of a trust estate when legally possible and to give aid in the administration of the same. If no trustee is appointed, or if a vacancy occurs, or if the trustee is removed, 101 or if the trustee refuses to act, 102 on an application made in behalf of the beneficiary or beneficiaries by next friend, equity will appoint a trustee. 103 If his powers are not defined, he is presumed to take an estate as large and extended as the necessities of the trust require.104

Administration of Charitable Trusts. 

§ 192.-History.-The history of the law as to charitable uses or trusts is extremely obscure. Such trusts probably have their origin in the charitable sentiments created by Christianity in the Roman Empire before that government publicly announced itself as Christian. Gifts for charitable purposes were known to the 

Christian emperors of Rome as "pious uses."

England was converted to Christianity while it was a Roman province; but, during the Anglo-Saxon conquest, the power and influence of Christianity largely disappeared in England, along with other evidences of Roman civilization. After conditions had become somewhat settled again, Christianity was firmly re-established in England by missionaries from Rome, the first of whom were Augustine and his band of monks, who arrived in 597 and established a monastery at Canterbury. From this center the conversion of the island was effected gradually. 

It is probable that the doctrine as to pious uses-charitable trusts was transferred from the civil law into the jurisprudence of England' as a result of the efforts of the Church.2 By concerning itself with more than the spiritual affairs of men, the Church accumulated great wealth during early English history. 

1. White v. White (1778), 1 Bro. C. 

C. 12; Moggridge v. Thackwell (1803), 7 Ves. Jr. 36, 69; Blackstone, vol. 2, page 327. 

2. See page 9 of chapter 1.

§ 192] 339 

CHARITABLE TRUSTS 

This wealth was represented to a large extent by land donated to the Church for various purposes.3 

The feudal barons became jealous of the wealth of the Church; there was no system of taxation like that of modern times, and the feudal barons were compelled to depend for taxes on such feudal dues as aids, relief, wardship and marriage, fines on alienation, forfeiture, and escheat.4 Lands held by the Church or monasteries were held in perpetuity and produced no such dues for the feudal lords. Lands thus held were held in mortmain, or by the dead hand of the Church.5

As a result of the desire of the feudal barons to prevent further conveyances of land to ecclesiastical corporations for pious uses, these barons forced King John at Runnymede, on June 15, 1266, to include in the Great Charter a provision that there should be no transfer of land to church corporations by a tenant without the approval of his lord. The ecclesiastics soon began to evade this provision of Magna Charta by causing lands to be conveyed directly to the ecclesiastics "for the use" of the Church or religious corporations. This situation led to the enactment by Parliament, in 1279, of the earliest complete statute of mortmain, known as the Statute de Religiosis. 

3. "In England, until the Reformation, and more particularly until the reign of Edward VI, pious and charitable gifts were not confined to aiding schools, churches, or living persons, but extended to masses, prayers, perpetual obits, and lights for the souls of the founders, their families and friends; but by force of statutes enacted in that reign and later, gifts for the latter purpose were abolished in England and became known as 'superstitious uses."" 11 C. J. 322.

Edward VI was king of England from 

1547 to 1553.

In Georgia, where religious tolerance is the rule, no restrictions as to religious beliefs are placed on charitable donations for religious or pious purposes. Therefore, a donation to any religious sect for any purpose or ceremonial, the efficacy of which is recognized by the members of such sect, will be upheld in Georgia unless such donation contravenes an express provision of law, or "is for a purpose forbidden by public policy."

This system of land tenure, devised by the ecclesiastics to evade the mortmain statutes by having land conveyed to some person "for the use" of the church corporations, 10 gradually evolved into general use not only by the ecclesiastics, but also by the laymen in their transactions pertaining to land. Under this system, the owner conveyed the legal title to some person or corporation for the benefit of the usee in whom the equitable title vested. The usee could be such owner himself." The owner of the legal title had nothing which he could enjoy. The cestui que use held the use or beneficial title to the land, which was the only valuable feature of it; the usee could convey this equitable title, either orally or in writing, publicly or secretly, by deed or by will, and could otherwise deal with his equitable estate as with any other tangible property. Thus, under this system, there were two titles or estates in the same land; the legal title or estate was vested in one person, and the equitable title or estate was vested in another. "By this course of putting lands into uses there were many inconveniences, as this use, which grew first from a reasonable cause, namely, to give men the power and liberty to dispose of their own, was turned to deceive many of their just and reasonable rights, as, namely, a man that had cause to sue for his land knew not against whom to bring his action nor who was the owner of it. The wife was defrauded of her thirds, the husband of being tenant by curtesy, the lord of his wardship, relief, heriot, and escheat, the creditor of his extent for debt, the poor tenant of his lease; for these rights and duties were given by law from him that was owner of the land, and none other, which was now the feoffee of the trust."12 "As various evasions of this statute were devised by the ecclesiastics, further acts were passed to defeat them, namely, 13 Edw. I cc 32, 33; 18 Edw. 

III c 3; 15 Rich. II c 5, which statutes imposed forfeiture of the lands on all direct or indirect gifts of lands to or for religious houses, and extended the law to guilds, fraternities, and municipal corporations." 11 C. J.

CHARITABLE TRUSTS 

Many statutes were passed between the passage of the first complete mortmain statute in 1279 and the enactment of the Statute of Uses in 1535, to cure or to prevent the hardships and evils caused by this system of land tenure. Finally, Parliament, in the reign of Henry VIII, enacted the famous Statute of Uses, 13 which annexed the legal title and the possession to the use, thereby making the use the very land itself. Thus, the beneficial use was converted into a legal estate; the statute executed the use, or converted it into lawful seizin and possession in the usee, thereby vesting both the legal and the equitable title in the usee and making him the complete owner in law and in equity.' 14 The Statute of Uses was enacted in hostility to all uses¹5 and was intended to destroy them altogether.16 The harshness of this statute in its purpose to strike down all trusts, including all donations to charitable purposes, religious or educational, resulted largely from the struggle of Henry VIII against the supremacy of the Pope. However, the charitable sentiments which Christianity inculcates were so prevalent, even at that time, that Parliament, soon after passing the Statute of Uses, began the enactment of statutes favorable to schools, colleges, universities, and hospitals, and for the relief of the poor.17 This legislation as to charitable purposes culminated in a statute enacted in 1601, in the fortythird year of the reign of Queen Elizabeth, 18 known as the Statute of Charitable Uses. This statute repealed all mortmain statutes 

13. Statutes of the Realm, vol. 3, pages 539-542; Blackstone, vol. 2, pages 332 and 375. "Many statutes were passed during a series of years to cure or to prevent these mischiefs or hardships. At last the statutes of uses, 27 Hen. VIII. c. 10, was enacted, which converted the beneficial use into the legal ownership; that is to say, if lands were conveyed to A. to the use of B., the statute executed or converted the use into a legal estate in B., and divested all title out of A. By the operation of this statute the Court of Chancery lost for a time much of its business; for after the statute the legal title as well as the beneficial use was in the cestui que use, and he could deal with his estate as his own in every respect; he was no longer compelled to appeal to the conscience of the feoffee to uses, nor to the equity powers of the court." Perry on Trusts, 7th ed., vol. 1, sec. 5.

§ 193.-Nature of Charitable Uses or Trusts.-Donations to be held for charitable purposes are usually called charitable or public trusts. Such trusts are created for the general benefit of an indefinite number of persons constituting the public at large or a portion thereof.22 

There are at least two important distinctions between private trusts and charitable trusts. In the first place, the beneficiary of a private trust must be some particular person23 who is designated in the trust instrument with sufficient certainty to be capable of ascertainment;24 such person then takes a vested equitable title into which the legal title, held by the trustee, merges when the disability which made the creation of the trust necessary has been removed. In a public or charitable trust, the legal title is vested in a trustee25 for the benefit of an uncertain and usually a fluctuatpurposes to which the property or income of such trust shall be applied; and no such gift, grant, devise or bequest, accompanied by such power of selection, shall be void because of uncertainty or indefiniteness." Code 108-209. "All gifts to the United States or to any State or to any subdivision thereof for any public purpose, shall be charitable." Code 108-210. "Sections 108-207 to 108-210, inclusive, shall affect and apply to all instruments created by will, deed or otherwise which may come into effect after the approval of said sections, and the same shall be applicable to any such instrument now in effect if the instrument contains the power in the trustee or trustees or other persons to designate the kind of charity to which the gift, grant, devise, or bequest shall be applied." Code 108-211.

"The rules governing the establishment and administration of charitable trusts are different from those applicable to private trusts, in giving effect to the intention of the donor and in establishing the charity. In private trusts, if the cestuis que trust are so uncertain or so incapable of taking, that they can not be identified or can not by legal or equitable proceedings claim the benefit conferred on them, the gift will fail and revert to the donor or his heirs. But if a gift is made for a public charitable purpose, it is immaterial that the trustee is uncertain or incapable of taking, or that the objects of the charity are uncertain and indefinite. It will, nevertheless, be sustained. Courts look with special favor upon such trusts."

§ 196. Statutory Restrictions on Right to Create Charitable Trusts. 

-Experience has taught that it is best to curtail to some extent the right to make charitable donations. People generally may not be so charitably inclined as to indulge in charitable donations to the extent that legislative restriction is necessary for the protection of their heirs ;47 yet, in order to give protection in all cases, the codifiers of our first Code48 deemed it wise to regulate charitable donations to the extent that certain heirs49 may not be deprived of all their rights of inheritance by charitable bequests and devises. The curtailment of the right to make donations to charitable purposes, like other rules of law, is the outgrowth of long years of experience.

One of the earliest forms of charitable donations consisted of gifts of land to monasteries and other religious institutions.50 As such gifts were held in perpetuity, the overlords were prevented from receiving the feudal benefits from the land held by such religious institutions.51 In order to prohibit gifts of land to the 

Church or to charitable institutions, as well as to temporal corporations, Parliament in 1279 enacted the first complete Statute of Mortmain.52 The ecclesiastics then invented the doctrine of

54. Superstitious Uses. "In England, until the Reformation, and more particularly until the reign of Edward VI, pious and charitable gifts were not confined to aiding schools, churches, or living persons, but extended to masses, prayers, perpetual obits, and lights for the souls of the founders, their families and friends; but by force of statutes enacted in that reign and later, gifts for the latter purpose were abolished in England and became known as 'superstitious uses.'" 11 C. 

J. 322.

In Georgia, where religious tolerance is the rule, no restrictions are placed on charitable donations for religious or pious purposes except for those which are immoral in their tendency or contrary to public policy. Therefore, a donation to any religious sect for any purpose or ceremonial, the efficacy of which is recognized by the members of such sect, will be upheld in Georgia unless such donation is for the furtherance of "doctrines licentious in their tendency, or inconsistent with the peace and safety of the State."

the charitable bequest or devise is void for uncertainty or other cause, the intention of the testator can not be effectuated by the doctrine of cy pres,69 but, if there is a charitable intention manifested by the testator which can not be effectuated in the exact mode indicated by the testator, or if the mode indicated by him should. become impossible by subsequent circumstances, equity will carry out his purpose, by approximation, in a manner similar to the method indicated by him.70 

As the intention of the testator controls, he may provide for the revocation or termination of a charitable donation after the lapse of a period of time, or he may provide that the donation shall vest in another donee upon mis-user or non-user by the first donee. Where no such provisions are made, and the charitable donation is a complete gift, the estate of the testator is completely divested of the title when the will goes into effect. Although a charitable trust may be created in perpetuity, experience has taught that the continual change in the course of human events ultimately may make impossible the manner of continuing the charity as prescribed by the testator. Then, the doctrine of cy pres comes to the rescue and continues the charity in a "manner next most consonant" with the intention of the testator. Where there occurs an entire failure of object or purpose for which the charity was created, the doctrine of cy pres does not apply, and the gift becomes void and reverts to the estate of the testator.71

[Ch. 15 § 199.-Jurisdiction-Construction.-In Georgia, equity has juris diction to carry into effect and supervise the charitable bequests and devises of a testator.72 The Statute of 43 Elizabeth,73 known as the Statute of Charitable Uses, defined what were the subjects of charity, but the jurisdiction of the English courts of chancery over charitable trusts did not arise by reason of this statute, as such jurisdiction had existed long prior thereto.74 Our courts of equity likewise have inherent jurisdiction over charitable trusts independent of statute,75 but this jurisdiction is conferred on them by statute also.76

In Georgia the terms of a will can be construed only in a court of equity.77

Consequently, when a testator creates a charitable trust, if it becomes necessary to construe the terms of the will pertaining to such trust or to supervise the same in any manner, application for such construction or supervision must be made to equity. When the will is construed, if it should be determined that the charitable donations therein were invalid for any reason, this fact would not destroy the whole will.79 The administration of the estate should continue according to the terms of the will, except that the void charitable devises or bequests should be administered according to the rules of testate administration.80 § 200.-Pleadings-Evidence.-Whenever it becomes necessary to appeal to equity to carry into effect a charitable bequest or devise, to supervise the same in any manner, to appoint a trustee, or to construe any of the terms or conditions of such donation, an equitable petition may be filed by one or more of the beneficiaries. If the construction of the terms of the will may involve the destruction of the charity, service should be made on the legatees or devisees or heirs at law who would benefit by such construction in order that they may be heard. However, a case like this will seldom arise; for, where the destruction of a charity is involved, those who would benefit by such termination usually will be found as the petitioners. If a beneficiary desires for any reason to bring the petition against the trustees of the charitable trust, such trustees are the proper parties defendant, and service should be made on them.82

In construing the terms of a will, the court may admit parol or other extrinsic evidence to explain ambiguities and uncertainties, but such evidence is not admissible for the purpose of varying the terms of the will or for the purpose of adding to it any provisions.83 The intentions of the testator govern and not the wishes

§ 202.-Administration of Charitable Trusts.-The administration of a charity does not begin until the executor has surrendered the charitable bequest or devise to the trustee. In the administration of the testator's estate, charitable bequests and devises are subject to abatement and to other administrative burdens in the same manner as other legacies and devises. When the trust property is surrendered to the trustee, his administration of it begins. If there is uncertainty as to the manner in which the trust is to be effectuated, the trustee should apply to equity for direction.93 95 It is the duty of trustees of private trusts to make an inventory94 of the trust property in their hands and file such inventory with the ordinary within three months after receiving it; they are also required to make annual and final returns to the ordinary.⁹ 

Trustees of charitable trusts are not required to make such inventory or returns,96 but like other trustees', their acts are subject to equitable supervision at any time. Such trustees may also apply to equity for instructions whenever they deem it necessary.97 § 203.-Taxation.-As a general rule, trust property, like all other property, is liable for taxes legally imposed upon it.98 However, under our Code,99 "all institutions of purely public charity" the legislature cannot confer such power on it; all that is meant is that it has not heretofore so done." 212. Testamentary Guardians. § 204. Generally.-"Testamentary powers" is a term broad enough to cover any act that a testator might do himself or any authority he might delegate to others. This expression is ordinarily used in the latter sense, and it will be so considered briefly in this chapter. When the meaning is thus narrowed, a testamentary power may be defined as an authority conferred by will upon one or more persons to perform certain acts after the testator's death. The person exercising the power acts, not by virtue of any title conveyed, but as a result of the power contained in the will. 1 A power is distinct from an estate,2 although it may be coupled with an interest in the property bequeathed or devised, as in case of a gift to the tenant for life with power of appointment or disposition of the fee. In such case, the fee does not vest in the tenant for life, but a legal exercise of the power by him will convey the fee to the purchaser.3 A power may be vested in a person to whom

S. E. 630; Beecher v. Newton (1923), 157 Ga. 113, 120 S. E. 779.

an interest in the realty or personalty is given, or it may be vested in a person who holds no interest in the estate conveyed. In the former case the power is coupled with an interest; in the latter it is not. In either case, the person to whom the power is granted may exercise it. 

§ 205.-Kinds of Testamentary Powers.-Testamentary powers may be classified as general or special. A power is general when the donee is given the privilege of exercising the power in favor of any person for any purpose satisfactory to himself. No condition or restriction is attached to the power either as to the estate which may be conveyed or as to the persons in whose favor the donee of the power may exercise it. A power is special if it can be exercised by the donee only for the benefit of particular persons or if it can be exercised only for some designated purpose. In other words, there is some condition or restriction attached to the power by which the donee must be governed in order to exercise the power legally. (1923), 156 Ga. 323, 118 S. E. 865; Newton v. Bullard (1935), 181 Ga. 448, 182

S. E. 614. 

"When by the terms of a will real and personal property is given to the wife for life with remainder to the children of the testator, a power conferred on the executrix, who was the wife of the testator, to sell any or all of the property devised and reinvest the proceeds, expressed in language which plainly and unequivocally limits the purpose for which any sale can be made to that of reinvestment only, does not, notwithstanding the will may contain broad and liberal provisions as to the manner in which this power may be exercised, empower the executrix to mortgage the property devised, nor to convey the title of such property as security for a debt created by her." McMillan v. Cox (1899), 109 Ga. 42 (1), 34 S. E. 341. 

4. "Power coupled with an interest" means that the donee is possessed of the legal estate or of a right therein.

369, 391, 21 S. E. 837. In order that a power may be a power coupled with an interest, the donee must have an interest derived from the power or from something else in the property or thing in reference to which the power was given. General powers, in the sense used above, are rare, for seldom does a testator see fit to donate to some other person the privilege of disposing of property without any restrictions or conditions. 

Occasionally, a case arises where the testator has granted a life estate with general power of disposition on the part of the life tenant.7 

§ 206.-Creation and Exercise of Powers.-At common law, if a life tenant attempted to convey the fee without express power of sale, he forfeited his life estate. The rule in Georgia is that any attempt on the part of the life tenant to convey the fee without the power to do so conveys only his life interest. If a power of sale is given to the life tenant without stipulation as to what interest he may convey under the power, such power will be construed to extend to a disposition of the fee unless, expressly or by necessary implication, it is limited to a smaller estate. A special power must be exercised by the donee according to the conditions prescribed by the testator, or the attempt to exercise the power will be invalid, at least so far as it departs from the terms of the power. The cardinal rule of construction that the intention of the testator, if legal, is to control applies in determining whether a power has been created or not by the will." A power of sale, whether general or special, is to be strictly construed and must be fairly exercised.14 The power is to be exercised in accordance with the testator's wishes. Thus, a special power given by the testator to "A" to sell certain property and apply the proceeds to a designated purpose would not be legally exercised if "A" conveyed a life estate to "B" with power to dispose of the fee for the purpose named by the testator.15 The donee of a special testamentary power can not confer the power upon his heirs or assigns in the absence of an expressed intention to that effect in the will.16 A donee of a general power may delegate the power, as such power is tantamount to ownership.17

Three executors were nominated and qualified. They sold and conveyed a lot of wild land. The ordinary of the county did not join in the conveyance, nor did it appear that he assented to the sale. Held: (a) A power conferred on a person who, at the time of the exercise of the power, may hold a particular office attaches to the individual filling the office, and not to the office. (b) The concurrence of the ordinary was necessary for the proper exercise of this power. (c) The subsequent passing by the ordinary of an order empowering the executors to sell the wild land of the testator at their discretion is not a ratification of the prior sale of a particular lot of wild land by the executors." Rowe v.

“‘And as a general disposition of the very property will amount to an execution of the power, so where there are several powers in one person over different estates, a like disposition of them all will operate as an execution of all the powers. 1 “‘If a man have two general powers over the same estate, with different circumstances, and do an act without referring to the powers which may be valid as an exercise of one of them, it will be deemed an execution of that power which will support the disposition.' 1 Sugden on Powers, side pages 356, 357. "'Where, however, the power is not referred to, the property comprised in it must be mentioned, so as to manifest that the disposition was intended to operate over it; the donee must do such an act as shows that he has in view the thing of which he had a power to dispose.' Id. 367. "C 'Upon these distinctions it has been held that, where otherwise part of the disposition would be void and the words remain unsatisfied, the words, if specific in their nature, will apply to the real estate in the power. Therefore, if the subject of the power be real estate, and the donee make a general devise of all his real and personal estate, and has no real estate, the estate subject to his appointment will pass, for the gift as to the real estate is specific, and as there is no other subject for it to attach upon, it must refer to that over which the testator has a power.' Id. 377. ""The power may be executed without reciting it, provided the act shows that the donee had in view the subject of the power. . . 

The general rule of construction, both as to deeds and wills, is, that if there be an interest and power existing together in the same person, over the same subject, and an act be done without a particular reference to the power, it will be applied to the interest and not to the power. If there be any legal interest on which the deed can attach, it will not execute a power. If an act will work two ways, the one by an interest, and the other by a power, and the act be indifferent, the law will attribute it to the interest and not to the authority, for fictio cedit veritati.' 4 Kent's Com., side pp. 234, 235. ""The donee of a power may execute it without expressly referring to it, or taking any notice of it, provided that it is apparent from the whole instrument that it was intended as an execution of the power. The execution of the power, however, must show that it was intended to be such execution; for if it is uncertain whether

[Ch. 16 

the act was intended to be an execution of the power, it will not be construed as an execution. The intention to execute a power will sufficiently appear-(1) when there is some reference to the power in the instrument of execution; (2) where there is a reference to the property which is the subject-matter on which execution of the power is to operate; and (3) where the instrument of execution would have no operation, but would be utterly insensible and absurd, if it was not the execution of a power. Thus, if a donee of a power to sell land have also an interest in his own right in the same. land, his deed of the land, making no reference to the power, will convey his own interest; for there is a subject-matter for the deed to operate upon, excluding the power, and, therefore, as it does not conclusively appear that the deed was intended to be an execution of the power as well as a conveyance of the grantor's interest in the land, it will be held not to be an execution of the power; but if the grantor has no interest in the land, his deed will be insensible and a mere absurdity, if not intended as an execution of the power; therefore, it will be held to be an execution of the power, if it refers to the subject-matter of the power, or describes the land over which his power extends. It will be seen that this last conclusion is a presumption of law; this presumption may be more or less strong, according to all the circumstances of the case and the condition of the property. If all the words of a deed or will can have an effect given to them, and an operation upon property or rights, without being taken as the execution of a power, they will not be an execution of such power. If a man has several powers, and refers to some and not to others, the execution will exclude those not referred to. From these propositions it may be seen why a conveyance of specific property, or a specific devise of property, will generally operate as the execution of a power, if the grantor or testator has no other interest in the property but the power, although he makes no reference to the owner in his deed or will.' § 213.—Kinds of Gifts.-The word gift' is sufficiently broad to cover every legacy or devise, for the usual consideration which moves a testator to remember others with his bounty is the approbation of his own conscience or the expected appreciation of the intended beneficiaries. However, by custom and by statute the word gift has been given a restricted meaning, so that it now signifies a transaction between the donor and the donee in which a delivery of the subject matter of the gift takes place during the lifetime of the donor. Thus considered, gifts may be either causa mortis² or inter vivos.³ Neither kind of gift is valid against the just claims of creditors, as the law requires every person to be just before it permits him to be generous.4 

A gift inter vivos may relate to any kind of realty or personalty, 1. 28 C. J. 621. 

2. Donatio causa mortis: Gift in contemplation of death. 

3. Donatio inter vivos: Gift between the living. 

4. Blackstone, vol. 2, page 512;

(1891), 109 Mo. 90, 18 S. W. 1139. "An insolvent person may not make a valid gift to the injury of his existing creditors; and where possession, partial or entire, shall remain with the donor, every parol gift shall be void against bona fide creditors and purchasers without notice." Code 48-110. 

5. "To constitute a valid parol gift of land it is necessary not only that the donee should take possession under the gift, but that he should make valuable improvements thereon upon the faith of the donor's promise, or declared intention, to make the gift.

Valuable improvements made and paid for by the donor, even though made by him for the benefit of the donee, or in the nature of a gift to the donee, can not be regarded as improvements made by the donee." Hodgson v. Hodgson (1922), 28 Ga. App. 250, 110 S. E. 754 (1).

[Ch. 17 

while a gift causa mortis can dispose of no property except personalty. A gift inter vivos operates immediately and irrevocably, while a gift causa mortis operates only in the event of death, the prospect of which causes the gift to be made; in both, a change of possession takes place immediately. As possession is acquired through the donor and not through his personal representative, either form of gift is of higher rank than general or special legacies or devises. 

Consequently, such gifts would not abate until all the other assets of the estate had been consumed in the payment of debts, and a gift inter vivos would not abate at all if it were made prior to the creation of the indebtedness which made abatement necessary. A gift causa mortis can not destroy the marital rights of the widow in the personal estate.7 § 214.-Gifts Causa Mortis.-A donatio causa mortis is an unrevoked gift of personal property made in contemplation of death resulting from illness or peril which is then existing and to which the donor is subject, and with the intention that, if the donor does not die of that particular illness or peril, the title shall revert to him; such gift must be consummated by actual or constructive delivery. In some respects a gift causa mortis is similar to a nuncupative will: Both are revocable during the life of the donor or testator; both are completed only by death, for, if the person making either recovers from the illness or peril then existing, it is void; both are made in contemplation of death, which at the time appears to be imminent; and both are proved by the words and acts of the donor or testator by the witnesses present at the time the transaction takes place. "In order to constitute a valid gift of personalty made by one in view of impending dissolution, it is not necessary that there should be a delivery of the property to the donee personally; but such delivery may be effected and the gift rendered valid by a delivery to a third person in trust and for the benefit of the donee." Dominion acquired by the donee after the death of the donor is not sufficient;16 dominion acquired before the donor makes the gift is sufficient; and in such case no further act of delivery is necessary if such dominion is affirmed by the donor by words or acts showing an intention to give.17 Such a gift would take effect, not from the time the dominion was acquired, but from the time the intent to give was expressed. 

Delivery need not be actual in order to complete a gift causa mortis; it may be symbolical. Thus a delivery of a key to a receptacle, not readily accessible, in which is stored the subject matter of the gift is a sufficient delivery if the key is delivered with an intent to make a gift. If the receptacle is readily accessible, like a trunk, bureau, or chest in the same room or house with the donor, the property should be delivered manually, if not too bulky or cumbersome, as an extra precaution; for delivery should be the best possible delivery under the circumstances. 18 Regardless of whether the delivery is actual or symbolical, our Code requires that a gift causa mortis be proved by at least one witness. 19

As such a gift is not complete until the death of the donor, he may revoke it at any time before his reasoning faculties25 forsake him, although the article given has actually been now well established that all things in action which consist of the promises or undertakings of third persons, not the donor himself, of which the legal or equitable title can pass by delivery, may be the subject of a valid gift, including promissory notes, bills of exchange, checks, bonds, mortgages, saving banks' pass-books, certificates of deposit and the like; and it is settled that a valid donation of negotiable instruments may thus be made without endorsement." If the donor should make a will after he had made the gift and if the will contained provisions contrary to the terms of the gift, this would indicate a change of intention on the part of the donor and properly should be termed an implied revocation of the gift.26 27 It is considered by some authorities that the death of the donee prior to the death of the donor also revokes a gift causa mortis.2 

It is true that the title does not vest and that the gift does not become complete in the donee until the death of the donor; the same is true as to wills, as title does not pass until the death of the testator. Yet under our Code28 a legacy or devise will not lapse if the legatee or devisee dies before the testator, leaving issue living at the death of the testator. This same rule would apply, in all probability, to gifts causa mortis where the donee, after acquiring possession of the thing given, died prior to the death of the donor, leaving issue who are living at the death of the donor. As a will is revoked by the birth of a child to the testator after the will has been executed,29 for which child no provision has been made in the will, and as a gift causa mortis is in some respects similar to a nuncupative will, doubtless a gift causa mortis would be revoked under the same circumstances. 30 § 218.-Impossible and Illegal Gifts.-If a gift fails from any cause and becomes impossible of accomplishment, it is, in a sense, a revoked gift. Evidence of any circumstances connected with the alleged gift is admissible to prove or disprove the essential elements of the gift. Motive of the donor in making the alleged gift may be proved in order to show the intention to make a gift. The opinion of a witness that a certain transaction constituted a gift would not be admissible, as whether or not the facts prove a gift is a question of law.40 Declarations of the donor made before or after the alleged gift are admissible as corroborative evidence of the gift,41 but the bare declarations of the donor alone are not sufficient, as delivery and acceptance must be shown.42 

Gifts causa mortis were recognized in the civil law and at common law. Doubtless, there was more necessity for their existence in those ancient days than at present, when learning is more nearly universal. If a man has sufficient personal estate to be of interest to him, he should not wait to make provisions for its post-mortem disposition until an exigency arises which compels him to make a gift causa mortis. At best, evidence of such gift is unsatisfactory and may lead to dissatisfaction among the parties interested in the estate. Gifts causa mortis should be prohibited by law, in this enlightened age, except as to jewelry, wearing apparel, pictures, and other such personal effects. 

§ 221.-Fraud, Undue Influence, and Mental Capacity.-In order that any gift may be valid, it must result from the free and voluntary act of a person mentally capable of comprehending the transaction. § 223. Generally. It is the policy of all civilized nations to permit the owner of an estate to give direction as to its disposition after his death; if such owner fails to make a will giving such direction, his estate will be distributed in the manner prescribed by the statutes of distribution. In order to distribute the estate according to the wishes of the deceased, or according to the terms of the law, when he has not legally expressed his wishes, it is necessary to appoint someone to represent him. This person is called the personal or legal representative. If he is acting under a will, he is called an executor; otherwise he is an administrator. The provisions of our Code¹ referring to the powers, duties, and lia-

bilities of administrators apply to executors also. Therefore, in discussing the administration of estates, it will be unnecessary to consider executors and administrators separately unless the subject matter in particular instances requires it. 

§ 224.-Temporary Administrators.-A temporary administrator is one appointed on an unrepresented estate for the purpose of collecting and taking care of the effects of the deceased until permanent letters are granted. He may be appointed without notice to anyone, and, unless removed from office,4 he continues to act until a permanent administrator has been qualified. When a temporary administrator has charge of an estate and an appeal is taken from the appointment of a permanent administrator, the temporary administrator continues as representative of the estate pending the appeal.5

Before the temporary administrator is qualified to act, he must give bond with good security, to be approved by the ordinary, in a sum at least double the value of the personal property of the estate. The temporary administrator and the sureties on his bond. are liable to the permanent administrator for any waste or misand liabilities, the mode of effecting sales, of making and receiving titles to property sold or purchased by their intestates, of investing the funds, of obtaining letters of dismission, of resigning their trusts, of removing proceedings to the county of their residence, of compelling settlements before the ordinary, of returns by representatives of deceased administrators, and in all other matters in their nature applicable to executors, shall be held and taken to apply to and include executors, to the same extent as if they were named therein." § 226.-Administrators de Bonis Non.-An administrator de bonis non28 is one appointed to complete the administration of an estate which has been partly administered but is unrepresented from any cause.29 Every administrator after the first is an administrator de bonis non.30 If the deceased died testate but no executor appears to qualify, letters of administration with the will annexed must be granted.31 If the person so appointed should be removed from his trust for any cause, the administrator appointed to take his place is called an administrator de bonis non cum testamento annexo.32 A testator may appoint a minor as his executor,33 but such minor can not qualify until he arrives at majority unless the will especially provides that he may do so. If no such provision is made, letters of administration with the will annexed may be granted to someone to represent the estate until such minor arrives at majority.34

389 Administrators de bonis non and administrators with the will annexed are appointed according to the rules for the appointment of administrators generally.35 The office must be vacant at the time of the appointment for the appointment to be valid.36 If the administrator is removed from his trust, it is necessary that the order of removal be granted before the order appointing his successor, as no vacancy occurs in such case until the order of removal is granted.37 An administrator who has been adjudged insane is disqualified further to act as such administrator, and the estate is left unrepresented.  § 230.-Executors de Son Tort.60-Under the provisions of our 

Codes "if any person, without authority of law, wrongfully intermeddles with,62 or converts to his own use, the personalty of a deceased individual whose estate has no legal representative, he shall be held and deemed an executor in his own wrong, and as such shall be liable to the creditors and heirs or legatees of such estate for double the values of the property so possessed or converted by him; nor shall such executor be allowed to set off any debt due to him by the deceased, or voluntarily paid64 by him out of the assets. If such executor dies, his legal representatives shall be liable in the same manner, and to the same extent, as he would be if he were still living."

At common law a person was considered an executor de son tort whenever he intermeddled with the goods of the deceased, without lawful authority, whether there was a duly qualified legal representative or not. Since the adoption of our Code, no person can

The statute vests the right to sue in the heirs and creditors, in the event there is no legal representative of the estate."

§ 231.-Foreign Executors and Administrators.—As a general rule, only citizens of the United States domiciled in Georgia are qualified to act as executors and administrators in this state.73 The only exception to this rule arises where a non-resident has an “equal, greater, or sole interest" in the estate of a deceased citizen of Georgia ;74 and, even then, such non-resident executor or administrator must give bond for double the value of the estate in Georgia, payable to the ordinary of the county where the administration was granted, with sureties resident in this state.75 The courts of ordinary have no authority to appoint a non-resident as administrator of an estate of a non-resident of Georgia, although such non-resident left assets in this state.76

§ 235.—Application for Appointment. Our Code120 requires that every application for letters of administration or for letters testamentary be made to the court of ordinary121 of the county of the domicile of the deceased.122 If the deceased is a non-resident, the application may be made in any county where the estate or some portion of it is located.123 

Under our law no particular time is fixed during which the application must be filed.124 In the interest of efficiency, application for appointment should be made promptly after the death of the testate or intestate, and the estate should be administered as quickly as is consistent with the circumstances. The sureties on the bond of an administrator or an executor bind themselves only to see that their principal faithfully performs his duty as required by law. 167 If he fails in the performance of this duty, creditors, heirs, legatees, devisees, or in some cases all of them, suffer financial loss as a result thereof. In order to obtain redress for their wrong, they may sue such personal representative alone, or they may sue him and one or more of the sureties in the same action; they may sue also one or more of the sureties in the first instance "if the administrator is beyond the jurisdiction of this State, or is dead, and his estate unrepresented, or is in such position that an attachment may be issued against him."168 

Prior to the Act of December 13, 1820,169 before suit could be instituted against the sureties on the bond of an administrator or an executor, it was necessary first to sue the administrator or the executor in his representative capacity and exhaust all the assets of the estate, and second, to sue him individually and exhaust all of his individual assets. When this had been done, suit could then be instituted against the sureties on the bond, thus making three actions necessary to reach the sureties. 170 This Act of 1820, in the interest of justice and efficiency, evidently had for its purpose the abolishment of the rule requiring the first two suits above mentioned to be instituted so that the administrator or the executor and his sureties could be sued in the first instance in the same action. However, our supreme court held that this act was intended to save only the first suit;171 that it was not permissible to join the sureties in the first action against the administrator in his representative capacity, representative in the first instance, and may recover judgment against the principal and his sureties without first suing the executor or administrator in his representative character."

Some of these differences will be noted briefly.216 

This act modifies the rule as to unregistered lands that, when an owner of lands in Georgia dies intestate, the title vests immediately in the heirs at law. Under this act, the title vests in the representative of the estate, whether the owner dies testate or intestate.217

In the event it becomes necessary for the representative of the estate to sell registered lands for the payment of debts or for distribution, he is permitted under this act to make such sale under the same rules under which personalty is sold. This dispenses with the preliminary advertisement for leave to sell and the order granting leave to sell required by our Code218 for the sale of unregistered lands.219

As hereinafter shown in this volume,220 an administrator can not sell unregistered lands while they are held adversely; he must first recover possession. This rule is abolished as to registered lands, "since none of the legal incidents of adverse possession affect registered lands.”221

Two very wholesome changes made by the Land Registration Act are: 1. "All questions as to the legality of the sale made by an executor or administrator, as the same may be, shall be settled at once and for all time, and shall not remain open to haunt the title like spectres throughout the future." 2. Where an estate is distributed without administration, descent and heirship can be established by a binding adjudication in advance as to who are the heirs of any decedent from whom registered lands descend.222

§ 250.-Compensation of Executors and Administrators.—It will be noticed from the preceding section that expenses of administration rank third in the order of payment of the legal charges of an estate. Our Code 50 provides that the commissions of executors and administrators are part of the necessary expenses of administration. For this reason, no claims against the estate, not even taxes, are superior to the right of the representative to compensation, except year's support and funeral expenses. The amount of compensation allowed is two and one-half per cent on all money received and a like commission on all sums paid out whether to creditors, legatees, or distributees.51 No commission is allowed (1847), 2 Ga. 370 (4); Nisbet v. § 251.-Release, Compromise, and Arbitration of Claims.—An exec utor or an administrator is authorized by our Code67 to compromise all contested or doubtful68 claims for or against any estate that either may represent, to submit such claims to arbitration, and to release a debtor if it is to the interest of the estate to do so. 

Such acts, in order to be valid against the beneficiaries of an estate, must be effected in a legal manner.69 It would not be legal for an executor or an administrator to settle claims against an estate where such executor or administrator by fraud had procured such claims to be contested in order to compromise or settle them under apparent authority of the law.70 The claims must be bona fide against the estate before the executor or administrator may compromise them legally. Otherwise, an unscrupulous executor who was relieved by the will from giving bond might enter into a collusive agreement with other persons to file suits against the estate on fake claims which he would compromise for a share of the spoils, thus defrauding the beneficiaries of the estate. 

When a settlement of a claim is made by the representative, such settlement is conclusive until it is set aside in a direct proceeding instituted for that purpose, and the representative of the estate is a necessary party in such proceeding.7

Murray v. Hawkins (1915), 144 Ga. 

613, 87 S. E. 1068; Walton v. Reid (1918), 148 Ga. 176, 96 S. E. 214; 

Tinsley v. Maddox (1933), 1.76 Ga. 471, 168 S. E. 297, 302.

 § 252.-Continuing the Business of Deceased.-An administrator may exercise his discretion in continuing the business of the deceased72 until the expiration of the calendar year73 in which the intestate died; but he acts at his own peril if he continues the business, without an order of court, longer than the year in which the intestate died, and debts incurred by the administrator while unlawfully conducting the business of the deceased are his own individual liabilities.74 If it is necessary to continue the business of the deceased after the expiration of the calendar year, the administrator may make the necessary contracts for carrying on such business, but such contracts, in order to bind the estate, must be approved by the ordinary.75 If the business is to be carried on after the expiration of the calendar year, the representative of the estate should be careful to obtain an order from the court of ordinary to that effect; for as a general rule a representative of an estate may not contract debts for such estate.76

Truth is so consistent with herself that every technical rule which arbitrarily construes an act contrary to the real intent of the parties will cause a perpetual struggle to get away from the technicality to the fact; and such has been the history of the rule as to descriptio personae. A deed signed 'A, executor of B,' will convey the title of the estate. Where the maker of a note signs his name ‘executor,' 'administrator,' or 'trustee,' he can not relieve himself of his individual liability and impose the debt on the estate. § 258.-Time Within Which Suits Must Be Filed.-Prior to the 

Act of 1883125 the statute of limitations did not operate against the claims of an estate against debtors while the estate was unrepresented, provided such period of unrepresentation was not longer than five years, 126 but the statute was not suspended in behalf of creditors when the estate was unrepresented. By this act, the same rule was made applicable to creditors of an estate, so that now the statute of limitations does not operate against the claims of creditors when the estate is unrepresented, provided that such period of unrepresentation does not exceed five years. 127 After a

"After a partnership is dissolved by the death of one of its members, the acceptance by a creditor of a renewal note executed in the firm name by one of the survivors, and extending the time of payment fixed by the note renewed, discharges the individual liability of all the partners except the one who executes the renewal note, but does not discharge the partnership assets. These remain liable, in equity at least, for the payment of the debt. "If, after the dissolution of a partnership by the death of one of its members, a surviving partner in the name of the firm conveyed land which constituted a portion of the partnership assets, in part payment of a debt for which neither the firm nor its assets were liable, the creditor holding such debt took nothing by the deed except the individual interest in the land of the partner who executed the deed, and took that interest subject to the payment of the partnership debts, and subject also to any prior conveyance of the land by that partner of which the creditor had notice. "If, after the dissolution of a partnership composed of three members, by the death of one of them, one of the two survivors, with the consent of the other, assumed possession and control of the partnership assets for the purpose of applying the same to the partnership debts, he thereby became the liquidating surviving partner, and could, without any express assent of the cosurvivor, apply such assets to any bona fide debt to which they were subject, although such debt was not one intended to be provided for in the arrangement between the two survivors, and was in fact unknown to the cosurvivor when the arrangement was made." At common law the title to land conveyed to a partnership vested in the partners as tenants in common.161 This is the rule in Georgia now, except where land is purchased in the name of the partnership, with partnership funds, and is used for partnership purposes.162 In such a case the surviving partner may treat the land as personalty, in so far as the payment of debts is concerned, and, in equity, the real estate of the partnership is considered personal property to the extent necessary to pay debts.163 The title to the personal property of the partnership vests in the surviving partner for the payment of debts and for the purpose of making distribution.164

Under our Code, when all the debts of the partnership have been paid, the assets may be divided in kind, as far as possible, between the surviving partners and the representative of the deceased partner, "by three disinterested appraisers, chosen by the parties as arbitrators or appointed by the ordinary of the county where the survivors reside, either in term or vacation, on application of either party. § 263.-Removal of Administration to Another County.-When ever, from any change of residence or other cause, an administrator or an executor may desire to remove the jurisdiction of his trust from the court of ordinary of the county of the residence of the testator or intestate to that of his own residence, he may do so by complying with the following provisions of our Code:168 "1. By obtaining a copy of all the records of the ordinary relative to his trust, and causing the same to be recorded by the ordinary of the county of his residence. "2. By giving to the ordinary of his county new bond, with good security, for the discharge of his duty as administrator, in the same manner as if the administration were originally granted there. "3. By filing with the ordinary of the county having original jurisdiction a certificate, under the seal of the ordinary of the county to which the trust is to be removed, that the foregoing provisions have been complied with. "4. The ordinary having jurisdiction shall then pass an order transferring the trust to the ordinary of the other county. "5. Upon compliance with the provisions of this section the whole of said trust is thereby removed from the one county to the other so that every question growing out of or affecting said trust shall be heard and tried only in that county to which said trust has been removed."

The right of inheritance and the right to make a will are 

169. Code 113-1902.

[Ch. 19 

protected by the laws of the government under which they are enjoyed. Therefore, for these rights and for this protection in the enjoyment of them, it is just that an inheritance tax or an estate tax should be imposed on the transfer of the net estate to the beneficiaries. When a person becomes the beneficiary of assets which he has not earned by his own labors, as in the case of testate or intestate transmission, and has the benefit of all the machinery of the government for his protection in the use and enjoyment of such assets, it is right and fair that the estate should be taxed before the transfer is made.

The legislative acts establishing the state and federal estate taxes, commonly called inheritance taxes, are of recent statutory creation, and since their creation there has been little statutory repose with reference to these acts. The federal estate tax was first imposed by the Act of September 8, 1916. This act, with its amendments, was supplanted by the Revenue Act of 1918. Estate taxes were also imposed by the Revenue Act of 1921 and the Revenue Act of 1924. All of these acts have been repealed, subject, however, to saving provisions continuing them in force for the assessment and collection of taxes which had accrued prior to their repeal and the imposition and collection of penalties in relation thereto.172

The present federal estate tax was enacted on February 26, 1926. It is neither a property nor a legacy tax, but is a tax imposed upon the transfer of the net estate of every citizen dying after 

February 26, 1926, whether a resident or a non-resident of the

United States. 173 The tax does not attach to any particular legacy, devise, or distributive share,174 but attaches to the net estate of the deceased.

The personal representative of an estate subject to federal estate tax, within two months after the decedent's death, or within a like period after qualifying as such personal representative, must give written notice thereof to the collector of internal revenue in whose district the decedent had his domicile at the time of his death; or, if there was no such domicile in the United States, then to the collector of the district in which the gross estate of the decedent is situated. If such gross estate is situated in more than one district, notice must be given to the collector of internal revenue of such district as may be designated by the commissioner of internal revenue. The personal representative must also file with the collector of internal revenue, at such times and in such manner as may be required by regulations made pursuant to law, a return under oath in duplicate, setting forth the value of the gross estate of the decedent at the time of his death, or in case of a non-resident, of that part of his gross estate situated in the United States, as well as such other supplemental data as may be necessary to establish the correct tax.

The tax is due and payable fifteen months after the decedent's death and should be paid by the personal representative to the collector of internal revenue of the district in which the administration is pending. The commissioner of internal revenue may extend the time for payment of any part of the tax, not to exceed ten years from due date, in the event he finds that the payment on the due date would impose undue hardship upon the estate. Any amount so extended bears interest at the rate of four per centum per annum from the expiration of six months after the due date of the tax, to the expiration of the period of the extension. 180 The tax is a lien for ten years on the gross estate of the decedent, unless it is paid, except that any part of the estate used in paying legal charges against the estate and costs and expenses of administration is discharged of such lien. 181
