§ 265.—Same-Georgia Estate Taxes.-At the regular session of the Legislature of Georgia in 1913 an inheritance tax act was enacted183 which provided for a tax upon the right to receive property transmitted to one by devise or inheritance or by deed, grant, or gift intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment after the death of the grantor or donor. This was strictly an inheritance tax act and was based on the theory exactly opposite from our present federal estate tax act. This inheritance tax act did not provide for a tax on the estate, but was a tax on the right to receive property by devise or inheritance, or by deed, grant, or gift intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment after the death of the grantor or donor. It was, therefore, a tax on the beneficiary rather than on the estate of the deceased. This inheritance tax act has been repealed.

The Congress of the United States on February 26, 1926, enacted the present estate tax act, section three hundred one (b) of which reads as follows: "The tax imposed by this section shall be credited with the amount of any estate, inheritance, legacy or succession taxes actually paid to any state or territory or the District of Columbia, in respect to any property included in the gross estate. 

The credit allowed by this subdivision shall not exceed 80 per centum of the tax imposed by this section, and shall include only such taxes as were actually paid and credit therefor claimed within three years after the filing of the return required by section 304,"184 The effect of this act of Congress was to return eighty per centum of the basic estate tax185 collected to each state having es-

§ 266.-Sales by Executors.-An executor may derive his authority to make a sale either from an order of court or from the will under which he is acting as executor. A testator has the right to designate in his will the time, place, manner, and terms under which his property shall be sold. If he fails to make such designations, the executor, in making sales, must follow the requirements of the law as to administrators' sales. If the testator in his will makes some of these designations but fails to provide for the others, the executor, as to those requisites of sale which have not been given to him by the will of the testator, must follow the provisions of the law for administrators' sales. The administrator should not apply for an order to sell the land of an estate unless it is necessary to do so for the purpose of paying the debts or for making a distribution or both.18 It is the policy of our courts to favor the heirs by a division in kind, 19 whenever a fair division of the estate in kind can be made; and, if it is unnecessary to sell for the payment of debts or for distribution, the heirs may file a caveat to the application for leave to sell.20 It is too late to object to such sale after it has been made where the order of sale was obtained regularly and no fraud was practiced. After the order for sale is granted, it is not necessary to advertise immediately and sell the property at the next regular sale day following the granting of the order, although this is the usual procedure. § 273.—Claims at Administrators' Sales. Under our Code, when an administrator, executor, guardian, or other trustee applies for leave to sell any property, real or personal, of the estate which he represents, any person claiming such realty or personalty may by himself, his agent, or his attorney at law file an affidavit, claiming such property, in the court of ordinary where such administration is pending.82 No bond and security is necessary to the validity of such claim, but the claimant is subject to have damages assessed against him by the jury, as in claims under execution sales, to be calculated on the basis of the value of the property claimed whenever it appears that such claim was interposed for delay only.84 

The claim affidavit may be filed immediately after the application for leave to sell is made, or it may be filed at any time after the order of sale is granted and before the sale occurs. When the claim affidavit is filed, a copy of the same must be served on the representative of the estate.85

The claim affidavit must be filed in the court of ordinary having jurisdiction of the administration. When notice of such claim has

§ 274] 487 

The right to file a claim to realty or personalty which the representative of an estate is attempting to sell applies only to sales which are judicial in their nature. A sale by an executor or an administrator under order of the court of ordinary is judicial in its nature, but a sale by an executor under a power in a will is not judicial in its nature, and, consequently, a claim can not be interposed to such a sale.93 The remedy of the person claiming the property in such a case would be an application to equity to enjoin the sale. If no equitable petition was filed to obtain an injunction and the sale took place, then the question of title could be settled by an ejectment suit in the case of realty, or trover in the case of personalty. 

§ 274.-Sales by Attorneys in Fact. The realty and personalty of an estate can be sold in this state only in the manner prescribed by law. If the decedent died intestate, the assets of his estate, if not distributed in kind, must be sold by the administrator, except in cases where no necessity of an administration exists; in such cases, the heirs may make the sale. If the decedent died testate, the assets of his estate must be sold by his executor in the manner prescribed by the will. If no provisions of sale are made in the will, then sales must be made by the executor or by the administrator de bonis non appointed to take the place of the executor, in the manner prescribed by law for sales by administrators.94 Under our Code,95 an executor or an administrator may delegate to an 

93. "A sale of land by an administrator or executor, under an order of the court of ordinary, is in the nature of a judicial sale. The sections of the code authorizing the interposition of claims where executors or administrators are proceeding to sell land, limit this right to cases where the sale is proceeding under an order, or where proceedings are being taken in such court for legal authority to make the sale. § 275.-Completing Sales Where Bonds for Title Given.-Whenever a vendor executes a bond for title to land and dies without executing a deed in compliance with such bond, the holder of the bond is entitled to apply to the court of ordinary having jurisdiction of the administration of such vendor's estate for an order requiring the administrator or the executor to make title according to the terms of the bond.98 The holder of such bond must comply with its conditions by making full payment of the purchase price and must make written application to the court for the order requiring the deed to be made, to which application should be attached a copy of the bond for title in question.99 

Written notice of such application must be served upon the representative of the estate at least fifteen days before the hearing. 

This notice may be served by the applicant personally or by anyone else for him, or it may be served by registered mail. In addition to this notice to the representative of the estate, notice must be given to the heirs at law of the deceased by publication once a week latter, and can not, over his protest, complete the sale; certainly not when there are present one or more persons willing to bid higher if allowed an opportunity to do so." Scales v. Chambers (1901), 113 Ga. 920 (2), 39 S. E. 396.

Equity may decree a sale of the entire interest in the land and distribute proceeds where estate is insolvent. "The administrator of an insolvent intestate, whose entire estate consists of a lot of land held under bond for titles, and which is worth more than the debt due the obligor, is entitled in equity to have the land sold and to receive the proceeds remaining after the extinguishment of the creditor's debt and the costs of the equitable proceeding." Streetman v. Streetman (1909), 133 Ga. 760 (1), 66 S. E. 883. "The general rule is, that, if there is an administration on the estate of a decedent, the right to bring suit to protect an equitable interest of such estate, arising from payments made by the decedent under a bond for title and a subsequent conveyance by the obligor to one who takes with notice, is in the administrator; but this rule is subject to modification under peculiar circumstances, such as collusion between the administrator and the obligor or the person to whom the latter conveyed, for the purpose of defrauding those interested in the estate, and obtaining a personal benefit for the administrator as an individual." "It makes no difference that the property was offered a second time, and bid off by another for the original bidder, and that the second bidder did not pay his bid, and the property was afterwards sold a third time, all the delays being at the instance of the first bidder. § 280.-Purchase at Own Sale.-An executor or an administrator occupies a place of trust and confidence; the law will not permit him to take advantage of those whom he represents. It makes no difference whether the representative of an estate acts in good faith or not in purchasing at his own sale. The widow may persuade him to purchase the property in order to prevent it from being sacrificed, and he may pay more than its value; nevertheless, the sale is voidable at the instance of heirs or others interested in the estate, regardless of the good faith that might have been shown by such representative. However, when the sale has been set aside and a resale ordered, the administrator is entitled to reimbursement for the amount of his previous bid where he has expended it legitimately for the benefit of the estate; if the proceeds are inadequate, the loss will fall upon him.159 

As a purchase by an executor or by an administrator at his own sale is voidable only, it follows that such sale passes a valid title until the sale has been set aside.160 If the executor or administrator who has purchased at his own sale conveys the property to an innocent third person before steps have been taken to set the sale aside, it is too late to set it aside, if both sales were for the reasonable value of the property. If the first sale was not for the reasonable value, the question of fraud would arise; and if, upon the trial of the case, it appeared that the purchaser from the administrator or executor who had purchased at his own sale was an innocent purchaser, then equity should hold the admin- 158. § 281. Sales May be Set Aside. As stated in the foregoing par agraph, sales may be set aside at the instance of those interested in an estate where the representative of the estate is the purchaser. 

A sale may be set aside also, at the instance of those interested in the estate where the administrator or executor and the purchaser have been guilty of fraud in obtaining an order for sale or in making the sale.165 If the motion is to the court of ordinary to set aside the judgment authorizing the sale and if letters of dismission have been granted to the representative of the estate, the judgment discharging him must be reopened before the motion to set the sale aside will be entertained.166 The order of discharge may be vacated and the sale set aside in one action in equity.167

§ 282.-Persons Entitled to Year's Support.-Year's support is an allowance out of an estate¹ for the support and maintenance of the widow² of the deceased, or for his minor children,³ or for both, for a period of twelve months.4 If a widow dies leaving a minor 

1. Before a year's support may be obtained, it must appear that the deceased had an estate. Griffin v. Davis (1882), 69 Ga. 760. 

2. Remarriage of widow does not prevent her from making application for a year's support out of the estate of her deceased husband. Swain v. 

Stewart (1896), 98 Ga. 366, 25 S. E. 

831; Bridges v. Barbree (1906), 127 

Ga. 679, 56 S. E. 1025; Grant v. Sosebee (1929), 169 Ga. 658, 151 S. E. 336. 

3. "A minor daughter, married at the time of her father's death and not a member of his household, but living with and supported by her husband, is not entitled to a year's support out of her deceased parent's estate." Goss V. 

Harris (1903), 117 Ga. 345 (1), 43 

S. E. 734.

Georgia Railway & Power Co. v. 

Beale (1920), 25 Ga. App. 364, 367, 103 

S. E. 434. Conveyance by heirs will not estop minor children from having year's support assigned. Jones V. 

Cooner (1911), 137 Ga. 681, 74 S. E. 51. 

An adult child is not entitled to a year's support. Miller v. Ennis (1899), 107 Ga. 663, 665, 34 S. E. 302. 

4. "The right to a year's support is purely statutory, and can be exercised only in the court of ordinary." Kerr v. McAnally (1936), 183 Ga. 365, 188 

S. E. 687. "Among the necessary expenses of administration, and to be preferred before all other debts, except as otherwise specially provided, is the provision for the support of the family, to be ascertained as follows: Upon the

[Ch. 21 

child a member of her family at the time of her death, such child is entitled to a year's support from her estate; if a married woman dies leaving a minor child and its father surviving, the child is not entitled to a year's support out of her estate, as the child and its father inherit equally. If there are two sets of minor children by different wives, each set of children is entitled to a year's support. 

Only one set of appraisers is necessary to set apart the year's support to the children of both marriages. In their return, however, the appraisers must specify the portions of the year's support which shall belong to each set of children; otherwise the children of the first marriage can claim no benefit in the same. If the return does not specify the portion for each set of children, those of the first marriage should object to the return of the appraisers in order that it may be corrected. If they fail to object, they can not claim an interest in the property set apart as a year's support. When the year's support is properly set apart to both sets of children, each set has a separate estate from the other. If one of either set dies, death of any person testate or intestate, leaving an estate solvent or insolvent, and leaving a widow, or a widow and minor child or children, or minor child or children only, it shall be the duty of the ordinary, on the application of the widow, or the guardian of the child or children, or any other person in their behalf, on notice to the representative of the estate (if there is one, and if none, without notice), to appoint five discreet appraisers; and it shall be the duty of such appraisers, or a majority of them, to set apart and assign to such widow and children, or children only, either in property or money, a sufficiency from the estate for their support and maintenance for the space of 12 months from the date of administration, in case there is administration on the estate, to be estimated according to the circumstances and standing of the family previous to the death of the testator or intestate, and keeping in view also the solvency of the estate. 

If there is a widow, the appraisers shall also set apart, for the use of herself and children, a sufficient amount of the household furniture. The amount set apart for the family shall in no event be less than the sum of $100; and if it shall appear upon a just appraisement of the estate that it does not exceed in value the sum of $500, it shall be the duty of the appraisers to set apart the whole of said estate for the support and maintenance of such widow and child or children, or, if no surviving widow, to the lawful guardian of the child or children, for their benefit." Code 113-1002.

§ 284. Jurisdiction and Procedure.-Application for dower is made in writing to the superior court,25 but application for year's support is made in writing to the court of ordinary.26 Upon presentation of the application for year's support, the ordinary is required to appoint five discreet appraisers to set aside the year's support, a majority of whom may act. These appraisers must be appointed by the ordinary having jurisdiction of the administration.27 (Civil Code, § 5912), as a homestead for the benefit of himself and family, and his widow lives upon the property for several months until her death, without making an application for a year's support out of the property or indicating any intention to do so, she will be held to have elected to take the homestead in the property, rather than the year's support; and her executor can not have the property set apart as a year's support to her estate under the provisions of the Civil Code, 3465." Ehrlich v. Silverstein (1904), 121 Ga. 54 (1), 48 S. E. 703; Donalson v. Yeates (1931), 173 Ga. 30, 159 S. E. 856; 

Philpot v. Ramsey & Hogan (1933), 47 Ga. App. 635, 171 S. E. 204.

27. In the first edition of this book, on page 566, the statement was made that, if the property out of which the year's support is sought is "located in two or more counties, then appraisers must be appointed in each county who must make their return to the court where the proceedings are pending."

The author, during the past ten years, has received several letters from attorneys expressing doubt as to this statement of the law and contending that the correct rule is that the appraisers should be citizens of the county of the administration and that the appraisers so appointed could go into any other county in the state and make appraisals of the value of the property of the estate located therein, out of which the year's support is to be set aside. The following authorities have been cited by different attorneys as indicating that the law is contrary to the statement of the author above indicated: McSwain v. Ricketson (1907), 129 Ga. 176, 58 S. E. 655; 

Carter v. Davidson (1912), 138 Ga. 

317, 75 S. E. 155 (4); Wessel-Duval & 

Co. v. Ramsey (1930), 170 Ga. 675, 153 

S. E. 744.

These decisions do not definitely settle the question, as it was not directly involved in any of them. Code 

113-1401, pertaining to the appointment of appraisers of an estate, provides that, after the qualification of an administrator, the ordinary shall issue a warrant, or, if the property is in different counties, warrants of appraisement, directed to five disinterested freeholders, citizens of the county where the property is located, any three of whom shall be qualified to act. Since the Code recognizes that appraisers should be appointed in different counties for the purpose of appraising the entire assets of the estate, and since the supreme court

[Ch. 21 

Our Code28 provides that the appraisers shall make a schedule of the property or a statement of the amount of money set apart by them and return it under their hands and seals within thirty days from the date of their appointment.29 This provision as to the has held, in the case of Kerr v. Mc- 

Anally (1936), 183 Ga. 365, 188 S. E. 

687, that the right to a year's support is purely statutory, the author is still of the opinion that, in setting apart a year's support out of property located in different counties, a careful practitioner would see that appraisers were appointed in each county where any of the assets are located out of which a year's support is sought. The rights of creditors are involved, as well as the rights of the widow and children.

Where the property is located in different counties, appraisers residing in the counties where the property is located are more familiar with its value and are more likely to give a just appraisement. If appraisers are appointed in all the counties, they must make their returns to the ordinary having jurisdiction over the administration. Any creditor or any other person interested may file objections to the returns of the appraisers and have his rights protected, as shown in the next section of this chapter. 

Since there is doubt as to whether the ordinary should appoint appraisers in all counties where any property of the deceased is located out of which a year's support is sought, or whether the appraisers should be appointed only in the county of the administration, this question should be settled by the legislature.

WILLS AND AdministrATION OF ESTATES 

The judgment of the court of ordinary is the judgment of a court of general jurisdiction, and the presumption is that everything necessary to authorize the rendition of such judgment was properly done.45 Therefore, a judgment setting apart a year's support can not be collaterally attacked.46 If the year's support has been legally set apart to the widow, minor children, or both, but the ordinary, through mistake or negligence, has failed to enter the return of record, it is legal for the ordinary thereafter, regardless of the lapse of time, to pass an order nunc pro tunc that the return be admitted to record, unless innocent persons' rights, acquired in the meantime, would be injuriously affected.47 

When a caveat has been filed to the return of the appraisers setting apart the year's support, the issue before the court of ordinary, or before the superior court on appeal, is not confined to the allowance or disallowance of the return. To confine the issue to these two questions would necessitate the reappointment of appraisers in case the first return was disallowed, with the resultant expense and delay, to the detriment of the rights of the widow and minor children. Upon the trial of such issue, the court of ordinary, in the first place, or the jury on appeal to the superior court, in the second place, may change or modify the return of the appraisers as to the amount or property set apart.

Under our Code a purchase-money mortgage on land75 or on personalty76 is superior to the right of the widow and minor children to a year's support in such mortgaged property. All mortgages which are not given for purchase money are inferior to this right.77

Our Code also provides that year's support is inferior to a landlord's special lien on the crops of a tenant for rent and for supplies furnished in the year during which the tenant dies.78 This applies only to the crops grown during the year of the tenant's death. If the tenant paid the rent and paid for the supplies furnished him during the year previous to his death, the fact that he owed the landlord for rent and supplies which accrued during the year in which he died would not entitle the landlord to take the crops of the previous year to the exclusion of the right of the widow and minor children to a year's support.

§ 289.-How Right Defeated.-A valid marriage is essential to the right of the widow to claim a year's support.85 When the alleged widow applies for a year's support, her marriage to the deceased may be collaterally attacked.86 A contract between husband and wife made for the purpose of promoting a dissolution of their marriage is contrary to public policy and will not defeat the right of the wife to claim a year's support and dower in the estate of the husband if he dies before a divorce is obtained or permanent alimony is allowed. Year's support is intended to be a provision for the maintenance of the widow and minor children for twelve months from the date of administration on the estate of the deceased husband and father.92 However, the right is not defeated by failure to apply during this twelve months' period. Delay in applying may furnish ground for defeating the application, especially where the applicants have lived on the assets of the estate for twelve months or more previous to their application.93 If the widow is fully informed of her rights and no fraud is practiced on her, she may make a binding agreement with the heirs to take a stipulated amount in lieu of her year's support. The acceptance of the stipulated amount under an agreement would operate as a bar to a subsequent application for a year's support.9 

A widow acting as administratrix of her husband's estate may defeat her right to year's support by paying out funds of the estate to creditors holding claims inferior in dignity to her year's support. 

Such misapplication of the funds of the estate does not defeat her claim for year's support absolutely; it simply postpones it until after the payment of the just claims still outstanding against the estate, 91. Swain v. Stewart (1896), 98 Ga.

§ 290.-Election in Lieu of Year's Support.-A testator by the terms of his will may require his widow to elect between provisions in the will and her right to year's support.97 Unless the terms of the will show that the testator intended to require such election, the widow may claim her year's support in addition to the benefits provided for her in the will.98 When the widow is required to elect between the provisions made for her in the will and a year's support, if she elects to take the legacy or devise, she is a quasi purchaser of it, in that she surrenders her vested right to a year's support for such legacy or devise. When property is set apart as a year's support for the benefit of a widow alone, she owns it in fee without restriction as to use, disposition, or encumbrance.113 Where property is set apart as a year's support for the joint benefit of a widow and her minor child or children, a conveyance or encumbrance of the same or any part thereof by the widow conveys or encumbers only her title and interest in such property. This act of the legislature uses the word "property" apparently in the sense of both real and personal property. If this act is strictly construed, then it will apply to both real and personal property set apart as a year's support. In such event, the widow could not sell any of the personal property without an order of court. In the majority of estates of country people the year's support consists of food products, cattle, horses, mules, and other animals, and some money. The widow usually finds it necessary to consume all such food products in the support of the family. She may find it necessary to sell a horse or a mule, or several cows, or even chickens which had been given to her and the children as part of the year's support. 

Certainly the legislature did not intend that she should apply to the ordinary to obtain an order granting her leave to sell the interest of the children in such property when she found it necessary to sell any of the same for the support of herself and children. should be amended so as to exclude foodstuffs, animals, and other such property set apart for the support of the widow and children, as the widow should be given the power to sell these in her own discretion for the support of herself and minor children in the same manner as she could have sold them prior to this act.

§ 295.-Homestead, Dower, and Year's Support Compared.-As homestead 130 is involved only occasionally in the administration of estates, it is not a proper subject to be treated in a work of this character. However, it will be interesting, and perhaps helpful, to compare it with dower and year's support, as the ultimate purpose of all these rights is the protection of those who are dependent upon the husband and father.131

Dower is a right given to the widow only.132 Homestead and year's support are rights provided for the widow or minor children or both.

Dower is a life estate for and during the life of the widow, whether she remarries or not. Year's support is intended as a temporary provision for the family only, but a fee-simple title vests in such beneficiaries. Homestead is an estate for life or for years or during the continuance of some disability. 

Dower may be assigned and year's support set apart only after the death of the husband and father. Homestead may be set apart either before or after his death for the benefit of those dependent upon him.134 Dower and year's support are not inconsistent, and

§ 296.-History. In the obscurity of early English history, the origin of dower seems to be interwoven to some extent with legend. 

According to Blackstone, "some have ascribed the introduction of dower to the Normans, as a branch of their local tenures; though we cannot expect any feudal reason for its invention, since it was not a part of the pure, primitive, simple laws of feuds." Blackstone also says that dower may be a relic of Danish custom; "since, according to the historians of that country, dower was introduced into Denmark by Sweyn, the father of our Canute the Great, out of gratitude to the Danish ladies, who sold all their jewels to ransom him when taken prisoner by the Vandals."2 Whatever may be the origin of dower or the cause of its adoption in England, a more practical reason for its existence is the one of making a pro- 

1. Blackstone, vol. 2, page 129. 

2. Blackstone, vol. 2, page 129. "If, indeed, dower had an origin so tinged with grateful gallantry, and having for its purpose the rewarding of the generous ladies of Denmark by conferring upon them a right in respect to their husband's lands, with or without the consent of the husbands, it is not surprising that, when it became a part of the law of England, it should have been often declared to be a favored right especially by the courts of equity, which delighted in being called 'courts of conscience."" Harris v. Powers (1907), 129 Ga. 74, 58 S. E. 1038.

At common law the widow's dower consisted of a life estate, for the term of her natural life, in one-third of all the lands and tenements of which her husband was seized in fee simple or in fee tail during the coverture and of which any issue which she might have had might have been heir. Under the common law the wife could not convey her inchoate right of dower or release it directly to her husband. In order to prevent the inconvenience of making land owned by a married man unsalable by reason of the inchoate right of his wife to dower, fictitious litigation was resorted to in order to free from the dower right land which the husband desired to sell. This litigation consisted of suffering a common recovery or levying a fine jointly with the husband. § 297.-Right to Dower.-The right to dower is exclusively in the widow; children, whether minors or not, have no right to dower.4 At common law, the widow's dower consisted of a life estate, for the term of her natural life, in one-third of all the lands and tenements of which her husband was seized in fee simple or in fee tail during the coverture, and of which any issue, which she might have had, might have been heir.5 A sale by the husband did not deprive the wife of her right of dower in the land sold unless she voluntarily released the same. The common law of force prior to May 14, 1776, was adopted as the law of Georgia by our adopting Act of February 25, 1784, so far as suited to our conditions and form of government. Since this adopting act, so many statutory modifications have been made in Georgia that it is seldom necessary to appeal to the common law to determine any right as to dower. § 298. A radical change in the common law as to dower is found in our first Code, in the following language: "Dower is the right of a wife to an estate for life in one-third of the lands, according to valuation, including the dwelling house (which is not to be valued unless in a town or city), of which the husband was seized and possessed at the time of his death, or to which the husband obtained title in right of his wife." 

This Code section has been copied verbatim in all subsequent Codes of Georgia. 10 The last clause of this Code section, "or to which the husband obtained title in right of his wife," applies only to cases arising prior to the Married Woman's Act of 1866." 

As we are so far removed from that date, this clause can be stricken from all future Codes without danger of affecting the rights of anyone.

Seizin of a legal title at common law was requisite to the right of dower, for a widow was not entitled to dower in lands to which her husband held only an equitable title. This common-law rule, that the husband must be seized of a legal title in order to entitle his widow to dower, has been modified by statute in Georgia to the extent that "dower may be assigned in lands held under deed, bond for title, or other instrument in writing having like effect, where a portion of the purchase money has been paid, but the estate in dower shall be liable for the unpaid purchase money where the vendee held under bond for titles or other instrument having the same effect, or under deed where contemporaneously with the execution of the deed the vendee encumbered the land with a mortgage for the purchase money. "15 This Code section refers to payment of part of the purchase money by the husband in his lifetime,16 and the exceptions to the common-law rule that dower can not be claimed in an equity are limited to the cases mentioned in this Code section.17 

It also refers to contracts for the purchase of lands and not to bonds to reconvey held by the vendor in a security deed. If the husband has conveyed the title to land as security, he has only an equity of redemption, and what he owes is borrowed money, not purchase money.  § 299.-Same-Redemption by Widow.-At common law there were some adjudications to the effect that the widow might redeem the land with her own funds and then apply for dower.20 These adjudications have caused some confusion in Georgia over this question. There are certain dicta21 by our supreme court to the effect that a widow may redeem the land and then claim her dower in it, and there is also one dissenting opinion in a case where part of the loan had been repaid by the husband in his lifetime, in which it is held that the widow should be allowed to pay the balance of the indebtedness and then claim her dower, especially as the estate was solvent,2 22 but the majority of the court in this case indicated that the widow was not entitled to pay the balance of the indebtedness and claim dower.23 paid, may have dower assigned to her out of such lands. That is not the present case. The present case is one of the conveyance by the owner of lands to secure a debt and the taking of a bond for title for the reconveyance upon the payment of that debt. 

To hold that a case like this falls within the provision of Code section 5248 would be adding to and widening the terms of that statute, which a court is not authorized to do. It is clear that but for the terms of the law embraced in section 5248 of the Code the wife would have no claim of a right of dower in the lots of land in controversy; and as she does not bring herself within the provisions of that statute, her claims can not be upheld."

541 No doubt arises as to the widow's inability to claim dower in an equity of redemption when she does not redeem the land from the indebtedness to secure which her husband, in his lifetime, conveyed the legal title; but, as stated above, there has been some disposition in the form of dicta to recognize the widow's right to dower, in such cases, where she redeems or offers to redeem the land with her own. funds. However, with due respect to the able judges who rendered these dicta in the cases mentioned, it seems that the correct rule, under strict construction of our statutes and under the common law, is that the status of the legal title at the time of the husband's death determines the widow's right to dower and that acts done by the widow after his death will not create a right of dower.24 This is a

The following is quoted from that brief as illustrative of the question under discussion: "At the outset of this discussion, we desire freely to concede that there are decisions in OTHER jurisdictions, based upon entirely DIFFERENT 

PRINCIPLES OF CONSTRUCTION ob taining there, to the effect that the widow might redeem such lands, and might be entitled to contribution from the legatees, or to some other right against the executor. Indeed, there may be OBITER DICTA from our own courts, which indicate this to be the rule in Georgia. But we insist that the 

LAW as it is laid down in THIS State, is PRECISELY THE REVERSE, as will be seen from a consideration of the principles underlying the actual decisions of our courts. "It must be borne in mind that dower is a mere interest in the REALTY of the estate, as distin guished from the PERSONALTY. The taking of dower has no effect whatever upon the widow's right to share in the PERSONALTY of the estate, but it excludes her from all other interest in the REALTY. Our Statutes of dis tribution provide an entirely DIF- 

FERENT system for the distribution of the REALTY on the one hand, and for the distribution of the PERSON- 

ALTY on the other. Indeed, if the widow simply does NOTHING, and neither elects to take a child's part or dower, she is NOT AN HEIR AT 

ALL AS TO THE LAND-for some POSITIVE ACTION on her part is necessary to enable her to share in the 

REALTY of her deceased husband, if he leaves any children. "Now, inasmuch as dower is a claim against the REALTY only, it follows that it must be a claim against such realty in the STATUS IN WHICH IT EXISTED AT THE TIME OF THE 

HUSBAND'S DEATH; and certainly, even if the widow were entitled to RE- DEEM LAND which the husband had conveyed by security deed (and thus were entitled to enable herself to take dower therein), she could certainly have no right to use the PERSON- ALTY of the estate for that purpose; for that would be INCREASING HER 

DOWER OUT OF THE PERSONALTY.

In either case, under our Code, the question is whether or not the husband died seized and possessed of the land; that is, did he have legal title to it at the time of his death ?26 If he did not, the widow is not dowable in such land, regardless of the value of the equity which belongs to the husband's estate. § 300.-Requisites to Right of Dower.-Three requisites are necessary to perfect the right of dower-marriage, seizin, and death.27 When the dower right has been perfected by the existence of these requisites, there remains one essential to the consummation of the dower estate-the widow must apply for her dower within seven years from the date of the death of the husband.28 

As dower is intended solely for the widow, it follows that there is no right of dower unless there is a valid marriage.29 A marriage which is void confers no right of dower.30 "While it is true that our Supreme Court Judges have several times intimated an opinion to the effect that the widow might have the right to redeem, and even one went so far as to say that this principle apparently had become embedded in our law, (referring to Harris v. The right of dower is vested without any act on the part of the widow, and it continues as a vested right until barred by the lapse of time77 or by an election by the widow to claim a child's part in the realty. The right to a child's part in the real estate is not a vested right; it is dependent on an election by the widow to claim it in lieu of dower within twelve months from the date of the granting of letters of administration or letters testamentary on her husband's estate.78

When the husband dies testate, the widow, in addition to her right to year's support, has the choice between claiming dower or claiming under the will, if the terms of the will require such choice.79 If real estate is devised to her, she is, by operation of law, required to elect between such devise and dower, unless a contrary intent appears in the will,80 but she is not required to elect between dower and the personalty bequeathed to her in the will, unless the will states that such personalty is given in lieu of dower.81

In Georgia the widow's right to dower is superior to all claims against the estate, with certain statutory exceptions as to purchase money.85 Consequently, there seems to be no valid reason why the widow should lose her priority when she exchanges her right of dower for a devise or bequest in a will.86 However, equity would not permit a testator to provide for his widow such an amount in lieu of dower as would be a fraud on the creditors. 

For illustration, it would be improper to permit a testator to devise all of a valuable estate to his wife in lieu of dower, thus allowing her to elect to claim all of the estate and thereby defeat the just claims of creditors. Where the claims of creditors have been affected in such a case, the amount of the legacy or devise would doubtless be considered, and equity would take charge of the estate and do justice to all the parties on the theory that a legal fraud was being perpetrated on the creditors by the terms of the will.87

In addition to the foregoing methods of barring the right of dower, this right may be barred by a decree for permanent alimony,96 or by contract between the husband and wife in which the wife releases her right to dower for a valuable consideration.97 

The right to dower may also be barred by a gift causa mortis made for that purpose and accepted by the wife, in lieu of dower, and retained by her after her husband's death.98 Such a gift would be in the nature of a contract between the husband and the wife in which the widow released her right to dower for a valuable consideration. The right of dower may be barred also by estoppel, as where the widow's conduct amounts to a waiver of dower. In such a case, it must appear that the widow had full knowledge of her rights at the time she committed the acts relied on as an estoppel and that some innocent person has relied on such acts.99 The mere failure to claim dower can not be relied on as an estoppel.

allowed except when expressly permitted by statute, while certiorari is a common-law remedy for reviewing judgments of inferior judicatories which is always allowed unless expressly taken away by statute. It, therefore, becomes proper to consider to what extent the right of appeal from judgments from the court of ordinary has been given and in what manner the right of certiorari has been. restricted by statute in Georgia. Under our constitution4 jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to the probate of wills and the administration of estates is vested in a "court of ordinary" for each county.5 The judge who presides over a court of ordinary is called the "ordinary," but he is vested with judicial authority independent of the "court of ordinary" in the performance of special duties imposed on him by law, as in the granting of homesteads and the supervising of county matters. 

Such duties as these devolve on him as "ordinary" and not on the "court of ordinary." By reason of this dual judicial authority, appeal may be proper from a decision of the "court of ordinary" which would not be proper under similar circumstances from a decision of the "ordinary." For illustration, appeal is the remedy for reviewing any decision of the "court of ordinary" pertaining to the probate of a will or the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, although only questions of law are involved, whereas certiorari is the exclusive remedy for reviewing questions of law decided by the "ordinary." This distinction is due to our statutory regulations.

Under our Code an appeal lies from any decision made by the "court of ordinary" except an order appointing a temporary administrator or an order probating a will in common form. Cer-

A surety on an appeal bond should be some person with sufficient property to cover his homestead exemption and the penalty of the appeal bond. Usually no difficulty is experienced in obtaining security for an appeal from the court of ordinary, as the bond on appeal is not an eventual condemnation money bond but a bond "for such further costs as may accrue." The person selected for surety must not be a party to the case. A co-defendant is already bound by the judgment; consequently, an appeal with a co-defendant as surety would be a nullity and could not be amended.30

APPEALS § 314.-Transmission of Appeal.-In most counties in Georgia the office of the ordinary and the office of the clerk of the superior court are on the same floor of the same building. Therefore, the. transmission of the original papers in appeal cases is a simple matter. It is the duty of the ordinary to deliver all the original papers47 filed in his office, in the case in which the appeal is taken, including his judgment in the case,48 to the clerk of the superior court at least ten days before the next term of the superior court.49 

These papers must be transmitted to the clerk of the superior court of the county in which the proceedings in the case were had before the court of ordinary. It is unnecessary that the ordinary transmit with the original papers a certificate showing that the costs have been paid,50 although the ordinary may refuse to enter the appeal unless the costs are paid.51 While the law makes it the duty of the ordinary to transmit the papers on appeal to the clerk of the superior court, he may authorize someone else to act for him; but no one can transmit the papers on appeal legally without authority ordinary, made under section 113-1229, such appeal shall not operate as a supersedeas, unless the executor or administrator shall first give a good and sufficient bond, payable to the ordinary and his successors in office, in such sum as the ordinary may require (not exceeding the amount of the estate in the hands of the administrator), conditioned to pay all costs and damages that may accrue to the estate pending the appeal." § 315.-Effect of Appeal.-The entry of an appeal acts as a super sedeas, as it suspends but does not vacate the judgment from which the appeal is taken.54 If the appeal is withdrawn55 or if it is dismissed in the superior court, the rights of the parties are the same as if no appeal had been entered.56 When the case has been tried in the superior court, the judgment of that court determines the rights of the parties. Jurisdiction on Appeal.-In trying an appeal from the court of ordinary, the superior court is merely an appellate court; it can reach no conclusion which could not have been reached in the court of ordinary, had the case been terminated there. Consequently, an equitable petition or amendment in aid of the appeal may not be filed in the superior court; for the court of ordinary from which the appeal was made has no equitable jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction of the appellate court is limited to that of the lower court. 64 If, for any reason, the court of ordinary or the superior court, on appeal, could not do full justice between the up by ordinary in transmitting appeal.

§ 318.-Descent.-Under our Code, upon the death intestate of the owner of any estate in realty, which estate survives him, the title vests immediately in his heirs at law.2 The title to all other property owned by such intestate vests in the administrator of his estate for the benefit of the creditors and then the heirs. The title to realty and personalty vests in the executor when the deceased dies testate, and the devisees and legatees take by purchase and not by

Upon the death of a wife without lineal descendants, the husband is her sole heir. If the wife leaves a surviving child or children or descendants of child or children, her estate shall be equally divided between the husband and said offspring per capita, except that descendants of children shall take per stirpes.14 A modification of this rule occurs where the husband and wife are living in a state of separation, in that the acquisitions of the wife and her children living with her are vested in the wife, free from the debts, contracts, or control of the husband, and at her death intestate, the same descend to her children, and, if there are none, then to her next of kin.15

§ 320.-Same-Rules of Canon Law.-As set forth in paragraph nine of the preceding section of this chapter, the degrees of relationship more remote than those mentioned in the preceding eight paragraphs of said section are determined by the rules of the canon law enforced by the English courts prior to the fourth day of July, 1776. The rules of the canon law for determining these remote degrees are as follows:

Count one degree for each generation from the intestate up to the common ancestor of such intestate and the claimant of the estate; thence one degree for each generation down the collateral line to the claimant. The number of degrees in the longer of these two lines is the degree of kindred between the intestate and the claimant. Determine the relationship of each claimant to the intestate in this manner, and the claimant most closely related is 16. Code 113-904, 113-905, 113-906; 

Pollard v. Gorman (1935), 52 Ga. App. 

127, 182 S. E. 678. "The plaintiff brought suit to recover a distributive share in the estate of his maternal grandfather, who died subsequently to the date of the death of plaintiff's mother. It appeared from the evidence that the plaintiff was a bastard. Being such, he was not capable of inheriting from the grandfather; and consequently the court did not err in holding that he could not recover, and in directing a verdict accordingly.” Thigpen v. Thigpen (1911), 136 Ga. 541 (1), 71 S. E. 790. 

Father may, by order of court, have illegitimate child made legitimate so as to inherit in same manner as if born in lawful wedlock. Code 74-103.

Adopted child may inherit from adopting father, but adopting father may not inherit from adopted child. Code 74-404.

[Ch. 24 entitled to the estate. It is seen from the foregoing that the common ancestor need not be the same person as to all the claimants. 

The common ancestor is the person from whom the relationship of the claimant and the intestate is traced. The case of Wetter v. 

Habersham17 serves as an excellent illustration of the method of determining remote degrees of relationship.

Miss Telfair died leaving a valuable estate. The Jones heirs, who were the grandchildren of an aunt of Miss Telfair, claimed the estate. The Wetters, who were great-grandchildren of Miss 

Telfair's brother, also claimed the estate. The question to determine was, which were the more closely related to Miss Telfairthe aunt's grandchildren or the brother's great-grandchildren? The following diagram illustrates this relationship:18 Aunt's Child

From this diagram it is seen that the common ancestor of Miss Telfair and the Joneses is the grandfather of Miss Telfair and that the father of Miss Telfair is the common ancestor of her and the Wetters. By counting one degree for each generation up to the common ancestor in each case, one sees that the longer of the two lines in each case is from the claimant up to the common ancestor and not from Miss Telfair to the common ancestor. The number of degrees counting one degree for each generation from the Joneses to the common ancestor the grandfather of Miss Telfair-is three; the number of degrees from the Wetters to the common ancestor-the father of Miss Telfair-is four. Thus the 

Joneses are related to Miss Telfair in the third degree and the Wetters in the fourth degree, and the Supreme Court of Georgia so held.

Under the fifth paragraph of Code section 113-903, the children or grandchildren of Thomas Telfair, had they been living, would have taken his place by representation and would have inherited Miss Telfair's estate to the exclusion of the Jones heirs, but his great-grandchildren could not.19 If all the aunt's grandchildren had been dead, leaving children then living, her great-grandchildren and the Wetters-brother's great-grandchildren—would have inherited per capita, as they would have all been related in the same degree to Miss Telfair, the intestate. 

§ 321. Inheritance Per Capita and Per Stirpes.-Little difficulty arises in determining who are the lineal heirs of an intestate or in what proportion they take, as our Code20 provides that "in all cases of inheritance from a lineal ancestor the distribution is per stirpes and not per capita."21 When there are no lineal descendants, the collateral kindred inherit, and it is often difficult to determine in what proportion they take.

Under the English statutes of distribution,22 representation among collateral relatives was not allowed further than to children of brothers and sisters of the intestate. This rule was followed in Georgia until 1859, when our legislature extended the right of representation to the children of brothers and sisters.23 Inheritance by more remote degrees is determined under our Code not by representation but by the rules of the canon law.2 24 As collateral relatives are allowed by our Code 

22. 22 and 23 Charles II c. 10 (1671). 

According to Blackstone, vol. 2, pages 

515-517, the settled rule for the construction of the English statutes of distribution is that, where all the collateral distributees stand in equal degree, they inherit per capita from the intestate, and where they stand in unequal degree, they inherit per stirpes, the more remote degrees taking by representation the share of the deceased ancestor. For illustration, "A," "B," "C," and "D" are brothers whose parents are dead. "B," "C," and "D" die, leaving one, three, and five children respectively. "A" then dies intestate leaving no wife or lineal heirs. His estate under such circumstances, would be divided under the English statutes of distribution above mentioned into nine equal parts and distributed equally per capita among the children of "B," "C," and "D," as they all would be related to the intestate in equal degree. However, if one of the brothers of "A" were living, then the heirs of "A" would stand in unequal degree and the distribution would be per stirpes under the English rule above mentioned.

Code 113-903 (5). This explains why the Wetters-brother's great-grandchildren-as shown in the diagram in the preceding section of this chapter, could not inherit, by representation, the estate of Miss Telfair. Representation stopped with the brother's grandchildren; so these great-grandchildren could inherit only by virtue of the rules of the canon law, and under these rules the Joneses were one degree closer to the intestate and inherited to the exclusion of the Wetters.

"Representation or that rule of law by which the children, or their descendants, of a deceased person who, if he had lived, would have taken property by virtue of an intestacy, stand in his place so as to take the property which he would have taken had he lived, is stated to be an admitted principle of the common law. 

By the Roman law, the right of representation continued in infinitum in the descending line, and, in all cases, the inheritance always descended in stirpes; but in collateral succession the rule of the Roman law differed from the common law, for, according

321] 583 

to inherit by representation only through three generationsbrothers and sisters; children of brothers and sisters, that is, nieces and nephews; grandchildren of brothers and sisters, that is, grandnieces and grand-nephews—the question arises as to whether these collateral relatives inherit per capita or per stirpes. If the intestate leaves only brothers and sisters as his heirs at law, necessarily they will inherit per capita, as they all stand in equal degree of relationship to the intestate. If the only heirs are a brother and a sister of the deceased and nieces and nephews-children of deceased brothers and sisters-the inheritance will necessarily be per stirpes, as the heirs stand in unequal degree of relationship to the intestate. For illustration, "A," "B," "C," and "D" are brothers whose parents are dead. "C" and "D" die, leaving three and five children respectively. "A" then dies intestate, leaving no wife or lineal heirs. His estate, under such circumstances, would be divided per stirpes, and "B" would receive one-third, the children of "C" one-ninth each, and the children of "D" one-fifteenth each, as these collateral heirs stand in unequal degree of relationship to the intestate. Now suppose "B" also had died prior to "A," leaving one child. Then there would be nine children related to "A" in equal degree, namely, the children of "B," "C," and "D." As the relationship is in equal degree, the distribution is per capita and each child would inherit a one-ninth interest in the estate of "A," for our Code provides: "If all the brothers and sisters be dead at the death of the intestate, then the distribution is between the nephews and nieces, per capita; and if any of the nephews and nieces be dead, leaving children, distribution is to be made as though the nephews and nieces were all alive, the children of the deceased nephew or niece standing in place of the parent."25 to the former, the division of the estate among collaterals per stirpes took place only where the persons succeeding to the inheritance were of unequal degree; representation had no place where such persons stood in equal degree. The right to take by representation is secured to the descendants of the intestate's children in probably all the states, but, among collaterals, it is generally limited so as not to extend beyond brothers' and sisters' children or descendants." 18 

C. J. 824.

Perhaps the rule now established by our Code provides for a more just distribution of the assets of brothers and sisters among their collateral relatives. § 322.-Same-First Cousins, Uncles, and Aunts.-An uncle or an aunt is one degree closer in blood to an intestate than a first cousin, had rendered two recent decisions pertaining to inheritance per capita and per stirpes by collateral relatives. 

Harrell v. Storey (1932), 175 Ga. 569, 165 S. E. 554; Brown v. Brown (1934), 179 Ga. 615, 176 S. E. 646. These two decisions indicate that the supreme court had reached the conclusion that, even though all the collaterals were related in the same degree, the inheritance would still be per stirpes. 

If these decisions conflict with the last sentence of Code 113-903 (5), then they must yield to it. The supreme court in the case of Harrell v. Storey indicated that a per stirpes distribution would be made even though the nieces and nephews were all equally related to the intestate because of the fact that the preceding sentence in said Code section states that: "The children or grandchildren of brothers and sisters deceased shall represent and stand in the place of their deceased parents."

The author is of the opinion that the words "represent and stand in the place of" were not used in the Act of 1859 and in subsequent Codes for the purpose of showing a per stirpes inheritance among collaterals. These words were used evidently for the purpose of showing that inheritance by representation by collateral relatives was extended one generation farther than that allowed by the common law before the canon law applied to the remote degrees. See footnote 24 of this chapter. The Code has now re-established the rule announced in the case of Houston v. Davidson (1871), 45 Ga. 574, by providing in effect that nieces and nephews inherit per capita when they all stand in the same degree of relationship to the intestate. For illustration, if there are three brothers whose parents are dead, and two of them die leaving respectively two children and five children, and then the other brother dies intestate without leaving a wife or lineal descendants, the nieces and nephews of the deceased brothers stand in equal degree to the intestate, and inherit per capita, each taking a one-seventh interest in the estate, because they take by representation, whereas, if they stood in the place of their deceased parents, they would take per stirpes. Our Code settles this question by adding the last sentence to paragraph 5 of section 113-903, which provides for per capita distribution under such circumstances, and extends the same rule to grandnieces and grand-nephews-grandchildren of brothers and sisters. The illustration given above with reference to brothers of course refers to sisters or brothers. 

26. See footnote 24 of this chapter.

§ 322] 585 

DESCENT, DISTRIBUTION, ANd Settlement for first cousins are children of uncles or aunts. Therefore, under the rules discussed in the preceding section of this chapter, uncles and aunts and first cousins apparently would inherit per stirpes, the uncles and aunts taking full shares and the first cousins taking the shares of their deceased parents. However, our Code27 provides that first cousins and uncles and aunts stand in the same degree; therefore, inheritance by them would be not per stirpes but per capita, as they are all related in equal degree to the intestate. Consequently, children of a living uncle28 would inherit from the estate of a first cousin equally with their father, thus creating the anomalous situation of a remoter degree in blood inheriting equally with a nearer degree in blood in the same branch. Such children, although they are only first cousins and their father is an uncle of the intestate, inherit per capita with their father and with the other first cousins and uncles and aunts. For illustration, "A," "B," “C,” and “D” are brothers29 whose parents are dead. "B," "C," and "D" die intestate, "B" leaving one child, "E," and "C" leaving two children, and "D" three children. Then "E" dies leaving no mother or lineal descendants living. "A," the uncle of "E,' is living and has four living children, and the five children of "C" and "D" are living. Who are the heirs of "E" and in what proportion do they take? 99 "A" is an uncle of "E"; his four children and the five children of "C" and "D" are all first cousins to "E." Should the estate be divided per stirpes, "A" getting one-third and the children of "C" one-third and the children of "D" one-third, or should it be divided per capita, "A" taking one-tenth, his children each onetenth, and the children of "C" and "D" each one-tenth? If the children of "A" took by representation, they could claim no share, as their father is living, but they do not take by representation but take as heirs of equal degree with their father by virtue of Code section 113-903 (8). Consequently, the estate of "E" should be divided into ten equal shares, "A" taking one-tenth and all the first cousins, including the children of “A," each taking one-tenth. The uncle "A" and his children and all the other first cousins, by virtue of the Code section above mentioned, are related to "E" in equal degree, and the distribution, is therefore per capita among all of

Annuities should be paid according to the directions given by the testator in his will. If no direction is given, they may be paid in advance, or they may be paid in installments or at the end of the year, in the discretion of the executor.38 § 324.-Division in Kind.-Usually, a division in kind of the assets of an estate is to be preferred over a sale of the assets and a division of the proceeds.39 A division in kind may be made by consent and agreement of those interested in the estate,40 but the rights of creditors can not be prejudiced thereby. No division in kind should be attempted until all the debts of the estate have been paid or satisfactorily arranged with the creditors. 

Where administration has been granted upon an estate, the usual method of making a division in kind is by application to the ordinary.41 This application may be made by the representative of the estate or by any distributee interested therein. In all cases, the applicant shall give at least twenty days' written notice to all parties in interest residing in this state. This notice may be served by the sheriff of the county of the residence of the person to be served, or service of such notice may be waived or acknowledged. If any person in interest is a minor, service must be made on his guardian; if such minor has no guardian, then service may be made on him, but a guardian ad litem must be appointed by the court to represent such minor. Service may be made on any person in interest residing out of the state of Georgia by publication at least twice a month for two months in the newspaper in which the ordinary's official notices are published in the county where the administration is pending.42

§ 325.-Advancements.-During the distribution of an estate in kind, or otherwise, each distributee must account for any advancements from the estate which were made to him in the intestate's lifetime. Our Code47 defines an advancement to be "any provision. made by a parent48 out of his estate, for and accepted49 by a child, either in money or property, during his lifetime, over and above the obligation of the parent for maintenance and education. 

Donations from affection, and not made with a view to an accounting, nor intended as advancements, shall not be accounted for as such; nor shall the support of a child under the parental roof, although past majority, nor the expenses of education, be held as advancements, unless charged as such by the parent."50 From this

Interest on Funds of Estate.-As creditors of an estate have twelve months within which to give notice of their claims, the representative can not safely distribute the assets or invest the same until the expiration of this period. For this reason, no executor, administrator, or guardian is liable to the distributees of the estate for interest during the first year after his appointment, unless he actually makes it,55 and then only for the amount so earned. The rule for charging interest on funds in the control of the representative of an estate is that a reasonable time,56 according to the facts of each case, should be allowed him to invest the funds of the estate; the object of charging the representative of the estate with interest is to require him to make such interest as a diligent man would make with his own funds.57 The representative is authorto account for them.  § 328.-Jurisdiction and Venue.-A court of equity has concur rent jurisdiction with the court of ordinary78 in the settlement of accounts of administrators and executors.79 An equitable petition for accounting and settlement must be filed in the county where one or more of the defendants reside; but an accounting and settlement before the ordinary may be had in the county where the administration is pending, regardless of whether the representative of the estate resides in that county or not. Whenever a person applies for letters of guardianship or of administration in a county different from that in which he resides, by that act he waives his right to be sued in the county of his residences in so far as an accounting and settlement of his trust are concerned. He is a quasi officer of the court appointing him, and is subject to the orders of that court pertaining to the administration and settlement of his trust. However, suits by creditors of an estate and equitable suits against the representative of an estate must be filed in the county where he resides.81

When an executor or administrator is cited to appear and settle his accounts before the ordinary having jurisdiction of the administration of the estate, if such executor or administrator is not a resident of that county, he may remove the proceedings to the county of his residence with the consent82 of all the parties in interest and by complying with the provisions of our Code pertaining to the removal of such cases.83 § 329.-Basis of Settlement.-Our Code84 provides that all statements for final settlement with executors or administrators shall be made upon the following basis: "1. The rate of interest charged against executors and administrators shall be the same as that provided by law. "2. No interest shall be charged either way for the first year, as one year is allowed by law for the collection of assets and to ascertain the indebtedness of an estate. "3. An executor or administrator, in the management of an estate, may retain in his hands, at the beginning of each year, an amount of money sufficient to pay the current expenses of said year; upon which amount no interest shall be charged in final settlement. "4. The executor or administrator shall, however, pay interest upon all balances left in his hands at the beginning of each year, over and above the payment of expenses for said year, the same to be ascertained and computed in final settlement. "5. When it shall so happen that, at the beginning of any year, an executor or administrator shall not have an amount in hand sufficient to pay the current expenses of said year, and his annual returns show that fact, he shall be allowed to charge, in final settlement, interest on the amount advanced by him during the year for such expenses. "6. The annual returns of executors or administrators shall be made out in the manner provided by law and practiced in this State; and the reservations, charges, and computations of interest set forth in this section shall be made when said parties come to make a statement for final settlement.

In the settlement of the accounts of the representative of an estate, his returns which have been allowed by the ordinary are considered as stated accounts, and the rule that anyone who objects to a stated account must surcharge or falsify applies. The pleadings in which such returns are attacked should point out specifically the items of the returns on which the attack is made and should disclose the cause or ground of attack.85 

The object of settling the accounts of the representative of an estate is to determine whether or not he has properly administered his trust. In order to determine this question, he shall be charged with all assets which have come into his hands for administration and shall be credited with all lawful expenditures made by him in payment of charges fixed by law against the estate, whether such assets or such credits are shown in his returns or not. 

§ 330.-Effect of Settlement.-The representative of an estate may be cited to settle his accounts at any time after the expiration of one year from the date administration was granted, whether the estate is ready for final distribution or not.86 However, a citation for settlement is usually made after the representative has had sufficient time and opportunity to complete the administration and in connection with an application for his discharge or removal. An order of court settling finally the accounts of the representative of an estate and granting a discharge is conclusive until reversed or set aside and is not subject to collateral attack except for fraud.87
