§ 7.-Kinds of Wills.-Saliba v. Saliba (1947), 202 Ga. 791, 44 S. E. 2d 744. 

§ 8.-Nature of Wills.-Nixon v. Nixon (1942), 194 Ga. 301, 21 S. E. 2d 702. 

"A will does not confer any present right at the time of its execution. Until the death of the testator, it has been called ambulatory. It has been compared to an undelivered deed, which contains an expression of a purpose that has not gone into effect." Payne v. Payne (1957) 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 S. E. 2d 450. "A limitation over to the 'heirs at law' of a person is a limitation over to his 'children.''' Lane v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1943), 195 Ga. 

828, 25 S. E. 2d 800 (6).

Acts 1952, pages 288, 289, as amended by Acts 1959, pages 299, 300 (Ga. Code 

Ann., § 113-909), prohibits one who maliciously kills another from inheriting or from receiving any property from such person so killed. This code section as amended is as follows: "113-909. Right of inheritance denied person who kills another for purpose of inheriting latter's property.-The right of inheritance is hereby denied any person who shall, with malice aforethought, kill any other person, or who shall conspire with another to kill or who shall procure another to kill any such person. This denial to inherit shall include any property which the person so killing would otherwise have inherited, whether real, personal or mixed, or any part thereof, belonging to such deceased person at the time of death, or any property which the person so killing would take by deed, will, or otherwise, at the death of the deceased; and all right, interest, and estate in and to said property shall go to such other heirs as may be entitled thereto by the laws of descent and distribution, or by will, deed, or other conveyance duly executed by the deceased in his or her lifetime. For the purpose of determining the descent and distribution through such person so killing, he shall be treated as though he had predeceased the person so killed. (Acts 1952, pp. 288, 289; Acts 1959, pp. 299, 300.)"

The fact that a person was acquitted in a criminal proceeding of the charge that he had with malice aforethought killed his wife would not be a bar to a civil action on the ground that such person by killing his wife with malice aforethought forfeited his right of inheritance under Code § 113-909. Webb v. 

McDaniel (1962), 218 Ga. 366, 127 S. E. 2d 900. 

§ 9.-Character of Wills.-Mills v. Tyus (1942), 195 Ga. 119, 23 S. E. 2d 

259; Comer v. Comer (1942), 195 Ga. 79, 23 S. E. 2d 420. "A will does not confer any present right at the time of its execution. Until the death of the testator, it has been called ambulatory. It has been compared

to an undelivered deed, which contains an expression of a purpose that has not gone into effect." Payne v. Payne (1957) 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 S. E. 2d 450. 

§ 10.-General Principles-Form of Wills.-Page v. Jones (1938), 186 Ga. 

485, 198 S. E. 63; Hungerford v. Spalding (1936), 183 Ga. 547, 189 S. E. 2; 

Nixon v. Nixon (1942), 194 Ga. 301, 21 S. E. 2d 702; Patellis v. Tanner (1944), 197 Ga. 471, 29 S. E. 2d 419; Smith v. Thomas (1945), 199 Ga. 396, 34 S. E. 2d 278. 

Code § 113-301, relating to the formalities of the executing of wills, the number of witnesses required, etc., was amended by Act 1958, page 658, which code section as amended is as follows: 

"113-301. All wills (except nuncupative wills) disposing of realty or personalty shall be in writing, signed by the party making the same or by some other person in his presence and by his express direction, and shall be attested and subscribed in the presence of the testator by two or more competent witnesses.' 

"An administrator of an estate, who is also an heir, may not take to his own use the entire estate or any part thereof, under a claim that deceased, sixteen years previously, had made a verbal agreement that he wanted his property disposed of in such manner, since, in absence of will, such a claim cannot be sustained." McNeely v. Booth (1939), 59 Ga. App. 906, 2 S. E. 2d 512 (3). "A deed to an immediate estate in land, made directly to a person not in esse, is void."

Singer v. First Nat. Bank & Trust Co. (1943), 195 Ga. 269, 

24 S. E. 2d 47 (7). "An instrument in form of deed reciting a valuable consideration, witnessed as a deed, delivered to one of grantees, and recorded in grantor's lifetime, was not a 'will,' so as to require attestation as such, merely because, in expressly reserving a life estate to grantor, instrument used the somewhat inappropriate words that the 'conveyance is inoperative until the death of the grantor.' Smaha v. George (1943), 195 Ga. 412, 24 S. E. 2d 385 (1). 

§ 11.-Property Which May Be Devised.-Bleckley v. Bleckley (1939), 189 

Ga. 47, 5 S. E. 2d 206; Byrd v. Goodman (1943), 195 Ga. 621, 25 S. E. 2d 34. 

'Generally, proceeds of life policy in which third person is named beneficiary belong exclusively to beneficiary as an individual and are not subject to administration as an estate of insured, but, where policy is held by creditor merely as security for debt of insured, creditor is entitled only to reimbursement and bound to account for balance to legal representative of insured.' 

Chapman v. Lipscomb-Ellis Co. (1942), 194 Ga. 640, 22 S. E. 2d 393 (2). "The proceeds of a life policy in which a third person is named as beneficiary belong exclusively to said beneficiary as an individual and are not subject to administration as an estate of insured." Wages v. Wages (1947), 202 Ga. 155, 42 S. E. 2d 481 (2).

One may not devise by will property which he has already conveyed by a valid oral agreement. Roseman v. Wright (1953), 209 Ga. 748, 76 S. E. 2d 7.

The trust having become executed, the testatrix had a devisable interest in her share of the trust property and could dispose of it by her will. Erskine v. 

Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 112, 126 S. E. 2d 755. 

§ 12.—Same-After-Acquired Property.—Linson v. Crapps (1948), 204 Ga. 

278, 49 S. E. 2d 522.

§ 13.-Same-Undevised Property.-Armstrong Junior College Commission v. 

Livesey (1940), 189 Ga. 825, 7 S. E. 2d 678. 

§ 15.-Contract to Make a Will.-Powell v. Bussell (1940), 64 Ga. App. 42, 

12 S. E. 2d 152; Mickle v. Moore (1941), 193 Ga. 150, 17 S. E. 2d 728; Sybilla v. Connally (1942), 66 Ga. App. 678, 18 S. E. 2d 783; Cagle v. Justus (1943), 196 Ga. 826, 28 S. E. 2d 255; Salmon v. McCrary (1944), 197 Ga. 281, 29 S. E. 

2d 58; Young v. Lewis (1944), 70 Ga. App. 627, 29 S. E. 2d 267; Roberts v. 

Wilson (1944), 198 Ga. 428, 31 S. E. 2d 707; Sparks v. Bell (1945), 198 Ga. 

827, 33 S. E. 2d 105; Mulligan v. Mulligan (1946), 201 Ga. 444, 39 S. E. 2d 

699; Matthews v. Blanos (1946), 201 Ga. 549, 40 S. E. 2d 715; Avary v. Avary (1947), 202 Ga. 22, 41 S. E. 2d 314; Griffin v. Driver (1947), 202 Ga. 111, 42 

S. E. 2d 368; Spinks v. Jenkins (1947), 75 Ga. App. 414, 43 S. E. 2d 586; 

Freeman v. Collier (1948), 204 Ga. 329, 50 S. E. 2d 61; Rogers v. Stamos (1948), 77 Ga. App. 285, 48 S. E. 2d 548; Hightower v. Scarborough (1949), 79 Ga. 

App. 342, 53 S. E. 2d 726; Holliday v. Pope (1949), 205 Ga. 301, 53 S. E. 2d 

350; Shadburn v. Tapp (1953), 209 Ga. 887, 77 S. E. 2d 7. "Contracts under which one of the contracting parties agrees with the other, for a valuable consideration, to make a will giving him property, real or personal, or both, have been sustained and enforced in America from the earliest times, and the validity of such contracts seems now to be settled beyond all doubt. And where the party in whose favor the will is to be made has performed of the contract and the other party dies without making the will, or leaves a will in which there is no compliance with the contract, or leaves a will which by its terms complies with the contract but is invalid for some reason, the disappointed party may apply to a court of equity for a decree against his estate enforcing the contract." Zachos v. C. & S. Natl. Bank (1957), 213 Ga. 619, 622, 100 S. E. 2d 418. "Contracts under which one of the contracting parties agrees with the other, for a valuable consideration, that he will make a will giving to the other property, either real or personal, have been sustained and enforced in America from the earliest times, and the validity of such contracts seems now to be beyond all doubt." Allen v. Bobo (1960), 215 Ga. 707, 710, 113 S. E. 2d 138. 

Contracts under which one of the contracting parties agrees with the other, for a valuable consideration, that he will make a will giving to the other property, either real or personal, have been sustained and enforced in America from the earliest times, and the validity of such contracts seems now to be beyond all doubt. However, a plaintiff seeking to enforce such a contract must prove the precise contract beyond a reasonable doubt. The contract must also be fair and just. The fairness of the contract is usually to be determined as of the date of its making. The persons seeking specific performance of such a contract must show, in addition to the contract, a substantial compliance with his part of the agreement. Rodgers v. Street (1960), 215 Ga. 643, 644, 112 S. E. 2d 598.

Equity will specifically enforce a parol agreement entered into between two persons, by the terms of which one is to perform certain services during the lifetime of the other, and the latter is to convey certain land at or before his death in consideration of such services, if the contract be definite and specific, based upon a full performance of consideration in the way of services performed on the one side and a failure or refusal to perform on the other. Allen v. Bobo (1960), 215 Ga. 707, 709, 113 S. E. 2d 138. "A party seeking specific performance of an alleged oral agreement to devise land in consideration of the performance of ordinary personal services,

SH must show the value of the land and the value of the services, in order that a court of equity may determine whether or not the contract is fair, just, and equitable; and a petition which fails to allege such values is subject to dismissal on general demurrer." Treadwell v. Treadwell (1960), 216 Ga. 156, 115 S. E. 2d 535.

If an alleged contract sued on is based on an oral agreement to convey or devise land in consideration of the performance of ordinary personal services, the petition must not only show that the contract is precise in its terms, but must also allege the value of such services and the value of the land or specific data from which such relative values can be determined. Exceptions to the general rule as to the necessity for averments as to the value of services may exist in cases involving virtual adoption or contracts between near relatives, where one goes into the home of the other agreeing to nurse and give the other personal, affectionate, and considerate attention, such as could not be readily be procured elsewhere, and where the value of such services could not be readily computed in money. Treadwell v. Treadwell (1960), 216 Ga. 156, 160, 115 S. E. 2d 535. However, the mere fact that the contracting parties are relatives is not enough to bring the case within the exception to the rule requiring allegations in regard to the values of the land and of the services rendered. Id. 

A contract or agreement that one shall have a child's part of an estate for services to be performed in taking care of another does not make such person an heir. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 895 (1), 114 S. E. 2d 12. "A contract by which one of the contracting parties agrees with the other that he will make a will containing a legacy fully compensating the latter for services rendered and to be rendered to the former during his lifetime is valid and enforceable. Upon the failure of one of the contracting parties in such a case to make the will containing an item providing compensation, a cause of action arises at his death in favor of the surviving party.” Zachos v. Zachos (1959), 214 Ga. 629, 106 S. E. 2d 775. "The cause of action for the breach of the contract arises at the death of the person promising to make the will." Zachos v. Zachos (1959), 214 Ga. 629, 106 S. E. 2d 775, citing Redfearn on Wills and Administration of Estates 

(Rev. ed.), page 27. And where a person who agrees to make a will for the benefit of another person is still in life, and where it was not agreed to make the will at a given date, no cause of action for specific performance can be maintained against the person so agreeing to make the will. Id. 

A contract by a person to adopt a child of another as his own is not selfoperating; heirship does not grow out of it. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 

Ga. 892, 895 (1), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

An unfulfilled promise to adopt another does not have the effect of constituting the promisee a child or heir of the promisor. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

The first essential of a contract for the adoption of a child, where no statutory adoption exists, is that it be made between persons competent to contract for the disposition of the child, and be based upon a sufficient legal consideration. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409, 412 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

Where husband and wife enter into a joint agreement to adopt a third person as their child, both are necessary parties to a proceeding to enforce the contract. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409 (3), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

Where parties agreeing to the adoption of an infant have no authority or legal right to assent to such adoption, the agreement is not a valid and binding contract, nor is it capable of being enforced where it is made upon a condition that, due to no fault of the prospective parents, was never performed by the opposite parties to the agreement. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

A petition which alleged a parol contract to adopt certain children, and a relinquishment of the rights of their natural parents, accompanied by a virtual though not a statutory adoption, said adoption being acted upon by all the parties during the obligors' life, a breach of which is alleged, and the refusal of the administratrix of the obligors' estate to recognize the plaintiffs as the children of the deceased, set forth a cause of action to enforce a parol contract to adopt the plaintiffs as the children of the defendant administratrix's intestate. Hollis v. Maxwell (1959), 215 Ga. 483, 111 S. E. 2d 72.

A parol agreement by a person to adopt the child of another as his own, accompanied by a virtual though not a statutory adoption, and acted upon by all parties concerned for many years during the obligor's life, may be enforced in equity upon the death of the obligor, by decreeing the child entitled as a child to the property of the obligor, undisposed of by will. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 895 (2), 114 S. E. 2d 12. "Contracts to adopt and contracts to devise may be enforced in an action for specific performance. 

"Where infant girl's mother, who had full parental authority over her by reason of the desertion of the girl by the father, surrendered the girl and all parental rights to a third person for the purpose of having the girl adopted by the third person, so that the mother thereby lost the parental rights, including the right to the companionship and services of the girl, and third person in turn agreed to adopt, care for, and rear the girl and leave to her one-half of his estate by will, a mutually binding and enforceable 'contract' arose. Savannah Bank & Trust Co. v. Wolff (1940), 191 Ga. 111, 11 S. E. 2d 766 (1, 2). "Where a mother surrenders possession of her infant girl to a third person, for the purpose of having the child adopted by him, in consideration of an alleged promise by the wife of said third person to leave to the mother her entire estate by will, such contract is void as against public policy." Savannah 

Bank & Trust Co. v. Hanley (1951), 208 Ga. 34, 65 S. E. 2d 26. "Where considered on general demurrer, the allegations by a wife that, while living separately from her husband, she agreed to relinquish valid grounds for divorce and resume her marital relations with him, and that she did so, show sufficient consideration for the husband's promise to leave her all his property and to deed her their home." Holsomback v. Caldwell (1962), 218 Ga. 393, 128 S. E. 2d 47. "Allegations that the petitioner's wife, for several years prior to her death, had on numerous occasions told the petitioner that she was going to leave her property to him at her death, and that, relying thereon, the petitioner made valuable improvements on the property, fail to set out a cause of action for specific performance of an oral contract to convey real and other property, as no agreement on the part of the wife to leave her property to him in consideration of what he might do is alleged.” Charles v. Simmons (1960), 215 

Ga. 794 (2), 113 S. E. 2d 604.

In a suit by a husband and his wife against himself and another as co-executors of an estate, seeking to require the executors to specifically perform an

alleged contract between the plaintiffs and the testatrix, whereby the testatrix agreed to will a certain house and lot to them in consideration of their rendering services to her, and the testatrix by her will devised the property to others, the plaintiff-husband, having qualified as a co-executor, was estopped from attempting to enforce the alleged contract. Spratlin v. Spratlin (1960), 216 Ga. 27, 114 S. E. 2d 370. "The petition did not state a cause of action for specific performance of an alleged oral contract to make a will devising the property of the deceased, in consideration of services to be performed by the petitioner, and it was error to overrule the general demurrers to the petition." Jackson v. Copeland (1961), 217 Ga. 420, 122 S. E. 2d 573. "The petition and the evidence submitted upon the trial did not bear out the defendant's contention that the plaintiff failed to show the value of her services and the value of the property the deceased was to devise to her." 

Daniel v. Weeks (1961), 217 Ga. 388 (2), 122 S. E. 2d 564.

Where a petition affirmatively shows that the petitioner's debtor bequeathed to him a life estate in certain realty in consideration of the personal services which the latter rendered the former and his wife during their lifetime; that the property so bequeathed to him had a value of $1,178.28; that he accepted the property so bequeathed to him; and that he has retained it and now has possession of it under the terms of his debtor's will, such allegations show accord and satisfaction of the claim or demand declared on; and since they do, the petition stated no cause of action against the defendants as the legal representatives of the testator's estate, and was properly dismissed on general demurrer. Matthews v. Sprayberry (1960), 216 Ga. 40, 41, 114 S. E. 2d 516.

A petition to enjoin further proceedings to probate a will, and other relief, should have been filed in the county of the residence of the defendant rather than in the county of the probate proceedings, as petitions for equitable relief must be filed in the county of residence of one of the defendants against whom substantial relief is sought, except in cases of injunction to stay pending proceedings, which may be filed in the county where the proceedings shall be pending provided no relief is prayed as to matters not included in such litigation. Spiller v. Chapman (1960), 216 Ga. 456, 457, 117 S. E. 2d 536. "The measure of damages for breach of contract to make will compensating promisee for services is the value of property promised to be devised." Gilmore v. Hammock (1945), 72 Ga. App. 35, 32 S. E. 2d 844 (5).

Where decedent contracted to devise more land than he owned, and the other party has performed and is willing to accept the land decedent actually had plus damages for the remainder, equity will so require specific performance. 

Bowles v. White (1950), 206 Ga. 433, 57 S. E. 2d 547.

Where eighty-four year-old man agreed to make will to plaintiff if she would look after him and allow him to live in her home until he died, plaintiff is entitled to specific performance against the executor where the precise contract has been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Mann v. Mosely (1951), 208 Ga. 

420, 67 S. E. 2d 128.

Where a wife, before her death, agreed to will to her husband her entire estate if he would return to the marital domicile and resume the marital status, which he did, but which agreement his wife failed to perform before her death, the husband has a cause of action against the deceased wife's executor. First 

Nat. Bank of Atlanta v. DeLoach (1953), 87 Ga. App. 639, 74 S. E. 2d 740.

"An attorney at law is incompetent, under Code § 38-1605, to testify as a witness, in a suit against the administrator of his client's estate by a third person to require the administrator to perform specifically an oral contract, allegedly entered into between the client and a third person, as to the oral instructions given to him in drafting the client's will, which was never executed by the client." DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255 (2), 109 S. E. 2d 777. 

A person in possession of land, who has fully performed his part of a valid contract to render services to another upon a promise that the latter will, as a consideration for the services, make a will giving the property to him, is in the same position as one who is in possession of land for which he has paid the purchase-price in full, and consequently holds a perfect equity. Under such circumstances, such contracts do not fall within the operation of the statute of frauds, and may, therefore, be enforced. Zachos v. C. & S. Natl. Bank (1957), 213 Ga. 619, 623, 100 S. E. 2d 418. 

§ 16.-Codicil.-Buchanan v. Nicholson (1941), 192 Ga. 754, 16 S. E. 2d 743. 

$ 18.-Definitions.-Robinson v. Haisten (1940), 63 Ga. App. 676, 11 S. H. 

2d 802. 

§ 18a. Filing of Wills.-Acts 1958, page 354, amended Code § 24-1804, by adding a new paragraph 12 to said section, which amendment makes provision for the filing of wills of persons still in life. Said amendment is as follows: 

"12. To Keep and Maintain Facilities for the Filing of Wills of 

Persons Still in Life: Any person having made a will may file it in the office of the ordinary of the county of his residence, and the ordinary shall maintain a docket in which he shall register the said will, the date on which deposited in his office, and the date of withdrawal of said will by the person making the same, or other person as the case may be, if the same be withdrawn. Such files shall be confidential and no person other than the person depositing the same or his legal representative, or his attorney in fact, shall have access to said file prior to the death of the person making and depositing said will. The docket maintained by the ordinary shall be public as are other dockets in such office. Nothing in this paragraph shall be construed so as to prohibit any person from revoking such will by the execution of a subsequent will or to change the ambulatory nature of the will of any person. § 20.-Definitions. Only two witnesses are now required for a nuncupative will. Code § 113-502, as amended by Acts 1958, page 659. 

§ 21.-Requisites to Validity of Nuncupative Will.-Biggers v. Gladin (1948), 

204 Ga. 481, 50 S. E. 2d 585.

Only two witnesses are now required for a nuncupative will. Code § 113-502, as amended by Acts 1958, page 659. 

Code § 113-502, providing the requisites for nuncupative wills, was amended by Acts 1958, page 659, and substituted in lieu thereof an entirely new section 

"113-502. No nuncupative will shall be good unless proved by the oaths of at least two competent witnesses who were present in

the making thereof; nor unless it shall be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the same, bade the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; nor unless such nuncupative will was made in the time of the last sickness of the deceased."

It should be noted that this section as amended omitted the requirements that the nuncupative will must have been made in the habitation or dwelling of the testator, or where he had been a resident for a space of ten days or more next before making such will, except where such person was surprised or taken sick, being away from his own home, and died before he returned to the place of his dwelling. § 24. In Time of His Last Sickness."-Where caveat was filed in proceedings to probate a nuncupative will which was made by testator forty days before he died of lung cancer and just before he entered hospital for treatment where he remained until a few days before his death, whether testator complied with all the statutory requirements as to execution of the nuncupative will was a question for the jury to decide. Durden v. Henderson (1957), 212 Ga. 

807, 96 S. E. 2d 362. § 25.-Witnesses to Nuncupative Will.-Only two witnesses are now required for a nuncupative will. Code § 113-502, as amended by Acts 1958, page 659. § 26.-Form of Nuncupative Will.-Only two witnesses are now required for a nuncupative will. Code § 113-502, as amended by Acts 1958, page 659. 

Code § 113-502, by Acts 1958, page 659, was stricken in its entirety and a new section was enacted in lieu thereof. The new section omitted the requirement that it was necessary for the maker of a nuncupative will to be in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he had been a resident for the space of 10 days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person was surprised or taken sick, being away from his own home, and died before he returned to the place of his dwelling. It follows, therefore, that when the nuncupative will is reduced to writing as required by Code § 113-503, the written will no longer is required to set forth these details. 

§ 27.-Probate of Nuncupative Will.-Acts 1958, page 664, amended Code 

§ 113-617, relating to the probate of nuncupative wills, by striking the section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "113-617. Application for probate of a nuncupative will shall be made before the court within six months after the death of the testator. The petition to probate a nuncupative will, in addition to other necessary averments, shall set forth the information required in a petition to probate a will in solemn form. The petition shall be verified and shall conclude with a prayer for the issuance of letters testamentary.”

Acts 1958, page 664, amended Code § 113-618, relating to the notice to be given upon the application for the probate of a nuncupative will, by striking the section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "113-618. Upon all applications for probate of nuncupative wills, the notice required on probate of other wills in solemn form shall

be given to the heirs at law. No acknowledgment of service in the case of nuncupative wills shall serve to expedite the probate thereof to any date prior to the date when the hearing on the application in due course is to be held."

A nuncupative will may now be proved by the oaths of only two witnesses. 

Code § 113-502, as amended by Acts 1958, page 659. 

In Denmark v. Rushing (1951), 208 Ga. 557, 67 S. E. 2d 766, it was held that where an essential witness to an alleged oral will is the sole beneficiary under the will, the devise to the witness is void, and the will inoperative, overruling the rule laid down in Smith v. Crotty, 112 Ga. 905, 38 S. E. 110.

The effect of the holding in Denmark v. Rushing, is that, where a witness to an oral will is also a beneficiary that such witness cannot take under the will. 

The witness should be competent, but the legacy or devise shall be void. 

§ 30.-Characteristics of Nuncupative Wills in Georgia. Since Acts 1958, page 659, amending Code § 113-502, only two witnesses are required for a nuncupative will for it to be valid. 

It should be noted that the Acts of 1958, page 659, amending Code § 113-502, omitted from the original section the requirement that a nuncupative will must be made in the habitation or dwelling of the testator, or where the testator had been resident for a space of ten days or more next before making such will, except where such person was surprised or taken sick, being away from his own home, and died before he returned to the place of dwelling. It would seem, therefore, that under this code section, as amended, that a nuncupative may be made at any place where the testator happens to be.

§ 31.-Who May Make a Will.-Moore v. Segars (1941), 192 Ga. 190, 14 S. E. 

2d 752; Smith v. Davis (1947), 203 Ga. 175, 45 S. E. 2d 609. "The weak have the same rights as the strong-minded to dispose of their property by will, and anything less than a total absence of mind does not destroy that capacity. If the testator has sufficient intellect to enable him to have a rational desire as to the disposition of his property, this is sufficient. 

And the condition of the testator's mind at the time of the execution of the will determines whether he can make a valid will." MeTyre v. King (1959), 215 Ga. 417, 420 (4), 110 S. E. 2d 651. § 37.-Mental Capacity.-Morgan v. Bell (1939), 189 Ga. 432, 5 S. E. 2d 897; 

Thompson v. Mitchell (1941), 192 Ga. 750, 16 S. E. 2d 540; Hopkins v. Brumbelow (1943), 195 Ga. 388, 24 S. E. 2d 318; Everitt v. LaSpeyre (1943), 195 Ga. 377, 24 S. E. 2d 381; Espy v. Preston (1945), 199 Ga. 608, 34 S. E. 

2d 705; Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 50 S. E. 2d 617; Beman v. Stem- 

Bridge 1955), 211 Ga. 274, 85 S. E. 2d 434. "If testator has sufficient intellect to enable him to have a decided and rational desire as to disposition of his property, testator possesses 'testamentary capacity.' Manley v. Combs (1944), 197 Ga. 768, 30 S. E. 2d 485 (5); 

Leventhal v. Baumgartner (1950), 207 Ga. 412, 61 S. E. 2d 924. 299

While under undue influence "whereby the will of another is substituted for the wishes of the testator' will invalidate a will, a testator can not be said to lack testamentary capacity because he executes a will under undue influence. Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "A person has testamentary capacity who understands the nature of a testament or will, viz., that it is a disposition of property to take effect after death, and who is capable of remembering generally the property subject to disposition and the persons related to him by the ties of blood and of affection, and also of conceiving and expressing by words, written or spoken, or by signs, or by both, any intelligible scheme of disposition. If the testator has sufficient intellect to enable him to have a decided and rational desire as to the disposition of his property, this will suffice." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 

Ga. 27, 29, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "While it is true that the law provides that absence of testamentary capacity will invalidate a will, and the law also provides that where the will of one wielding undue influence or practicing fraud or other act upon the testator is substituted for the will of the testator himself, the testament will likewise be invalidated, yet neither of these rules is directed to the abridgment of the right of the citizen to make a will. The testamentary-capacity rule does not abridge this right, but simply recognizes the inability of one who comes within the operation of the rule to exercise the right which he unquestionably has. The undue-influence rule not only does not challenge the right, but contemplates added protection of that right, and works destruction to any disposition by will and testament of property by any person other than the person entitled to make disposition thereof." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "The admission in the present case that the testator had testamentary capacity at the time of the execution of the will eliminated any issue made by the caveat that the testator was laboring under any mental disability to execute the will, including monomania from which the will resulted; but did not eliminate the issue of undue influence and mistake of fact." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "We conclude that the admission of 'testamentary capacity' of the testator by the caveatrix eliminated any consideration of the ground of caveat that the testator was afflicted with monomania from which the will resulted." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "The fact that the will is ungrammatical or inaccurate does not of itself establish mental incapacity to execute a will." McGahee v. Phillips (1954) 

211 Ga. 118, 84 S. E. 2d 19. 

§ 40.-Insanity.-Espy v. Preston (1945), 199 Ga. 608, 34 S. E. 2d 705. 

§ 41.-Monomania and Insane Delusions.-Boland v. Aycock (1940), 191 Ga. 

327, 12 S. E. 2d 319; Brumbelow v. Hopkins (1944), 197 Ga. 247, 29 S. E. 2d 

42; Yarbrough v. Yarbrough (1947), 202 Ga. 391, 43 S. E. 2d 329; Culpepper v. Bower (1948), 203 Ga. 784, 48 S. E. 2d 369. "Our Code recognizes such a thing as monomania as affecting testamentary capacity. But it means a mental disease, not merely the unreasonable conduct of a sane person. It is a species of insanity. . . It is not every delusion which will deprive one of testamentary capacity. It must be an insane delusion.

The subject-matter of the insane delusion must have no foundation in fact, and must spring from a diseased condition of mind." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757.

In considering the question of monomania the amount of intellect necessary to constitute testamentary capacity is that which is necessary to enable the party to have a decided and rational desire as to the disposition of his property. A decided and rational desire does not exist where the testator is partially insane, and the will is in any way the effect or result of that insanity. 

Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "We conclude that the admission of 'testamentary capacity' of the testator by the caveatrix eliminated any consideration of the ground of caveat that the testator was afflicted with monomania from which the will resulted." 

Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757.

The mere dislike of certain persons, or ill feelings towards them, causing their exclusion from a will, is not monomania. Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 

Ga. 480, 485, 128 S. E. 2d 744. "The attesting witnesses having testified that at the time of the execution of the will testatrix was of sound and disposing mind and memory, and there being no evidence that testatrix was suffering from monomania, the court properly directed a verdict for propounder on the ground of the caveat based on monomania." Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 744. "The admission in the present case that the testator had testamentary capacity at the time of the execution of the will eliminated any issue made by the caveat that the testator was laboring under any mental disability to execute the will, including monomania from which the will resulted; but did not eliminate the issue of undue influence and mistake of fact." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757.

§ 46. Reasonableness and Unreasonableness.-Crutchfield v. McCallie (1939).

Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 S. E.

Where probate of a will is contested for incapacity of the maker, or for fraud or undue influence, it is proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable and accord with the state of the testator's family relations, or to the contrary. The source from which the property disposed of by the will came into decedent's possession may be shown, as well as the reasonableness of the provisions of the will. Worrell v. § 47.-Proof of Mental Capacity.-Morgan v. Bell (1939), 189 Ga. 432, 5 

S. E. 2d 897; Boland v. Aycock (1940), 191 Ga. 327, 12 S. E. 2d 319; Scott v. 

Gibson (1942), 194 Ga. 503, 22 S. E. 2d 51; Hopkins v. Brumbelow (1943), 195 Ga. 388, 24 S. E. 2d 318; Fowler v. Fowler (1943), 197 Ga. 53, 28 S. E. 

2d 458; Davis v. Aultman (1945), 199 Ga. 129, 33 S. E. 2d 317; Fehn v. Shaw

(1945), 199 Ga. 747, 35 S. E. 2d 253; Spivey v. Spivey (1947), 202 Ga. 644. 

44 S. E. 2d 224; Allen v. Heys (1949), 204 Ga. 635, 51 S. E. 2d 417; Bassett v. Hunter (1949), 205 Ga. 417, 53 S. E. 2d 909; Whitfield v. Pitts (1949), 205 

Ga. 259, 53 S. E. 2d 549; Orr v. Orr (1951), 208 Ga. 431, 67 S. E. 2d 209; Hodo v. Jenkins (1952), 209 Ga. 4, 70 S. E. 2d 452. "It is undoubtedly true that where a will is attacked upon the ground of the mental incapacity of the testatrix, and of undue influence in the procurement of it, it is always proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable, and in accord with the state of testatrix's 'family relations or the contrary.''' Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 S. E. 

2d 89. "Where there is an issue as to the testamentary capacity of the testator, as in this case, the opinion as to the sanity of the testator may be given in evidence by a witness who attested the will without first stating the facts upon which he bases such opinion." Brooker v. Brooker (1951), 208 Ga. 387, 67 S. E. 2d 117. "What is mental capacity to make a will is a question of law. On the trial of an issue of devisat vel non, whether the alleged testatrix had mental capacity to make a will at the time of signing the paper is a question for decision by the jury, and a witness can not testify as to such legal conclusion." Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16.

An adjudication of insanity of the deceased before the execution of a will raises a presumption of incapacity to make a will. While such presumption is rebuttable, it is sufficient to raise a question for the jury. Belk v. Colleas (1950), 207 Ga. 328, 61 S. E. 2d 464.

Testamentary capacity is to be determined by the condition of the testator's mind at the time the will was executed. Nash v. Poss (1956), 212 Ga. 590, 593, 94 S. E. 2d 409. "Where a condition of incapacity is shown to exist prior to the execution of a will, and it is further shown that this condition continues for a period of time subsequent to the date of execution, it is evidence showing incapacity at the time of execution.'' Ware v. Hill (1952), 209 Ga. 214, 71 S. E. 2d 630.

Where two surviving attesting witnesses make a prima facie case for probate of will by their positive testimony that, at the time of the execution thereof, the testator acted freely and voluntarily, and was of sound mind, a verdict for the propounder was demanded. Nash v. Poss (1956), 212 Ga. 590, 94 S. E. 

2d 409. "A person has testamentary capacity who understands the nature of a testament or will, viz., that it is a disposition of property to take effect after death, and who is capable of remembering generally the property subject to disposition and the persons related to him by the ties of blood and of affection, and also of conceiving and expressing by words, written or spoken, or by signs, or by both, any intelligible scheme of disposition. If the testator has sufficient intellect to enable him to have a decided and rational desire as to the disposition of his property, this will suffice." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 

Ga. 27, 29, 120 S. E. 2d 757. 'The weak have the same rights as the strong-minded to dispose of their property by will, and anything less than a total absence of mind does not destroy that capacity. If the testator has sufficient intellect to enable him to have a rational desire as to the disposition of his property, this is sufficient.

And the condition of the testator's mind at the time of the execution of the will determines whether he can make a valid will." McTyre v. King (1959), 215 Ga. 417, 420 (4), 110 S. E. 2d 651.

Where the evidence did not make an issue as to the mental capacity of the testator to make a will, and it was not erroneous for the trial judge to direct the jury to find that the testator had testamentary capacity. Gornto v. Gornto (1961), 217 Ga. 136, 141, 121 S. E. 2d 139. "On the question of devisavit vel non and revocavit vel non declarations of the testator 'made prior to or at the time of the execution of the will or its revocation are clearly admissible.'''Sheffield v. Sheffield (1959), 215 Ga. 546, 551, 111 S. E. 2d 218. "Where the question is revocavit vel non, parol evidence, as to the acts and declarations of the testator, are admissible although made at any time between the making of the will and the death of the testator." King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 349, 110 S. E. 2d 772. "Evidence is properly admitted which tends to establish mental incapacity of the testator prior or subsequently to the execution of a will, as illustrating the condition of the testator's mind. But where it is sought to establish testamentary incapacity by such evidence, it is not sufficient to controvert the positive testimony of the subscribing witnesses, unless it would be proof of testamentary incapacity at the time the will was executed." Gornto v. Gornto (1961), 217 Ga. 136, 139 (1), 121 S. E. 2d 139. "The testimony of the subscribing witnesses having made a prima facie case of testamentary capacity for the propounder, and caveator having offered no evidence tending to show incapacity, the trial court propertly directed a verdict for propounder on this issue.'' Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480, 485, 128 S. E. 2d 744. 

§ 48.-Same-Opinions of Witnesses.-Scott v. Gibson (1942), 194 Ga. 503, 

22 S. E. 2d 51; Lyons v. Bloodworth (1945), 199 Ga. 44, 33 S. E. 2d 314. "What is mental capacity to make a will is a question of law. On the trial of an issue of devisat vel non, whether the alleged testatrix had mental capacity to make a will at the time of signing the paper is a question for decision by the jury, and a witness can not testify as to such legal conclusion." 

Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16. "The opinions of subscribing witnesses to a will, as to sanity of testator, are admissible, without stating facts upon which opinions are founded. Code 

1933, § 38-1708." Morgan v. Bell (1939), 189 Ga. 432, 5 S. E. 2d 897 (2); 

Smith v. Davis (1947), 203 Ga. 175, 43 S. E. 2d 609; Brooker v. Brooker (1951), 208 Ga. 387, 67 S. E. 2d 117; Reid v. Wilson (1951), 208 Ga. 235, 65 S. E. 2d 913.

Where two surviving attesting witnesses make a prima facie case for probate of will by their positive testimony that, at the time of the execution thereof, the testator acted freely and voluntarily, and was of sound mind, a verdict for the propounder was demanded. Nash v. Poss (1956), 212 Ga. 590, 94 S. E. 

2d 409.

Where a caveat raised two grounds of objection, mental capacity and undue influence, the admission over objection of testimony of one of the caveators, that the will offered for probate did not contain the same provisions as the will read to witness and other relatives by the propounder a day or two after the death of the testatrix, was held to be prejudicial error. This was so held because there was nothing in the pleadings raising the issue that the will

offered for probate was not in fact the will made by the testatrix. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16. 

§ 49.-Undue Influence Generally.-Marlin v. Hill (1941), 192 Ga. 434, 15 

S. E. 2d 473; Moreland v. Word (1953), 209 Ga. 463, 74 S. E. 2d 82; Northwestern University v. Crisp (1955), 211 Ga. 636, 86 S. E. 2d 26. "While it is true that the law provides that absence of testamentary capacity will invalidate a will, and the law also provides that where the will of one wielding undue influence or practicing fraud or other act upon the testator is substituted for the will of the testator himself, the testament will likewise be invalidated, yet neither of these rules is directed to the abridgement of the right of the citizen to make a will. The testamentary-capacity rule does not abridge this right, but simply recognizes the inability of one who comes within the operation of the rule to exercise the right which he unquestionably has. The undue-influence rule not only does not challenge the right, but contemplates added protection of that right, and works destruction to any disposition by will and testament of property by any person other than the person entitled to make disposition thereof." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 

2d 757.

While under undue influence "whereby the will of another is substituted for the wishes of the testator" will invalidate a will, a testator can not be said to lack testamentary capacity because he executes a will under undue influence. 

Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 30, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "The trial court was authorized to conclude that the evidence did not contain sufficient facts of mental incapacity of the testator to justify the opinion of the witness that he was insame, and there was no error in excluding from the evidence such conclusions." Martin v. Baldwin (1959), 215 Ga. 293, 294 (5), 110 S. E. 2d 344. 

§ 50.-Undue Influence Defined. Scott v. Wimberly (1939), 188 Ga. 148, 3 

S. E. 2d 71; Orr v. Blalock (1943), 195 Ga. 863, 25 S. E. 2d 668; Butler v. 

Lashley (1944), 197 Ga. 461, 29 S. E. 2d 508.

The influence must be what the law regards as undue influence; such influence that is obtained by flattery, inportunity, superiority of will, mind, or character, which would give dominion over the will to such an extent as to destroy free agency, or constrain one to do against his will what he is unable to refuse. Such is the kind of influence which the law condemns as undue. 

Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 559, 50 S. E. 2d 617. "The 'undue influence' which the statute contemplates as a ground to invalidate a properly executed will must be such as amounts to fraud, deceit force, or coercion, destroying the testator's free agency, and it must also be operative at the time the will is executed, and not merely at some other time. 

Code 1933, § 113-208." Boland v. Aycock (1940), 191 Ga. 327, 12 S. E 

2d 319 (2); Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 50 S. E. 2d 617; Ehlers v. 

Rheinberger (1948), 204 Ga. 226, 49 S. E. 2d 535. "Fraud is a distinct head of objection to the validity of a will, from importunity and undue influence; usually they are the very opposites of each other. 

Both are equally destructive of the validity of a will." Stephens v. Brady (1952), 209 Ga. 428, 73 S. E. 2d 182.

A will by its very nature must be voluntary, and anything which destroys freedom of volition whereby will of another is substituted for that of the

testator will invalidate the will. Northwestern University v. Crisp (1955), 211 Ga. 636, 86 S. E. 2d 26. "Code § 113-106 provides that one may bequeath his entire estate to strangers to the exclusion of his wife and children but in such cases the will should be closely scrutinized, and upon the slightest evidence of the aberration of intellect, or collusion or fraud, or any undue influence or unfair dealing, probate should be refused." Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53.

Fraud which will invalidate a will must be fraud which operates upon the testator, i.e., a procurement of the execution of the will by misrepresentations made to him. It exists only when it is shown that the testator relied on such a representation and was deceived. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53.

To invalidate a will on the ground of undue influence the evidence must show that such influence amounted to fear, force, overpersuasion or coercion to the extent of destroying the free will power of the testator and in effect make the will the mental offspring of another and it must be shown that the undue influence was operating on the mind of the testator at the time the will was executed and published. Evidence which does no more than show opportunity for exerting influence falls short of showing the exercise of undue influence required to invalidate the will. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 

Ga. 369, 370 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53. "Undue influence, to invalidate a will, must amount to force or fear-must, in effect, make the will the mental offispring of some other person, and must be operative on the mind of the testator at the time the will is executied. It must destroy the free agency of the testator and constrain him to do what is against his will, but what he is unable to refuse." Gornto v. Gornto (1961), 217 Ga. 136, 142, 121 S. E. 2d 139. 

§ 51.-Undue Influence-Burden of Proof.-Marlin v. Hill (1941), 192 Ga. 

434, 15 S. E. 2d 473; Orr v. Blalock (1943), 195 Ga. 863, 25 S. E. 2d 668; 

Shaw v. Fehn (1943), 196 Ga. 661, 27 S. E. 2d 406.

To invalidate a will on the ground of undue influence the evidence must show that such influence amounted to fear, force, overpersuasion or coersion to the extent of destroying the free will power of the testator and in effect make the will the mental offspring of another and it must be shown that the undue influence was operating on the mind of the testator at the time the will was executed and published. Evidence which does no more than show opportunity for exerting influence falls short of showing the exercise of undue influence required to invalidate a will. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 

369, 370, 128 S. E. 2d 53. 

§ 52.-Proof-Admissibility of Evidence.-Orr v. Blalock (1943), 195 Ga. 

863, 25 S. E. 2d 668; Shaw v. Fehn (1943), 196 Ga. 661, 27 S. E. 2d 406; 

Fowler v. Fowler (1943), 197 Ga. 53, 28 S. E. 2d 458; Brumbelow v. Hopkins (1944), 197 Ga. 247, 29 S. E. 2d 42; Norman v. Hubbard (1948), 203 Ga. 530, 47 S. E. 2d 574.

Where probate of a will is contested for incapacity of the maker, or for fraud or undue influence, it is proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable and accord with the state of the testator's family

relations, or to the contrary. The source from which the property disposed of by the will came into decedent's possession may be shown, as well as the reasonableness of the provisions of the will. Worrell v. Ganns (1959), 214 Ga. 

708 (3), 107 S. E. 2d 186.

Undue influence may be proved by circumstantial evidence. Bowman v. 

Bowman (1949), 205 Ga. 796, 55 S. E. 2d 298; Moreland v. Word (1953), 209 

Ga. 463, 74 S. E. 2d 82. "A very wide range of testimony is permissible on the issue of undue influence. This is due to the fact that undue influence seldom can be shown except by circumstantial evidence. It results from the circumstances and surroundings of the testator and his associations with the person or persons exercising the undue influence. For this reason it is proper on this issue, to consider the testator's dealings and associations with the beneficiaries; his habits, motives, feelings; his strength or weakness of character; his confidential, family, social, and business relations; the reasonableness of the will; his mental and physical condition at the time the will was made; his manner and conduct; and generally every fact which will throw light on the issue raised by the charge of undue influence." Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 840, 102 S. E. 2d 16. "It is undoubtedly true that where a will is attacked upon the ground of the mental incapacity of the testatrix, and of undue influence in the procurement of it, it is always proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable, and in accord with the state of the testatrix's 'family relations or the contrary.'"' Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 

S. E. 2d 89.

To be sufficient to invalidate a will on the ground of undue influence, the evidence must show that such influence amounted to fear, force, overpersuasion, or coercion, to the extent of destroying the free agency and will power of the testator, and in effect made the will the mental offspring of another. Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 559, 50 S. E. 2d 617.

And it must be shown that the undue influence was operative on the mind of the testator at the time the will was actually executed and published. Id. "Evidence which does no more than show opportunity to influence falls short of 'undue influence' as defined in the Code, § 113-208. 

Orr v. 

Blalock (1943), 195 Ga. 863, 866, 25 S. E. 2d 668; Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 559, 50 S. E. 2d 617; Kellar v. Edwards (1959), 214 Ga. 633, 106 S. E. 2d 787.

Where a caveat raised two grounds of objection, mental capacity and undue influence, the admission over objection of testimony of one of the caveators, that the will offered for probate did not contain the same provisions as the will read to witness and other relatives by the propounder a day or two after the death of the testatrix, was held to be prejudicial error. This was so held because there was nothing in the pleadings raising the issue that the will offered for probate was not in fact the will made by the testatrix. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16. "While undue influence may be proved by circumstances, merely to show an opportunity to exert it by one who occupies a confidential relation to the alleged testator, and who receives a substantial benefit under the instrument sought to be propounded, is not sufficient to prove it." Gornto v. Gornto (1961), 217 Ga. 136, 142, 121 S. E. 2d 139.

Where the beneficiaries of the will were not present when the testator gave instructions as to the provisions of his will, nor were they present at the time of its execution, the circumstances relied on by the caveators, merely show an opportunity for the beneficiaries to exercise under influence, which might continue to operate on the mind of the testator until the will was executed, were insufficient to make an issue as to undue influence. Gornto v. Gornto (1961), 217 Ga. 136, 142, 121 S. E. 2d 139. "While equity raises the presumption of undue influence where persons standing in a confidential of fiduciary relationship with the donor or grantor derive a possible benefit from a deed, gift, contract, or the like, since the law implies a condition of superiority to such party, yet where the evidence on the trial is in conflict, it is a question for the jury to determine, and there being ample evidence to support the verdict, the court did not err in denying the motion on the general grounds of the motion for new trial." McGahee v. 

Walden (1960), 216 Ga. 352, 353 (3), 116 S. E. 2d 559. "On the trial of a proceeding to probate in solemn form, the evidence demanding a finding that the will was not executed as a result of (1) undue influence, (2) fraud, (3) misrepresentation, or (4) mistake of fact, as asserted in the caveat, it was not error to direct a verdict in favor of the propounder.” 

Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53. 

§ 53.-Inadmissible Evidence.-Bloodworth v. McCook (1941), 193 Ga. 53, 

17 S. E. 2d 73.

Where a caveat raised two grounds of objection, mental capacity and undue influence, the admission over objection of testimony of one of the caveators, that the will offered for probate did not contain the same provisions as the will read to witness and other relatives by the propounder a day or two after the death of the testatrix, was held to be prejudicial error. This was so held because there was nothing in the pleadings raising the issue that the will offered for probate was not in fact the will made by the testatrix. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16. § 54.-Hearsay Evidence-Declarations.-Where a will is sought to be invalidated on the ground of fraud or undue influence, the declarations of the testator tending to show the state of the testator's mind are admissible on these issues, but are not admissible for the purpose of showing the truth of the facts stated by him. Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 33, 120 S. E. 2d 757. 

§ 55.-Inequalities or Injustice as Evidence.-Shaw v. Fehn (1943), 196 Ga. 

661, 27 S. E. 2d 406. "It is undoubtedly true that where a will is attacked upon the ground of the mental incapacity of the testatrix, and of undue influence in the procurement of it, it is always proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable, and in accord with the state of the testatrix's 'family relations or the contrary.''' Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681 (101 S. E. 

2d 89. 

§ 56.-Confidential Relations.-Marlin v. Hill (1941), 192 Ga. 434, 15 S. E. 

2d 473; Fowler v. Fowler (1943), 197 Ga. 53, 28 S. E. 2d 458.

A person standing in confidential relation to another is not prohibited from exercising any influence whatever to obtain a benefit to himself. The influence

must be what the law regards as undue influence; such influence that is obtained by flattery, importunity, superiority of will, mind, or character, which would give dominion over the will to such an extent as to destroy free agency, or constrain one to do against his will what he is unable to refuse. Such is the kind of influence which the law condemns as undue. Bailey v. Bailey (1948), 204 Ga. 556, 559, 50 S. E. 2d 617. "While equity raises the presumption of undue influence where persons standing in a confidential or fiduciary relationship with the donor or grantor derive a possible benefit from a deed, gift, contract, or the like, since the law implies a condition of superiority to such party, yet where the evidence on the trial is in conflict, it is a question for the jury to determine, and there being ample evidence to support the verdict, the court did not err in denying the motion on the general grounds of the motion for new trial." McGahee v. 

Walden (1960), 216 Ga. 352, 353 (3), 116 S. E. 2d 559. § 58.-Same-Other Relations.-"It is undoubtedly true that where a will is attacked upon the ground of the mental incapacity of the testatrix, and of undue influence in the procurement of it, it is always proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable, and in accord with the state of the testatrix's 'family relations or the contrary.'" Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 S. E. 2d 89. "Unless otherwise provided by statute, communications, by a client to the attorney who drafted his will, in respect to that document and transactions between them leading up to its execution, are not privileged, after the client's death, in a suit between devisees under the will and heirs at law, or other parties who all claim under him. The principal reason is that the general rule is designated for the protection of the client, and it is deemed not for the interests of the testator, in a controversy between the parties, all of whom claim under him, to have those declarations and transactions excluded which promote a proper fulfillment of his will. Also a witness to a will, although attorney for the testator, is permitted to disclose everything which he knew concerning his attestation and the circumstances surrounding and leading up to it." DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255, 260, 109 S. E. 2d 777.

An exception to the common-law rule of privileged communications is that communications by a client to the attorney who prepared his will, in respect to that document, and transactions occurring between them and leading up to its execution, are not, after the client's death, within the protection of the rule, in a suit between the testator's devisees and heirs at law, or other persons who claim under them. DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255, 259, 109

S. E. 2d 777. 

§ 61.-Pleading.-Bloodworth v. McCook (1941), 193 Ga. 53, 17 S. E. 2d 73. 

§ 63.-Signature of Testator.-Crutchfield v. McCallie (1939), 188 Ga. 833, 

5 S. E. 2d 33. § 67. Alterations, Interlineations, and Additions.-"If a will was duly executed, and when propounded for probate it appears that certain provisions thereof have been changed, altered, or destroyed by a third person without the knowledge or consent of the testator, and it can be shown by the will itself, or by extrinsic evidence, what such stricken or destroyed provisions were, they could be restored, and the will as originally executed admitted to probate." Nassau v. Sheffield (1954), 211 Ga. 66, 84 S. E. 2d 4.

The cases cited in Note 29 of the original hold that in order for alterations and changes in a will to be valid must be made with intent and must be executed with the same formalities as a will. Prior to the amendment to Code § 113-301 (Acts 1958, p. 657), three witnesses were required. This code section as amended calls for "two or more competent witnesses." It follows, therefore, that any alterations or changes made in will must be attested and subscribed in the presence of the testator and by two or more competent witnesses. 

§ 69.-Knowledge of Contents.-Davis v. Aultman (1945), 199 Ga. 867, 33 

S. E. 2d 317. "When the person who prepares a will, or conducts the execution of it, is himself benefited by the disposition, evidence of the signing alone would not be sufficient, but the proof must go to the knowledge of the contents of the will. The rule of law is that whenever the capacity of the testatrix, at the time of the execution of the will, is in any degree doubtful, there must be proof of instructions given, or reading it over." However, a propounder who conducted the execution of a will, is only named the executor, does not constitute a benefit within the rule. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 842, 102 S. E. 2d 16. 

§ 70.-Foreign Wills.-The legislature in 1946 changed the rule heretofore recognized in Georgia that a foreign will devising real estate located in Georgia should be executed according to the laws of Georgia. This new statute was approved January 31, 1946, and reads as follows: "That Section 113-709 of the Code of Georgia (Acts of 1908, page 85) be amended by striking the word 'Georgia' in the second line thereof and substituting in lieu thereof the words 'said state,' so that said Section, as amended, shall read as follows:-'All wills executed in another State and witnessed according to the laws of said State, which shall be hereafter probated in another State, shall constitute muniments of title for the transfer and conveyance of real property in this State to the distributees or devisees mentioned in such wills, and the same shall be admitted in evidence in this State as such muniments of title without being probated in this State, when accompanied by an exemplification of the record admitting the will to probate in another State, certified according to the provisions of section 38-627, and when said will so exemplified is recorded in the office of the clerk of the Superior Court of the county in which the land is situated, in the record where deeds are recorded in this State.'" Acts 1946, page 84; Ga. Code Ann. 113-709.

A will which is executed in another state and witnessed according to the laws of that state, and which is thereafter probated in another state, shall constitute a muniment of title for the transfer and conveyance of real property in this state to the distributees or devisees mentioned in said will when accompanied by an exemplification of the record admitting it to probate, certified according to Code § 38-627, and properly recorded in the office of the clerk of the superior court of the county where the land is situated. Tripp v. Hutchins (1958), 214 Ga. 330 (1), 104 S. E. 2d 423.

WILLS AND ADMINISTRATION OF Estates § 72.-Parol Evidence.—In Baumbach v. Dickens (1957), 213 Ga. 745, 101 

S. E. 2d 702, it was held, in a proceeding to probate an alleged will, that the evidence sustained the verdict in favor of the caveators that the testatrix had not signed or executed the document propounded as her will, there being testimony by witnesses, including that of two handwriting experts, that the purported signature was not that of the deceased, and none of the alleged witnesses to the alleged will were present at the hearing to testify. 

On the question of devisavit vel non and revocavit vel non declarations of the testator "made prior to or at the time of the execution of the will or its revocation are clearly admissible." Sheffield v. Sheffield (1959), 215 Ga. 546, 551, 111 S. E. 2d 218. "Where the question is revocavit vel non, parol evidence, as to the acts and declarations of the testator, are admissible although made at any time between the making of the will and the death of the testator." King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 349, 110 S. E. 2d 772. 

§ 73.-Form, Seal, Revenue Stamp, Date, Bad Grammar.-Sproull v. Graves 

(1942), 194 Ga. 66, 20 S. E. 2d 613. 

§ 75.—Attestation of Wills-Generally.—Fraser v. Rummele (1943), 195 

Ga. 839, 25 S. E. 2d 662. § 77.-Attestation Clause.-"A person may be a 'witness' to a will although his signature precedes the attestation clause." Whitfield v. Pitts (1949), 205 

Ga. 259, 53 S. E. 2d 549. "'Attestation' is the act of witnessing the actual execution of a paper and subscribing one's name as a witness to that fact and the fact that the Code uses two terms 'attested' and 'subscribed' is of no special significance."' 

Bloodworth v. McCook (1941), 193 Ga. 53, 17 S. E. 2d 73 (3, 4). 

§ 78.-Competency of Witnesses to Wills.-Manley v. Combs (1944), 197 Ga. 

768, 30 S. E. 2d 485. "A will devising and bequeathing all of testatrix' property to a named person was not invalid because legatee's wife was one of the subscribing witnesses." Bryant v. Bryant (1949), 204 Ga. 747, 51 S. E. 2d 797. "When the person who prepares a will, or conducts the execution of it, is himself benefited by the disposition, evidence of the signing alone would not be sufficient, but the proof must go to the knowledge of the contents of the will. The rule of law is that whenever the capacity of the testatrix, at the time of the execution of the will, is in any degree doubtful, there must be proof of instructions given, or reading it over." However, a propounder who conducted the execution of a will, is only named the executor, does not constitute a benefit within the rule. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 842, 102 S. E. 2d 16. "An attorney at law is incompetent, under Code § 38-1605, to testify as a witness, in a suit against the administrator of his client's estate by a third person to require the administrator to perform specifically an oral contract, allegedly entered into between the client and a third person, as to the oral instructions given to him in drafting the client's will, which was never executed by the client." DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255 (2), 109 S. E. 2d 777.

§ 79.-Interest as Affecting Competency. "When the person who prepares a will, or conducts the execution of it, is himself benefited by the disposition, evidence of the signing alone would not be sufficient, but the proof must go to the knowledge of the contents of the will. The rule of law is that whenever the capacity of the testatrix, at the time of the execution of the will, is in any degree doubtful, there must be proof of instructions given, or reading it over." However, a propounder who conducted the execution of a will, is only named the executor, does not constitute a benefit within the rule. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 842, 102 S. E. 2d 16. 

§ 82.-Signatures of Witnesses Must Be In Presence of Testator.-Middleton v. Waters (1949), 205 Ga. 847, 55 S. E. 2d 359.

The attesting witnesses must sign in the presence of the testator. The testator must either sign in the presence of the attesting witnesses or acknowledge his signature to each of them in whose presence he did not sign. The witnesses need not sign in the presence of each other. Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 

Ga. 480, 481, 128 S. E. 2d 744. § 85.-History of Revocation.-In connection with footnote 4, page 117 of the Revised Edition, note that the former rule that murder of a testator did not defeat the right to take under a will has now been changed by statute. 

See Ga. Code Ann. 113-909, and section 8 of this supplement. § 86.-Methods of Revocation.-Experience has found it necessary to limit, within certain fixed bounds, the modes in which wills may be revoked. Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 S. E. 2d 450. "A will does not confer any present right at the time of its execution. Until the death of the testator, it has been called ambulatory. It has been compared to an undelivered deed, which contains an expression of a purpose that has not gone into effect. In the absence of all statutory regulations, it would be revocable by any act or declaration that the purpose of the testator had changed, and that the paper no longer expressed his testamentary wish. This would, of course, leave wills open to attack by parol to a dangerous extent. 

To guard against such latitude, statutes have been passed and an act which will revoke a will must be one prescribed in the statute." Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 S. E. 2d 450.

In Georgia revocation may be either express or implied. Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 100 S. E. 2d 450. "Joint operation of act and intention is necessary to revoke a will.'' Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 615, 100 S. E. 2d 450. "An express revocation may be effected by any destruction or obliteration of the will by the testator, or by someone else at his direction, when the act of destruction or obliteration is coupled with an intention on the testator's part to revoke it." Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 So. 2d 450. 

§ 87. Revocation by Subsequent Writing.-Cummings v. Cummings (1954), 

89 Ga. App. 529, 80 S. E. 2d 204.

When a testator executes a valid will containing a clause expressly revoking all former wills made by him, such revocation takes effect immediately and is no way dependent upon the ultimate fate of the latter will. Cash v. Cash (1956), 212 Ga. 416, 93 S. E. 2d 346. "While revocation of a will cannot be established by proof of parol declarations by the testator, a clause in a later written instrument, properly executed

by the testator, expressly revoking a former will is not rendered ineffective merely by the loss or destruction of the instrument which contains it, and proof of the revocation clause in a later lost or destroyed will may be made by parol." Driver v. Sheffield (1955), 211 Ga. 316, 85 S. E. 2d 766. See also, Cash v. Cash (1956), 212 Ga. 416, 93 S. E. 2d 346. 

§ 88.-Implied Revocation by Subsequent Inconsistent Will.-Where a caveat was filed to a will offered for probate on the ground that the writing offiered was not the last will and testament of the deceased because there was a subsequent will which had been lost and which specifically revoked the former will, or which by inconsistent provisions revoked the will offered for probate, it was held that even if the alleged subsequent will was inconsistent with the prior will, the sole legatee named in the subsequent will having died prior to the testatrix, the subsequent will had lapsed and therefore did not have the effect of revoking the prior will by implication. Miller v. Marchman (1958), 214 Ga. 355, 104 S. E. 2d 888. 

§ 89.-Revocation by Obliteration or Destruction.-Cummings v. Cummings 

(1954), 89 Ga. App. 529, 80 S. E. 2d 204. "All the destroying in the world without intention will not revoke a will; nor all the intention in the world without destroying it; there must be the two." Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 615, 100 S. E. 2d 450. "Joint operation of act and intention is necessary to revoke a will. The destroying of a will without intention to revoke it would not revoke the will, neither would the intention to destroy a will without actually doing so revoke the will; there must be both." Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 615, 100 

So. 2d 450. "An express revocation may be effected by any destruction or obliteration of the will by the testator, or by someone else at his direction, when the act of destruction or obliteration is coupled with an intention on the testator's part to revoke it." Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 614, 100 So. 2d 450.

An act which revokes a will must be one prescribed by the statute; and, in this state, revocation of a will is not accomplished by only an attempt to destroy or obliterate it by the maker, though the unsuccessful act employed by him be coupled with an intention on his part to expressly revoke it. Payne v. Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 100 S. E. 2d 450. 

In Payne v. 

Payne (1957), 213 Ga. 613, 100 S. E. 2d 450, the testator, in the presence of his wife and another witness, threw his will into the fire, saying, "I am going to get rid of this damn will right now." The testator then left the room immediately and his wife rescued the will from the fire after it was only singed on the ends of two of the pages. It was held on appeal that such acts on the part of the testator did not revoke his will. "We have found no case in Georgia contray to the rule that, where the revocation of a will must be presumed because of its destruction in a material part, declarations of the testator are admissible to support or rebut the presumption that the destruction was the act of the testator with the intention to revoke. The trial judge in the present case properly considered the testimony in regard to the declarations of the testatrix as to her intention to revoke her will by destroying it." King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 350, 110

S. E. 2d 772.

"Where a paper found among a decedent's papers is offered for probate as a will, and appears to have been canceled or obliterated in a material part, a presumption arises that the cancellations or obliterations were made by the deceased and that he intended them to operate as a revocation." King v. 

Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 348, 110 S. E. 2d 772.

Where it is shown that the paper offered as a will for probate, which had been mutilated in material parts, had been in the custody of the deceased up to the time of her death, the propounder was met with the presumption that the cancellation or obliterations were made by the deceased and that he intended them to operate as a revocation. King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 348, 110 S. E. 2d 772. "The condition of the will when found among the papers of the testatrix, torn in four pieces, the signature torn from it, and missing, certainly shows its cancellation in a material portion, the signature of a will being essential to its validity. This evidence of the condition of the original will, which was in the custody of the testatrix until her death, raised a presumption that the cancellation was done by the testatrix and that she intended to revoke the will.'' 

King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 349, 110 S. E. 2d 772.

Where it is shown that the copy retained by the testatrix of a will executed in triplicate, which had been in her custody until her death, was found among her papers torn in four parts, and with the signature torn from it, a presumption arises that the destruction was done by the deceased with the intention to revoke the will. King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345 (2), 110 S. E. 2d 772.

Where there has been a multiple execution of a will, the destruction of one of the executed copies of the testatrix with intention to revoke the will would have the effect of revoking all of the copies, and the same presumption of intention to revoke arises from the destruction of one of the duplicates as would arise if the destroyed copy were the only one. King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345 (1), 110 S. E. 2d 772. 

§ 90.-Revocation by Obliteration or Destruction-Evidence.-Fletcher v. 

Gillespie (1946), 201 Ga. 377, 40 S. E. 2d 45; Saliba v. Saliba (1946), 201 Ga. 

577, 681, 40 S. E. 2d 511; Langan v. Cheshire (1951), 208 Ga. 107, 65 S. E. 2d 415.

On the question of devisavit vel non and revocavit vel non declarations of the testator "made prior to or at the time of the execution of the will or its revocation are clearly admissible." Sheffield v. Sheffield (1959), 215 Ga. 546, 551, 111 S. E. 2d 218. "Where a will cannot be found after the death of the testator, there is a strong presumption that it was destroyed or revoked by the testator, and this presumption stands in the place of positive proof; and one who seeks to establish a lost or destroyed will assumes the burden of overcoming this presumption by adequate proof." Sheffield v. Sheffield (1959), 215 Ga. 546, 548, 111 S. E. 2d 218. "Where the question is revocavit vel non, parol evidence, as to the acts and declarations of the testator, are admissible although made at any time between the making of the will and the death of the testator." King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345, 349, 110 S. E. 2d 772.

In a case where such presumption has arisen because of the destruction of the will, declarations of the testatrix as to her intention to revoke her will by destroying it are admissible in evidence. King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345 (3), 110 8. E. 2d 772.
