King v. Bennett (1959), 215 Ga. 345 (2), 110 S. E. 2d 772. 

§ 94.-Revocation by Marriage or Birth of Issue.-Williams v. Lane (1942), 

193 Ga. 306, 18 S. E. 2d 481; Saliba v. Saliba (1947), 202 Ga. 279, 42 S. E. 2d 

748; Mitchell v. Arnall (1948), 203 Ga. 384, 47 S. E. 2d 258.

While a valid marriage will revoke a will not made in contemplation thereof, an invalid marriage will not. Graves v. Carter (1950), 207 Ga. 308, 61 S. E. 

2d 282.

In connection with footnotes 102 and 103, page 138 of the Revised Edition, note: "An antecedent will, which makes no provision in contemplation of an adoption, is revoked by implication or inference of law by the testatrix's legal adoption of a minor child. The act of adopting a child, under the provisions of our adoption statute of 1941 as amended by the act of 1949, (Acts 1941, p. 305; 1949, p. 1157; Ga. Code Ann. 74-414) is the equivalent in law of the birth of a child." Thornton v. Anderson (1951), 207 Ga. 714, 64 S. E. 2d 186.

Divorce was added as a ground of revocation of a will by the General Assembly in 1952. This enactment constitutes an amendment to Ga. Code section 

113-408. The amended section will be found in the Ga. Code Ann. as follows: "113-408. (3923) Revocation by marriage of testator, total divorce, or birth of child. In all cases, the marriage of the testator, total divorce or the birth of a child to him, subsequent to the making of a will in which no provision is made in contemplation of such an event, shall be a revocation of the will. (Act 1834, Cobb, 347; 1952, pp. 196, 197.)"

Code § 113-408, as amended by acts 1952, pages 196, 197, providing that the total divorce of the testator, when no provision of his will is made in contemplation of such event, shall be a revocation of the will, is applicable in a case where both the execution of the will and the divorce occurred prior to the passage of the act. Friedman v. Cohen (1960), 215 Ga. 859, 114 S. E. 

2d 24. "A statute providing that the divorce of the testator subsequent to the execution of the will revokes the will as to the divorced spouse controls a will of a testator who died after its effective date, although the execution of the will and the subsequent divorce both occurred before the effective date." 

Friedman v. Cohen (1960), 215 Ga. 859, 114 S. E. 2d 24. 

§ 95.-Revocation by Alienation or Loss of Property.-Cummings v. Cum mings (1954), 89 Ga. App. 529, 80 S. E. 2d 204. § 99.-Revocavit Vel Non.-Where a will is offered for probate in solemn form, and a caveat is filed thereto which admits a prima facie case in favor of propounders and contests the probate of the will upon the sole ground that the testator had executed a subsequent valid will containing a clause revoking all prior wills, the only issue to be determined on appeal is that of revocavit vel non-did he revoke or not. Cash v. Cash (1956), 212 Ga. 416, 93 S. E. 2d 346. 

§ 101.-Methods of Republication.-Code § 113-409, relating to the manner in which a will may be republished, was amended by Acts 1958, pages 658,

659, and Acts 1959, pages 136, 137 by changing the requirement from three to two witnesses. Said code section as amended is as follows: "113-409. A codicil properly executed and annexed to a revoked will shall amount to a republication of the same. Any writing executed with all the formalities required for a will may operate as a republication. A republication of the same paper in the presence of two witnesses, who shall subscribe as additional attesting witnesses shall be good. A parol republication in the presence of the original witnesses to the will shall be good." § 102.-Republication by Codicil.-Code § 113-409, relating to the manner in which a will may be republished, was amended by Acts 1958, pages 658, 659, and Acts 1959, pages 136, 137, by changing the requirement from three to two witnesses. A parol republication in the presence of the original witnesses to the will shall be good." § 108.-Purpose and Necessity of Probate.-"An exemplified copy of a will from the ordinary's office is presumptive proof that it was properly probated. 

Code 1933, §§ 38-206, 113-612.'' Davis v. Tyson (1939), 60 Ga. App. 714, 4 S. E. 2d 704 (1). "Where amendment to petition for establishment and probate of will alleged that remaindermen and heirs of remaindermen did not know it was their duty or privilege to cite life tenant in ordinary's court and require probate of will, and that all parties thereto were ignorant of legal effect of not probating will and that their mistake was mutual, amendment was insufficient to meet demurrer on ground of laches because of delay of more than 40 years in probating will." Fitzgerald v. Morgan (1946), 200 Ga. 651, 36 S. E. 2d 171 (3).

Where a copy of a will is introduced into evidence without having been certified by the clerk of the court of ordinary, it is not legal evidence of title even though admitted without objection, the same having no probative value. 

Goolsby v. Nails (1961), 217 Ga. 348 (1), 122 S. E. 2d 248.

In order to use a will as a muniment of title, a copy certified by the clerk of the court of ordinary must be introduced showing the probate of the will. 

However, a copy of a will duly certified that it came from the court of ordinary's office raises the presumption that such will has been probated. But such copy must be certified by the clerk of the court of ordinary, who has jurisdiction over such records. Goolsby v. Nails (1961), 217 Ga. 348, 349, 122 S. E. 

2d 248. 

§ 109.-Place of Probate and Who May Propound.-Stevens v. Duncan 

(1940), 189 Ga. 730, 7 S. E. 2d 745; Samples v. Samples (1942), 194 Ga. 383, 21 S. E. 2d 601. "The court of ordinary has original and exclusive jurisdiction, in the first instance, of the probate of wills; and a court of equity in the exercise of its equity powers has no jurisdiction to enjoin the custodian of an alleged will from offering it for probate, or for any reason to decree cancellation of an alleged will on which no action has been taken by the court of Ordinary." 

Willis v. Willis (1957), 213 Ga. 45, 96 S. E. 2d 591.

A petition to enjoin further proceedings to probate a will, and other relief, should have been filed in the county of the residence of the defendant rather than in the county of the probate proceedings, as petitions for equitable relief must be filed in the county of residence of one of the defendants against whom substanial relief is sought, except in cases of injunction to stay pending proceedings, which may be filed in the county where the proceedings shall be pending provided no relief is prayed as to matters not included in such litigation. Spiller v. Chapman (1960), 216 Ga. 456, 457, 117 S. E. 2d 536.

§ 110. Jurisdiction.-Bowers v. Dolen (1939), 187 Ga. 653, 1 S. E. 2d 734; 

Furr v. Jordan (1943), 196 Ga. 862, 27 S. E. 2d 861; Jackson v. Sapp (1953), 210 Ga. 134, 78 S. E. 2d 23. "The court of ordinary has original and exclusive jurisdiction, in the first instance, of the probate of wills; and a court of equity in the exercise of its equity powers has no jurisdiction to enjoin the custodian of an alleged will from offering it for probate, or for any reason to decree cancellation of an alleged will on which no action has been taken by the court of Ordinary.” 

Willis v. Willis (1957), 213 Ga. 45, 96 S. E. 2d 591.

House Bill Number 107 of the 1963 General Assembly superseded Code 

§ 24-2104, which section provides when business may be transacted with the ordinary. Said Code section as amended is as follows: "The ordinary of each county may close his office at 12:00 o'clock noon on not more than two days out of each week, or at his election close his office for one entire day out of each week, Sundays and holidays excluded. The ordinary's office shall not be open for transaction of business on any Sunday or legal holiday. No will shall be admitted to record, or letters testamentary, of administration, or any order for the sale of real estate, shall be granted, except at a regular term of said court." "Prior to the enactment of Ga. L. 1959, pp. 136, 137, and Ga. L. 1959, p. 312, which amended Code Ann. §§ 113-602 and 24-2104, respectively, a will could not be probated in solemn form at a time other than during a regular term of the court of ordinary. Since these enactments became effective, a will may be probated in solemn form and letters testamentary thereupon issue in vacation, provided 'all of the heirs at law are sui juris and shall acknowledge service of the petition and notice, and shall in such acknowledgment assent thereto.' The contention of the plaintiff that a will cannot be probated in solemn form at a time other than a regular term of the court of ordinary is without merit." Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 224, 225 (2), 121 S. E. 

2d 340. Evidently the holding in the above case is superseded by House Bill 

Number 107 of the 1963 General Assembly which states: "No will shall be admitted to record, or letters testamentary, of administration, or any order of sale of real estate, shall be granted, except at a regular term of said court." 

The probate in solemn form was not void because the court of ordinary rendered its judgment on the first Monday in September, a public and legal holiday in this State. Accordingly, the caveat to such probate, filed on the following day, was not in time and was properly denied by the court of ordinary. Therefore, the superior court properly dismissed the appeal taken from such denial by the court of ordinary. Moore v. Dearing (1961), 216 Ga. 596 (1-3), 118 S. E. 2d 366. 

A court of ordinary alone has original, exclusive, and general jurisdiction to probate will, and likewise has jurisdiction alone to probate a copy of a lost will. Dockery v. Findley (1961), 216 Ga. 807 (1), 120 S. E. 2d 608.

The assent of a testator's son, a devisee, who had acknowledge service of application to probate a will in solemn form, that it be probated in solemn form without further delay, and the failure to appear at the hearing when the will was probated in solemn form, did not operate as a waiver or an estoppel preventing the son from pursuing a suit to set aside or void judgment of probate. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 224, 121 S. E. 2d 340.

A petition to enjoin further proceedings to probate a will, and other relief, should have been filed in the county of the residence of the defendant rather than in the county of the probate proceedings, as petitions for equitable relief must be filed in the county of residence of one of the defendants against whom substantial relief is sought, except in cases of injunction to stay pending proceedings, which may be filed in the county where the proceedings shall be pending provided no relief is prayed as to matters not included in such litigation. Spiller v. Chapman (1960), 216 Ga. 456, 457, 117 S. E. 2d 536. "Equity has jurisdiction to set aside a judgment granting letters of administration, where such judgment was obtained by fraud." Lefkoff v. Sicro (1939), 189 Ga. 554, 6 S. E. 2d 687 (20). "Where there is no administration of the estate of a deceased, a plaintiff may proceed in equity against deceased's heir at law and persons holding under deceased.' "" Hughes v. Cobb (1942), 195 Ga. 213, 23 S. E. 2d 701 (2).

The Supreme Court of the United States, in the case of Riley v. New York 

Trust Co. (1942), 315 U. S. 343, 86 L. ed. 885, declined to apply the full faith and credit clause (Article IV, section 1) of the Federal Constitution, in such manner as to give the Georgia judgment of probate in solemn form, in the case of Hungerford v. Spalding (1936), 183 Ga. 547, 189 S. E. 2, extraterritorial effect upon assets in other states. The Supreme Court of the United States in that case said: "So far as the assets in Georgia are concerned the Georgia 

Judgment of probate is in rem; so far as it affects personalty beyond the state, it is in personam and can bind only parties thereto or their privies." "Judgments of courts of ordinary may be set aside by court of equity in direct proceeding for that purpose on the ground that they were procured by fraud." Johnson v. Bogdis (1949), 205 Ga. 535, 54 S. E. 2d 620. 

§ 112-Proof of Death.-Pfenning v. Life Ins. Co. of Virginia (1939), 60 Ga. 

App. 706, 4 S. E. 2d 682; Cartwright v. State (1940), 64 Ga. App. 51, 12 S. E. 

2d 370; Payne v. Home Sav. Bank (1942), 193 Ga. 406, 18 S. E. 2d 770; Jackson v. Sapp (1953), 210 Ga. 134, 78 S. E. 2d 23. "Proof that defendant is living at a particular time gives rise to an inference, within logical and legal limits, that he is alive at a subsequent time." 

Chapman v. Chapman (1939), 59 Ga. App. 602, 1 S. E. 2d 697 (1). "The presumption of duration of life, with respect to a person of whom no account can be given, ends at the expiration of seven years from the time when he was last heard of as living. Code 1933, § 38-118." Pilgrim Health & 

Life Ins. Co. v. Shows (1939), 60 Ga. App. 872, 5 S. E. 2d 585 (1).

In Samples v. Samples (1942), 194 Ga. 383, 388, 21 S. E. 2d 601, it was held that when an executor has probated a will in common form and the heirs at law require a probate in solemn form, the executor is entitled to have the court costs and counsel fees paid out of the estate and that this is true even though the caveat is successful and probate in solemn form is refused, unless the probate in common form was originally made in bad faith on the part of the executor in an attempt to defraud the heirs at law. And Acts 1953, page 423, codified as Code § 113-619, further extends the rule enunciated above by including probate of a will in both solemn and common form. However, it should be remembered that a caveat may not be filed to an application to probate a will in common form. See section 123 of the main volume. Said 

Code § 113-619 is as follows: 

"Those who are named as executors in purported wills of decedents shall be entitled to recover from the estate of the decedent expenses, including a reasonable attorney's fee if the services of an attorney are employed for offering for probate will in solemn or common form, even though the will is subsequently determined not to be the valid will of the testator: Provided, however, such persons shall not be entitled to recover from the estate the expenses and attorney's fees incurred in the effort to sustain the will in the event of a contest, unless the person so named proceeds in good faith; the court of ordinary shall determine upon the petition of a person so named, the amount of expenses, and the amount to be paid the attorney so employed, and its order shall be subject to appeal to the superior court as is now in other cases provided." 

§ 114.-Probate in Solemn Form.-By the Acts 1958, page 660, and Acts 

1959, pages 136, 137, Code § 133-602 was amended by striking this section in its entirety and in lieu thereof substituted the following: “113-602. Probate by the witnesses, or probate in solemn form, is the proving of the will, after due notice to all devisees and legatees and all the heirs at law, by all the witnesses in life and within the jurisdiction of the court, or by proof of their signatures and that of the testator, if the witnesses are dead, blind, incompetent or inaccessible, and the ordering to record of the will so proved. Such probate is conclusive upon all the parties notified, and all devisees and legatees under the will who are represented in the executor. The petition to probate a will in solemn form shall be verified by the oath of the applicant, and shall set forth the full name, place of domicile, the legal residence, the date of the death of the testator, the post office address of the petitioner, and the names, ages and addresses of the surviving spouse and all the heirs at law, stating their relationship to the testator, and in the event full particulars are lacking, the petition shall state the reasons for

such omission. Every such petition shall conclude with a prayer for the issuance of letters testamentary, and if all the heirs at law, devisees and legatees are sui juris and shall acknowledge service of the petition and notice, and shall in such acknowledgment assent thereto, the will may be admitted to record on proper proof, and letters may thereupon issue without further delay whether in term or vacation."

House Bill Number 107 of the 1963 General Assembly superseded Code 

§ 24-2104, which section provides when business may be transacted with the ordinary. Said Code section as amended is as follows: "The ordinary of each county may close his office at 12:00 o'clock noon on not more than two days out of each week, or at his election close his office for one entire day out of each week, Sundays and holidays excluded. The ordinary's office shall not be open for transaction of business on any Sunday or legal holiday. No will shall be admitted to record, or letters testamentary, or administration, or any order for the sale of real estate, shall be granted, except at a regular term of said court." "Prior to the enactment of Ga. L. 1959, pp. 136, 137, and Ga. L. 1959, p. 312, which amended Code Ann. §§ 113-602 and 24-2104, respectively, a will could not be probated in solemn form at a time other than during a regular term of the court of ordinary. Since these enactments became effective, a will may be probated in solemn form and letters testamentary thereupon issue in vacation, provided 'all of the heirs at law are sui juris and shall acknowledge service of the petition and notice, and shall in such acknowledgement assent thereto. The contention of the plaintiff that a will cannot be probated in solemn form at a time other than at a regular term of the court of ordinary is without merit." Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 224, 225 (2), 121 S. E. 

2d 340. Evidently the holding on the above case was superseded by House 

Bill Number 107 of the 1963 General Assembly which provides: "No will shall be admitted to record, or letters testamentary, of administration, or any order for the sale of real estate, shall be granted, except at a regular term of court." 

A will cannot be probated in solemn form upon the affidavit of the subscribing witnesses to the will. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 224, 225 (3), 121 S. E. 2d 340. However, in all proceedings for the probate of a will in common form, and in all proceedings for the probate of a will in solemn form when all of the heirs at law of the testator are sui juris and acknowledge services of the petition and notice and assent to the admission of the will to record upon proper proof without further delay, may be probated by inter rogatories. Code § 113-621 et seq.

The assent of a testator's son, a devisee, who had acknowledged service of application to probate a will in solemn form, that it be probated in solemn form without further delay, and the failure to appear at the hearing when the will was probated in solemn form, did not operate as a waiver or an estoppel preventing the son from pursuing a suit to set aside or void judgment of probate. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 224, 121 S. E. 2d 340.

Probate in solemn form requires that all witnesses be produced, if they be in life and within the jurisdiction of the court. To make out a prima facie case, and to be entitled to a judgment of probate in solemn form, the propounder must introduce at the hearing all subscribing witnesses, if living and accessible, or proof of their signatures, if dead or inaccessible. They must be introduced, for examination, even though the propounder knows that their testimony will be unfavorable to him. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 

224, 225 (3), 121 S. E. 2d 340.

The main reason of the rule for calling all witnesses in a proceeding for probate in solemn form is to give the other party an opportunity of crossexamining them. Accordingly, the failure of the plaintiff to appear at the hearing when the will was probated would neither estop the plaintiff nor constitute a failure to exercise due diligence for the reason that had the plaintiff appeared, there would have been no witnesses to cross-examine. The law prescribes certain essential prerequisites before a valid judgment probating a will in solemn form can be rendered. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App. 

224, 226, 121 S. E. 2d 340.

Where a petition to set aside a judgment probating a will affirmatively alleges that judgment is void, in that subscribing witnesses were not produced as witnesses, as required by law, or their absence accouned for, and that all of the witnesses were sui juris and available to court, treating allegations of the petition as true, the judgment probating the will in solemn form is void, and the court erred in sustaining a general demurrer thereto. Miller v. Miller (1961), 104 Ga. App 224, 225, 121 S. E. 2d 340. 

Jones v. Dean (1939), 188 Ga. 319, 3 S. E. 2d 894; Benton v. Turk (1939), 188 Ga. 710, 4 S. E. 2d 580; Bloodworth v. McCook (1941), 193 Ga. 53, 17 S. E. 

2d 73; Samples v. Samples (1942), 194 Ga. 383, 21 S. E. 2d 601; Orr v. Blalock (1943), 195 Ga. 863, 25 S. E. 2d 668; Foster v. Allen (1946), 201 Ga. 348, 40 

S. E. 2d 57; Culpepper v. Bower (1948), 203 Ga. 784, 48 S. E. 2d 369; Byrd v. Riggs (1955), 211 Ga. 493, 86 S. E. 2d 285. law. "The question of what is mental capacity to make a will is a question of "On the trial of an issue of devisavit vel non, whether the alleged testatrix had mental capacity to make a will at the time of signing the paper is for jury, and a witness cannot testify as to such legal conclusion. "In will contest proceeding, permitting a witness of the caveator, over objection, to testify that the alleged testatrix had not sufficient capacity to make a will, was error as against objection that witness was testifying to a mixed question of law and fact." Smoot v. Alexander (1939), 188 Ga. 203, 3 S. E. 2d 593 (1, 2, 3). "In will contest, caveator can admit prima facie case for propounder of will, and thereby obtain the opening and concluding argument." Tilley v. 

King (1940), 190 Ga. 421, 9 S. E. 2d 670 (3).

"The probate of will revoked letters of administration as to assets unadministered, which was equivalent to removal of administrator. Code, § 113-2204." 

Hudmon v. Thomasson (1946), 74 Ga. App. 31, 38 S. E. 2d 683 (3).

The legislature in 1945 provided that, where it is desired to take the testimony of a witness to a will who resides outside the state of Georgia, a photostatic copy of the will may be exhibited to such witness at the time of taking his testimony and returned with said commission. This obviates the necessity of sending the original will outside the state. Acts 1945, page 142; Ga. Code 

Ann. 113-609.1.

In 1945 the legislature added a new section to Code 113-6 providing for the establishment of a will when one or more of the subscribing witnesses to the will are connected with the armed forces of the United States or with the merchant marine. Acts 1945, page 401; Ga. Code Ann. 113-620.

In the probate of a will in solemn form, the absence from the State at the time of the probate of an heir at law who resides within this State, solely because of service in the armed forces of the United States, does not change his domicile or residence so as to authorize service on him of a notice of such proceeding by publication. Foster v. Foster (1951), 207 Ga. 519, 63 S. E. 2d 318.

Where four persons affixed their signatures below the signature of the testatrix, and three were present at the probate proceedings and testified, and the fourth who was out of the state and her signature was proved by her mother, all four persons were therefore properly accounted for. Thornton v. 

Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480, 481, 128 S. E. 2d 744. "The testimony of the subscribing witnesses having made a prima facie case of testamentary capacity for the propounder, and caveator having offered no evidence tending to show incapicity, the trial court properly directed a verdict for propunder on this issue." Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480, 485, 128 S. E. 2d 744.

The introduction into evidence of the will containing a proper attestation clause having raised a presumption that the will was executed in the manner prescribed by law, and the caveator having introduced no evidence tending to show a failure to comply with the formalities of execution as to three of the attesting witnesses, one more than required by law for this will, the trial court correctly directed a verdict for propounder on the issue of execution. 

Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 744. 

In Baumbach v. Dickens (1957), 213 Ga. 745, 101 S. E. 702, it was held, in a proceeding to probate an alleged will, that the evidence sustained the verdict in favor of the caveators that the testatrix had not signed or executed the document propounded as her will, there being testimony by witnesses, including that of two handwriting experts, that the purported signature was not that of the deceased, and none of the alleged witnesses to the alleged will were present at the hearing to testify. 

The probate in solemn form was not void because the court of ordinary rendered its judgment on the first Monday in September, a public and legal holiday in this State. Accordingly, the caveat to such probate, filed on the following day, was not in time and was properly denied by the court of ordinary. Therefore, the superior court properly dismissed the appeal taken from such denial by the court of ordinary. Moore v. Dearing (1961), 216 Ga. 

596 (1-3), 118 S. E. 2d 366.

Plaintiff, claiming under an agreement to adopt and leave property, was entitled to notice of proceedings to probate will. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 896 (3), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

A judgment admitting a paper to probate in solemn form as a will is not binding upon heirs at law who had no notice of the application for such probate. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 896 (3), 114 S. E. 2d 12. 

§ 116.-Contract Not to Offer Will for Probate.-Sutton v. Ward (1943), 

195 Ga. 314, 24 S. E. 2d 17; Foster v. Allen (1946), 201 Ga. 348, 40 S. E. 2d 

57; Cone v. Johnston (1947), 202 Ga. 420, 43 S. E. 2d 545.

It is well settled that agreements among the heirs at law to distribute or divide property devised under a will, in lieu of that manner provided by the will, are valid and enforceable. Such agreements have as their consideration the termination of family controversies, and are upheld "albeit perhaps resting on grounds which would not have been satisfactory if the transaction had occurred between mere strangers." They partake of the nature of family arrangements and are, in essence, solely contractual and governed by rules applicable to all contracts. West v. Downer (1962), 218 Ga. 235, 241 (5), 127 

S. E. 2d 359. "Even where the instrument is an absolute nullity by reason of improper attestation or other invalidating cause, if it is probated and admitted to record as a will on the written consent of the heirs, although such consent and probate would not clothe the putative will with the requisites of validity, all the heirs who were sui juris and parties to the contract are estopped to deny the will's validity or the probate thereof." West v. Downer (1962), 218 Ga. 

235, 240, 127 S. E. 2d 359.

Where a contract to divide property shows on its face that it is lacking in mutuality, and that such lack of mutuality can be cured only by a meeting of the condition therein expressed, the petition in failing to allege a meeting of the condition, fails to set forth a cause of action for specific performance. 

West v. Downer (1962), 218 Ga. 235, 243, 127 S. E. 2d 359. § 117.-Collateral Attack on Order of Probate.- -"An exemplified copy of a will from the ordinary's office is presumptive proof that it was properly pro bated. Code 1933, §§ 38-206, 113-612.'' Davis v. Tyson (1939), 60 Ga. 

App. 714, 4 8. E. 2d 704 (1).

A latter will will not be probated in the absence of the setting aside of the probate of the prior will. Byrd v. Riggs (1953), 209 Ga. 930, 76 S. E. 2d 774. 

§ 118.-Proceedings to Set Aside Probate.-Womack v. Williford (1942), 

194 Ga. 688, 22 S. E. 2d 510.

A court of ordinary has no jurisdiction to entertain a petition to set aside a judgment probating a will in solemn form on the ground that a later will has been discovered, since in reality such petition is an extraordinary motion for new trial. Byrd v. Riggs (1954), 210 Ga. 473, 80 S. E. 2d 785.

A judgment admitting a paper to probate in solemn form as a will is not binding upon heirs at law who had no notice of the application for such probate. Banes v. Berricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 896 (3), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

A superior court in the exercise of its equitable jurisdiction may set aside a judgment of a court of ordinary, procured by fraud, upon proper allegations and proof. However, courts of equity grant relief only in favor of the diligent,

in the State of Georgia to sell the real estate located in Georgia and to pay over the proceeds to the testator's wife a sum certain and the balance to the trust estate therein created, the title thereto vested in the ancillary executor and the testator's wife, even though the executor therein named failed to qualify and, in fact, could not qualify since the will could not be probated in this state. "'Where testator dies after having executed two purported wills, proceedings to probate the instrument last executed should be tried first." Smith v. Davis (1946), 200 Ga. 317, 37 S. Ga. 428, 73 S. E. 2d 182.

A caveat to a will offered for probate in solemn form which admits a prima facie case in favor of propounders and contests the will on the sole ground of a subsequent valid will having a clause revoking all prior wills, the only issue for the jury on appeal is that of revocavit vel non-did he revoke or not.

Code § 113-619. § 124.-Same-Mistake, Fraud, or Forgery.-Butler v. Lashley (1944), 197 

Ga. 461, 29 S. E. 2d 508; Stephens v. Brady (1952), 209 Ga. 428, 73 S. E. 2d 182. "Code § 113-106 provides that one may bequeath his entire estate to strangers to the exclusion of his wife and children but in such cases the will should be closely scrutinized, and upon the slightest evidence of the aberration of intellect, or collusion or fraud, or any undue influence or unfair dealing, probate should be refused." Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53.

Fraud which will invalidate a will must be fraud which operated upon the testator, i.e., a procurement of the execution of the will by misrepresentations made to him. It exists only when it is shown that the testator relied on such a representation and was deceived. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370, 128 S. E. 2d 53.

A will executed "under a mistake of fact as to the existence or conduct of an heir at law of the testator" is inoperative only insofar as such heir is concerned, and where a testator has several heirs and the mistake of fact exists only as to a part of his heirs, the entire will is not necessarily void. Lee v. 

Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "The admission in the present case that the testator had testamentary capacity at the time of the execution of the will eliminated any issue made by the caveat that the testator was laboring under any mental disability to execute the will, including monomania from which the will resulted; but did not eliminate the issue of undue influence and mistake of fact." Lee v. Boyer (1961) 217 Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757.

Declarations of a testator on the issue of mistake of fact as to the conduct of an heir are admissible to show what operated on the testator's mind, in consideration of the issue of mistake of fact as to the conduct of the caveatrix. 

Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 34, 120 S. E. 2d 757. "On the trial of a proceeding to probate in solemn form, the evidence demanding a finding that the will was not executed as a result of (1) undue influence, (2) fraud, (3) misrepresentation, or (4) mistake of fact, as asserted in the caveat, it was not error to direct a verdict in favor of the propounder." 

Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 53. "The evidence showing no more than an erroneous deduction or conclusion by testatrix that because caveator once asserted a right to one-half of the property, he was continuing to do so, this being at most an error of judgment rather than an ignorance of basic facts, and not constituting a mistake of fact within the meaning of Code § 113-210, the court properly directed a verdict for propounder on the issue of whether or not the will was executed under a mistake of fact as to the conduct of caveator." Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480 (3), 128 S. E. 2d 744. "There is a difference between a 'mistake' arising from mere ignorance and one which results from an error of judgment after investigation or from neg-

ligent or wilful failure to make a proper investigation by means of which the truth could be readily and surely ascertained. It is to such a mistake as that first indicated that section 3262 [Code § 113-210] applies." Thornton v. Hulme 

(1962), 218 Ga. 480, 486, 128 S. E. 2d 744.

Petitioner should have applied to the ordinary for a citation calling on the propounder to prove the will in solemn form and by a caveat in that proceeding he could have questioned the validity of the intestate's will.

E. 2d 806. § 125.-Same-Uncertainty and Injustice.—A caveat to a will offered for probate in solemn form which admits a prima facie case in favor of propounders and contests the will on the sole ground of a subsequent valid will having a clause revoking all prior wills, the only issue for the jury on appeal is that of revocavit vel non-did he revoke or not. Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 S. E. 

2d 89.

Nuncupative will of testator that named his only living brother and his wife as beneficiaries was not an unreasonable disposition of property. Durden v. 

Henderson (1957), 212 Ga. 807, 96 S. E. 2d 362. 

§ 126.-Burden of Proof.-Tilley v. King (1940), 190 Ga. 421, 9 S. E. 2d 670; 

Butler v. Lashley (1944), 197 Ga. 461, 29 S. E. 2d 508; Brazil v. Roberts (1944), 198 Ga. 477, 32 S. E. 2d 171; Spivey v. Spivey (1947), 44 S. E. 2d 224. "In will contest, where court charged that burden was on propounder to show that will was executed freely and voluntarily at a time when testatrix had sufficient mental capacity to make a will, charge that caveators had burden of sustaining their objections by a preponderance of the evidence was not erroneous as limiting burden placed on propounder." Franklin v. First Nat. 

Bank of Atlanta (1938), 187 Ga. 268, 200 S. E. 679 (3). "On the trial of an issue of devisavit vel non, the burden, in the first instance, is upon propounder of alleged will to make out a prima facie case by showing the factum of the will and that at time of its execution the testator apparently had sufficient mental capacity to make it, and, in making it, acted voluntarily, and, when this is done, the burden shifts to the caveators." 

Smoot v. Alexander (1939), 188 Ga. 203, 3 S. E. 2d 593 (4); Smith v. Davis (1947), 203 Ga. 175, 43 S. E. 2d 609; Ehlers v. Rheinberger (1948), 204 Ga. 

226, 49 S. E. 2d 535; Langan v. Cheshire (1951), 208 Ga. 107, 65 S. E. 2d 415. 

§ 127.-Evidence-Witnesses.-Brazil v. Roberts (1944), 198 Ga. 477, 32 

S. E. 2d 171. "It is undoubtedly true that where a will is attacked upon the ground of the mental incapacity of the testatrix, and of undue influence in the procure-

ment of it, it is always proper to inquire whether the provisions of the will are just and reasonable, and in accord with the state of testatrix's 'family relations or the contrary.' '"' Knox v. Knox (1957), 213 Ga. 677, 681, 101 S. E. 

2d 89.

Where a caveat raised two grounds of objection, mental capacity and undue influence, the admission over objection of testimony of one of the caveators, that the will offered for probate did not contain the same provisions as the will read to witness and other relatives by the propounder a day or two after the death of the testatrix, was held to be prejudicial error. This was so held because there was nothing in the pleadings raising the issue that the will offered for probate was not in fact the will made by the testatrix. Hawkins v. Hodges (1958), 213 Ga. 837, 841, 102 S. E. 2d 16. "Since the contention of the caveatrix that the son of the propounder was the scrivener of the will, and that it was never read to the testatrix, or read by her in the presence of any of the subscribing witnesses to the will, and that for this reason the will should not be admitted to probate, was first raised by an amendment filed and allowed after the evidence had closed and during the argument of counsel, it was not an abuse of discretion on the part of the trial judge to reopen the case on motion of counsel for the propounder and permit them to offer evidence on the issue thus raised." Bodeker v. Purdy (1953), 209 Ga. 648, 74 S. E. 2d 856.

The introduction into evidence of the will containing a proper attestation clause having raised a presumption that the will was executed in the manner prescribed by law, and the caveator having introduced no evidence tending to show a failure to comply with the formalities of execution as to three of the attesting witnesses, one more than required by law for this will, the trial court correctly directed a verdict for propounder on the issue of execution. Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 744. "The attesting witnesses having testified that at the time of the execution of the will testatrix was of sound and disposing mind and memory, and there being no evidence that testatrix was suffering from monomania, the court properly directed a verdict for propounder on the ground of the caveat based on monomania." Thornton v. Hulme (1962), 218 Ga. 480 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 744. "On the trial of a proceeding to probate in solemn form, the evidence demanding a finding that the will was not executed as a result of (1) undue influence, (2) fraud, (3) misrepresentation, or (4) mistake of fact, as asserted in the caveat, it was not error to direct a verdict in favor of the propounder." 

Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 744. 

In Baumbach v. Dickens (1957), 213 Ga. 745, 101 S. E. 2d 702, it was held, in a proceeding to probate an alleged will, that the evidence sustained the verdict in favor of the caveators that the testatrix had not signed or executed the document propounded as her will, there being testimony by witnesses, including that of two handwriting experts, that the purported signature was not that of the deceased, and none of the alleged witnesses to the alleged will were present at the hearing to testify. "Unless otherwise provided by statute, communications, by a client to the attorney who drafted his will, in respect to that document and transactions between them leading up to its execution, are not privileged, after the client's death, in a suit between devisees under the will and heirs at law, or other parties who all claim under him. The principal reason is that the general rule is designed for the protection of the client, and it is deemed not for the

interests of the testator, in a controversy between the parties, all of whom claim under him, to have those declarations and transactions excluded which promote a proper fulfillment of his will. Also a witness to a will, although attorney for the testator, is permitted to disclose everything which he knew concerning his attestation and the circumstances surrounding and leading up to it." DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255, 260, 109 S. E. 2d 777.

An exception to the common-law rule of privileged communications is that communications by a client to the attorney who prepared his will, in respect to that document, and transactions occurring between them and leading up to its execution, are not, after the client's death, within the protection of the rule, in a suit between the testator's devisees and heirs at law, or other persons who claim under them. DeLoach v. Myers (1959), 215 Ga. 255, 259, 109 S. E. 2d 777. 

§ 128.-Construction of Wills Jurisdiction.-Moss v. Youngblood (1938), 

187 Ga. 188, 200 S. E. 689; Gormley v. Cleaveland (1939), 187 Ga. 457, 200 

S. E. 793; Cone V. Johnston (1947), 202 Ga. 420, 43 S. E. 2d 545.

Construction of wills is an ancient head of equity jurisdiction and has long been practiced in this State. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 692, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

Acts 1943, pages 409, 444 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1423), relating to the necessity of construing a will or trust upon an accounting the same shall be transferred to the superior court, is as follows: "The court of ordinary upon its own motion, or upon motion of any party at interest whenever it shall appear that a question of construction of a will or trust instrument is involved in said accounting, shall enter an order transferring said accounting to the superior court for the determination of all such questions which shall be presented to, heard and determined by the superior court as appeals from the court of ordinary are presented, heard and determined, and after the determination of such questions of construction by the superior court, the court of ordinary shall proceed with said accounting.' " See Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

As to authority of superior courts to enter declaratory decrees arising in the administration of estates or trusts, including questions of construction of wills or other writings, see Acts 1945, page 137; Acts 1959, page 236; Ga. Code 

Ann. 110-1101 et seq.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, in which it was sought a construction of a will and an accounting, with an injunction against an executor's sale of the property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting, relief is not to be denied because of the availability of claim procedure provided by Code §§ 113-1801 and 113-1802; neither is it to be denied because of an order of the court of ordinary authorizing a sale of the property in question; and, nor is it to be denied because of the prior but related litigation in the same case. 

Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105. 

In Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105, it was held that even though a petition was insufficient to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, the petition was maintainable as one in equity for the construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment under the Declaratory Judgment Act (Code § 110-1101 et seq.), this

failure does not affect the right to any other relief to which the plaintiff may be entitled, and the petition is maintainable as one in equity for construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

Where a petition is filed in a court of ordinary for a full accounting by the executor, in order to ascertain the rights of the parties and to ascertain whether or not the executor has completed his duties under the will and whether it is his duty to account and to turn over the property bequeathed and devised by the will, a construction of the will is necessary. As the court of ordinary has no power or authority to construe a will, the superior court on an appeal from the court of ordinary likewise has no authority to construe the will. Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

Under Code § 37-403, a legatee or devisee cannot under normal circumstances maintain a petition for mere construction of a will, since that is the duty and prerogative of the executor. Yet, the right of a legatee or devisee, under stated circumstances, to seek and obtain construction is recognized. Brewton v. 

McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 692, 119 S. E. 2d 105. § 129.-Same-Superior Courts.-The legislature in 1945 enacted a declaratory judgments statute which authorizes the superior courts of Georgia to render declaratory judgments. Among the powers granted to the superior courts by this statute is the power, on the petition of any person interested "as or through an executor, administrator, trustee, guardian, or other fiduciary, creditor, devisee, legatee, heir, ward, next of kin, cestui que trust... "(a) To ascertain any class of creditors, devisees, legatees, heirs, next of kin or others, or "(b) To direct the executor, administrator, or trustee to do or abstain from doing any particular act in their fiduciary capacity, or "(c) To determine any question arising in the administration of the estate or trust, including questions of construction of wills and other writings. (Acts 1945, pp. 137, 138.)" Ga. Code Ann. 110-1107. 

Taylor v. Taylor (1949), 205 Ga. 483, 53 S. E. 2d 769.

Acts 1943, pages 409, 444 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1423), relating to the necessity of construing a will or trust upon an accounting the same shall be transferred to the superior court, is as follows: "The court of ordinary upon its own motion, or upon motion of any party at interest whenever it shall appear that a question of construction of a will or trust instrument is involved in said accounting, shall enter an order transferring said accounting to the superior court for the determination of all such questions which shall be presented to, heard and determined by the superior court as appeals from the court of ordinary are presented, heard and determined, and after the determination of such questions of construction by the superior court, the court of ordinary shall pro-

ceed with said accounting." See Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. 

App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment under the Declaratory Judgment Act (Code § 110-1101 et seq.), this failure does not affect the right to any other relief to which the plaintiff may be entitled, and the petition is maintainable as one in equity for construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105. 

In Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105, it was held that even though a petition was insufficient to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, the petition was maintainable as one in equity for the construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, in which it was sought a construction of a will and an accounting, with an injunction against an executor's sale of the property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting, relief is not to be denied because of the availability of claim procedure provided by Code §§ 113-1801 and 113-1802; neither is it to be denied because of an order of the court of ordinary authorizing a sale of the property in question; and, nor is it to be denied because of the prior but related litigation in the same case. 

Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105. "Equity will not assume jurisdiction of an estate and thereby obstruct the orderly procedure for the administration of an estate under the guise of construing the will." Bandy v. Smith (1954), 211 Ga. 192, 84 S. E. 2d 449.

Construction of wills is an ancient head of equity jurisdiction and has long been practiced in this State. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 692, 119 S. E. 2d 105. 

In Gray v. Trust Company of Georgia (1955), 211 Ga. 332, 85 S. E. 2d 721, pending a proceeding for the construction of a will all the beneficiaries under the will entered into an agreement providing for the distribution and management of the property devised. The superior court approved the agreement and made it a part of the final decree which the court rendered in the construction proceeding. The jurisdiction of the superior court in this matter was upheld by the Supreme Court, and by implication, the Court upheld the validity of such agreements. 

Where a petition is filed in a court of ordinary for a full accounting by the executor, in order to ascertain the rights of the parties and to ascertain whether or not the executor has completed his duties under the will and whether it is his duty to account and to turn over the property bequeathed and devised by the will, a construction of the will is necessary. As the court of ordinary has no power or authority to construe a will, the superior court on an appeal from the court of ordinary likewise has no authority to construe the will. Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 495, 95 S. E. 2d 42. 

§ 131.-Same-Other Courts-Deeds and Wills Distinguished."A deed if testamentary in character, would be of no effect where it was not executed in the manner which would entitle it to probate as a will."' 

Childs v. 

Mitchell (1948), 204 Ga. 542, 50 S. E. 2d 216.

§ 132.-Pleadings-Parties.-Campbell v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1943), 197 

Ga. 37, 28 S. E. 2d 471; Fowler v. Latham (1946), 201 Ga. 68, 38 S. E. 2d 732; 

Williams v. J. M. High Co. (1946), 200 Ga. 230, 36 S. E. 2d 667; Wright v. 

Heffernan (1949), 205 Ga. 75, 52 S. E. 2d 289. "In petition by executor for construction of a will, all persons named in will as legatees are proper parties. Code 1933, § 37-404." Watts v. Finley (1939), 187 Ga. 629, 1 S. E. 2d 723 (2). "In a limited sense all executors, like administrators, are 'trustees' even as to the usual fiduciary duties imposed on them by law or under the will, but such general fiduciary relationship does not constitute a 'trust' in the sense that only equity court can impose its supervision." McDowell v. McDowell (1942), 68 Ga. App. 363, 22 S. E. 2d 851 (1). "A devisee under the will cannot maintain a petition for construction of the will, as only the representative of the estate may seek direction of a court." Rainey v. Woodcock (1954), 211 Ga. 101, 84 S. E. 2d 41. 

§ 133.-General Principles Governing Construction.-Cooper v. Harkness 

(1939), 188 Ga. 121, 2 S. E. 2d 918; Hungerford v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 190 Ga. 387, 9 S. E. 2d 630; Bratton v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 191 Ga. 49, 11 S. E. 2d 204; Boykin v. Bradley (1941), 192 Ga. 212, 14 S. E. 2d 734; 

Buchanan v. Nicholson (1941), 192 Ga. 754, 16 S. E. 2d 743; Snellings v. 

Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; Sproull v. Graves (1942), 194 Ga. 66, 20 S. E. 2d 613; Yerbey v. Chandler (1942), 194 Ga. 263, 21 S. E. 

2d 636; Mills v. Tyus (1942), 195 Ga. 119, 23 S. E. 2d 259; Comer v. Comer (1942), 195 Ga. 79, 23 S. E. 2d 420; Everitt v. LaSpeyre (1943), 195 Ga. 377, 24 S. E. 2d 381; Moody v. Baxley Turpentine Corporation (1943), 195 Ga. 

482, 24 S. E. 2d 652; Fraser v. Martin (1943), 195 Ga. 683, 25 S. E. 2d 307; 

Lane v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1943), 195 Ga. 828, 25 S. E. 2d 800; 

Yancey v. Grafton (1943), 197 Ga. 117, 27 S. E. 2d 857; Gilmore v. Gilmore (1944), 197 Ga. 303, 29 S. E. 2d 74; Blakeman v. Harwell (1944), 198 Ga. 165, 31 S. E. 2d 50; Armstrong v. Merts (1947), 202 Ga. 483, 43 S. E. 2d 512; Houston v. Mills Memorial Home (1947), 202 Ga. 540, 43 S. E. 2d 680; Young v. 

Young (1947), 202 Ga. 694, 44 S. E. 2d 659; Schriber v. Anderson (1949), 205 

Ga. 343, 53 S. E. 2d 490; Stahl v. Russell (1950), 206 Ga. 699, 58 S. E. 2d 135;

Graves v. Carter (1951), 208 Ga. 5, 64 S. E. 2d 450; Butts v. Trust Co. of 

Georgia (1953), 209 Ga. 787, 75 S. E. 2d 745; Aiken v. Aiken (1953), 209 Ga. 

819, 76 S. E. 2d 481; Whitney v. Citizens & Southern National Bank (1959), 214 Ga. 674, 107 S. E. 2d 191. "In the construction of wills, the intention of the testator should be the first and great object of inquiry. And this is to be sought for by looking to the whole will, and not to detached parts of it." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 

Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553.

The cardinal rule of construction of a will is for the court to seek the intention of the testator. Chamblee v. Guy (1962), 218 Ga. 56, 57 (2a), 126 

S. E. 2d 205. "It is a cardinal rule in the construction of wills to give effect to the intention of the testator, when the same can be done without violating any settled principle of law." Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (1), 127 

S. E. 2d 19.

In the construction of a will, the paramount object is the ascertainment of the intention of the testator by looking to "Its four corners' and giving consideration to all of its parts. Lewis v. Mitchell (1961), 216 Ga. 526, 527 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 901.

It is well settled that the general intention of the testator, as gathered from the entire will, must prevail over a particular intention gathered from a part of the will. Taylor v. Rapp (1962), 217 Ga. 654, 656, 124 S. E. 2d 271.

The circumstances surrounding the execution of a will must be considered in determining the intention of the testator. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 

148, 151, 109 S. E. 2d 741.

It is the duty of the court to effectuate the intent of the testator insofar as his intent is consistent with established rules of law. Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671 (1a), - S. E. 2d

In the construction of all legacies, the court shall seek diligently for the intention of the testator and give effect to the same as far as it may be consistent with the rules of law, the cardinal rule of construction being to ascertain the intention of the parties. Carnegie v. First National Bank of 

Brunswick (1963), 218 Ga. 585, 589, 129 S. E. 2d 780. "A will affecting property should never be so construed as to exclude some of it from its operation, unless demanded by the context or some rule prohibiting the disposition." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 69, 102 S. E. 

2d 553. "The natural and reasonable presumption is that when so solemn and important an instrument as a will is executed, the testator intends to dispose of his whole estate, and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, which presumption is overcome only where the intention of the testator to do otherwise is plain and unambiguous, or is necessarily implied." 

Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 69, 102 S. E. 2d 553; Lewis v. Mitchell (1961), 216 Ga. 526, 527 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 901.

The law presumes that a testator intends to dispose of the whole of his estate and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, unless the intention of the testator is otherwise plain and unambiguous, or must be necessarily implied. Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 471, 99 

S. E. 2d 827; McKain v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822, 108 S. E. 2d 319; 

Roberts v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822, 108 S. E. 2d 319, 73 A.L.R. 2d 479. "A testator is presumed to have intended to bequeath only what he actually owned and could lawfully dispose of." First Nat. Bank & Trust Co. in Macon v. Roberts (1939), 187 Ga. 472, 1 S. E. 2d 12 (13).

Where the language of a will is clear and can be given legal effect as it stands, the courts will not, by construction, give the will a different effect." 

Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 301, 116 S. E. 2d 223. "If two clauses of a will are so inconsistent that both cannot stand, the later will prevail, but the whole will is to be taken together and operation is to be given every part of it, if this can be done without violating its terms or the intention of the testator. Code 1933, § 113-806." Watts v. Finley (1939), 187 Ga. 629, 1 S. E. 2d 723 (8); Rigdon v. Cooper (1948), 203 Ga. 547, 47 S. E. 2d 633.

Where there are provisions in a will which are so inconsistent and irreconcilable that both cannot stand, the latter provision shall prevail. Chamblee v. 

Guy (1962), 218 Ga. 56 (2a), 126 S. E. 2d 205.

Where there are inconsistent provisions in the same will, the latter provision shall prevail, yet it is a settled rule that a court will not by construction reduce an estate once devised absolutely in fee, by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will, unless the intent to limit the devise is clearly and un-

mistakably manifested. Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 103 (2), 109 

S. E. 2d 41.

Code § 113-106 provides that one may bequeath his entire estate to strangers to the exclusion of his wife and children but in such case the will should be closely scrutinized, and upon the slightest evidence of the aberration of intellect, or collusion or fraud, or any undue influence or unfair dealing, probate should be refused. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370, 128 S. E. 2d 53. 

Where "a reading of the will shows clearly that the property is devised to the wife absolutely and in fee simple, and the estate thus created is not reduced by subsequent parts of the will, and it can not be reduced as prayed for in the petition." Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 104, 109 S. E. 2d 41. "Courts will not by construction reduce an estate once devised absolutely in fee by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will unless the intention to limit the devise is clearly and unmistakably manifest.'' Frost v. Dixon (1948), 204 Ga. 268, 49 S. E. 2d 664; McDonald v. Suarez (1956), 212 

Ga. 360, 93 S. E. 2d 16; Callaway v. Faust (1956), 212 Ga. 596, 94 S. E. 2d 379.

As a general rule, courts will not by construction of a will reduce an estate once devised absolutely and in fee, by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will unless the intention to limit or reduce is clearly and unmistakabaly manifested. Lewis v. Mitchell (1961), 216 Ga. 526, 527 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 901; 

Chamblee v. Guy (1962), 218 Ga. 56 (2b), 126 S. E. 2d 205. "An expressed devise cannot be cut down by a subsequent item of doubtful meaning." Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 103 (2), 109 S. E. 2d 41.

Language employed in a codicil, "Any of my children dying without heirs the property they get of me shall be divided between the others," relates entirely to the effective date of the will, the death of the testator. Davant v. 

Shaw (1950), 206 Ga. 843, 59 S. E. 2d 500. "Under the will here involved, which provided that three-sevenths of the testator's estate 'shall be divided equally among any and all children of my deceased brothers and sisters, showing no preference,' the manifest intention of the testator was that the distribution to the nieces and nephews should be per capita, and not per stirpes." Barfield v. Aiken (1953), 209 Ga. 483, 74 

S. E. 2d 100. "While the protective powers of a court of chancery over trust estates and the estates of wards of chancery are broad, comprehensive, and plenary, in construing a will, the intention of the testator must be sought, and the court has no power to devise a new scheme or to make a new will." First Nat. Bank of Atlanta v. Robinson (1953), 209 Ga. 582, 74 S. E. 2d 875. "In the construction of wills, the courts should look to that interpretation which carries out the provisions of the statute of distribution, rather than that which defeats them, and, in the absence of anything in the will to the contrary, the presumption is that the ancestor intended that his property should go where the law carries it, which is supposed to be the channel of natural descent; also that the use of such terms as 'in equal shares' or 'equally divided' will not alone be sufficient to overcome this presumption.' 

Butts v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1953), 209 Ga. 787, 75 S. E. 2d 745. 

"When a testator devises land to one in fee simple, and provides that, if the devisee should die without children, the estate will go to another, a defeasible fee with an executory limitation is created." Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 470, 99 S. E. 2.d 827.

The word "child" used in a statute, will, deed, or other conveyance generally means a legitimate child, unless the context shows a different meaning, or the circumstances surrounding the execution of a paper are such as to make the words include an illegitimate child. Pasley v. State (1960), 215 Ga. 

768, 769 (2), 113 S. E. 2d 454.

Acts 1959, page 99, enacted Code § 113-1528, giving executors and administrators the legal right to borrow money and bind the estate by the execution of a promissory note therefor, and the right to pledge any or all the property of the estate for the payment of the same by mortgage, trust deed, deed to secure debt or other security instrument, for the purpose of paying any gift, estate, inheritance, income, sales or ad valorem taxes due the United States, the State or any municipality or county thereof which constitute a claim or demand against said estate. This section also gives the procedure to be followed by such representative desirous of borrowing money for such purposes. 

§ 134.-Words and Phrases Construed.-Bryant v. Green (1938), 187 Ga. 89, 199 S. E. 804; Armstrong Junior College Commission v. Livesey (1940), 189 

Ga. 825, 7 S. E. 2d 678; Providence Washington Ins. Co. v. Pass (1940), 64 

Ga. App. 221, 12 S. E. 2d 460; Buchanan v. Nicholson (1941), 192 Ga. 754, 16 S. E. 2d 743; Pharis v. Perry (1941), 193 Ga. 125, 17 S. E. 2d 545; Snellings v. Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; Mills v. Tyus (1942), 195 

Ga. 119, 23 S. E. 2d 259; Everitt v. LaSpeyre (1943), 195 Ga. 377, 24 S. E.

E. 2d 522. “In a narrow sense the word 'legatee' means one to whom personal property is bequeathed by a will, but in the popular or broader sense, and where no contrary intent appears in the will, it is applied by the courts of this State as meaning one to whom property, either real or personal, is given under a will.” 

Darnell v. Tate (1951), 84 Ga. App. 831, 67 S. E. 2d 819.

Devise to "my children, share and share alike" held to grant nothing to illegitimate child. Wilson v. Ingram (1950), 207 Ga. 271, 61 S. E. 2d 126. "Bodily heirs' means children. Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 302, 116 

S. E. 2d 223.

The word "heirs" construed as meaning "distributees"; and the word "distributees'' means all of next of kin. Butts v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1953), 209 Ga. 787, 75 S. E. 2d 745.

The ordinary meaning of the words "my surviving children' is the children of the testator surviving him at his death. Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 301, 116 S. E. 2d 223. "Nearest of kin then surviving" was construed as meaning the same as "next of kin." Butts v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1953), 209 Ga. 787, 75 S. E. 

2d 745. "Grandchildren can not take in a will, under a bequest to children, unless there is something in the will to indicate and effectuate such intention by the testator." Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 469, 99 S. E. 2d 827; Chambers v. 

Dooley (1961), 217 Ga. 291, 292, 122 S. E. 2d 92.

"Grandchildren take nothing in a will under a bequest to children as a class, unless there be something to indicate and effectuate an intention that they should take the interest of their parent who dies before the testatrix.” 

Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 301, 116 S. E. 2d 223.

Where no trust, will or deed is involved, as where the question is one of intestates succession, the status of legitimacy is created by the law of the domicile of the parent whose relationship to the child is in question; but a trust of movables created by an instrument inter vivos is administered by the trustee according to the law of the state where the instrument creating the trust locates the administration of the trust. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 

S. E. 2d 147. 

§ 135.-Parol Evidence.—Watts v. Finley (1939), 187 Ga. 629, 1 S. E. 723; 

Hungerford v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 190 Ga. 387, 9 S. E. 2d 630; Snellings v. Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; Blakeman v. Harwell (1944), 198 Ga. 165, 31 S. E. 2d 50. "When called on to construe a will, a court may hear parol testimony of the circumstances of the testator at the time of the execution of the will, and may hear parol testimony to explain all ambiguities, both latent and patent. Code 

1933, § 113-807.'' Bratton v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 191 Ga. 49, 11 S. E. 2d 204 (3); Lining v. Jackson (1947), 203 Ga. 22, 45 S. E. 2d 410.
