E. 2d 328 (3). § 137.-Will Following Rules of Inheritance.-Everitt v. LaSpeyre (1943), 195 Ga. 377, 24 S. E. 2d 381. § 141.-Estates. The law presumes that a testator intends to dispose of the whole of his estate and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, unless the intention of the testator is otherwise plain and unambiguous, or must be necessarily implied. Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 471, 99 S. E. 2d 827; McKain v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822; 108 S. E. 2d 

319; Roberts v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822, 108 S. E. 2d 319, 73 A.L.R. 2d 479. "The natural and reasonable presumption is that when so solemn and important an instrument as a will is executed, the testator intends to dispose of his whole estate, and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, which presumption is overcome only where the intention of the testator to do otherwise is plain and unambiguous, or is necessarily implied."' 

Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 69, 102 S. E. 2d 553. § 142.-Legatees and Devisees.-"An infant en ventre sa mere, or in the mother's womb, is supposed in law to be born for many purposes. It is capable of having a legacy, or a surrender of a copyhold estate, made to it. It may have a guardian assigned to it; and it is enabled to have an estate limited to its use, and to take afterwards by such limitation, as if it were then actually born. And in this point the civil law agrees with ours. Tucker v. Howard 

K. Carmichael & Sons (1951), 208 Ga. 201, 65 S. E. 2d 909. 

In Gray v. Trust Company of Georgia (1955), 211 Ga. 332, 85 S. E. 2d 

721, pending a proceeding for the construction of a will all the beneficiaries under the will entered into an agreement providing for the distribution and

management of the property devised. The superior court approved the agreement and made it a part of the final decree which the court rendered in the construction proceeding. The jurisdiction of the superior court in this matter was upheld by the Supreme Court, and by implication, the Court upheld the validity of such agreements. 

Code § 113-106 provides that one may bequeath his entire estate to strangers to the exclusion of his wife and children but in such case the will should be closely scrutinized, and upon the slightest evidence of the aberration of intellect, or collusion or fraud, or any undue influence or unfair dealing, probate should be refused. Crawford v. Crawford (1962), 218 Ga. 369, 370, 128 S. E. 2d 53. 

§ 144.-Kinds of Legacies and Devises.-Lake v. McComb (1938), 186 Ga. 

658, 198 S. E. 701; Snellings v. Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; 

Young v. Young (1947), 202 Ga. 694, 44 S. E. 2d 659. "A 'special legacy' is one which operates on property specifically designated, while a 'specific legatee' is one to whom a particular thing, as distinguished from all others of the same kind, is bequeathed. Code 1933, § 113-808."' 

Regents of the University System v. Trust Company of Georgia (1938), 186 

Ga. 498, 198 S. E. 345 (2). "A devise to testator's uncle of the remainder of testator's estate, especially all his rights in particularly described property, constituted a 'specific devise' as to the particularly described property, and hence the devise was not subject to abatement because of insufficiency of assets to pay all the debts and ex penses of administration and specific devises. Code 1933, §§ 113-806, 113-808.'' 

Henderson v. First Nat. Bank of Rome (1939), 189 Ga. 175, 5 S. E. 2d 636 (4). 

A residuary legacy is a general legacy. Johnson v. Bogdis (1951), 84 Ga. 

App. 741, 67 S. E. 2d 189.

Provision in will that plaintiff should be paid a salary of $75 per week as long as he should serve as manager of company did not constitute a legacy, and such salary could properly be terminated upon his discharge as manager. Savannah Bank & Trust Co. v. Mason (1952), 209 Ga. 364, 72 S. E. 2d 720. 

§ 145.-Abatement.-In Redfearn on Wills and Administration of Estates in 

Georgia, Revised Edition, section 145, page 238, the statement is made that a money legacy to an executor as additional compensation for his services as such executor is a general legacy and subject to abate under the same rules as other general legacies. This rule would not apply to compensatory devises and bequests to executors in lieu of the statutory compensation allowed executors under Ga. Code Ann. 113-2001. "Testators making wills in this State shall have the power of giving and bequeathing to the persons nominated as executors, as compensation for the services to be rendered by such executors in the execution of the trusts reposed in them, such property or money as the testators may devise, and all such gifts and bequests shall take precedence over any other special gifts or bequests made by said testators: Provided, that such gifts or bequests to executors shall not interfere with the rights of creditors of such testators. (Acts 1869, p. 163.)" Ga. Code Ann. 113-823.

§ 146.-Ademption.-Kaylor v. Kaylor (1945), 199 Ga. 516, 35 S. E. 2d 1; 

Roberts v. Wilson (1946), 200 Ga. 201, 36 S. E. 2d 758; Thompson v. Long (1947), 202 Ga. 718, 44 S. E. 2d 651.

Where a person acquired certain property from her mother by purchase, and later, as a devisee under her mother's will quitclaimed to the executor all right to such property which she might have acquired under such will, such quitclaim did not affect her title by purchase. Covington v. Anderson (1950), 82 Ga. 

App. 622, 61 S. E. 2d 924.

In connection with footnote 70, p. 241 of the Revised Edition, "Where money or property is transferred by parent to child and is accepted, whether transfer is to be treated as advancement depends on intention of parent at time of transaction without regard to concurrence on part of child." Berry v. Berry (1951), 208 Ga. 285, 66 S. E. 2d 336. "A memorandum in a will, of advancement to a legatee, is conclusive of the fact, and is not subject to change by parol evidence." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 

Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757. § 147.-Lapse.-Snellings v. Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; 

Mills v. Tyus (1942), 195 Ga. 119, 23 S. E. 2d 259.

In absence of provision to contrary, legacy will lapse upon death of legatee without issue before death of testator. Collier v. Citizens & Sou. Nat. Bank (1950), 206 Ga. 857, 59 S. E. 2d 385. “When, upon the trial of the application to probate a will, the stipulated facts showed that the sole legatee who was named therein, and to whom the entire estate was devised, predeceased the testator and left no lineal heirs, a judgment denying probate was demanded." Lawson v. Hurt (1962), 217 Ga. 

827, 125 S. E. 2d 480. "A petition to cancel a deed, brought by the sole heirs at law of the maker, is properly dismissed on general demurrer thereto where it appears from the petition that such grantor left a will devising the same land to the defendant, that the will has been offered for probate in solemn form, that a caveat has been filed thereto by the heirs at law, and that the issue as thus made is still pending on appeal for a de novo determination in a court of competent jurisdiction." McKie v. McKie (1959), 215 Ga. 312, 110 S. E. 2d 372. § 149.-Taxation of Legacies and Devises.-"An administrator who had knowledge of tax liability before making distribution of estate to sole heir at law distributed estate at his peril and could not be relieved from personal liability for the tax. Code 1933, §§ 92-6701 et seq., 113-1505."' Hardin v. Reynolds (1939), 189 Ga. 534, 6 S. E. 2d 328 (10). 

§ 150.-Assent of Executor.-Miller v. Harris County (1938), 186 Ga. 648, 

198 S. E. 673; Lewis v. Patterson (1940), 191 Ga. 348, 12 S. E. 2d 593; Pound v. Faulkner (1942), 193 Ga. 413, 18 S. E. 2d 749; Matson v. Crowe (1942), 193 

Ga. 578, 19 S. E. 2d 288; Perdue v. McKenzie (1942), 194 Ga. 356, 21 S. E. 

2d 705; American Telephone & Telegraph Co. v. Smith (1943), 196 Ga. 626, 27 S. E. 2d 305; Strickland v. Jenkins (1944), 198 Ga. 15, 31 S. E. 2d 18; 

Clark v. Woody (1944), 197 Ga. 683, 30 S. E. 2d 181; Holcombe v. Stauffacher (1946), 201 Ga. 38, 38 S. E. 2d 818; Pope v. Stanley (1947), 202 Ga. 180, 42 

S. E. 2d 488; Armstrong v. Merts (1948), 76 Ga. App. 465, 46 S. E. 2d 529; 

Biggers v. Gladin (1948), 204 Ga. 481, 50 S. E. 2d 585; Jackson v. Brown (1948), 203 Ga. 602, 47 S. E. 2d 867; McGahee v. McGahee (1948), 204 Ga. 

91, 48 S. E. 2d 675; Thornton v. Hardin (1949), 205 Ga. 215, 52 S. E. 2d 841; 

Thornton v. Hardin (1949), 205 Ga. 769, 55 S. E. 2d 154.

Title to property remains in the executor until he assents to the devise. 

After such assent is given the land is no longer part of the estate. State Highway Department v. Stewart (1961), 104 Ga. App. 178, 181, 121 S. E. 2d 278.

Code § 113-802, relating to the assent of an executor to a devise or legacy, was amended by Acts 1958, page 665, by striking this section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "113-802. The assent of the executor may be express or may be presumed from his conduct. Assent should be evidenced by a conveyance of realty or tangible personalty or by an assignment or transfer of a chose in action. In the absence of a prior assent, the discharge of the executor shall be conclusive evidence of his assent. 

If no assent has been given within one year after the executor has qualified, a devisee or legatee may cite the executor in the court of ordinary to show cause why his assent should not be given or may compel him to assent by an equitable proceeding. The executor may not, by assenting to legacies, interfere with the rights of creditors, nor can he, by capriciously withholding his assent, destroy the legacy."

Under Code § 113-801 before title passes to a devisee and before a devisee is entitled to possession of the property devised, there must be assent of the executor. This code section applies with equal force to an administrator cum testamento annexo. Nash v. Williamson (1957), 95 Ga. App. 616, 619, 98 S. E. 

2d 239. "The statute providing that, all property being assets to pay debts, no devise or legacy passes title until assent of executor is given, applies with equal force to an administrator cum testamento annexo. Code 1933, 113. 

801." Whatley v. Musselwhite (1939), 189 Ga. 91, 5 S. E. 2d 227 (3). "Upon death of owner of an estate in realty which estate survived him, title vests immediately in his heirs at law, subject to administration by legal representatives and the right of recovery is in the legal representative, if there is one, otherwise the heirs may sue in their own name. Code, § 113-901." 

Slade v. Barber (1946), 200 Ga. 405, 37 S. E. 2d 143 (4). "It is no ground of caveat to the application of the executor to the ordinary for leave to sell land that the executor has assented to a devise in the will of the testator. The caveator's remedy is a claim.'' Salter v. Wetmore (1954), 90 Ga. App. 672, 83 S. E. 2d 852.

Until there has been an assent of the executor, or an administrator cum testamento annexo, to a legacy, either express or implied, and until the debts of the estate have been paid, no action can be maintained for an accounting and for a partitioning of property. Nash v. Williamson (1957), 95 Ga. App. 

616, 98 S. E. 2d 239. § 152.-Election.-"Where a will confers upon a legatee a benefit while attempting to dispose of legatee's own property, legatee must elect whether to accept the benefit under the will or retain his property. Code 1933, §§ 37-501, 37-502, 37-503. 

A devisee's acceptance of a bequest to him will not estop him from asserting his interest contrary to the will if the acceptance is made in ignorance of a material fact, the knowledge of which was necessary to allow him to make an intelligent choice, and where one is called upon to make an election between

a grant in a deed and a bequest in a will, he is entitled to have actual knowledge of all the facts affecting the choice. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 

52, 54, 129 S. E. 2d 82. "The doctrine of election as to wills does not apply where testamentary disposition describes no specific property so as to identify it with that of legatee but describes property only generally. Code 1933, §§ 37-501, 37-502, 37-503.'' 

First Nat. Bank & Trust Co. in Macon v. Roberts (1939), 187 Ga. 472, 1 

S. E. 2d 12 (11, 12). 

§ 154.-Charge on Legacies and Devises. "The action of a beneficiary under a will, in instituting an ejectment suit against the executors to recover land specifically devised to another, forfeited all benefits of such beneficiary under the will in virute of item 25 thereof which, in substance, provides that the institution of proceedings by any beneficiary to invalidate the will or any of its provisions shall annul all benefits which the will provides for such beneficiary. 

The action of three other beneficiaries in instituting ejectment proceedings to recover property not specifically devised by the will did not forfeit benefits provided for them in such a will." Fuller v. Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (1), 122 S. E. 2d 234.

A charge is most often found in cases where the testator has given property to one person with the provision that he pay a certain sum to another person. 

Broach v. Hester (1961), 217 Ga. 59, 61, 121 S. E. 2d 111. 

§ 155.-Devises to a Class.-Bryant v. Green (1938), 187 Ga. 89, 199 S. E. 

804; Gibson v. Stone (1939), 188 Ga. 199, 3 S. E. 2d 676; Armstrong Junior 

College Commission v. Livesey (1940), 189 Ga. 825, 7 S. E. 2d 678; Jefferson v. Bright (1940), 189 Ga. 866, 8 S. E. 2d 21; Hungerford v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 190 Ga. 387, 9 S. E. 2d 630; Nixon v. Nixon (1941), 192 Ga. 629, 15 

S. E. 2d 883; Snellings v. Downer (1942), 193 Ga. 340, 18 S. E. 2d 531; Renney v. Kimberly (1955), 211 Ga. 396, 86 S. E. 2d 217. "Generally, where there is a devise to a class, the members of the class are to be ascertained upon the death of the testator, since the will takes effect on that date. “Under a devise to children as a class by way of remainder, children in esse at death of testator take vested interests." Walters v. Suarez (1939), 188 Ga. 190, 3 S. E. 2d 575 (1, 2). 

In executory devises to children as a class where there are children in esse at the time of the testator's death, the latter take vested interests on the death of the testator unless there is a clear manifestation of a contrary intent on the part of the testator. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (2), 126 S. E. 2d 776. "In a devise to children as a class by way of remainder, children in esse at the time of the testator take vested interests, this rule applies to an executory devise, as well as to a remainder." Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137, 141, 126 S. E. 2d 776. "It is the general rule that, in a devise to a class, the members of the class are to be ascertained as of the date of the death of the testator, and to take a case out of the general rule, the intention to do so must be shown by clear and unambiguous language." Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 301, 116 S. E. 2d 223. 

Devise by mother to children share and share alike is a devise to a class, and goes to those members of the class who survive the testatrix. Where all the members of such class except one son execute a writing to the effect that

all the property shall go to such son in consideration of his expenditures for the mother, and such writing is entered on the will, a waiver is effected. Hurst v. McKissack (1952), 209 Ga. 440, 73 S. E. 2d 91. “Grandchildren can not take in a will, under a bequest to children, unless there is something in the will to indicate and effectuate such intention by the testator." Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 469, 99 S. E. 2d 827.

A devise to children as a class means immediate offspring and does not include grandchildren. Chambers v. Dooley (1961), 217 Ga. 291, 292, 122 S. E. 2d 92. “Grandchildren take nothing in a will under a bequest to children as a class, unless there be something to indicate and effectuate an intention that they should take the interest of their parent who dies before the testatrix.' 

Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 301, 116 S. E. 2d 223. 

Where, under the language of a will, 

property is given to said children for and during the term of their natural lives only, and after their death to their children . . ." without more would clearly and indisputably give to the grandchildren a vested remainder in the estate of their grandfather, which would vest at the time of the birth of the first grandchild, subject to open and let in afterborn grandchildren. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 148, 150, 109 

S. E. 2d 741. 

§ 156.-Distribution.-In Gray v. Trust Company of Georgia (1955), 211 Ga. 

332, 85 S. E. 2d 721, pending a proceeding for the construction of a will all the beneficiaries under the will entered into an agreement providing for the distribution and management of the property devised. The superior court approved the agreement and made it a part of the final decree which the court rendered in the construction proceeding. The jurisdiction of the su perior court in this matter was upheld by the Supreme Court, and by implication, the Court upheld the validity of such agreements. 

Until there has been an assent of the executor, or an administrator cum testamento annexo, to a legacy, either express or implied, and until the debts of the state have been paid, no action can be maintained for an accounting and for a partitioning of property. Nash v. Williamson (1957), 95 Ga. App. 

616, 98 S. E. 2d 239. 

§ 157.-Estates-Definitions.-Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. v. Hall (1940), 191 

Ga. 294, 12 S. E. 2d 53; Warehouses, Inc. v. Wetherbee (1948), 203 Ga. 483, 46 S. E. 2d 894; Bush v. Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1949), 79 Ga. 

App. 25, 52 S. E. 2d 515. "The natural and reasonable presumption is that when so solemn and important an instrument as a will is executed, the testator intends to dispose of his whole estate, and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, which presumption is overcome only where the intention of the testator to do otherwise is plain and unambiguous, or is necessarily implied.' 

Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 69, 102 S. E. 2d 553. 

The law presumes that a testator intends to dispose of the whole of his estate and does not intend to die intestate as to any part of his property, unless the intention of the testator is otherwise plain and unambiguous, or must be necessarily implied. Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 471, 99 

S. E. 2d 827; McKain v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822, 108 S. E. 2d 319; 

Roberts v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 822, 108 S. E. 2d 319, 73 A.L.R. 2d 479; 

Lewis v. Mitchell (1961), 216 Ga. 526, 527 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 901.

As a general rule, courts will not by construction of a wlil reduce an estate once devised absolutely and in fee, by limitations contained in subsequent parts

of the will unless the intention to limit or reduce is clearly and unmistakably manifested. Lewis v. Mitchell (1961), 216 Ga. 526, 527 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 901. 

§ 158.-Fee-Simple Estates.-Singer v. First Nat. Bank & Trust Co. (1943), 

195 Ga. 269, 24 S. E. 2d 47; Moody v. Baxley Turpentine Corporation (1943), 195 Ga. 482, 24 S. E. 2d 652; Jenkins v. Shuften (1950), 206 Ga. 315, 57 S. E. 

2d 283. "An estate in fee simple is the greatest estate that a person can hold in property. Code 1933, § 85-501.'' Regents of the University System v. Trust 

Company of Georgia (1938), 186 Ga. 498, 198 S. E. 345 (1). "An estate in fee simple is the entire and absolute property in the land; no person can have a greater estate or interest." Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 102 (1), 109 S. E. 2d 41.

Absolute estate in fee will not be reduced unless intent to limit devise is clearly evidenced by the language of the will or codicil. Davant v. Shaw (1950), 206 Ga. 843, 59 S. E. 2d 500. "It is a settled rule that a court will not by construction reduce an estate once devised absolutely in fee, by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will, unless the intent to limit the devise is clearly and unmistakably manifested. If the expression relied upon to limit the fee once devised be doubtful, the doubt should be resolved in favor of absolute estate." Dillard v. Dillard (1961), 217 Ga. 176, 178, 121 S. E. 2d 766.

Where "a reading of the will shows clearly that the property is devised to the wife absolutely and in fee simple, and the estate thus created is not reduced by subsequent parts of the will, and it can not be reduced as prayed for in the petition." Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 104, 109 S. E. 2d 41.

While as a general rule a court will not by construction reduce an estate once devised absolutely in fee by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will, yet a court will do so when the intent to limit the devise is clearly and unmistakably manifested. Chamblee v. Guy (1962), 218 Ga. 56 (2b), 126 

S. E. 2d 205.

Where a fee-simple estate is vested in the remaindermen, an attempted curtailment of their rights of alienation is ineffective, as being repugnant to the estate granted. Bussey v. Bussey (1952), 208 Ga. 760, 69 S. E. 2d 569. "It is the rule in Georgia that a power to dispose of property annexed to a life estate will not enlarge the estate given to a fee." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553. "A power is not property but a mere authority, and an absolute power of disposal is not inconsistent with an estate for life only. The gift of such power will not enlarge the life-estate previously given, but confers an authority in addition thereto." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553. 

In Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 102 S. E. 2d 553, it was held that the will of the testator, construed as a whole, which first provided for the payment of testator's just debts and funeral expenses, and then provided "The remainder I devise and bequeath to my beloved wife, . . . to have and to hold and keep as her property as long as she lives unless she sees fit to sell such things as she cannot use;" and, "I will that my said property be kept intact except such property that it requires to cover my debts and funeral expenses, unless my said wife . . . sees fit to dispose of such property as will be of no benefit to her until the youngest child becomes twenty-one years of age," gave widow a fee simple title rather a mere life estate.

"A fee simple estate passed to the survivor of the makers of a joint will which contained the following item: 'Upon the death of either of us, all the property of the deceased is given, devised and bequeathed to the survivor.' 

Said fee simple estate was not limited or qualified by a subsequent item stating that, 'It is the will of each of us that upon the death of the survivor, or upon the simultaneous death of both the makers hereof, that all of our estate and the estate of the survivor, both real and personal, wheresoever the same may be located, shall go in equal shares absolutely and in fee simple to Tommy B. 

Dillard and Patricia F. Dillard.''' Dillard v. Dillard (1961), 217 Ga. 176, 121

S. E. 2d 766. 

Merger of estates. McDaniel v. Bagby (1949), 204 Ga. 750, 51 S. E. 2d 805. 

§ 159.-Life Estates.—O'Hara v. Jacobs (1940), 191 Ga. 5, 11 S. E. 2d 199; 

Bienvenu v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1941), 193 Ga. 101, 17 S. E. 2d 

257; Yerbey v. Chandler (1942), 194 Ga. 263, 21 S. E. 2d 636; Singer v. First 

Nat. Bank & Trust Co. (1943), 195 Ga. 269, 24 S. E. 2d 47; Gilmore v. Gilmore (1944), 197 Ga. 303, 29 S. E. 2d 74; Raines v. Shipley (1945), 199 Ga. 316, 34 S. E. 2d 281; Williams v. J. M. High Co. (1946), 200 Ga. 230, 36 S. E. 2d 

667; Wright v. Conner (1946), 200 Ga. 413, 37 S. E. 2d 353; Campbell v. Barnard (1946), 74 Ga. App. 272, 39 S. E. 2d 420; Folds v. Hartry (1947), 201 Ga. 783, 41 S. E. 2d 142; Frost v. Dixon (1948), 204 Ga. 268, 49 S. E. 2d 664. "It has long been established that life estates subject to termination under particular circumstances may be created." Mid-State Homes, Inc. v. Johnson (1962), 218 Ga. 397, 399, 128 S. E. 2d 197.

Contingent remainders and life estate being alienable, they could be the subject matter of a conveyance by a testatrix to trustees and to her children. 

Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 112, 116, 126 S. E. 2d 755. "It is the rule in Georgia that a power to dispose of property annexed to a life estate will not enlarge the estate given to a fee." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553. "A power is not property but a mere authority, and an absolute power of disposal is not inconsistent with an estate for life only. The gift of such power will not enlarge the life-estate previously given, but confers an authority in addition thereto." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553. "Where property is held by a life tenant and taxes are assessed and executions issued against him in personam only, the liens represented thereby exist as such only against the life estate and are not enforceable against the remainder estate, and the same rule applies where returns are made by one who is an agent of the life tenant only and executions are issued against agent merely in personam. Coleman v. Durden (1941), 193 Ga. 76, 17 S. E. 2d 176 (1). 

"Generally, the assent of the executor to a legacy to the tenant for life inures to benefit of the remainderman, but the rule is otherwise where executor by will has a trust to perform, arising out of the property, after death of the life tenant." Dixon v. Richardson (1942), 194 Ga. 443, 21 S. E. 2d 854 (1). "A testator may authorize a widow, given a life estate in personalty, to encroach upon corpus by actual consumption of such personal assets for her support in the event she should so desire with a remainder over only in the unconsumed portion." Keen v. Rodgers (1948), 203 Ga. 578, 47 S. E. 2d 567.

Ordinarily a contingent remainderman, or a remainderman whose estate is subject to be divested, cannot during the existence of the preceding life estate

proceed against the life tenant or trustee for an accounting, etc. Fulton Nat. 

Bank v. Randall (1950), 207 Ga. 245, 61 S. E. 2d 122.

Where a remainder estate vested in the petitioner upon the death of the testator, subject to being divested in the event of her pre-deceasing the defendant, the petitioner alone is the proper person to prosecute an action for waste and want of care as to authorize a forfeiture of the life estate and to give immediate possession to the remainderman. Smith v. Minich (1959), 215 

Ga. 386, 110 S. E. 2d 649.

A vested interest for life and a contingent interest thereafter, depending upon survivorship, is such an interest as can be conveyed and assigned. It is not, therefore, necessary that devisees be owners indefeasibly in fee in order to convey their interest in property to the "remaining heirs, as provided by the will of the testator. Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 471, 99 S. E. 

2d 827. 

Where uncontradicted evidence shows that all pine timber growing on a tract of land was sold prior to the execution of a deed which created a remainder interest in the plaintiff, and the evidence further shows without question that the plaintiff had knowledge of the sale, the remainderman took no interest in that timber and could not complain of waste because of the cutting and removal of timber. Klias v. Conley (1961), 216 Ga. 832 (1), 120 

S. E. 2d 306.

Where a testator gave his estate to his wife for life and provided that on her death his three sons were to receive the net income therefrom and that upon the death of the last surviving son the corpus of the estate was to be divided among his grandchildren, the terms and provisions of the testator's will clearly show that it was his intention that the corpus of his estate be held intact for the ultimate benefit of his grandchildren, and that his wife, during her lifetime and his three sons, should, after her death, personally have and receive annually the entire net income of his estate and that any profit arising from a sale of capital assets of his estate became a part of the corpus of the estate, and that the petitioners have no rights to receive the same as a part of the income of the estate. Also, that it was the intention of the testator that any loss sustained by his estate through he sale of capital assets should be treated as a loss of corpus, and that the petitioners as executors of the estate are not required to deduct a corpus loss from the annual income of the estate before distributing to themselves as life beneficiaries under the will the net income of the estate for any given year. Hirsch v. Hirsch (1960), 216 Ga. 379, 116 S. E. 2d 318.

Where testator gave his wife a life estate in all of his property, real and personal, subject only to the right of his executor, in his discretion, to advance specified amounts to his children before assenting to the devise, this did not deprive his wife of a full life estate in all sums remaining. Whitlock v. 

Michael (1951), 208 Ga. 229, 65 S. E. 2d 797.

A life estate is subject to levy and sale under an execution against the life tenant. Whitlock v. Michael (1951), 208 Ga. 229, 65 S. E. 2d 797.

Where wife was left property for her natural life, with power of disposition, subject only to obligation of paying taxes, keeping up insurance, and preserving it, with further provision for sale and disposition on her death, she took a life estate with a power of disposal. Townsley v. Townsley (1952). 209 Ga. 323, 72 S. E. 2d 289.

When, upon the happening of a certain condition provided for by will, certain property was to go to the testator's daughters for life and to the

heirs of their bodies, daughter who died without issue had only a life estate in the portion which, by agreement of all the daughters, was her share, and since the will had no residuary clause, this daughter's legacy lapsed, and there was an interstacy as to her share. Smallpiece v. Johnson (1954), 210 

Ga. 310, 80 S. E. 2d 296.

In Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 102 S. E. 2d 553, it was held that the will of the testator, construed as a whole, which first provided for the payment of testator's just debts and funeral expenses, and then provided "The remainder I devise and bequeath to my beloved wife, . . . to have and to hold and keep as her property as long as she lives unless she sees fit to sell such things as she cannot use;" and, "I will that my said property be kept intact except such property that it requires to cover my debts and funeral expenses, unless my said wife sees fit to dispose of such property as will be of no benefit to her until the youngest child becomes twenty-one years of age,'' gave widow a fee simple title rather a mere life estate. 

Where a settlor provided that the trust should be divided into as many parts as he had children, and that each child was to receive the proceeds from his or her trust for and during his or her natural life, and then provided remainders to the issue of his children upon the death of said children, and the trust set out in detail how the remainders were to be paid and administered, the children of settlor took a life interest in the corpus of the trust estate with remainder to their issue and not a fee simple interest, the trusts being held executory since the remaindermen could not be determined until the children of the settlor die. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 292, 104 S. E. 2d 461. § 160.-Estate for Years.-The rule in this state is that a trust in which contingent remainders follow a life estate and are embraced by the trust will remain executory until such time as the persons who are to take the remainders can be ascertained. Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 111, 119, 126 S. E. 2d 755.

Where, under the language of a will, property "" is given to said children for and during the term of their natural lives only, and after their death to their children ." without more would clearly and indisputably give to the grandchildren a vested remainder in the estate of their grandfather, which would vest at the time of the birth of the first grandchild, subject to open and let in afterborn grandchildren. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 148, 150, 109 

S. E. 2d 741. 

§ 161.-Estates Tail-Singer v. First Nat. Bank & Trust Co. (1943), 195 

Ga. 269, 24 S. E. 2d 47. "Bodily heirs" means children. Veal v. King (1960), 216 Ga. 298, 302, 116

Where a will created a trust estate with a limitation over to his heirs at law who might be in life at the time of the termination of the trust estate, under the provisions of Code § 85-504, the words "heirs at law" would mean children and descendants of children, and since the only children of the testator have died without issue, it now appears that this remainder failed, and the reversionary interest in the testator's estate vested, upon his death, in those who were then his heirs at law, with the right of possession postponed until the death of the last life tenant. Dodson v. Trust Company of Georgia (1960), 216 

Ga. 499 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 331. 

§ 162.-Estates Tail-"Children"-Rule in Wild's Case.-Bryant v. Green 

(1938), 187 Ga. 89, 199 S. E. 804; Grant v. Grant (1939), 187 Ga. 807, 2 S. E. 

2d 421; Cooper v. Harkness (1939), 188 Ga. 121, 2 S. E. 2d 918; Singer v. First

Nat. Bank & Trust Co. (1943), 195 Ga. 269, 24 S. E. 2d 47; Moody v. Baxley 

Turpentine Corporation (1943), 195 Ga. 482, 24 S. E. 2d 652; Lane v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1943), 195 Ga. 828, 25 S. E. 2d 800; Patellis v. Tanner (1944), 197 Ga. 471, 29 S. E. 2d 419. "The rule that grant or devise to named person and 'heirs of her body' vests fee simple title in her is inapplicable where less estate has been carved out and term 'heirs of her body' or words of similar import are used in connection with a limitation over in remainder." Lewis v. Fry (1943), 69 Ga. 

App. 461, 26 S. E. 2d 122 (5). "Grandchildren can not take in a will, under a bequest to children, unless there is something in the will to indicate and effectuate such intention by the testator." Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 Ga. 466, 469, 99 S. E. 2d 827.

Where a will created a trust estate with a limitation over to his heirs at law who might be in life at the time of the termination of the trust estate, under the provisions of Code § 85-504, the words "heirs at law" would mean children and descendants of children, and since the only children of the testator have died without issue, it now appears that this remainder failed, and the reversionary interest in the testator's estate vested, upon his death, in those who were then his heirs at law, with the right of possession postponed until the death of the last life tenant. Dodson v. Trust Company of Georgia (1960), 216 

Ga. 499 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 331. 

§ 163.-Rule in Shelley's Case.-"Rule in Shelley's Case is abolished so far as it affects limitations over but it still applies in case of a deed or devise to 'A and his heirs' which is treated as putting absolute fee in A. Code 1933, 

"Under statute declaring that phrase 'his heirs' and words of like import shall mean 'children' whenever they occur in limitations over, in a deed or devise to 'A for life' with remainder to his 'heirs,' words 'his heirs' are treated as words of purchase and not of limitation, and instrument is construed as creating two estates, one to 'A' for life, and at his death, another estate to his children. Code 1933, § 85-504. "Under statute providing that the phrase 'his heirs,' and words of like import shall mean 'children' whenever used in limitations over, 'limitation over' includes any estate in the same property created or contemplated by the conveyance to be enjoyed after the first estate granted expires or is exhausted. 

Code 1933, § 85-504." Cooper v. Harkness (1939), 188 Ga. 121, 2 S. E. 

2d 918 (2, 3, 4). 

Grandchildren cannot take by the description of children unless there be something in the will to manifest that intention. Chambers v. Dooley (1961), 217 Ga. 291, 292, 122 S. E. 2d 92. "The law does not require the probate of a foreign will in this State in order for such a will to constitute a valid muniment of title." Nuckolls v. 

Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 35, 37, 114 S. E. 2d 427. 

§ 164.-Executory Devise.-Bryant v. Green (1938), 187 Ga. 89, 199 S. E. 

804; Sanders v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1939), 189 Ga. 450, 6 S. E. 2d 294; 

Jenkins v. Shuften (1950), 206 Ga. 315, 57 S. E. 2d 283.

The right of testator to place an executory limitation upon an estate devised by his will is not such a condition repugnant to the estate granted, as is prohibited by Ga. Code Ann., § 85-903. McDonald v. Suarez (1956), 212 Ga. 360, 362, 93 S. E. 2d 16.

A defeasible fee with an executory limitation is created when a testator devises land to one in fee simple, and subsequently provides in his will that, if a certain event does or does not happen, the estate will go to another. 

McDonald v. Suarez (1956), 212 Ga. 360 (2), 93 S. E. 2d 16. "When a testator devises land to one in fee simple, and provides that, if the devisee should die without children, the estate will go to another, a defeasible fee with an executory limitation is created." Johnson v. Johnson (1957), 213 

Ga. 466, 470, 99 S. E. 2d 827.

A devise of the residue of testatrix's estate to one person, and if she should die without children to another, conveys to the first devisee an estate in fee defeasible on her dying childless, and where, as here, the second devisee survived the testatrix, but predeceased the first devisee, upon the death of the first without child or children, the property passed to the heirs of the second devisee. Scranton-Lackawanna Trust Company v. Bruen (1950), 206 Ga. 

872, 59 S. E. 2d 397.

In executory devises to children as a class where there are children in esse at the time of the testator's death, the latter take vested interests on the death of the testator unless there is a clear manifestation of a contrary intent on the part of the testator. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (2), 126 S. E. 2d 776.

The rule in this state is that a trust in which contingent remainders follow a life estate and are embraced by the trust will remain executory until such time as the persons who are to take the remainders can be ascertained. Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 111, 119, 126 S. E. 2d 755. "In a devise to children as a class by way of remainder, children in esse at the time of the testator take vested interests, this rule applies to an executory devise, as well as to a remainder." Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137, 141, 126 S. E. 2d 776.

Even if a gift would have failed at common law as a remainder for want of a particular estate to support it, it is still good as an executory devise. 

Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (1), 126 S. E. 2d 776. 

§ 165.-Perpetuities.-Regents of the University System v. Trust Company of Georgia (1938), 186 Ga. 498, 198 S. E. 345; Murphy v. Johnston (1940), 190 

Ga. 23, 8 S. E. 2d 23; Perkins v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1940), 190 

Ga. 29, 8 S. E. 2d 28; Taylor v. Trustees of Jesse Parker Williams Hospital (1940), 190 Ga. 349, 9 S. E. 2d 165; Boykin v. Bradley (1941), 192 Ga. 212, 14 

S. E. 2d 734; Brown v. Mathis (1947), 201 Ga. 740, 41 S. E. 2d 137.

The aim of and reason for the rule against perpetuities, which is to prevent the tying up of property for an unreasonable length of time and to prohibit unreasonable restraint upon the alienation of property. So long as the settlor of an inter vivos trust has the absolute right to revoke or terminate the trust for his own exclusive personal benefit, there is no tying up of property and no restraint upon the alienability of the property in the trust fund, and thus no reason to include this time during which the trust is so destructible in determining whether a limitation is violative of the rule against perpetuities. 

Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461.

The rule against perpetuities is concerned with remoteness of vesting. Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 112, 117, 126 S. E. 2d 755.

The rule against perpetuities applies only to remoteness of vesting of title and not to postponement of enjoyment after a vesting not too remote. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (3), 126 S. E. 2d 776.

The rule against perpetuities applies to conditions subsequent, and where there is a possibility that a condition might occur at a time too remote, that condition is void. Where the condition is divesting in nature, and fails due to remoteness, the defeasible fee becomes indefeasible. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (4), 126 S. E. 2d 776. "The period of time during which an interest is destructible, pursuant to the uncontrolled volition, and for the exclusive personal benefit of the person having such a power of destruction is not included in determining whether the limitation is invalid under the rule against perpetuities. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461.

When a settlor has the power during his lifetime to revoke or destroy the trust estate for his own exclusive personal benefit, the question whether interests, or any of them, created by an instrument or deed of trust are void, because in violation of the rule against perpetuities, is to be determined as of the date of the settlor's death and not as of the date the instrument is executed and delivered. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461. "A perpetual lease or perpetual right to renew a lease does not violate rule against perpetuities or statutes limiting period during which absolute power of alienation may be suspended." Williams v. J. M. High Co. (1946), 200 

Ga. 230, 36 S. E. 2d 667 (2).

The will of the testator provided for a trust of income for the benefit of three sisters, and at their death, for the benefit of his "nieces in equal parts and the trust held intact as long as anyone of them is living and 21 years thereafter." The gift to the nieces was held to constitute a gift to a class, subject to open, and possible of being extended through the lives of some not in being at the time the limitations became effective plus more than 21 years thereafter. Such gift was held to violate the rule against perpetuities. 

Landrum v. National City Bank of Rome (1954), 210 Ga. 316, 80 S. E. 2d 300. "As vested remainders are not subject to the rule against perpetuities, it follows that the rule against perpetuities does not apply to reversions. The logical deduction from this conclusion is that a grantor or a testator may create a vested estate for any number of years, and such estate will not be destroyed by the rule against perpetuities. For illustration, a testator or a grantor may create a present estate to endure for any number of years, either more or less than one thousand years, provided such estate is followed by a reversion to the maker of the instrument, or to his heirs, or by a vested remainder in fee.” 

Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 112, 117, 126 S. E. 2d 755, quoting Redfearn,

Wills and Administration of Estates, § 165, p. 287. 

"Where the will seeks to set up a trust for the benefit of a number of persons as well as institutions, but the duration of a life of anyone in being constitutes no part of the specified duration of the trust, and it is provided therein that it shall not endure for more than 25 years, it is a clear violation of the rule against perpetuities, and the trust is absolutely void." Fuller v. 

Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (2), 122 S. E. 2d 234. 

§ 166.-Estates in Remainder.—Gormley v. Cleaveland (1939), 187 Ga. 457, 

200 S. E. 793; Pound v. Faulkner (1942), 193 Ga. 413, 18 S. E. 2d 749; Guess v. Morgan (1943), 196 Ga. 265, 26 S. E. 2d 424; Britt v. Fincher (1947), Ga. 661, 44 S. E. 2d 372. 202 "The distinction between a 'vested' and a 'contingent' interest is the uncertainty of the right of enjoyment in the future and not the uncertainty of enjoyment in the future.

"A remainder is 'vested' if it is subject to no condition precedent save the termination of the preceding estates." Grant v. Grant (1939), 187 Ga. 807, 2 S. E. 2d 421 (2, 3). 

A remainder estate is not necessarily the entire estate that is left after a previous estate is determined. A legatee may have an estate for life, his own or that of some other person, and still be a remainderman. Dodson v. Trust 

Company of Georgia (1960), 216 Ga. 499, 505, 117 S. E. 2d 331.

There being an intestacy as to a remainder estate, the reversionary interest in the testator's estate vested, upon his death, in those who were then his heirs at law, with the right of possession postponed until the death of the last life tenant. Dodson v. Trust Company of Georgia (1960), 216 Ga. 499, 503, 117 S. E. 2d 331. "In a devise to children as a class by way of remainder, children in esse at the time of the testator take vested interests, this rule applies to an executory devise, as well as to a remainder. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 

137, 141, 126 S. E. 2d 776.

Even if a gift would have failed at common law as a remainder for want of a particular estate to support it, it is still good as an executory devise. 

Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137 (1), 126 S. E. 2d 776.

The petitioner, as a remainderman, cannot require a distribution of the estate of the testator, until the termination of the estate of the life tenant. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668 (1), 119 S. E. 2d 28.

Where uncontradicted evidence shows that all pine timber growing on a tract of land was sold prior to the execution of a deed which created a remainder interest in the plaintiff, and the evidence further shows without question that the plaintiff had knowledge of the sale, the remainderman took no interest in that timber and could not complain of waste because of the cutting and removal of timber. Klias v. Conley (1961), 216 Ga. 832 (1), 120

A vested interest for life and a contingent interest thereafter, depending upon survivorship, is such an interest as can be conveyed and assigned. A vested remainderman in lands has a present estate or interest therein which has the character of absolute ownership and though the enjoyment of the interest is postponed to the future, it is, nevertheless, a present interest

which may be sold by conveyance, devised by will, or levied on, and sold under process. Oliver v. Irvin (1962), 105 Ga. App. 844, 845 (1), 125 S. E. 2d 695.

It is well established that in Georgia the policy of the law is to favor the vesting or remainders at the earliest possible time unless the intention of the testator is clearly manifest to the contrary. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 

148, 150, 109 S. E. 2d 741. "While it is recognized that remaindermen are not joint tenants with the life tenant, they do, nevertheless, have such an interest in the estate in common with the life tenant that they are necessary parties to the processioning proceeding." Oliver v. Irvin (1962), 105 Ga. App. 844, 845 (1), 125 S. E. 2d 695.

The petitioner, as a remainderman, cannot require a distribution of the estate of the testator, until the termination of the estate of the life tenant. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668 (1), 119 S. E. 2d 28.

There being an intestacy as to a remainder estate, the reversionary interest in the testator's estate vested, upon his death, in those who were then his heirs at law, with the right of possession postponed until the death of the last life tenant. Dodson v. Trust Company of Georgia (1960), 216 Ga. 499, 503, 117 

S. E. 2d 331.

Where there are inconsistent provisions in the same will, the latter provision shall prevail, yet it is a settled rule that a court will not by construction reduce an estate once devised absolutely in fee, by limitations contained in subsequent parts of the will, unless the intent to limit the devise is clearly and unmistakably manifested. Houston v. Coram (1959), 215 Ga. 101, 103 (2), 109 S. E. 2d 41. 

Divesting clauses, especially as to remainders, following the grant of an absolute estate should be strictly construed so as to vest the estate absolutely at the earliest possible time. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 148, 151, 109 

S. E. 2d 741.

Where an instrument is susceptible to two constructions, the one favorable to vested and unfavorable to contingent remainders should be adopted. Miller v. Brown (1959), 215 Ga. 148, 150, 109 S. E. 2d 741. "Prescription does not begin to run against remaindermen until the death of the life tenant.' Futch v. Jarrard (1947), 203 Ga. 47, 45 S. E. 2d 420.

Devise of realty was "to 'N' during life and at her death to such of her children as survive her, and to representatives of any that may be dead." 

Where "N" and her only child, "E", survived testator, "E" had a vested remainder subject to be divested by his dying before "N", and where he did so die, a child of "E" would prevail over a grantee in a deed made jointly by "N" and "E". Shedden v. Donaldson (1950), 207 Ga. 77, 60 S. E. 2d 158.

Bequest to trustee for benefit of "A" during her life, with remainder to be paid at her death to "B" and "C", if they survive, or to the children of "B" and "C" should such children survive them, constitutes defeasible vested interest in such children of "B" and "C", and assignment by "B" and "C" of their interests to "A" would not bring about such merger of interests as to cut off rights of such children. Hardison v. Bridges (1959), 215 Ga. 562, 111 S. E. 2d 138. "The defeasible fee is a present, possessory freehold estate of inheritance.

It has the attributes of a fee interest, such as general inheritability, but is not a fee simple due to the fact that it may be defeased. WILLS AND ADMINISTRATION OF Estates 

with the provision that should the husband remarry, "then in this event the life estate herein granted is to cease, and said property is to go to my nephew,' was held to mean that the nephew took a vested remainder interest in the described real property on the death of the testatrix, to be enjoyed, at any event, upon the death or remarriage of the life tenant. McKain v. Allen (1959), 214 Ga. 820, 108 S. E. 2d 319. "In terrorem" is defined as follows: "In terror or warning; by way of threat. Applied to legacies given upon condition that the recipient shall not dispute the validity or the dispositions of the will." Taylor v. Rapp (1962), 217 Ga. 654, 655 (1), 124 S. E. 2d 271. "In terrorem" is defined as "In terror or warning; by way of threat. 

Applied to legacies given upon condition that the recipient shall not dispute the validity or the dispositions of the will; such a condition being usually regarded as a mere threat." Broach v. Hester (1961), 217 Ga. 59, 61, 121 

S. E. 2d 111. A condition in terrorem" is a provision in a will which threatens the beneficiaries under the will with forfeiture of their legacies or bequests should they contest the validity or dispositions of the will. Taylor v. Rapp (1962), 217 Ga. 654 (1), 124 S. E. 2d 271.

In terrorem clauses are valid in this state so long as there is a limitation over to some other person and so long as the condition imposed is not impossible, illegal, or against public policy. Taylor v. Rapp (1962), 217 Ga. 654, 656, 124 S. E. 2d 271.

Even though Code § 53-107 provides that every effort to restrain or discourage marriage by contract, condition, limitation, or otherwise, shall be invalid and void, said section also provides that prohibiting marriage to a particular person or persons, or before a certain reasonable age, or other prudential provisions looking only to the interest of the person to be benefited, and not in general restrain of the marriage will be allowed and held valid. 

Therefore, and in terrorem provision in a will which only restrains the plaintiff from marrying a particular person, is not void. Taylor v. Rapp (1962), 217 

Ga. 654, 656, 124 S. E. 2d 271. "A condition in terrorem is valid where there are limitations over. A declaratory judgment action seeking to invalidate the present will violates the will's in terrorem clause and voids the plaintiff's interest under the will." 

Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137, 138 (5), 126 S. E. 2d 776. "The action of a beneficiary under a will, in instituting an ejectment suit against the executors to recover land specifically devised to another, forfeited all benefits of such beneficiary under the will in virtue of item 25 thereof which, in substance, provides that the institution of proceedings by any beneficiary to invalidate the will or any of its provisions shall annul all benefits which the will provides for such beneficiary. The action of three other beneficiaries in instituting ejectment proceedings to recover property not specifically devised by the will did not forfeit benefits provided for them in such a will." 

Fuller v. 

Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (1), 122 S. E. 2d 234. "A condition in terrorem will be sustained where the will especially directs that the share of the person violating the condition shall fall into the residue; but a mere general gift of the residue, or a gift over to the testator's estate, is not such a gift over as will take the case out of the operation of the foregoing rule as to conditions in terrorem, although there is some authority to the contrary. A general residuary clause is not of itself regarded as a substitute

for, or as the equivalent of, a gift over; and a gift to heirs may not be a gift over. "Broach v. Hester (1961), 217 Ga. 59, 62, 121 S. E. 2d 111.

A will provided: "I desire my property to be handled with the least possible expense and herein direct and provide that if any one of my said children take any steps to cause any expense in probating this my will or contesting same any way, that such child shall forfeit any and all benefits under terms hereof." 

It was held, there being no limitation over to some other person as is required by Code § 113-820 in order to enforce conditions in terrorem such condition in the will was void and the caveat to the application of the executors for discharge should have been sustained. Broach v. Hester (1961), 217 Ga. 59, 121 

S. E. 2d 111.

An item in a will, “In the event that any beneficiary under my will shall bring any action in any court to contest the validity of my will or of any provision thereof, any bequest or benefit set out in my will in behalf of such beneficiary shall be revoked and rescinded and the share of such beneficiary shall go pro rata to the remaining beneficiaries," contains limitations over and does not violate public policy. Therefore, a declaratory judgment action seeking to invalidate the will violates the will's in terrorem clause and voids the plaintiffs' interest under the will. Lanier v. Lanier (1962), 218 Ga. 137, 145 (5), 126 S. E. 2d 776.

A provision in a will of a decedent, who was given a power of appointment over certain property and who executed certain inter vivos agreement giving named grandchildren a one and one-half per cent undivided interest, respectively, in the property, was void insofar as such provision of the will attempted to impose a forfeiture of any legacy under the will by virtue of a claim of rights under the instruments executed by decedent in favor of her grandchildren. Browne v. Hendley (1960), 216 Ga. 411, 116 S. E. 2d 537. 

§ 175.-Definition and Nature of Trusts.-Pittman v. Pittman (1943), 196 

Ga. 397, 26 S. E. 2d 764. "Trusts are either express or implied; implied trusts are such as are inferred by law from the nature of the transaction or from the conduct of the parties. Code § 108-104. Trusts are implied whenever the legal title is in one person, but the beneficial interest, either from the payment of the purchase money or other circumstances, is either wholly or partially in another. Code § 108-106." Bullard v. Bullard (1958), 214 Ga. 122, 123, 103 S. E. 2d 570.

No particular form is necessary to create a trust estate, but there is only required a manifest intention that another person shall have the benefit of the property, in which case the grantee of the property is a trustee for the other person. Wright v. Piedmont Engineering & Construction Corporation (1962), 

106 Ga. App. 401, 403, 128 S. E. 2d 865.

The primary purpose of a trust is to provide for the beneficiaries thereof. 

The ultimate effect of a trust is payment to the beneficiaries; but before payment can be made, the beneficiaries must be determined. Therefore, to determine the effect of a trust, the beneficiaries must be determined. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 S. E. 2d 147.

The beneficial interest, where property is held in trust, is in some other person than the one holding the title. Wright v. Piedmont Engineering & Construction Corporation (1962), 106 Ga. App. 401, 403, 128 S. E. 2d 865. "Where the will seeks to set up a trust for the benefit of a number of persons as well as institutions, but the duration of the life of anyone in being

constitutes no part of the specified duration of the trust, and it is provided therein that it shall not endure for more than 25 years, it is a clear violation of the rule against perpetuities, and the trust is absolutely void." Fuller v. 

Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (2), 122 S. E. 2d 234. "In construing a trust instrument, it is the duty of a court to find the intention of the settlor and to effectuate that intention so far as the language used and the rules of law will permit. The intention of the settlor is to be determined from the whole instrument and not from isolated portions or statements contained therein." Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 887, 891, 102 S. E. 2d 488. 

In Rockefeller v. First Nat. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 154 F. Supp. 122, it was held that the construction of a trust involving property located in Georgia, and the rights and powers of the trustee over such property, are controlled by the laws of Georgia. 

In 1953, the General Assembly enacted a provision to the effect that a trust may be created to hold title to properties used or useful in furnishing utilities or other services to secure an obligation to furnish such utilities or services. 

This act is codified as Ga. Code Ann. § 108-119. (Acts 1953, page 496.) 

§ 176.-Trusts Created by Deed and by Will.-Perdue v. McKenzie (1942), 

194 Ga. 356, 21 S. E. 2d 705; Flemister v. Billups (1947), 202 Ga. 132, 42 S. E. 

2d 376. "Our Code (§ 108-114) provides that a trust estate may be created by a deed which shall be recorded where the cestui que trust resides within three months from its execution and a failure so to record shall make the deed void." Wright v. Piedmont Engineering & Construction Corporation (1962), 106 Ga. App. 401, 

404, 128 S. E. 2d 865.

In an action to compel defendants to deed certain undivided interest in described land, which petition alleged that said property was deeded to the defendant in order to settle the estate of their deceased father, held to state a cause of action, because such deed operated merely as a power of attorney, and any attempt to appropriate land thereunder would constitute a fraud against which equity would relieve and was not an attempt to engraft a parol trust on an absolute deed, the legal title being conveyed only for a particular purpose. Carter v. Rayford (1959), 215 Ga. 261, 109 S. E. 2d 608. 

In Rockefeller v. First Nat. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 766, 102

S. E. 2d 28, a trust was set up by the terms of a will which had for its purpose the keeping together of property as a place of residence and recreation for the children of the testatrix so long as any of them lived. Then, as an exception to this testamentary scheme, it was provided that a majority of the living children might in their discretion request a sale of the property or any portion of the same. This was construed to be a pure personal right given to the children, and was in no way coupled with a trust, and the trustee was held to have no voice in the decision of the children to sell the trust property. 

The power to sell was a mere naked power, purely discretionary with the donee. The only surviving child of the testatrix, for reasons sufficient to herself, for a valuable consideration, and at a time when she was competent to act, executed a release of her power to request the trustee to sell any of the property belonging to the trust estate. She subsequently became incompetent. 

The trustee then filed a petition asking the authority of the court to execute a mineral lease covering a portion of the lands of the trust estate. (See 

Rockefeller v. First Natl. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 493, 100 So. 2d 

279, the first appearance of this case in the Supreme Court.). It was held that

since the donee had executed a release of her power to request the trustee to sell any of the property belonging to the trust estate, which release was executed by the donee when she was capable of acting, the courts were without authority to change or modify what the donee did, and had no authority to permit the execution of the lease since the court can not do for the incompetent party something that she, if competent, could not do herself. Also, this being true, under the terms of the will, the property in question could not be sold so long as the surviving child of the testatrix is in life. 

§ 177.-Express Trusts.-Archer v. Kelley (1942), 194 Ga. 117, 21 S. E. 2d 

51; McDowell v. McDowell (1942), 68 Ga. App. 363, 22 S. E. 2d 851; Pantone v. 

Pantone (1947), 202 Ga. 733, 44 S. E. 2d 548. "In construing a trust instrument, it is the duty of a court to find the intention of the settlor and to effectuate that intention insofar as the language used and the rules of law permit." King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 

S. E. 2d 147. "The laws of Georgia, where the trusts were executed, where, at the time they were signed and delivered, all the parties including the trustors, the trustees, and the beneficiaries lived, and where the trust res has always since been kept and managed, will govern in determining whether or not persons are 'children' within the meaning of the trusts." King v. King (1962), 218 

Ga. 534, 129 S. E. 2d 147. "Trusts are either express or implied; implied trusts are such as are inferred by law from the nature of the transaction or from the conduct of the parties. Code § 108-104. Trusts are implied whenever the legal title is in one person, but the beneficial interest, either from the payment of the purchase money or other circumstances, is either wholly or partially in another. Code § 108-106." Bullard v. Bullard (1958), 214 Ga. 122, 123, 103 S. E. 2d 570.

No particular form is necessary to create a trust estate, but there is only required a manifest intention that another person shall have the benefit of the property, in which case the grantee of the property is a trustee for the other person. Wright v. Piedmont Engineering & Construction Corporation (1962), 

106 Ga. App. 401, 403, 128 S. E. 2d 865.

An express trust cannot be made by parol agreement. Nor can an allegation of an express, oral trust be employed to defeat a resulting trust. Wells v. Wells (1960), 216 Ga. 384, 386, 116 S. E. 2d 586. "In construing a trust instrument, it is the duty of a court to find the intention of the settlor and to effectuate that intention so far as the language used and the rules of law will permit. The intention of the settlor is to be determined from the whole instrument and not from isolated portions or statements contained therein." Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 

887, 891, 102 S. E. 2d 488. 

In Rockefeller v. First Nat. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 154 F. Supp. 122, it was held that the construction of a trust involving property located in Georgia, and the rights and powers of the trustee over such property, are controlled by the laws of Georgia.

The aim of and the reason for the rule against perpetuities, is to prevent the tying up of property for an unreasonable length of time and to prohibit unreasonable restraint upon the alienation of property. So long as the settlor of an inter vivos trust has the absolute right to revoke or terminate the trust for his own exclusive personal benefit, there is no tying up of property and

no restraint upon the alienability of the property in the trust fund, and thus no reason to include this time during which the trust is so destructible in determining whether a limitation is violative of the rule against perpetuities. 

Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461.

Where a will created a trust for a niece and nephew the trustee to hold said property until the youngest reached the age of twenty-one years, and when the testatrix died both named under the trust was over twenty-one years of age, the uses therein entirely failed, and under the provisions of Code § 108-106 (4), a resulting trust arose for the benefit of the heirs at law of the testatrix. First National Bank of Brunswick v. Stewart (1959), 215 Ga. 141, 109 S. E. 2d 606.

When a settlor has the power during his lifetime to revoke or destroy the trust estate for his own exclusive personal benefit, the question whether interests, or any of them, created by an instrument or deed of trust are void, because in violation of the rule against perpetuities, is to be determined as of the date of the settlor's death and not as of the date the instrument is executed and delivered. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461. 

In Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 887, 102 S. E. 2d 488, a trust provided that it should include grandchildren of the settlor, whether born at the time the instrument was executed or thereafter; provided that the corpus of the trust was to be distributed to any beneficiary upon reaching the age of twenty one years in fee simple and free of any trust, or to the estate of any beneficiary dying before reaching twenty one years of age; and, provided further, in order that the trust might not extend beyond the time permitted by the rule against perpetuities, any other provision in the trust to the contrary notwithstanding, that the trust should end twenty years and eleven months after the death of the last surviving beneficiary living at the time the trust agreement was executed. It was held that grandchildren who might be born after the execution of the trust agreement were entitled to share in the trust, notwithstanding the provision providing that the corpus of the estate was to be distributed to the beneficiaries when each reached the age of twenty one years. That such provision was subordinate to the provision including grandchildren whether born or unborn, and, therefore, no distribution of the trust could be made so long as settlor had living children. 

In Harvey v. First National Bank of Atlanta (1954), 210 Ga. 528, 81 S. E. 

2d 481, the testator by his will gave the residue of his estate to trustees to hold until his daughter reached the age of twenty-one or died. Until the daughter died or became twenty-one the daughter and the widow were to have the use and benefit of the family residence. It was held that it was the intention of the testator to include the residence in the trust estate, and thus, by the will, the trust estate was liable for upkeep. 

Where a settlor provided that the trust should be divided into as many parts as he had children, and that each child was to receive the proceeds from his or her trust for and during his or her natural life, and then provided remainders to the issue of his children upon the death of said children, and the trust set out in detail how the remainders were to be paid and administered, the children of settlor took a life interest in the corpus of the trust estate with remainder to their issue and not a fee simple interest, the trusts being held executory since the remaindermen could not be determined until the children of the settlor die. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 292, 104 

S. E. 2d 461.

Ga. 814, 55 S. E. 2d 217. "Trusts are either express or implied; implied trusts are such as are inferred by law from the nature of the transaction or from the conduct of the parties. Code § 108-104. Trusts are implied whenever the legal title is in one person, but the beneficial interest, either from the payment of the purchase money or other circumstances, is either wholly or partially in another. Code § 108-106.'' Bullard v. Bullard (1958), 214 Ga. 122, 123, 103 S. E. 2d 570. "An implied trust results from the fact that one person's money has been invested in land and the conveyance taken in the name of another. It is a mere creature of equity. (a) An implied trust may arise from a payment of a portion of the purchase-money. (b) An express oral promise by the grantee to hold in trust for another will not operate to defeat a resulting trust, where, on the special equities growing out of the transaction, the law would, in the

Bullard (1958), 214 Ga. 122, 123, 103 S. E. 2d 570. "In order to establish an implied trust, it must be shown that some definite portion of the purchase price was furnished by the party claiming the trust. 

It must further be shown that the payment was made at or before the time of purchase. " Bullard v. Bullard (1958), 214 Ga. 122, 126, 103 S. E. 2d 570. "It is not only in express or implied trusts, but in other fiduciary relations, that limitations will not begin to run so long as trust or duty with regard to specific property continues, is acknowledged to be subsisting, and there is no change of status to show adverse holding of such property. Code 1933, 

§ 3-713. 

"As long as persons in possession of another's property, using it for owner's benefit, recognize such ownership, no lapse of time will bar owner from asserting his title as against person in possession. "Where executor made deposit prima facie belonging to estate, never asserted adverse claim or exercised adverse control with reference thereto, and beneficiaries of estate had no notice or knowledge as to existence of fund until fiduciary depositor died and executor of his will took charge of deposit and notified beneficiaries as to its existence, petition for accounting and recovery as to deposit promptly brought after such notice was not barred by limitations or laches. Code 1933, §§ 3-709, 3-713." Reynolds v. Dorsey (1939), 188 

Ga. 218, 3 S. E. 2d 564 (3, 4, 7).

Where no beneficial interest in property was retained in the five children who made quitclaim deeds for a valuable consideration conveying all their interests in the property to their father; where fraud in the procurement of the deeds is not alleged; and where, from the nature of the transaction, it is not manifest that it was the intention of the parties that the father, who took the legal title, should have no beneficial interest in the property, the petition fails to establish an implied trust. Lucas v. Bonner (1960), 216 Ga. 334 (4), 116 S. E. 2d 548.

In an action to compel defendants to deed certain undivided interest in described land, which petition alleged that said property was deeded to the defendant in order to settle the estate of their deceased father, held to state a cause of action, because such deed operated merely as a power of attorney, and any attempt to appropriate land thereunder would constitute a fraud against which equity would relieve and was not an attempt to engraft a parol trust on an absolute deed, the legal title being conveyed only for a particular purpose. Carter v. Rayford (1959), 215 Ga. 261, 109 S. E. 2d 608.

Where petition to declare an implied trust for land showed that title and permissive possession had been in defendant for 18 years, but that defendant had asserted a claim adverse to plaintiff only since 1950, the action, having been instituted within seven years after notice of such adverse claim, is not barred by the statute of limitations or laches, and stated a cause of action. 

Epps v. Epps (1953), 209 Ga. 643, 75 S. E. 2d 165.

An action to enforce an implied trust must generally be brought within seven years of the time the cause of action arose. A claimant is not barred from asserting his right, however, where it appears that the cause of action

arose in 1929, and such claimant had been in continuous possession of the realty in question for over 20 years prior to the institution of the suit. 

Richards v. Richards (1953), 209 Ga. 839, 76 S. E. 2d 492.

A widow may claim an implied trust of lands held by her husband before his death when the land was a product of their joint endeavors. Joseph v. 

Citizens & Southern National Bank (1953), 210 Ga. 111, 78 S. E. 2d 193. "Where a man and woman, engaged to be married, agree that they will both contribute funds toward the purchase of a lot and the building of a home thereon, and in pursuance of such agreement a lot is purchased and title taken in the name of the wife, and subsequently to their marriage the antenuptial agreement is kept in force and a house is erected on the lot from funds contributed by both parties, and all of this was done with the understanding and agreement between the parties that they would be just and equal owners of the property, and where after a separation of the parties the wife refuses to recognize her husband's claim of ownership, the law will imply a trust in favor of the husband for an undivided interest in the real estate in proportion to the amount of the purchase money paid by him. Hemphill v. Hemphill, 176 Ga. 

585 (168 S. E. 878); Jackson v. Jackson, 150 Ga. 544 (104 S. E. 236).” Adams v. Adams (1958), 213 Ga. 875, 880, 102 So. 2d 566.

Where land is bought by a member of a partnership with money belonging to the firm, and the legal title thereto is placed in the name of only one member, an implied trust arises in favor of the other partners, who become equitable owners, and tenants in common, of such land. Varellas v. Varellas (1962), 218 Ga. 125 (1), 126 S. E. 2d 680.

A petition seeking to establish an implied trust will fail where all the allegations are based solely upon an oral agreement setting up an invalid express trust. However, where, from the nature of the transaction and the conduct of the parties, the law would imply a trust, an express oral agreement that one of the partners will hold the title to partnership property for the partners, with each partner owning an undivided one-third interest therein, will not defeat the trust. Varellas v. Varellas (1962), 218 Ga. 125 (2), 126 

S. E. 2d 680. § 181.-Same Resulting Trusts.-Lewis v. Patterson (1940), 191 Ga. 348, 12

623, 54 S. E. 2d 578; Baker v. Schneider (1954), 210 Ga. 493, 80 S. E. 2d 783. "An implied trust results from the fact that one person's money has been invested in land and the conveyance taken in the name of another. It is a mere creature of equity. (a) An implied trust may arise from a payment of a portion of the purchase-money. (b) An express oral promise by the grantee to hold in trust for another will not operate to defeat a resulting trust, where, on the special equities growing out of the transaction, the law would, in the absence of such agreement, imply a trust." Wells v. Wells (1960), 216 Ga.
