Where a will created a trust for a niece and nephew the trustee to hold said property until the youngest reached the age of twenty-one years, and when the testatrix died both named under the trust was over twenty-one years of age, the uses therein entirely failed, and under the provisions of Code § 108-106 (4), a resulting trust arose for the benefit of the heirs at law of the testatrix. First National Bank of Brunswick v. Stewart (1959), 215 Ga. 141, 109 S. E. 2d 606.

"As between husband and wife, payment of purchase money by one and causing conveyance to be made to the other is presumed to be a 'gift,' but the presumption is rebuttable and a resulting trust in favor of the one paying the money may be shown. "If husband paid purchase money for land and conveyance was made to wife, the law would presume existence of a 'gift' by husband to wife, but the presumption would not be conclusive and might be rebutted by clear testimony." Statham v. Council (1940), 190 Ga. 517, 9 S. E. 2d 768 (12, 13). "Where a husband pays purchase money of land from his own funds and has land conveyed to his wife, the presumption which the law makes is that husband intended to make a gift to his wife, but the presumption is a rebuttable one, and a resulting trust in favor of husband may be shown. Code, § 108-106." "An absolute gift will not be cut down by implication into a trust merely because donor hoped and believed, at time gift was made, that donee would share beneficial interest in the property with him or with a third person. Code, § 108-106." Williams v. Thomas (1946), 200 Ga. 767, 38 S. E. 2d 603 (1, 4).

In an action to set up a resulting trust, parol evidence of an oral agreement between the parties at the time the legal title was taken by the defendant with regard to the purposes of the conveyance is admissible to rebut an inference of gift. Clark v. Griffon (1950), 207 Ga. 255, 61 S. E. 2d 128. "The testator here having created an executory trust, vesting the full title to property of the testator in the trustees, no right of reversion or other interest whatsoever remained in the testator at the time of his death which could be inherited by his wife. Upon the failure of the life beneficiary to exercise the power of appointment, a resulting trust by operation of law was created upon her death, reinvesting the property in the estate of the estate of the testator, and the heirs of the testator must be determined as of the date of the death of the wife, and not at the time of his death."' Butler v. 

Citizens & Southern National Bank (1955), 211 Ga. 414, 86 S. E. 2d 520.

A resulting trust will be implied for the benefit of the testator, which of course means the testator's estate, rather than for the benefit of his heirs or next of kin when his will contains a residuary clause which disposes of all the rest or residue of his estate, a trust having been created in another provision of his will but no express disposition of the remainder thereafter having been made. Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671, 674, S. E. 2d

The resulting trust of the remaining portion of a trust estate after the termination of the trust will be implied for the benefit of a testator's estate where the testator in one provision of his will creates a trust for the benefit of a person for her life and makes no express disposition of that remaining portion but by the residuary clause of his will disposes of all the residue of his estate. The reason for the rule is that intestacies in construing wills are not favored and it will be presumed that the testator intended by his will to dispose of his entire estate. Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671 (1c), S. E. 2d

Resulting or implied trusts are within the statute of limitations. As stated in this case, there appears to be some conflict in the authorities as to whether the statutory period of limitations is ten years (Garner v. Lankford, 147 Ga. 

235, 93 S. E. 411) or seven years (Wallace v. Mize, 153 Ga. 374, 112 S. E. 724), and it would seem to be the rule whether the seven year or the ten year period is applicable would depend upon the circumstances of the particular case. Denson v. Denson (1958), 214 Ga. 8, 102 S. E. 2d 605.

When the trustee in an implied trust recognizes the trust, and treats it as subsisting within seven years next preceding the institution of an action to enforce it, such suit is not barred by the statute of limitations. However, when there has been notice of an adverse claim by the trustee or such change of circumstances as it calculated to put a reasonably prudent person on notice that the trust is no longer recognized as subsisting, or something to indicate to a reasonably prudent person that the relation of trustee and cestui trust has ceased, the statute of limitations will commence to run. Denson v. Denson (1958), 214 Ga. 8, 102 S. E. 2d 605. 

§ 182.-Same-Constructive Trusts.-Cordovano v. State (1940), 61 Ga. App. 

590, 7 S. E. 2d 45; Grant v. Hart (1941), 192 Ga. 153, 14 S. E. 2d 860; Ross v. Rambo (1942), 195 Ga. 100, 23 S. E. 2d 687; Murray County v. Pickering (1943), 196 Ga. 208, 26 S. E. 2d 287; Harris v. Rowe (1946), 200 Ga. 265, 36

"Constructive trusts are such as are raised by equity in respect of property which has been acquired by fraud, or where. though acquired originally without fraud, it is against equity that it should be retained by him who holds it." 

Brown v. Brown (1953), 209 Ga. 620, 75 S. E. 2d 13.

An express trust cannot be made by parol agreement. Nor can an allegation of an express, oral trust be employed to defeat a resulting trust. Wells v. Wells (1960), 216 Ga. 384, 386, 116 S. E. 2d 586.

One who seeks relief based on doctrine of trusts ex maleficio must allege more than a breach of a verbal promise. There must be an unequivocal allegation of positive fraud accompanying the promise, by means of which the acquisition of the legal title was consummated. General allegations as to an entire course of fraudulent conduct are not sufficient, in the absence of a specific averment that the promise was made to be broken. Mays v. Perry (1943), 196 Ga. 729, 27 S. E. 2d 698; Westbrook v. Westbrook (1956), 212 

Ga. 472, 93 S. E. 2d 683.

235, 93 S. E. 411) or seven years (Wallace v. Mize, 153 Ga. 374, 112 S. E. 

724), and it would seem to be the rule whether the seven year or the ten year period is applicable would depend upon the circumstances of the particular case. Denson v. Denson (1958), 214 Ga. 8, 102 S. E. 2d 605.

When the trustee in an implied trust recognizes the trust, and treats it as subsisting within seven years next preceding the institution of an action to enforce it, such suit is not barred by the statute of limitations. However, when there has been notice of an adverse claim by the trustee or such change of circumstances as it calculated to put a reasonably prudent person on notice that the trust is no longer recognized as subsisting, or something to indicate to a reasonably prudent person that the relation of trustee and cestui trust has ceased, the statute of limitations will commence to run. Denson v. Denson (1958), 214 Ga. 8, 102 S. E. 2d 605.

The legislature at the 1950 adjourned session enacted a new statute per taining to Trusts reading as follows: 

"A trust shall be executory, and the legal estate shall remain in the trustee, whether or not the beneficiary or beneficiaries be sui juris and whether or not any remainder interest be created, so long as the trustee has any powers or duties in regard to the trust property such as to preserve or protect, to manage, to invest or reinvest, to collect income or proceeds, to sell or otherwise dispose of, to ascertain the objects or the beneficiaries, or to distribute income or principal." Code § 108-111.1. 

Where a trust was created prior to the enactment of the above Code section (§ 108-111.1), cestui que trust had vested right in having it executed, and this section did not continue the trust in force. Blanchard v. Gilmore (1952), 208 

Ga. 846, 849, 69 S. E. 2d 753.

The primary purpose of a trust is to provide for the beneficiaries thereof. 

The ultimate effect of a trust is payment to the beneficiaries; but before payment can be made, the beneficiaries must be determined. Therefore, to determine the effect of a trust, the beneficiaries must be determined. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 S. E. 2d 147. "The laws of Georgia, where the trusts were executed, where, at the time they were signed and delivered, all the parties including the trustors, the trustees, and the beneficiaries lived, and where the trust res has always since been kept and managed, will govern in determining whether or not persons are 'children' within the meaning of the trusts." King v. King (1962), 218 

Ga. 534, 129 S. E. 2d 147.

Whether or not the testator's intent to create a trust for the benefit of his widow for life may be effectuated depends upon the law in force at the time of the testator's death. Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671 (2-a), 130 

S. E. 2d 208.

Where a will which incorporated a trust was executed in Pennsylvania and probated both in Pennsylvania and Georgia, the law of Georgia governs trust property located in Georgia but the intestate law of Pennsylvania governs in determining remindermen and whether certain items of the will were intended to refer to natural or blood relationships to the exclusion of adopted children. 

Carnegie v. First National Bank of Brunswick (1963), 218 Ga. 585, 588 (la), 129 S. E. 2d 780. 

In Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671, 130 S. E. 2d 208, the testator died in 1946 and his will was admitted to probate during that year. In his will he created a trust for life for his wife but made no provision for the

disposition of the trust res at her death. But by the residuary clause of his will he disposed of all the residue of his estate. His widow made written demand upon the trustee to deliver to her in fee the corpus of the trust on the ground that the trust had become executed by operation of the statute of uses as codified in Georgia. The trustee brought an action for construction of the will and for direction as to the rights and interests of the various parties. It was held that whether or not the testator intended to create a trust for the benefit of his widow for life depended upon the law in force at the time of the testator's death in 1946 and that under the law of Georgia in force at that date a trust could not be created in property for the sole benefit of an adult who was sui juris and who was not a spendthrift and that Code § 108-111.1 (Acts 1950, page 310, 311), which provides that "a trust shall be executory, and the legal estate shall remain in the trustee, whether or not the beneficiary or beneficiaries be sui juris and whether or not any remainder interest be created, so long as the trustee has any powers or duties in regard to the trust property such as to preserve or protect, to manage, to invest or reinvest, to collect income or proceeds, to sell or otherwise dispose of, to ascertain the objects or the beneficiaries, or to distribute income or principal" could not be considered in deciding the issues involved. The court further held that the trust therefor being executed, the intended life income beneficiary takes a legal estate equivalent to the equitable estate she was intended to have, to wit: a legal life estate. The reversionary interest in fee in the trust property passed by an implied resulting trust to the testator's estate and thence by the residuary clause of his will to his residuary legatees. 

And the fact that the trustees were given a power to encroach upon the corpus of the trust for the benefit of the life beneficiary does not have the effect of increasing her legal life estate (the trust having been executed) into a fee. 

A trust is executory when something remains to be done by the trustee, either to secure the property, to ascertain the objects of the trust, to distribute according to a specified mode, or some other act, the doing of which requires the trustee to retain the legal title. Budreau v. Mingledorff (1951), 207 Ga. 538, 63 S. E. 2d 326.

Where the obvious intent of the trustor was to vest title to the res in the trustees, with a discretionary power in the trustees to turn over the res to the cestui que trust if he becomes capable of looking after his own interests, a court of equity will not control the exercise of such discretion. Id. 

The rule in this state is that a trust in which contingent remainders follow a life estate and are embraced by the trust will remain executory until such time as the persons who are to take the remainders can be ascertained. Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 111, 119, 126 S. E. 4d 755. 

§ 188.-Execution of Trusts.-McBride v. Bullard (1939), 188 Ga. 354, 4 

S. E. 2d 149; Wilson v. Fulton Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1939), 188 Ga. 691, 4 S. E. 2d 660.

The courts have not determined what effect Acts 1950, page 310 (Code 

108-111.1), has on the execution of trust when the beneficiary becomes sui juris. This Code section provides that a trust shall be executory, and the legal estate shall remain in the trustee, whether or not the beneficiary or beneficiaries is sui juris and whether or not any remainder interest be created, so long as the trustee has any powers or duties in regard to the trust property such as to preserve or protect, to manage, to invest or reinvest, to collect income or proceeds, to sell or otherwise dispose of, to ascertain the objects or the beneficiaries, or to distribute income or principal. The only case that

can be found which mentions this section is the case of Blanchard v. Gilmore (1952), 208 Ga. 846, 849, 69 S. E. 2d 753, wherein it was held that where a trust was created prior to the enactment of this section, the cestui que trust had a vested right in having it executed and this section did not continue the trust in force. "A trust wherein beneficiary's estate is a defeasible fee, with executory devise in favor of others limited thereon, does not become an 'executed trust' by beneficiary's arrival at age of 21 years and by fact that he is under no legal disabilities, but trust continues to be 'executory' until contingency on which beneficiary's estate is defeasible is no longer capable of defeating it. Code 

1933, §§ 85-103, 85-708, 108-111, 108-112, 108-114." Sanders v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1939), 189 Ga. 450, 6 S. E. 2d 294 (3).

Where remainderman of trust estate attains majority, he is entitled to delivery of the property, without benefit of a trustee, despite an equitable lien in favor of testator's widow. Blanchard v. Gilmore (1952), 208 Ga. 846, 69 

S. E. 2d 753.

Upon the execution of a trust, the legal title in the trustee and the equitable title in the beneficiaries become merged and the interest of the trustee terminates. Mason v. Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (2), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

A devise in trust for the life of a first taker, and at his death to go in remainder, creates an equitable estate in remainder and is not a legal estate, and that such trust is executory until the death of the life tenant. Mason v. 

Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (2), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

The trust having become executed, the testatrix had a devisable interest in her share of the trust property and could dispose of it by her will. Erskine v. Klein (1962), 218 Ga. 112, 126 S. E. 2d 755.

Where a will created a trust for a niece and nephew the trustee to hold said property until the youngest reached the age of twenty-one years, and when the testatrix died both named under the trust was over twenty-one years of age, the uses therein entirely failed, and under the provisions of Code § 108-106 (4), a resulting trust arose for the benefit of the heirs at law of the testatrix. First National Bank of Brunswick v. Stewart (1959), 215 Ga. 

141, 109 S. E. 2d 606. 

In Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671, 208 S. E. 2d 130, the testator died in 1946 and his will was admitted to probate during that year. In his will he created a trust for life for his wife but made no provision for the disposition of the trust res at her death. But by the residuary clause of his will he disposed of all the residue of his estate. His widow made written demand upon the trustee to deliver to her in fee the corpus of the trust on the ground that the trust had become executed by operation of the statute of uses as codified in Georgia. The trustee brought an action for construction of the will and for direction as to the rights and interests of the various parties. It was held that whether or not the testator intended to create a trust for the benefit of his widow for life depended upon the law in force at the time of the testator's death in 1946 and that under the law of Georgia enforced at that date a trust could not be created in property for the sole benefit of an adult who was sui juris and who was not a spendthrift and that Code § 108-111.1 (Acts 1950, page 310, 311), which provides that "a trust shall be executory, and the legal estate shall remain in the trustee, whether or not the beneficiary or beneficiaries be sui juris and whether or not any remainder interest be created, so long as the trustee has any powers or duties

in regard to the trust property such as to preserve or protect, to manage, to invest or reinvest, to collect income or proceeds, to sell or otherwise dispose of, to ascertain the objects or the beneficiaries, or to distribute income or principal" could not be considered in deciding the issues involved. The court further held that the trust therefor being executed, the intended life income beneficiary takes a legal estate equivalent to the equitable estate she was intended to have, to wit: a legal life estate. The reversionary interest in fee in the trust property passed by an implied resulting trust to the testator's estate and thence by the residuary clause of his will to his residuary legatees. 

And the fact that the trustees were given a power to encroach upon the corpus of the trust for the benefit of the life beneficiary does not have the effect of increasing her legal life estate (the trust having been executed) into a fee. 

188a.-Construction of Trusts—Jurisdiction.— 

Acts 1943, pages 409, 444 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1423), relating to the necessity of construing a will or trust upon an accounting the same shall be transferred to the superior court, is as follows: "The court of ordinary upon its own motion, or upon motion of any party at interest whenever it shall appear that a question of construction of a will or trust instrument is involved in said accounting, shall enter an order transferring said accounting to the superior court for the determination of all such questions which shall be presented to, heard and determined by the superior court as appeals from the court of ordinary are presented, heard and determined, and after the determi nation of such questions of construction by the superior court, the court of ordinary shall proceed with said accounting." See Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 

Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42. 

In Rockefeller v. First Nat. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 154 F. Supp. 122, it was held that the construction of a trust involving property located in Georgia, and the rights and powers of the trustees over such property, are controlled by the laws of Georgia. 

§ 189.-Administration of Trust Estates.-National City Bank of Rome v. First Nat. Bank of Birmingham, Ala. (1942), 193 Ga. 477, 19 S. E. 2d 19; 

Perdue v. McKenzie (1942), 194 Ga. 356, 21 S. E. 2d 705; Kaiser v. Kaiser (1942), 194 Ga. 658, 22 S. E. 2d 390.

If an executor is also designated trustee under a will he comes into possession as executor, and his election afterward to hold as trustee must be manifested by some plain and unequivocal act. Evans v. Citizens & Sou. Nat. Bank (1950), 206 Ga. 441, 57 S. E. 2d 541.

In creating a trust estate, legal title to the property conveyed vests in the trustee, and the equitable title in the cestui que trust for whom the trust was created. Mason v. Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (3), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

Upon the execution of a trust, the legal title in the trustee and the equitable title in the beneficiaries become merged and the interest of the trustee terminates. Mason v. Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (2), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

A devise in trust for the life of a first taker, and at his death to go in remainder, creates an equitable estate in remainder and is not a legal estate, and that such trust is executory until the death of the life tenant. Mason v. 

Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (2), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

The aim of and reason for the rule against perpetuities, which is to prevent the tying up of property for an unreasonable length of time and to prohibit

unreasonable restraint upon the alienation of property. So long as the settlor of an inter vivos trust has the absolute right to revoke or terminate the trust for his own exclusive personal benefit, there is no tying up of property and no restraint upon the alienability of the property in the trust fund, and thus no reason to include this time during which the trust is so destructible in determining whether a limitation is violative of the rule against perpetuities. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461.

When a settlor has the power during his lifetime to revoke or destroy the trust estate for his own exclusive personal benefit, the question whether interests, or any of them, created by an instrument or deed of trust are void, because in violation of the rule against perpetuities, is to be determined as of the date of the settlor's death and not as of the date the instrument is executed and delivered. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 293, 104 S. E. 2d 461. 

In Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 887, 102 S. E. 2d 488, a trust provided that it should include grandchildren of the settlor, whether born at the time the instrument was executed or thereafter; provided that the corpus of the trust was to be distributed to any beneficiary upon reaching the age of twenty one years in fee simple and free of any trust, or to the estate of any beneficiary dying before reaching twenty one years of age; and, provided further, in order that the trust might not extend beyond the time permitted by the rule against perpetuities, any other provision in the trust to the contrary notwithstanding, that the trust should end twenty years and eleven months after death of the last surviving beneficiary living at the time the trust agreement was executed. It was held that grandchildren who might be born after the execution of the trust agreement were entitled to share in the trust, notwithstanding the provision providing that the corpus of the estate was to be distributed to the beneficiaries when each reached the age of twenty one years. That such provision was subordinate to the provision including grandchildren whether born or unborn, and, therefore, no distribution of the trust could be made so long as settlor had living children. 

A trustee may be held liable individually on a contract which the trustee has negotiated on behalf of the trust estate and for its benefit. Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336 (la), 116 S. E. 2d 308.

Under the common-law rule a trustee can be held liable individually on a contract which he has negotiated on behalf of the trust estate, where the contract was for the benefit of the estate, and it is immaterial that the contract was made by the trustee in the proper performance of his duties as trustee, and that he contracted as trustee and not individually, and that he purported to bind the beneficiary personally. Such contracts bind the trustee personally unless it is otherwise provided in the contract. Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336, 337, 116 S. E. 2d 308.

Code §§ 108-501 et seq. do not abolish the common-law liability of the trustee personally in contract, but are merely cumulative and offer an additional method by which a claimant might reach directly the assets of an estate. 

Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336 (1a), 116 S. E. 2d 308.

This section shall apply to all such property held by such fiduciary on the effective date of this section under estates or trusts previously created, except that it shall not relieve any such fiduciary from liability for loss which shall have already accrued on or before the effective date of this section for losses that have already occurred." Whether or not the testator's intent to create a trust for the benefit of his widow for life may be effectuated depends upon the law in force at the time of the testator's death. Stephens v. Stephens (1963), 218 Ga. 671 (2a), S. E. 2d 208. 130 Acts 1960, page 194, codified as Code §§ 108-445 through 108-447, provides that where the trust instrument is silent as to the time of distribution of income and the frequency thereof, that all trustees of all trusts subject to the laws of this state, whether heretofore or hereafter established, shall distribute all net income derived from the property comprising such trust at least annually, on a calendar or fiscal year basis. However, in the case of any trust now in existence or created after the passage of the act where the trust instrument expressly directs or permits net income to be distributed less frequently than annually, the express provision of such instrument shall govern the time and manner of making distributions of income. "Net income" as used in the act means gross income less expenses,

Said act also provides if two or more fiduciaries are acting jointly in reference to any securities, it shall be lawful to register the property in the name of any nominee or any joint corporate fiduciary and in the event more than one corporate fiduciary is acting, it shall be lawful to register securities in the name of any nominee of any one of said corporate fiduciaries.

§ 190.-Same-Trustees.-Parnelle v. Cavanaugh (1941), 191 Ga. 464, 12 S. E. 

2d 877; Watkins v. Watkins (1941), 64 Ga. App. 344, 13 S. E. 2d 100; Dixon v.

Ga. 100, 23 S. E. 2d 687; Campbell v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1943), 197 Ga. 37, 28 S. E. 2d 471; Williams v. J. M. High Co. (1946), 200 Ga. 230, 36 S. E. 2d 

667; Gilmore v. Gilmore (1947), 201 Ga. 770, 41 S. E. 2d 229.

Code § 108-315, as amended by Acts 1959, page 324, provides for the appointment of successor trustees by the superior courts where the sole or surviving trustee shall have departed this life or removed beyond the jurisdiction of the courts of the state or have resigned or shall have otherwise become disqualified. This section also provides the notice and manner of such appointment, the duties and requirements of such successor trustee or trustees. 

An application for the appointment of a successor trustee cannot be made by one claiming adversely to the estate. Mason v. Young (1947), 203 Ga. 

121 (3), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

It is the established law of this State that, where the powers conferred by deed or will upon a trustee in the management and control of property for named beneficiaries are personal and discretionary to the trustee, such powers cannot be exercised by a successor; but that, if the exercise of the powers so conferred is imperative or mandatory in all events, the powers are incident to the office and may be exercised by a successor trustee, whether appointed by the court or provided for in the trust instrument. Gilmore v. Gilmore (1947), 201 Ga. 770, 776, 41 S. E. 2d 229.

The powers conferred by the testator in his will upon the person named as executor and as trustee of his estate, being powers which were personal and discretionary, and not imperative or mandatory, did not attach to the office of trustee, and could not be exercised by a successor trustee. Id. 

Where such testator by another item of his will conferred upon the named executor and trustee the authority to provide by will for a successor trustee "to handle the estate" for a specified period of time, but without providing that such successor trustee should exercise the same powers lodged in the original trustee, the trustees appointed by the will of the original trustee, "with all the powers lodged" in him by the will under which he was appointed trustee, did not become vested with such authority. Id. "The note sued upon in this case being made payable to 'A. G. Smith, Trustee,' the legal title to said obligation was vested in Smith individually and not in his representative capacity; and upon his death the right to collect said note in an action at law accrued to his personal representative and not to his successor in trust." Hardwick v. Avary (1962), 107 Ga. App. 79, 129 

S. E. 2d 379. "An executor or other trustee acts in a representative capacity and for the benefit of the cestui que trust. Persons dealing with him are bound to know the extent of his powers and, in absence of ratification by the cestui que trust the latter is not bound by the executor's acts in excess of his authority.. 

This rule is necessary for the protection of the cestui que trust against unlawful acts of the trustee." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 557, 118 

8. E. 2d 456.

A trustee may be held liable individually on a contract which the trustee has negotiated on behalf of the trust estate and for its benefit. Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336 (la), 116 S. E. 2d 308.

Under the common-law rule a trustee can be held liable individually on a contract he has negotiated on behalf of the trust estate, where the contract was for the benefit of the estate, and it is immaterial that the contract was made by the trustee in the proper performance of his duties as trustee, and that he contracted as trustee and not individually, and that he purported to bind the beneficiary personally. Such contracts bind the trustee personally unless it is otherwise provided in the contract. Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336, 337, 116 S. E. 2d 308.

Code §§ 108-501 et seq. do not abolish the common-law liability of the trustee personally in contract, but are merely cumulative and offer an additional method by which a claimant might reach directly the assets of an estate. 

Oberdorfer v. Smith (1960), 102 Ga. App. 336 (1a), 116 S. E. 2d 308.

In creating a trust estate, legal title to the property conveyed vests in the trustee, and the equitable title in the cestui que trust for whom the trust was created. Mason v. Young (1947), 203 Ga. 121 (3), 45 S. E. 2d 643.

In Rockefeller v. First Nat. Bank of Brunswick (1947), 154 F. Supp. 122, it was held that the construction of a trust involving property located in Georgia, and the rights and powers of the trustee over such property, are controlled by the laws of Georgia. 

Where a settlor provided that the trust should be divided into as many parts as he had children, and that each child was to receive the proceeds from his or her trust for and during his or her natural life, and then provided remainders to the issue of his children upon the death of said children, and the trust set out in detail how the remainders were to be paid and administered, the children of settlor took a life interest in the corpus of the trust estate with remainder to their issue and not a fee simple interest, the trusts being held executory since the remaindermen could not be determined until the children of the settlor die. Cook v. Horn (1958), 214 Ga. 289, 292, 105 S. E. 

2d 461. "Where a trustee in violation of his trust has changed the trust property or its proceeds into other property, the cestui que trust has his option, either to hold the substituted property liable to the original trust, or hold the trustee liable for breach of trust." This right or option of the cestui que trust belongs exclusively to him, and it is not in the power of the trustee to deprive him of it." Turner v. Trust Company of Georgia (1958), 214 Ga. 339, 348, 105 

S. E. 2d 22. "Where the title to property is put in one person for the benefit of others, the latter take cum onere. The skill, ability, and solvency of the trustee operate to their advantage. But as to acts within the scope of his express or implied powers, they must suffer the consequences when they ultimately prove detrimental to the beneficiaries. The remedy in such a case is not to undo what has lawfully been done, but to proceed against the trustee (Clark v. Flannery, 99 

Ga. 239), whose personal and financial fitness were passed upon by the grantor when giving the land. The very instrument which created the estate put forward the trustee as the person who was to represent those interested therein when it became necessary to deal with third persons. On this principle cestuis que trust are bound by his non-action for a time long enough for him to be barred by the statute (Civil Code [1895] § 3773 [now Code § 3-710]); they are bound by his loss of a loan made in good faith to a person then solvent (Walker v. Walker, 42 Ga. 135); by his receipt of funds which other prudent men then took as currency (Campbell v. Miller, 38 Ga. 304); by a compromise honestly and in good faith made by him (Maynard v. Cleveland, 76 Ga. 53 (6)). They are likewise bound by the results of suits instituted or defended by him for the benefit of the estate (Gunn v. James, 120 Ga. 482); and this is so even if the judgment is rendered by default. Sanders v. Houston, 107 Ga. 59 (4). See Ferris v. Van Ingen, 110 Ga. 102 (6, 7), where the minor was held bound by the conduct of the mother to whom a year's support for herself and child had been set apart." Turner v. Trust Company of Georgia (1958), 214 Ga. 339, 346, 105 S. E. 2d 22.

While the beneficiaries of a trust may apply to a court of equity to protect the trust property upon the refusal or failure of the trustee to do so, where the instrument creating the trust confers upon the trustee discretionary power to be exercised according to its judgment, and it has instituted an equitable proceeding respecting a particular transaction and subject matter, a court of equity will not interfere to control the trustee acting bona fide in the reasonable exercise of its discretion, and will restrain the beneficiaries from maintaining an independent proceeding subsequently instituted respecting the same transaction and subject matter. All parties who have asserted any rights in the subject matter in either of the proceedings here involved being parties to

the proceeding instituted by the trustee, they may all be heard, and their rights and liabilities settled in that proceeding, and the whole matter finally adjudicated. Turner v. Trust Company of Georgia (1958), 214 Ga. 339 (1), 105 S. E. 2d 22.

E. 2d 488, a trust provided that it should include grandchildren of the settlor, whether born at the time the instrument was executed or thereafter; provided that the corpus of the trust was to be distributed to any beneficiary upon reaching the age of twenty one years in fee simple and free of any trust, or to the estate of any beneficiary dying before reaching twenty one years of age; and, provided further, in order that the trust might not extend beyond the time permitted by the rule against perpetuities, any other provision in the trust to the contrary notwithstanding, that the trust should end twenty years and eleven months after death of the last surviving beneficiary living at the time the trust agreement was executed. It was held that grandchildren who might be born after the execution of the trust agreement were entitled to share in the trust, notwithstanding the provision providing that the corpus of the estate was to be distributed to the beneficiaries when each reached the age of twenty one years. That such provision was subordinate to the provision including grandchildren whether born or unborn, and, therefore, no distribution of the trust could be made so long as settlor had living children. "Code §§ 37-1201, 37-1303, 37-1304, 81-204, 81-205, and 108-408 prescribe the manner and procedure to be followed in applications for sales of property belonging to trust estates; provide that the application for such authority may be made to the judge of the superior court in vacation on full notice to all parties in interest and that the order for such sale may be granted at chambers; and empower a court of chancery, upon such an application, to authorize a trustee to sell and convey the corpus of his trust estate, where such sale is authorized or is not prohibited by the instrument creating the trust." Rockefeller v. First Natl. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 493 (1), 100 S. E. 2d 

279; 213 Ga. 766, 102 S. E. 2d 28. "Where the beneficiary of a trust has been adjudged incompetent, and is not capable of giving his valid consent to the conveyance of property which has been placed in trust for him prior to his becoming incompetent, and which may be conveyed by the trustee with his consent, a court of equity, in the exercise of its broad, comprehensive, and plenary jurisdiction of trusts and the estates of wards of chancery, may make the election for such incompetent, and authorize the trustee to convey the property." Rockefeller v. First Natl. 

Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 493 (3), 100 So. 2d 279, 213 Ga. 766, 102 

S. E. 2d 28. "General allegations of a breach of trust are unavailing even against a general demurrer." Malone v. Armor Insulating Co. (1940), 191 Ga. 146, 12 

S. E. 2d 299 (4).

Code § 113-1725. 

In 1953, the Legislature set up a procedure for the execution of leases of trust property. Thus it is provided in Section 1 of Acts 1953, page 44 et seq. that: "When the assets of a trust include an interest in real property the trustee may apply to the superior court for an order authorizing such trustee to lease such real property or a part thereof for a term of years which may or will continue beyond the termination of the trust and the superior court in the execution of the protective powers of equity over trust estates and the estates of wards in chancery shall have power and jurisdiction to pass an order authorizing the execu tion of such a lease." 

The word "trust," wherever used in the Act, includes the estate held by an executor, administrator, guardian, or trustee, whether held or in existence at the time of the passage of the Act or later coming into existence. There is provision for action upon the application in vacation and at chambers and for notice to all living beneficiaries as may be ordered by the court. Provision is also made for the appointment of guardians ad litem wherever necessary. 

A lease so executed is binding upon all beneficiaries in life or born subsequent to its execution during the existence of the lease. It is further provided by 

Section 6 of the Act that: 

"It shall be the duty of the superior court to hear evidence that may be tendered by the trustee and if the court is satisfied from the proceedings that the lease to be authorized is expedient, the court shall pass an order authorizing the trustee to execute the lease subject, however, to such terms as the court shall deem proper and necessary to protect the value of the trust estate. The granting of such application is not precluded by the fact that the instrument creating the trust only authorizes leases for terms not extending beyond the duration of the trust."

This Act is codified as Ga. Code Ann § 108-439 through 108-444. 

Since contracts for the sale of mineral lands or minerals are governed in the main by principles applicable to sales of real property generally, a "lease" of the minerals in place is a sale of a portion of the land, and the authority to sell all or any portion of trust property includes the right to sell or lease the minerals in place thereon. Rockefeller v. Rockefeller (1947), 213 Ga. 493, 503, 100 

So. (2d) 279; 213 Ga. 766, 102 S. E. 2d 28.

In Rockefeller v. First Natl. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 

766, 102 S. E. 2d 28, a trust was set up by the terms of a will which had for its purpose the keeping together of property as a place of residence and recreation for the children of the testatrix so long as any of them lived. Then, as an exception to this testamentary scheme, it was provided that a majority of the living children might in their discretion request a sale of the property or any portion of the same. This was construed to be a pure personal right given to the children, and was in no way coupled with a trust, and the trustee was held to have no voice in the decision of the children to sell the trust property. The power to sell was a mere naked power, purely discretionary with the donee. The only surviving child of the testatrix, for reasons sufficient to herself, for a valuable consideration, and at a time when she was competent to act, executed a release of her power to request the trustee to sell any of the property belonging to the trust estate. She subsequently became incompetent. The trustee then filed a petition asking the authority of the court to execute a mineral lease covering a portion of the lands of the trust estate. (See Rockefeller v. First Natl. Bank of Brunswick (1957), 213 Ga. 439, 100 So. 2d 279, the first appearance of this case in the

Supreme Court.) It was held that since the donee had executed a release of her power to request the trustee to sell any of the property belonging to the trust estate, which release was executed by the donee when she was capable of acting, the courts were without authority to change or modify what the donee did, and had no authority to permit the execution of the lease since the court cannot do for the incompetent party something that she, if competent, could not do herself. Also, this being true, under the terms of the will, the property in question could not be sold so long as the surviving 

Ichild of the testatrix is in life. "A trustee who has a power to sell in addition to a power to lease, whether the latter is express or implied, does not ordinarily have the power to give a lessee an option of purchase for a definite sum during the term of the lease. 

The purpose of this rule is to compel the trustee to exercise his judgment at the time of the sale and not at the time of the making of the lease as to whether the sale is beneficial to the trust estate." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 

Ga. 553, 555 (1), 118 S. E. 2d 456. 66 'Where, by the terms of a will creating a trust estate for named beneficiaries, the executor-trustees are empowered and directed to invest, reinvest, sell, lease, or transfer any of the property of the estate upon such terms as to them seem best, at public or private sale, without any order of any court and without reporting to any court, the power granted by the will, not having expressly included the right of the executor-trustees to encumber real property of the estate by a long-term option to purchase, will ordinarily not be enlarged to include such right." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553 (1), 118 

S. E. 2d 456.

The legislature in 1943 provided that any administrator, executor, committee, guardian, trustee, or other fiduciary for whom a bond or other obligation

is required may agree that a bank or trust company, or other depository approved by the court or a judge thereof, may act in joint control of moneys or other assets of the estate. This provision is found in a new Code section, 561117, Acts 1943, page 296.

Suspension during war service. If any guardian, trustee, executor, or administrator is engaged in war service, a new representative may be appointed to serve in his place. Acts 1943, page 416; Ga. Code Ann. 113-2503, 113-2504. 

Acts 1960, page 194, codified as Code §§ 108-445 through 108-447, provides that where the trust instrument is silent as to the time of distribution of income and the frequency thereof, that all trustees of all trusts subject to the laws of this state, whether heretofore or hereafter established, shall distribute all net income derived from the property comprising such trust at least annually, on a calendar or fiscal year basis. However, in the case of any trust now in existence or created after the passage of the act where the trust instrument expressly directs or permits net income to be distributed less frequently than annually, the express provision of such instrument shall govern the time and manner of making distributions of income. "Net income" as used in the act means gross income less expenses, other proper charges, and such reserves as may be necessary under the trust instrument to preserve the trust property. 

Where a testator gave his estate to his wife for life and provided that on her death his three sons were to receive the net income therefrom and that upon the death of the last surviving son the corpus of the estate was to be divided among his grandchildren, the terms and provisions of the testator's will clearly show that it was his intention that the corpus of his estate be held intact for the ultimate benefit of his grandchildren, and that his wife, during her lifetime and his three sons, should, after her death, personally have and receive annually the entire net income of his estate and that any profit arising from a sale of capital assets of his estate became a part of the corpus of the estate, and that the petitioners have no rights to receive the same as a part of the income of the estate. Also, that it was the intention of the testator that any loss sustained by his estate through the sale of capital assets should be treated as a loss of corpus, and that the petitioners as executors of the estate are not required to deduct a corpus loss from the annual income of the estate before distributing to themselves as life beneficiaries under the will the net income of the estate for any given year. Hirsch v. Hirsch (1960), 216 Ga. 379, 116 S. E. 2d 318.

The legislature in 1949 enacted "The Trustee Savings Act." For the nature of this act see Acts 1949, page 1123. The Trustee Savings Act now appears in the Code of Georgia as sections 109-701 to 109-711 inclusive. 

By Acts 1953, page 178 et seq., the General Assembly set up a procedure for the regulation of foreign trustees as to lands in Georgia. The Act requires each such trustee to designate and keep designated some person within the State to act as his agent for service. This designation is required to be filed in the office of the Secretary of State, giving the name of the agent and the address for the purpose of service. The foreign trustee may also designate the 

Secretary of State as his agent for service. Where the foreign trustee fails to designate anyone as an agent for service, notice of process may still be made

apon such trustee by leaving a copy, together with a fee of $2, in the hands of the Secretary of State.

All actions brought against such nonresident trustees are to be brought in the county where the land, or some portion thereof, lies. Where the agent for service resides in a county other than that in which the land lies, he may be served by second original. 

The Act further provides that all such foreign trustees shall be subject to removal, giving bond, and direction of superior court to the same extent as resident trustees.

It is required that all foreign trustees comply with this Act by May 1, 1953, on failure whereof they shall cease to exercise control or dominion over the trust estate and new trustees shall be appointed. The Act is expressly made cumulative of other laws on the same general subject, and provides that it shall not be construed to authorize the appointment of nonresidents to act as trustees who would not be otherwise authorized. This Act is codified as Ga. Code Ann. 

108-701 through 108-707.

Acts 1961, page 188, superseded Code 113-1518, which provides for the investment of trust funds in state bonds and other securities which said new Code section is as follows: 

"Executors, administrators, guardians, and trustees are authorized, unless otherwise provided in the fiduciary instrument, to retain the property received by them on the creation of the estate, guardianship or trust (including, in the case of a corporate fiduciary, stock or other securities of its own issue), even though such property may not otherwise be a legal investment, and shall not be liable for such retention, except for gross neglect. In the case of corporate securities, they may likewise retain the securities into which the securities originally received may be converted or which may be derived therefrom as a result of merger, consolidation, stock dividends, splits, liquidations, and similar procedures (and they may exercise by purchase or otherwise any rights, warrants or conversion features attaching to any such securities). This section shall apply to all such property held by such fiduciary on the effective date of this section under estates or trusts previously created, except that it shall not relieve any such fiduciary from liability for loss which shall have already accrued on or before the effective date of this section for losses that have already occurred." Code § 113-1518. 

Acts 1961, page 414, codified as Code §§ 108-448 and 108-449, provides that whenever a bank or trust company is duly authorized to and is acting as a fiduciary, which term shall include an executor, administrator, trustee or guardian, and has a nominee or nominees in whose name securities, including, without limitation, bonds,

stocks, notes and other evidences of title to intangible personal property held as fiduciary may be registered, it shall be lawful to register securities in the name of such nominee or nominees without mention of the fiduciary relationship in the instrument evidencing such securities or on the books of the issuer of same: Provided, (a) The records of such corporate fiduciary shall at all times clearly show that such securities are held by the corporate fiduciary in its capacity as fiduciary, together with the beneficial owner or owners thereof and all facts relating to its ownership, possession and holding thereof; and (b) Such corporate fiduciary shall not be relieved of liability for the safe custody, control and proper distribution of such securities by reason of the registration of same in the name of any nominee. 

Said act also provides if two or more fiduciaries are acting jointly in reference to any securities, it shall be lawful to register the property in the name of any nominee or any joint corporate fiduciary and in the event more than one corporate fiduciary is acting, it shall be lawful to register securities in the name of any nominee of any one of said corporate fiduciaries.

Upon cancellation of the authorization, the bank or lessor may require the presence of all lessees or renters for access. 

§ 191.-Taxation of Trust Estates.-The legislature in 1939 changed the rule as to the taxation of intangible trust assets by providing: "The taxable situs of all intangible trust property, which trust was or is created by a resident of this State, is hereby fixed and declared to be the county of the State of Georgia of which the settler or maker of the trust is a resident, if living, and the county of the State of Georgia of which the settler or maker of the trust was a resident at the time of his death, if deceased. (Acts 1939, p. 100.)" Ga. Code Ann. 92-160.

In Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 887, 893, 102 S. E. 2d 488, a trust instrument provided, among other things, that the trustees "shall not have power to use income or corpus of the trust fund or any part thereof for the purpose of discharging any legal obligations or debts of the donor. It was held that while under 26 U. S. C. A. 2502 (d), it is provided that the gift tax shall be paid by the donor, 26 U. S. C. A. 6324 (b) provides that, if the tax is not paid when due, the donee of any gift shall be personally liable for such tax to the extent of his gift. Under this latter section, no matter what the reason and whether or not any attempt has been made to collect the tax from the donor, the tax then becomes an immediate and direct liability of the donee. That the gift tax in this case was, therefore, a direct obligation upon the trust fund, and that the Treasury Department was authorized under 26 U. S. C. A. (b), to collect the tax from the trustees. 

§ 192.-History.-"Code Ann. § 113-107 is a limitation on testamentary power and applies only to those persons named in the statute. The prohibition is not made in the public interest, but only for the prevention of what the statute regards as a private wrong to a widow, child or the descendants of a child. Such statute does not prohibit a devise for charitable uses; on the contrary, such devises are expressly authorized by law, and are favored by the declared policy of the State." Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 185 (3), 127 S. E. 2d 19.

A testator may by his will make provision for his wife in lieu of a year's support and dower. And where, the testator made certain bequests to his wife, but expressly provided that they were in lieu of a year's support and dower and she applied for and received both from his estate, she, by such an election, completely excluded herself from his will. Therefore, the testator's widow by electing not to take under the will was in no position to invoke the provision of Code § 113-107 which prohibits a testator from devising more than one-third of his estate to any charitable use to the exclusion of his wife, child or the descendants of a child; and this is especially true, since an invocation of that section could not possibly result in any benefit to her after she had taken both a year's support and dower from his estate which are expressly declared to be in lieu of any provision his will made for her. Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (2), 127 S. E. 2d 19. 

§ 193.-Nature of Charitable Uses or Trusts.-Murphy v. Johnston (1940), 

190 Ga. 23, 8 S. E. 2d 23; Perkins v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1940), 190 

Ga. 29, 8 S. E. 2d 28; Taylor v. Trustees of Jesse Parker Williams Hospital (1940), 190 Ga. 349, 9 S. E. 2d 165; Pace v. Dukes (1949), 205 Ga. 835, 55 

S. E. 2d 367.

According to the Acts of 1952, pp. 256, 257, the trustees of certain charitable trusts, having as their object the relief of aged, impotent, diseased, and poor people by providing hospitals and hospital services, may be relieved of certain of their responsibilities under stipulated conditions. This provision will be found in the Ga. Code Ann. as follows: "108-215. Liability of trustees for operation or management of hospital facilities.-The trustees of such charitable trusts shall not be responsible for the operation or management of any hospital facility constructed or operated by any hospital authority with which they may contract, and after the payment of funds from the trust estate represented by such trustees to such hospital authority, said trustee or trustees shall be relieved of any liability to the trust estate

or any beneficiary, whether known or unknown, or to any class of beneficiaries. (Acts 1952, pp. 256, 257.)" "The devise for the purpose of defraying medical expenses of blood relatives of the testator who because of poverty or old age were unable to pay for such services, and for educational loans to deserving persons who were dependents of testator's blood relatives, was not a devise for public charity.” 

Thus, the devise violated the rule against perpetuities. Hardage v. Hardage (1954), 211 Ga. 80, 84 S. E. 2d 54. "Where the will seeks to set up a trust for the benefit of a number of persons as well as institutions, but the duration of the life of anyone in being constitutes no part of the specified duration of the trust, and it is provided therein that it shall not endure for more than 25 years, it is a clear violation of the rule against perpetuities, and the trust is absolutely void." Fuller v. Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (2), 122 S. E. 2d 234. § 195.-Same-Definiteness.-"In the instant case the testator bequeathed the residue of his estate to five trustees and authorized them to use it for the purpose of establishing and maintaining a home for indigent colored people residing in Augusta, Ga., who were sixty years of age or older. He authorized and empowered such trustees and their successors to select those persons who came within the provisions of the bequest and to furnish them living quarters, food, laundry and bed linen without charge therefor. Hence, there is clearly no merit in the contention that the charitable trust which the testator created is void for uncertainty and for that reason unenforceable under the laws of this state." Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (1), 127 S. E. 2d 19. 

§ 196. Statutory Restrictions on Right to Create Charitable Trusts.-"Code 

Ann. § 113-107 is a limitation on testamentary power and applies only to those persons named in the statute. The prohibition is not made in the public interest, but only for the prevention of what the statute regards as a private wrong to a widow, child or the descendants of a child. Such statute does not prohibit a devise for charitable uses; on the contrary, such devises are expressly authorized by law, and are favored by the declared policy of the State." Strother v. 

Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 185 (3), 127 S. E. 2d 19.

A testator may by his will make provision for his wife in lieu of a year's support and dower. And where, the testator made certain bequests to his wife, but expressly provided that they were in lieu of a year's support and dower and she applied for and received both from his estate, she, by such an election, completely excluded herself from his will. Therefore, the testator's widow by electing not to take under the will was in no position to invoke the provision of Code § 113-107 which prohibits a testator from devising more than onethird of his estate to any charitable use to the exclusion of his wife, child or the descendants of a child; and this is especially true, since an invocation of that section could not possibly result in any benefit to her after she had taken both a year's support and dower from his estate which are expressly declared to be in lieu of any provision his will made for her. Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (2), 127 S. E. 2d 19. 

§ 197.-Conditions.-Sproull v. Graves (1942), 194 Ga. 66, 20 S. E. 2d 613. 

Where, in a conveyance of realty to named trustees of a church for use solely for type of religious worship set out in the conveyance, a majority of the members of the unincorporated association vote to devote the property and funds in the hands of the trustees to the use of another religious group, without the unanimous consent of the members, a decree enjoining the trustees from turning over the property and funds to the other church would be proper since

such action would constitute a diversion from the trust. Chatfield v. Dennington (1950), 206 Ga. 762, 58 S. E. 2d 842. § 198.-Cy Pres.-"A bequest to governing authorities of designated 'orphans' home located at Macon, Georgia,' was sufficiently definite and specific to be capable of execution as a charitable trust for benefit of orphans as a class, wherein designated 'governing authorities' were merely to perform office of trustee." Goree v. Georgia Industrial Home (1938), 187 Ga. 368, 200 S. E. 684 (1). "Where . . the manifest intention was to create a charitable trust for tubercular children, and even though the charitable institution named never existed, the purpose and object for which the trust was created still exists and the legacy does not lapse, and the cy pres doctrine applies.'' 

Creech v.

Scottish Rite Hospital for Cripple Children (1954), 211 Ga. 195, 84 S. E. 

2d 563. 

§ 199. Jurisdiction-Construction.-By Acts 1952, page 121, and amended by Acts 1962, page 524, the Legislature made the Attorney General or the solicitor general of the circuit wherein the major portion of the trust res lies, the legal representative of the beneficiaries of charitable trusts and of the interest of the state in their welfare. These acts are codified as Code § 108-212, and is as follows: “In all cases in which the rights of beneficiaries under a charitable trust shall be involved, the Attorney General of the State of Georgia shall, in his official capacity, or the solicitor general of the circuit wherein the major portion of trust res lies, represent the interests of such persons and the interests of the State of Georgia as parens patriae in all legal matters pertaining to the administration and disposition of such trusts; and, in this capacity, he may sue or be sued, and, insofar as a suit of this nature may be deemed a suit against the State, the State of Georgia expressly give its consent to suit; the venue of such suits may be in any county in the State where a substantial number of persons who are the beneficiaries of said trusts shall reside. Process shall be directed to the Attorney 

General of the State of Georgia, in his official capacity, or the solicitor general of the circuit wherein the major portion of trust res lies. 

Service may be perfected by mailing a copy of the petition and process by the clerk of the superior court wherein it is filed to the Attorney General or the solicitor general of the circuit wherein the major portion of trust res lies and by his entry of his action upon the issue docket, and it shall be the duty of said clerk to do the acts herein stated instanter upon the filing of the petition. Any judgment determining rights under any charitable trusts shall be binding on the beneficiaries when the Attorney General or the solicitor general of the circuit wherein the major portion of trust res lies is a party and is served as herein provided." were sixty years of age or older. He authorized and empowered such trustees and their successors to select those persons who came within the provisions of the bequest and to furnish them living quarters, food, laundry and bed linen without charge therefor. Hence, there is clearly no merit in the contention that of the charitable trust which the testator created is void for uncertainty and for that reason unenforceable under the laws of this state." Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (1), 127 S. E. 2d 19. 

§ 203.-Taxation.-Regents of University System of Georgia v. Trust Co. 

of Georgia (1942), 194 Ga. 255, 21 S. E. 2d 691.

In Church of God of the Union Assembly, Inc. v. City of Dalton (1961), 216 Ga. 659, 119 S. E. 2d 11, it was held that under Code § 92-201 and under the 

Constitution, Code § 2-5404, as amended by the Act of 1953 (Acts 1953, Nov.- 

Dec. Sess., page 70), that property owned by a church but used as rented apartments and dwellings, on which rent was paid, are not tax exempt; but that restaurant located in main church building, used primarily for church purposes, but where some meals are served to public for pay is tax exempt. In construing the above Code section and article of the constitution which provides that certain property belonging to religious groups and other charitable institutions are exempt from taxation provided the property so exempt be not used for the purpose of private or corporate profit and income, distributable to shareholders in corporation owning such property and any income from such property is used exclusively for religious purposes and for the purpose of maintaining and operating such institutions but that this exemption shall not apply to real estate or buildings other than those used for the operation in such institution and which are rented, leased or otherwise used for the primary purpose of securing an income therefrom, held that the fact that property is used to make a profit which would in turn be given or used by the church for church purposes in no degree confers tax exemption thereupon. When this case was in the supreme court on the pleadings (Church of God of the Union Assembly v. 

City of Dalton (1957), 213 Ga. 76, 97 S. E. 2d 132) that since it was alleged that no dividends, income, or profits had been, or would be, distributable for purpose of profit or personal gain, that the property upon which the execution had been levied was a place of religious worship and was used in maintaining and operating a church that income derived therefrom was used exclusively for religious purposes that the primary purpose of such real estate was not that of securing an income therefrom for the primary reason was that of providing a meeting place and quarters for the members or affiliates of the church, such allegations would place the church squarely within the constitutional and statutory exemption. However, when the case was decided on the merits, as will be noted above, the supreme court did not follow this line of reasoning. Therefore, it would seem to follow, in view of the above, that charitable institutions owning property that is rented is subject to ad valorem taxes since such property would not be used exclusively by such institutions even though the income derived from the rental thereof was paid over to and used exclusively by such institutions for charitable purposes. 

'Despite the declaration of purpose found in the charter of a hospital corporation, the court will examine and ascertain whether the property itself is dedicated to a beneficent purpose and used exclusively as an institution of purely public charity. The evidence discloses that the hospital in question was engaged principally for non-charitable purposes and apparently chiefly for the benefit of its staff. Hence, the trial judge did not err in dissolving a temporary injunction obtained under a petition by the hospital corporation, seeking to restrain and enjoin the levy and future collection of ad valorem taxes on its

property and alleging that it was entitled to an exemption as being a purely public charitable institution." Georgia Osteopathic Hospital, Inc. v. Alford (1962), 217 Ga. 663, 124 S. E. 2d 402. 

See section 191 of this supplement. 

§ 204.-Testamentary Powers-Generally.—"A 'power' is not 'property' 

but a mere authority, and an absolute power of disposal is not inconsistent with an estate for life only." Bienvenu v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1941), 193 Ga. 101, 17 S. E. 2d 257 (4); Keen v. Rodgers (1948), 203 Ga. 578, 47 

S. E. 2d 567. "A power is not property but a mere authority, and an absolute power of disposal is not inconsistent with an estate for life only. The gift of such power will not enlarge the life-estate previously given, but confers an authority in addition thereto." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553. "It is the rule in Georgia that a power to dispose of property annexed to a life estate will not enlarge the estate given to a fee." Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 68, 102 S. E. 2d 553.

In Harper v. Fuller (1958), 214 Ga. 67, 102 S. E. 2d 553, it was held that the will of the testator, construed as a whole, which first provided for the payment of testator's just debts and funeral expenses, and then provided "The remainder I devise and bequeath to my beloved wife to have and to hold and keep as her property as long as she lives unless she sees fit to sell such things as she cannot use"; and, "I will that my said property be kept intact except such property that it requires to cover my debts and funeral expenses, unless my said wife sees fit to dispose of such property as will be of no benefit to her until the youngest child becomes twenty-one years of age,' gave widow a fee simple title rather than a mere life estate. 

Where a widow had a power of appointment under a will which provided that she might, by her last will and testament, direct or appoint, such widow could not make a gift in praesenti to certain of her named grandchildren, although the widow provided in certain instruments in which she attempted to make present gifts to specified grandchildren of one and one-half per cent undivided interest in the property involved, that she thereby released her right to exercise her power of appointment in regard to the gifts to her grandchildren, such purported release of power of appointment did not convey any right to the grandchildren, in view of the fact it was not in favor of members of a limited class but in favor of specific individuals and therefore not the kind of release as is authorized by Code § 37-612. Browne v. Hendley (1960), 216 Ga. 

411, 116 S. E. 2d 537. 

§ 206.-Creation and Exercise of Powers.-Bienvenu v. First Nat. Bank of 

Atlanta (1941), 193 Ga. 101, 17 S. E. 2d 257. "The donee of a power of appointment, who is also appointed executor or trustee by the will creating the power, is not deprived of his right to exercise it by renouncing, resigning or being discharged from his office or trust, unless the power was given him simply virtute officii. "In determining who has the right to exercise a power in a will, the intention of the testator is to be sought." Bratton v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1940), 191 Ga. 49, 11 S. E. 2d 204 (4, 5). "A power of appointment for disposal of land can be exercised only in the manner specified by donor of the power." Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. v. Hail (1940), 191 Ga. 294, 12 S. E. 2d 53 (9).

One of the rules of law applicable to all wills, where the will confers upon an executor a power involving a purely personal trust or confidence, and it is apparent that the testator expected and intended that the person appointed to carry out his direction shall exercise a personal discretion in so doing, the power conferred will not pass to a successor appointed by a court. Therefore, where a will conferred upon an executrix a discretionary power as to how land devised under the will was to be divided, such power did not pass to a successor administrator de bonis non with will annexed. Marsh v. Anderson (1959), 214 Ga. 667, 107 S. E. 2d 188.

It is the established law of this State that, where the powers conferred by deed or will upon a trustee in the management and control of property for named beneficiaries are personal and discretionary to the trustee, such powers cannot be exercised by a successor; but that, if the exercise of the powers so conferred is imperative or mandatory in all events, the powers are incident to the office and may be exercised by a successor trustee, whether appointed by the court or provided for in the trust instrument. Gilmore v. Gilmore (1947), 201 Ga. 770, 776, 41 S. E. 2d 229.

The powers conferred by the testator in his will upon the person named as executor and as trustee of his estate, being powers which were personal and discretionary, and not imperative or mandatory, did not attach to the office of trustee, and could not be exercised by a successor trustee. Id. 

Where such testator by another item of his will conferred upon the named executor and trustee the authority to provide by will for a successor trustee "to handle the estate" for a specified period of time, but without providing that such successor trustee should exercise the same powers lodged in the original trustee, the trustees appointed by the will of the original trustee, "with all the powers lodged" in him by the will under which he was appointed trustee, did not become vested with such authority. Id. "In the absence of any authority for that purpose conferred by a will, the executor nominated therein and subsequently qualified has no authority to enter into a contract granting an option to a certain person to purchase at private sale land belonging to the estate for a specified price." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 556, 118 S. E. 2d 456. "Where, by the terms of a will creating a trust estate for named beneficiaries, the executor-trustees are empowered and directed to invest, reinvest, sell, lease, or transfer any of the property of the estate upon such terms as to them seem best, at public or private sale, without any order of any court and without reporting to any court, the power granted by the will, not having expressly included the right of the executor-trustees to encumber real property of the estate by a long-term option to purchase, will ordinarily not be enlarged to include such right." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553 (1), 118 S. E. 2d 456.

Where a widow had a power of appointment under a will which provided that she might, by her last will and testament, direct or appoint, such widow could not make a gift in praesenti to certain of her named grandchildren, although the widow provided in certain instruments in which she attempted to make present gifts to specified grandchildren of one and one-half per cent undivided interest in the property involved, that she thereby released her right to exercise her power of appointment in regard to the gifts to her grandchildren, such purported release of power of appointment did not convey any right to the grandchildren, in view of the fact it was not in favor of members of a limited class but in favor of specific individuals and therefore not the kind of release as is authorized by Code § 37-612. Browse v. Hendley (1960), 

216 Ga. 411, 116 S. E. 2d 537.

A provision in a will of a decedent, who was given a power of appointment over certain property and who executed certain intervivos agreement giving named grandchildren a one and one-half per cent undivided interest, respectively, in the property, was void insofar as such provision of the will attempted to impose a forfeiture of any legacy under the will by virtue of a claim of rights under the instruments executed by decedent in favor of her grandchildren. Browne v. Hendley (1960), 216 Ga. 411, 116 S. E. 2d 537. 

§ 208.-Manner of Executing Powers.-Regents of University System of 

Georgia v. Trust Co. of Georgia (1942), 194 Ga. 255, 21 S. E. 2d 691; Jenkins v. 

Shuften (1950), 206 Ga. 315, 57 S. E. 2d 283.

Acts 1945, page 340, codified as Code §§ 37-612 et seq., provides the manner for the release of powers of appointment.

Where a widow had a power of appointment under a will which provided that she might, by her last will and testament, direct or appoint, such widow could not make a gift in praesenti to certain of her named grandchildren, although the widow provided in certain instruments in which she attempted to make present gifts to specified grandchildren of one and one-half per cent undivided interest in the property involved, that she thereby released her right to exercise her power of appointment in regard to the gifts to her grandchildren, such purported release of power of appointment did not convey any right to the grandchildren, in view of the fact it was not in favor of members of a limited class but in favor of specific individuals and therefore not the kind of release as is authorized by Code § 37-612. Browne v. Hendley (1960), 216 

Ga. 411, 116 S. E. 2d 537.

A provision in a will of a decedent, who was given a power of appointment over certain property and who executed certain intervivos agreement giving named grandchildren a one and one-half per cent undivided interest, respectively, in the property, was void insofar as such provision of the will attempted to impose a forfeiture of any legacy under the will by virtue of a claim of rights under the instruments executed by decedent in favor of her grandchildren.
