Under the federal laws the estate of a donee of a valid power of appointment is subject to estate tax to the extent of the value of any property over which such decedent had a power of appointment. To avoid this tax, the donee of a power may release it; the time for release has been extended by 

Congress to June 30, 1947. If the donee of the power fails to make such release before that time, his estate will be subject to tax to the extent of the value of the property subject to the power of appointment; and, if the donee releases the power of appointment after that time, he will be subject to a gift tax. 26 U.S.C.A., sec. 811 (f), 826 (d). § 210.-Discretion of Donee.-Regents of the University System v. Trust 

Company of Georgia (1938), 186 Ga. 498, 198 S. E. 345. "A discretionary power in a trustee is not beyond the reach of judicial inquiry. A court will interfere whenever the exercise of discretion by the trustee is infected with fraud or bad faith, misbehavior, or misconduct, arbitrariness, abuse of authority or perversion of the trust, oppression of the beneficiary, or want of ordinary skill or judgment." Cates v. Cates (1962), 217 Ga. 626, 632, 124 S. E. 2d 375. "If the power of appointment given by will is merely personal to the donee by reason of trust and confidence placed in him by the testator, the power does

not follow the office of the donee as executor or trustee." 

Co. of Georgia (1940), 191 Ga. 49, 11 S. E. 2d 204 (6).

Bratton v. Trust 

"The courts will not ordinarily interpose to restrain the execution of a power, except where abuse of discretion, bad faith, or fraud is shown, or where the power is attempted to be exercised in a manner different from that authorized by the donor." Cates v. Cates (1962), 217 Ga. 626, 632, 124 S. E. 2d 375.

One of the rules of law applicable to all wills, where the will confers upon an executor a power involving a purely personal trust or confidence, and it is apparent that the testator expected and intended that the person appointed to carry out his direction shall exercise a personal discretion in so doing, the power conferred will not pass to a successor appointed by a court. Therefore, where a will conferred upon an executrix a discretionary power as to how land devised under the will was to be divided, such power did not pass to a successor administrator de bonis non with will annexed. Marsh v. Anderson (1959), 214 Ga. 667, 107 S. E. 2d 188.

It is the established law of this State that, where the powers conferred by deed or will upon a trustee in the management and control of property for named beneficiaries are personal and discretionary to the trustee, such powers cannot be exercised by a successor; but that, if the exercise of the powers so conferred is imperative or mandatory in all events, the powers are incident to the office and may be exercised by a successor trustee, whether appointed by the court or provided for in the trust instrument. Gilmore v. Gilmore (1947), 201 Ga. 770, 776, 41 S. E. 2d 229.

The powers conferred by the testator in his will upon the person named as executor and as trustee of his estate, being powers which were personal and discretionary, and not imperative or mandatory, did not attach to the office of trustee, and could not be exercised by a successor trustee. Id. 

Where such testator by another item of his will conferred upon the named executor and trustee the authority to provide by will for a successor trustee "to handle the estate" for a specified period of time, but without providing that such successor trustee should exercise the same powers lodged in the original trustee, the trustees appointed by the will of the original trustee, "with all the powers lodged" in him by the will under which he was appointed trustee, did not become vested with such authority. Id. § 211.-Equity Jurisdiction.-"A discretionary power in a trustee is not beyond the reach of judicial inquiry. A court will interfere whenever the exercise of discretion by the trustee is infected with fraud or bad faith, misbehavior, or misconduct, arbitrariness, abuse of authority or perversion of the trust, oppression of the beneficiary, or want of ordinary skill or judgment."' 

Cates v. Cates (1962), 217 Ga. 626, 632, 124 S. E. 2d 375. "The courts will not ordinarily interpose to restrain the execution of a power, except where abuse of discretion, bad faith, or fraud is shown, or where the power is attempted to be exercised in a manner different from that authorized by the donor." Cates v. Cates (1962), 217 Ga. 626, 632, 124 S. E. 2d 375. 

§ 213.-Kinds of Gifts.-Cannon v. Williams (1942), 194 Ga. 808, 22 S. E. 

2d 838; Harden v. Morton (1943), 195 Ga. 471, 24 S. E. 2d 685; McLendon v. Johnson (1943), 69 Ga. App. 214, 25 S. E. 2d 53.

To constitute a valid gift, there must be the intention to give by the donor, acceptance by the donee, and delivery of the article given, or some act accepted by the law in lieu thereof. It is generally settled that there must be a present

intention to give, full completion and execution of the gift by the donor, and acceptance of the gift by the donee, and furthermore that the donor must have renounced all dominion over the subject matter of the gift, in order to make the transaction binding. Brannen v. Cubbedge (1960), 101 Ga. App. 343, 344, 114 S. E. 2d 152.

Where there is no present intention to give indicated, there is no complete renunciation of right by the giver over the thing given, there is no complete relinquishment of the power of revocation shown and no full delivery of possession as a gift, it follows that there is no valid gift. Brannen v. Cubbedge (1960), 101 Ga. App. 393, 114 S. E. 2d 152.

A joint deposit by an aunt and her nephew, the retaining power to control and withdraw the money held no gift. Brannen v. Cubbedge (1960), 101 

Ga. App. 393, 114 S. E. 2d 152. 

§ 214.-Gifts Causa Mortis.-Higgs v. Willis (1949), 205 Ga. 857, 55 S. E. 

2d 372; Guest v. Stone (1949), 206 Ga. 239, 56 S. E. 2d 247. "Allegations that the petitioner's wife, for several years prior to her death, had on numerous occasions told the petitioner that she was going to leave her property to him at her death, and that, relying thereon, the petitioner made valuable improvements on the property, fail to set out a cause of action for specific performance of an oral contract to convey real and other property, as no agreement on the part of the wife to leave her property to him in consideration of what he might do is alleged." Charles v. Simmons (1960), 215 Ga. 794 (2), 113 S. E. 2d 604. 

8 215.-Gifts-Delivery.-Godwin v. Mitchell (1939), 60 Ga. App. 713, 4 

S. E. 2d 678; Young v. Locknit (1941), 64 Ga. App. 438, 13 S. E. 2d 525; 

Felder v. Felder (1944), 71 Ga. App. 860, 32 S. E. 2d 550; Upchurch v. Upchurch (1947), 76 Ga. App. 215, 45 S. E. 2d 855; Knight v. Wingate (1949), 205 Ga. 133, 52 S. E. 2d 604.

To constitute a valid gift, there must be the intention to give by the donor, acceptance by the donee, and delivery of the article given, or some act accepted by the law in lieu thereof. It is generally settled that there must be a present intention to give, full completion and execution of the gift by the donor, and acceptance of the gift by the donee, and furthermore that the donor must have renounced all dominion over the subject matter of the gift, in order to make the transaction binding. Brannen v. Cubbedge (1960), 101 Ga. App. 343, 344, 114 S. E. 2d 152.

Where there is no present intention to give indicated, there is no complete renunciation of right by the giver over the thing given, there is no complete relinquishment of the power of revocation shown and no full delivery of possession as a gift, it follows that there is no valid gift. Brannen v. Cubbedge (1960), 101 Ga. App. 393, 144 S. E. 2d 152. "The administrator of a donor of a gift causa mortis has no right to possession of the subject of the gift for administration, and the gift is not subject to the ordinary course of administration, save that the administrator may, upon a proper showing, cause the donee to account for the value of the gift provided there is no other sufficient estate to satisfy creditors.'' Cannon v. Williams (1942), 194 Ga. 808, 22 S. E. 2d 838 (17). "The rule that alleged contract of deceased to execute will leaving to claimant all of deceased's realty must be established so clearly, strongly, and satisfactorily as to leave no reasonable doubt as to the contract, does not apply

§ 222.-Gifts Inter Vivos.-Trustees of Jesse Parker Williams Hospital v. 

Nisbet (1940), 189 Ga. 807, 7 S. E. 2d 737; Guffin v. Kelly (1941), 191 Ga. 889, 14 S. E. 2d 50; Moore v. Segars (1941), 192 Ga. 190, 14 S. E. 2d 752; Cannon v. Williams (1942), 194 Ga. 808, 22 S. To constitute a valid gift, there shall be the intention to give by the donor, acceptance by the donee, and delivery of the article given or some act accepted by the law in lieu thereof. Code § 48-101; Banks v. Harvey (1958), 98 Ga.

Actual manual delivery shall not be essential to the validity of a gift. Any act which shall indicate a renunciation of dominion by the donor, and the transfer of dominion by the donor, shall be a constructive delivery. Id. 

The delivery of keys to personal property accompanied by a declaration that the donor is giving the property to the donee is sufficient evidence to sustain a finding there has been a constructive delivery of the object. Id.. 

Where the circumstances are not such as to negative delivery of a gift, declarations of the donor that he has given personal property to another living on the premises with him are sufficient to authorize a recovery by the donee. Id. 

Where a petition alleges an oral promise to give a certain tract of land, a good consideration, an entry into possession in pursuance of the promise, and the making of valuable improvements on the property. This is sufficient to state a cause of action for specific performance of a voluntary promise. Yates v. 

Yates (1959), 214 Ga. 843, 844 (1), 102 S. E. 2d 330. 

§ 223.-Executors and Administrators Generally.-Samples v. Samples 

(1942), 194 Ga. 383, 21 S. E. 2d 601. "It has several times been held that where a person dies without having an estate, no administrator should be appointed." Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 531, 533, 109 S. E. 2d 289.

No administrator should be appointed where, under statute, all the estate should be set aside as a year's support. Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 

Ga. App. 531, 533, 109 S. E. 2d 289.

An executor is not only the personal representative of the decedent, but occupies the position of a trustee for the legatees and devisees. The required notice of an application for a year's support and the return of the appraisers is not for the benefit of the widow, but for the benefit of persons whose interest would be affected by the judgment. Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524, 527, 123 S. E. 2d 728. "An executor or other trustee acts in a representative capacity and for the benefit of the cestui que trust. Persons dealing with him are bound to know the extent of his powers and, in absence of ratification by the cestui que trust the latter is not bound by the executor's acts in excess of his authority. 

This rule is necessary for the protection of the cestui que trust against unlawful acts of the trustee.” Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 557, 118 

S. E. 2d 456. 

"The executor of testator's estate is testator's administrative representative, with property and testamentary rights, and a quasi court officer owing duty to stand in testator's place and administer estate as directed by court." 

Dobbs v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1941), 65 Ga. App. 796, 16 S. E. 2d 485 (8). 

Acts 1958, page 672, which provides that executors, administrators and other fiduciaries may permit others to enter safety deposit boxes, etc., is as follows: "When safety deposit boxes, or receptacles are leased or rented to fiduciaries, including executors, administrators, guardians, trustees, custodians, receivers, and the like, the fiduciary or fiduciaries, as lessee or renter, shall have the right to authorize the entering of the box or receptacle by one or by fewer than all of the fiduciaries or by any other person, without the presence or consent of the fiduciary or other person, and upon the receipt of such written authorization the bank or lessor may authorize access to the box or receptacle in accordance therewith, and without any liability. Upon cancellation of the authorization, the bank or lessor may require the presence of all lessees or renters for access.

"The word 'administrator,' within statute giving administrator or executor right to recover for benefit of next of kin for tortious homicide of decedent when next of kin is dependent upon decedent or to whose support decedent contributed, embraces a 'temporary administrator.' Code 1933, §§ 105-1309, 113-1511." Wilson v. Pollard (1940), 190 Ga. 74, 8 S. E. 2d 380 (2). "A temporary administrator of deceased's estate is authorized to maintain suit under statute providing that where a person killed as a result of negligence leaves no child, spouse, or dependent parent surviving, the 'administrator' or executor may recover for benefit of next of kin if dependent on decedent, or if decedent contributed to their support. Code 1933, § 1051309." Wilson v. Pollard (1940), 62 Ga. App. 781, 10 S. E. 2d 407 (1).

In Redfearn on Wills and Administration of Estates in Georgia, Revised Edition, page 385, footnote 8, the statement is made that a temporary admin-

istrator has no authority to continue the business of the deceased. This statement is based on the decision of the Supreme Court of Georgia in the case of 

Irvine v. Wiley (1916), 145 Ga. 867, 90 S. E. 69. This was changed by the

Acts of 1935, page 326, now codified in the following language: "Temporary administrators, pending the appointment of a permanent administrator, and executors, pending litigation of caveats to wills, are authorized to carry out existing contracts of the deceased, carry on the business of the deceased, and do such acts as might be required of a receiver in the superior court, provided proper orders are secured from the court of ordinary, after due notice to all parties at interest. (Acts 1935, p. 326.)" Ga. Code Ann. 113-1527. 

Acts 1953, page 451, provided for the discharge of temporary administrators as follows: 

'Where there is no necessity for the appointment of a permanent administrator and a temporary administrator has been appointed, the temporary administrator may be discharged in the same manner as provided for discharge of permanent administrators." 

This Act is codified as Ga. Code Ann. 113-1240. 

Temporary administrators may institute suits for the collection of the assets of the estate of their intestates, and particularly to ask for an injunction to protect the estate until the affairs of the estate can be investigated. However, a temporary administrator cannot bring an action to recover land. Royal v. 

Lane (1958), 214 Ga. 375, (1), 104 S. E. 2d 901.

A temporary administrator may not maintain an action for the recovery of land belonging to the estate. Peyton v. Rylee (1950), 206 Ga. 520, 57 S. E. 

2d 565.

On the question of appointment of an administrator de bonis non, an appeal to the superior court from that of the ordinary is a de novo investigation, and the judgment of the superior court supported by evidence is valid, even though contrary to that in the court of ordinary, which was also supported by evidence.

At the 1952 session, the General Assembly provided a definite statutory procedure for the appointment of an administrator de bonis non with will annexed. This procedure may be found in Acts 1952, pp. 87, 88, and is set out in the Ga. Code Ann. as follows: "113-1210.1. Appointment of administrator de bonis non with will annexed upon application of interested persons when only qualified executor of first estate dies.-In all cases when the only qualified and acting executor of the estate of a decedent dies testate himself, any person or persons having an interest in the estate of such first decedent shall have the right to apply to the court of ordinary having jurisdiction of the administration of such first estate for the appointment of an administrator de bonis non with the will annexed of such first testator. (Acts 1952, p. 87.) "113-1210.2. Same; application and hearing.-Upon the hearing of said application, after the issuance and publication of citation as in other cases of applications for letters of administration, the ordinary shall inquire into the circumstances of the case and determine whether the interest of such first estate and the persons interested therein will be best served by the appointment of an administrator de bonis non with will annexed or by permitting the executor appointed under the will of such deceased executor to be or become, as the case may be, the executor of such first estate by operation of law. (Acts 1952, pp. 87, 88.) "113-1210.3. Same; grant of application, when.-Should the ordinary find that the interest of such first estate and of the persons interested therein will be best served by the granting of said application the same shall be granted, otherwise said application shall be denied. (Acts 1952, pp. 87, 88.)" "The plaintiff as the sole beneficiary under the will of the first decedent was a person 'having an interest in the estate of such first decedent' within the purview of the act of 1952 (Ga. L. 1952, p. 87; Code Ann. §§ 113-1210.1, 1210.2, 1210.3) and was therefore entitled under the provisions of said act to apply to the court of ordinary having jurisdiction of such first estate for the appointment of an administrator de bonis non with the will annexed of such first testator." McCray v. The First National Bank (1961), 103 Ga. App. 506, 120 S. E. 2d 26. "Where an administrator has been appointed to administer the estate of a deceased who supposedly died intestate the later production and probate of a

By Acts 1952, pp. 189, 190, the General Assembly amended Ga. Code § 13-2048 by providing that where a depositor has more than $600 on deposit, the payment of $600 to an authorized person shall not act as a full and final acquittance to the bank of all liability to the estate, but only as to the liability for such amount as might have been paid. This amendment was probably intended as a necessary clarification of the language of the section, and more adequately expresses the original legislative intent. The Code section was again amended in 1955 by raising the amount of the deposit to $1000. It now reads: "13-2048. Payment of deposit of deceased depositor.-Upon the death of any person intestate, having a deposit in the bank of not more than $1000, such bank shall be authorized to pay over such deposit: (a) to the husband or wife of the depositor; (b) if no husband or wife, to the children; (c) if no children, to the father, if living, if not, to the mother of the depositor; (d) if no children or parent, then to the brothers or sisters of the depositor. The receipt of such person or persons shall be a full and final acquittance to the bank and relieve it of all liability to the

estate of said deceased depositor or the representative thereof, should one be appointed: Provided, however, that in any case in which a deceased depositor has more than $1000 on deposit in the bank such bank shall be authorized to pay over any amount up to $1000 to any of the persons so authorized by this section to receive said deposit, such receipt shall not act as a full and final acquittance to the bank of all liability, however, but only as to the liability for such amount as might be paid. (Acts 1919, p. 211; 1927, p. 204; 1943, p. 253;

In 1945 the legislature enacted a law pertaining to administration unnecessary in certain cases. This law provides that, when a person has died intestate and there has been no administration in Georgia on his estate, any heir at law of such deceased may file a petition in the court of ordinary of the county of the residence of the deceased, if he was a resident of this state, or, if he was not, in the county in which property belonging to the deceased is located, praying for an order that no administration of the estate is necessary. The statute provides in detail the procedure to be followed. It is a modern law and perhaps should be amended to apply also to testate estates in which, after a will has been probated, no necessity exists for further administration. Acts 1945, page 167; Ga. Code Ann. 113-1232 et seq. 

Acts 1958, pages 355-358, repealed Acts 1945, page 167 (Codified as Ga. Code 

Ann., §§ 113-1232 thru 113-1239), relating to no administration of estates necessary. The 1958 Act, however, enacted the same law as did the 1945 Act, with only a few variations. About the only major change was the addition of the following proviso to section one of the act (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1232): "Provided, however, that property subject to an outstanding security deed, although such indebtedness is a charge against the estate, may be subject to like administration if the holder of the security deed consents or is served and makes no objection thereto, or in instances where there are known debts and all of the known creditors join in a written consent to the order." 

Where all of the assets of an estate are set aside to the widow as a year's support, no administration of the deceased's estate is necessary. Taylor v. 

Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 24, 120 S. E. 2d 874.

Courts of ordinary have authority to exercise original, exclusive, and general jurisdiction in the granting of letters testamentary, of administration, the repeal or revocation of the same, and all controversies in relation to the right of executorship or administration. Whenever the ordinary knows, or is informed by any person having an interest in the estate, that the administrator for any reason is unfit for the trust reposed in him, after citation and hearing, the ordinary may, in his discretion revoke the letters of administration. The word unfit is not limited to physical, mental, or moral conditions, but is sufficiently broad to include a legal disqualification under a will or otherwise. Therefore, where it was established that an executor had violated the terms of the will, violated the law and the will by binding the estate for borrowed money, and that the executor was in extremely poor health, such executor was properly removed. McLendon v. McLendon (1957), 96 Ga. App. 

197, 99 S. E. 2d 489.

The jurisdiction of the court of ordinary to revoke letters of executorship and to require the executor to make an accounting and settlement to the heirs is limited to the case as one at law. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567. See Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 

517. The case was transferred to the Court of Appeals, it being held that such an action was one at law and therefore the Supreme Court did not have jurisdiction of the appellate proceedings. "Where all allegations in a suit to remove an administrator and to have equity court administer an estate showed that court of ordinary, which had taken charge of administering estate, could give full and adequate relief, petition alleged no cause of action and should be dismissed on demurrer. Code 

1933, §§ 37-403, 113-1229, 113-1408, 113-2203." Beecher v. Carter (1939), 189 

Ga. 234, 5 S. E. 2d 648 (8); Turner v. Turner (1954), 210 Ga. 586, 82 S. E. 

2d 137.

On appeal to the superior court from the court of ordinary in a proceeding to remove an administrator, or executor, the discretion which by law has been vested in the ordinary is to be exercised by the jury. McLendon v. McLendon (1957), 96 Ga. App. 197 (2), 99 S. E. 2d 489.

Petition showing that administrator was not citizen of State, that bond was insufficient, and that he had been appointed through fraud on the court of ordinary, stated cause of action for his removal. Jue v. Joe (1950), 207 Ga. 119, 60 S. E. 2d 442.

Previous litigation between the same parties wherein it was held than an administratrix could not assert a claim as an individual against herself as administratrix of the estate she represented for services rendered by her to the intestate and to enforce an alleged contract of the intestate to will property to her, constituted a final adjudication against the right of such administratrix to assert such a claim in her individual capacity against the estate which she represented so long as she continued to represent the estate; however, such ruling would not constitute an adjudication as to her fitness to serve as administratrix as no such question was presented or could have been presented in that litigation; therefore, it follows that the trial judge, in instructing the jury that the fact that the administratrix had filed a claim against the estate was a matter which the jury could take into consideration in ascertaining

whether her interest was so adverse to the estate as to render her unfit to serve as administratrix, did not charge contrary to the previous judgment and decision of the Supreme Court rendered in an entirely separate and distinct case between the same parties. Maxwell v. Hollis (1961), 104 Ga. App. 237, 239 (4), 121 S. E. 2d 409.

The ordinary had jurisdiction on a petition filed at the same term at which he granted the discharge to set aside the discharge on a petition merely showing irregularities in the administration. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Com pany v. Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14, 19, 126 S. E. 2d 289.

A judgment of discharge obtained by an executor cannot be set aside by adult heirs who are sui juris, unless they attack it by a proceeding commenced within three years from the date of its rendition. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 896 (4), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

A petition to set aside judgment discharging the executor, 13 years after the discharge, must contain specific allegations of actual fraud on the part of the executor deterring and debarring the plaintiffs from a more timely suit in order to toll the statute of limitations. Immediately upon the qualification of every administrator, the ordinary shall issue a warrant of appraisement directed to five disinterested freeholders, citizens of the county where the administration is pending, any three of whom shall be qualified to act, requiring them on oath fairly and justly to appraise and value all

of the personal property of the deceased produced to them by the administrator, and also all real estate belonging to the deceased, whether said real estate be situated, lying and being in the county where the administration is pending or in any other county of the 

State of Georga." Acts 1947, page 862. 

Administrator's duty does not include collecting rents accruing after death. 

Ray v. Dooley (1952), 208 Ga. 811, 69 S. E. 2d 766; Turner v. Turner (1954), 210 Ga. 586, 82 S. E. 2d 137.

This act was approved on March 19, 1943. On the next day a conflicting act was approved which provides for the repeal of all laws or parts of laws in conflict with it. Consequently it appears that the act of March 19, 1943, was repealed by the act of March 20, 1943, which provides: "Within sixty days after the anniversary date of his qualification, in each year, every administrator, executor, guardan and trustee and other fiducary now required by the laws of this State to make annual returns, shall make a true and just accounting upon oath of his receipts and expenditures in behalf of the estate during the year preceding such anniversary date of qualification, together with a note or memorandum of any other fact necessary to the exhibition of the true condition of such estate. (Acts 1943, pp. 409, 410.)"

The title to realty is immediately vested in the heirs of an intestate upon his or her death. However, if there be a legal representative, the right to recover for the benefit of the heirs is in such representative. If there be no representative, the heirs may sue in their own names to clear title to land. In the case of personalty, heirs cannot sue except in some special circumstances, such as the refusal of the administrator to act, or fraud. City of Griffin v. McKneely (1960), 101 Ga. App. 811, 816, 115 S. E. 2d 463.

An administrator is a proper party to bring suit for the recovery of damages to personal property. City of Griffin v. McKneely (1960), 101 Ga. App. 811 (2), 115 S. E. 2d 463.

An administrator is a proper party to bring suit for the recovery of damages to real property. City of Griffin v. McKneely (1960), 101 Ga. App. 811 (1), 115 S. E. 2d 463. "An administrator may not sell property held adversely to the estate by a third person, he shall first recover possession." Moore v. Hartford Accident & 

Indemnity Company (1960), 102 Ga. App. 514, 517, 117 S. E. 2d 206. "In suit by heirs at law to recover land allegedly occupied by their father as owner under a deed at time of his death, refusal to charge that if plaintiff's proved that their father was in possession claiming as owner and that while in possession he made valuable improvements at his own expense, plaintiffs would be entitled to recover unless defendant proved that she had title to land, was not error. "" Sharp v. Autry (1938), 186 Ga. 805, 199 S. E. 129 (6). "An executor in possession of money belonging to legatee has an equitable lien thereon, upon final settlement of estate, in nature of a retainer as against debt owing by legatee to deceased, and may appropriate money to extent necessary to discharge debt, notwithstanding that debt is barred by statute of limitations." Cox v. Brady (1938), 58 Ga. App. 498, 199 S. E. 242 (1). "Generally, an interest in realty belonging to a decedent may be recovered in an action against a person not an heir or a purchaser from an heir without necessity of showing existence of debts or need for distribution.” 

Nixon v. 

Nixon (1941), 192 Ga. 629, 15 S. E. 2d 883 (3). "The administrator is the proper representative to sue on life policy where estate of insured or his executors, administrators, etc., are named as beneficiary." Fenn v. Castelana (1943), 196 Ga. 22, 25 S. E. 2d 796 (2).

In 1943 the legislature amended Ga. Code Ann. 113-908, pertaining to recovery of possession from heirs or their assigns, by adding a comma after the word "debts" in line six, by striking the words "or making a proper distribution" from lines six and seven, and by adding in lieu thereof the words "making a proper distribution, or for other purposes provided for in this Title." Acts 1943, page 237.

Where husband and wife agreed that each should have an equal right of entry to safe deposit box, widow and administrator of husband's estate have the same rights. Mandeville v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1950), 206 Ga. 

426, 57 S. E. 2d 553. "While an heir may bring an action to recover property of his intestate where there is no administrator, or where the administrator consents to the action, the law plainly gives the administrator the right to recover property held adversely to the estate of his intestate." Andrews v. Walden (1951), 208 Ga. 340, 66 S. E. 2d 801.

The statutory provision set out on p. 429 of the Revised Edition, "As the right of possession to all the estate is in the administrator, he may recover possession of any part or all of the lands from an heir or from a purchaser from an heir, provided he alleges and proves either that the land sued for has been in his possession and without his consent is being held by the defendant, or that it is necessary for him to have possession for the purpose of paying the debts or making a proper distribution,'' is not applicable where the administrator seeks to recover an interest in land from purchasers of a cotenant of his intestate, such cotenant not being an heir at law of the administrator's intestate. Andrews v. Walden (1951), 208 Ga. 340, 66 S. E. 2d 801. "Where the administrator is insolvent, commits a fraud upon the estate or is in collusion with others to do so, fails to collect assets of the estate and refuses to sue, the heirs may sue in their own name. This is an exception to the rule requiring heirs to show that there is no representation of the estate or assent of the representative." Harrison v. Holsenbeck (1951), 208 Ga. 

410, 67 S. E. 2d 311. "As against one who by fraud during the lifetime of the deceased induced the latter to execute to him a deed to realty, equity will afford the widow, as such personal representative, a remedy to cancel and set aside the deed and incidentally to preserve and apply rents issuing from such realty. Upon like principle equity will afford the widow as such personal representative a remedy to cancel and set aside a judgment obtained against her deceased husband during his lifetime, upon the ground of fraud or other sufficient cause."' Ealy v. 

Tolbert (1953), 209 Ga. 575, 74 S. E. 2d 867.

The petitioner in an action to cancel a deed of the deceased does not set out a cause of action when he fails to show that he is the proper party to bring suit. In Smith v. Smith (1954), 210 Ga. 354, 80 S. E. 2d 196, it was held that the petition did not set out a cause of action, since there were no allegations as to whether or not there was an administration on the estate of the deceased, whether or not the petitioner was the administrator, or whether or not an administration was necessary, or whether or not the petitioner was the widow and sole heir at law. 

Where one dies intestate, leaving no debts, and there is no administration on his estate, all the heirs of such decedent may jointly maintain action to cancel deed of their ancestor, upon ground that it is illegal and void and is a cloud upon their title. White v. Pratt (1955), 211 Ga. 891, 89 S. E. 2d 479. "Where the proceeds of property condemned were claimed by an alleged widow, an alleged heir of the mortgagee, and the administrator of the estate of the deceased holder of the record title to the property, the trial judge properly awarded the funds to the administrator. The conflicting claims of the parties can be asserted against the administrator who may bring an action for determination of heirship." Boswell v. Underwood (1962), 106 Ga. App. 675, 127 S. E. 2d 870. 

§ 248.-Payment of Debts.-Clarkson v. Clarkson (1940), 64 Ga. App. 1, 12 

S. E. 2d 468; Parnelle v. Cavanaugh (1941), 191 Ga. 464, 12 S. E. 2d 877;

Acts 1958, pages 666, 667, amended Code § 113-1505, relating to the notice to creditors to render their accounts, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "113-1505. Every administrator shall give four (4) weeks notice by advertisement in the official newspaper of the county, and the administrator shall publish such notices four (4) weeks within sixty (60) days from date of qualification as administrator, for creditors of the estate to render an account of their demand. The administrator shall be allowed 12 months from the date of his qualification, to ascertain the condition of the estate. Creditors failing to give notice within six months from the date of publication of last notice lose all rights to an equal participation with creditors of equal dignity to whom distribution is made before notice of such claims is brought to the administrator; nor can they hold the administrator liable for a misappropriation of the funds; if, however, there are assets in the hands of the administrator sufficient to pay such debts, and no claims of higher dignity are unpaid, the assets shall be thus appropriated notwithstanding failure to give notice." "An executor cannot, after he has accepted the trust, set up a title adverse to the trust. Code 1933, 38-117. "A claim which may be presented by an administrator, as heir, next of kin, or creditor of deceased, does not have the effect of setting up a title adverse to the trust which has been accepted by the administrator so as to fall within rule that executor cannot, after accepting trust, set up title adverse thereto. 

Code 1933, §§ 38-117, 113-1202." Crummey v. Crummey (1940), 190 Ga.

595, 23 S. E. 2d 272 (7).

Testator not having by his will charged certain property upon which debts were due and bills of sale to secure debt were outstanding with the payment of those debts, the debts were payable out of his residuary estate. Chamblee v. 

Guy (1962), 218 Ga. 56 (1), 126 8. E. 2d 205.

Where husband and wife while separated entered into a contract which provided for monthly payments to the wife as long as she lived and also provided payments to minor children until they reached a specified age, and where contract subsequently was made part of the final divorce decree, the death of the husband did not destroy his obligation, and his estate must continue to make monthly payments. Ramsay v. Sims (1952), 209 Ga. 228, 71 S. E. 2d 639. 

§ 249.-Same-Priority of Payment.-Clarkson v. Clarkson (1940), 64 Ga.

Code 1933, 113-1508, subd. 6." Benfield v. McMillan (1939), 188 Ga. 52, 2 S. E. 2d 600 (1).

Son was entitled to reimbursement for paying decedent's funeral expenses, where same were charged to the estate. He was not a volunteer and his claim came ahead of purchase-money mortgagee's. King v. Dalton (1952), 85 Ga.

Acts 1962, page 610, amended Code § 113-2001, providing commissions to be paid to administrators. Said Code section as amended is as follows: "As compensation for his services, the administrator shall have a commission of two and one-half per cent. on all sums of money received by him on account of the estate (except money loaned by him and repaid to him), and a like commission on all sums paid out by him, either for debts, legacies, or distributive shares. Such commissions are part of the expense of administration, and shall be paid from the general estate, if any; if none, they shall be deducted from the debt or legacy paid. Whenever any portion of the dividends, interest or rents payable to an administrator are required by law of the United States or other governmental unit to be withheld by the person paying the same for income tax purposes, the amount so withheld shall be deemed to have been collected by the administrator. The provisions of this Code section shall likewise apply to commissions payable to executors, trustees and guardians." Code 

§ 113-2001. 

"Though rate or amount of executor's or administrator's compensation fixed by statute is ordinarily controlling, agreement by him to serve for less than such compensation is valid and enforceable." Cagle v. Cagle (1939), 60 Ga. 

App. 769, 5 S. E. 2d 100 (1). "Testators making wills in this State shall have the power of giving and bequeathing to the persons nominated as executors, as compensation for the services to be rendered by such executors in the execution of the trusts reposed in them, such property or money as the testators may devise, and all such gifts and bequests shall take precedence over any other special gifts or bequests made by said testators: Provided, that such gifts or bequests to executors shall not interfere with the rights of creditors of such testators. (Acts 1869, p. 163.)" Ga. Code Ann. 113-823.

The legislature in 1941 authorized the payment of compensation to executors and administrators when property, tangible or intangible, is delivered in kind, even though there has been no appraisement of such property. Not more than

three per cent of the fair value of such property, such value to be determined by the ordinary, shall be allowed as compensation for delivering any property in kind to the beneficiaries. Acts 1941, page 299; Ga. Code Ann. 113-2004. 

See section 324.

Under the provisions of Code § 113-2008 the administrator may be allowed additional compensation for extraordinary services, and under § 113-2009 he may also be authorized to pay the expenses of employing such agents as he finds necessary to employ for the estate. The allowance of such extra compensation to the administrator and the allowance of expenses for employing agents can only be made after a showing to the ordinary and a finding by him of the necessity therefor. But, where the case is one of appeal from the court of ordinary brought to the superior court to review the ordinary's action in approving or disapproving the administrator's acts in dealing with the estate, and where the proceeding in the superior court takes upon itself the nature of a general accounting and winding up of the estate, that court has jurisdiction to allow or not to allow these items of expense on the same basis as the ordinary would have had. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cochran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14, 21, 126 S. E. 2d 289.

In the trial of an appeal from the court of ordinary before a jury in the superior court, the jury has jurisdiction to allow extra compensation to the administrator under Code § 113-2008 or to approve the expense of employing agents to assist in the administration of the estate on the same basis as the ordinary upon a showing that these expenses and charges were reasonably necessary to the prudent and sound administration of the estate. Hartford 

Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 108 Ga. App. 14, 15 (4), 126 S. E. 2d 289.

Acts 1958, page 672, amended Code § 113-2010, providing for the expenses of giving bond by administrators and executors, by striking said section in its entirety and enacting in lieu thereof the following: "113-2010. Administrators or executors who are required by law to give bond as such, who have given as security on such bonds one or more guaranty companies, surety companies, fidelity insurance companies, or fidelity and deposit companies, as authorized by law, may include as part of their lawful expenses or costs of administration the cost of such bond premium or bond premiums.' 

An executor named in a purported will is entitled to expenses, including reasonable attorney's fees if an attorney is employed, in offering a will for probate, even though the will may subsequently be declared invalid. Acts 

1943, page 423; Ga. Code Ann. 113-619. "An administrator will not be allowed attorney fees out of the estate for the purpose of protecting him from his misdeeds in relation to it." Estes v. 

Collum (1954), 91 Ga. App. 186, 85 S. E. 2d 561. "As to the plaintiff's claim for extra compensation for services as administratrix, it appears from the petition that this estate is being administered in the court of ordinary. That court, under Code § 113-2008, has jurisdiction to award extra compensation in cases of extraordinary services. The claim for extra compensation is peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the court of ordinary." Maxwell v. Hollis (1960), 216 Ga. 224, 227, 115 S. E. 2d 360.

"A court of ordinary is without jurisdiction to assess and award attorney's fees to an attorney representing an estate in an action brought by the attorney for that purpose in the court of ordinary." Cromer v. Chambers (1961), 104 

Ga. App. 196, 121 S. E. 2d 397.

An administrator is authorized to provide for the estate competent legal counsel. Such counsel fees are legitimate expenses of the estate according to the particular facts and circumstances of each case. In employing counsel, an administrator should use the same care as a prudent man would exercise in employing competent legal counsel in a matter in which he is personally concerned. Such contracts of employment, when made under such circumstances, need not be sanctioned or approved by the ordinary before they become valid and binding. Cromer v. Chambers (1961), 104 Ga. App. 196, 197, 121 S. E. 2d 397. 

In Samples v. Samples (1942), 194 Ga. 383, 388, 21 S. E. 2d 601, it was held that when an executor has probated a will in common form and the heirs at law require a probate in solemn form, the executor is entitled to have the court costs and counsel fees paid out of the estate and that this is true even though the caveat is successful and probate in solemn form is refused, unless the probate in common form was originally made in bad faith on the part of the executor in an attempt to defraud the heirs at law. And Acts 1943, page 

423, codified as Code § 113-620 further extends the rule enunciated above by including probate of will in both solemn and common form. However, it should be remembered that a caveat may not be filed to an application to probate a will in common form. See section 123 of the main volume. Said Code § 113-619 is as follows: "Those who are named as executors in purported wills of decedents shall be entitled to recover from the estate of the decedent expenses, including a reasonable attorney's fee if the services of an attorney are employed for offering for probate wills in solemn or common form, even though the will is subsequently determined not to be the valid will of the testator: 

Provided, however, such persons shall not be entitled to recover from the estate the expenses and attorney's fees incurred in the effort to sustain the will in the event of a contest, unless the person so named proceeds in good faith; the court of ordinary shall determine upon the petition of a person so named, the amount of expenses, and the amount to be paid the attorney so employed, and its order shall be subject to appeal to the superior court as is now in other cases provided." 

§ 251.-Release, Compromise, and Arbitration of Claims.-An administrator is only authorized to compromise debts owing the estate after strictly complying with Code § 113-1515 which requires that he first obtain an order from the ordinary directing the compromise and that he make oath to the ordinary that such settlement was made in good faith and to the best interest of the estate. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. 

App. 14 (3), 126 S. E. 2d 289.

(1938), 187 Ga. 340, 200 S. E. 283; Harris v. O'Quinn (1941), 66 Ga. App. 226, 17 S. E. 2d 758; Fisher v. Pair (1943), 69 Ga. App. 492, 26 S. E. 2d 187; Morris v. Nicholson (1944), 198 Ga. 450, 31 S. E. 2d 786; Bickerstaff v. Ellis (1949), 204 Ga. 734, 51 S. E. 2d 821.

Acts 1959, page 99, enacted Code § 113-1528, giving executors and administrators the legal right to borrow money and bind the estate by the execution of a promissory note therefor, and the right to pledge any or all the property of the estate for the payment of the same by mortgage, trust deed, deed to secure debt or other security instrument, for the purpose of paying any gift, estate, inheritance, income, sales or ad valorem taxes due the United States, the State or any municipality or county thereof which constitute a claim or demand against said estate. "An executor or administrator cannot bind an estate he represents by note or by encumbrance without having been given such authority by the testator in a will. See McFarlin v. Stinson, 56 Ga. 396, 397; Gaudy v. Babbitt, 56 Ga. 

640; Lynch v. Kirby, 65 Ga. 279; Howard v. Cassels, 105 Ga. 412 (31 S. E. 

562, 70 Am. St. R. 44); Brannon v. Ober & Sons Co., 106 Ga. 168, 170 (32 S. E.

416, 418, 105 S. E. 2d 807.

An administrator may not make a note as agent for an estate. If such a note is made it is held to be an individual undertaking. And an administrator may not seek a revocation of a note made by him in order to show that the note was executed by him as agent for the estate as the law does not permit an administrator to sign a note in such a capacity. Burk v. Hammond (1958), 98 Ga. App. 416, 418, 105 S. E. 2d 807.

In 1953, the Legislature set up a procedure for the execution of leases of trust property. Thus it is provided in Section 1 of Acts 1953, page 44 et seq. that: "When the assets of a trust include an interest in real property the trustee may apply to the superior court for an order authorizing such trustee to lease such real property or a part thereof for a term of years which may or will continue beyond the termination of the trust and the superior court in the execution of the protective powers of equity over trust estates and the estates of wards in chancery shall have power and jurisdiction to pass an order authorizing the execution of such a lease."

The word "trust," wherever used in the Act, includes the estate held by an executor, administrator, guardian, or trustee, whether held or in existence at the time of the passage of the Act or later coming into existence. There is provision for action upon the application in vacation and at chambers and for notice to all living beneficiaries as may be ordered by the court. Provision is also made for the appointment of guardians ad litem wherever necessary. 

A lease so executed is binding upon all beneficiaries in life or born subsequent to its execution during the existence of the lease. It is further provided by 

Section 6 of the Act that: 

"It shall be the duty of the superior court to hear evidence that may be tendered by the trustee and if the court is satisfied from the proceedings that the lease to be authorized is expedient, the court shall pass an order authorizing the trustee to execute the lease subject, however, to such terms as the court shall deem proper and necessary to protect the value of the trust estate. The granting of such application is not precluded by the fact that the instrument creating the trust only authorizes leases for terms not extending beyond the duration of the trust."

This Act is codified as Ga. Code Ann. 108-439 through 108-444. "In the absence of any authority for that purpose conferred by a will, the executor nominated therein and subsequently qualified has no authority to enter into a contract granting an option to a certain person to purchase at private sale land belonging to the estate for a specified price." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 556, 118 S. E. 2d 456. "A trustee who has a power to sell in addition to a power to lease, whether the latter is express or implied, does not ordinarily have the power to give a lessee an option of purchase for a definite sum during the term of the lease. 

The purpose of this rule is to compel the trustee to exercise his judgment at the time of the sale and not at the time of the making of the lease as to whether the sale is beneficial to the trust estate." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 555 (1), 118 S. E. 2d 456. 

§ 254.—Liability for Negligence and Mismanagement.—Watson v. Watson 

(1940), 61 Ga. App. 825, 7 S. E. 2d 614; Beaudry, Inc. v. Freeman (1946), 73 

Ga. App. 736, 38 S. E. 2d 40. "Generally, the estate of a decedent is not liable for tortious acts of an administrator or executor committed in course of administration of estate. 

Where pecuniary gain results to an estate of a decedent from tortious of an executor, the estate may be liable." Fife v. Richards (1948), 77 Ga. App. 

698, 49 S. E. 2d 772.

When a petition for transfer of the administration of an estate from a court of ordinary to a court of equity and for damages does not allege that the executor was insolvent or that there was danger of loss or irreparable injury to the estate, the petition does not state any reason why such transfer should be made. Bandy v. Smith (1954), 211 Ga. 192, 84 S. E. 2d 449.

In the absence of any authority conferred by will, an executor has no power, by virtue of his appointment as such, to borrow money and bind the estate. 

McLendon v. McLendon (1957), 96 Ga. App. 197 (3), 99 S. E. 2d 489. However, Acts 1959, page 99 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1528), provide that an executor

or administrator may borrow money and bind the estate by giving security therefor for the purpose of paying any gifts estate, inheritance, income or ad valorem taxes. This act sets forth the procedure to be followed. 

Acts 1958, page 672, which provides that executors, administrators and other fiduciaries may permit others to enter safety deposit boxes, etc., is 

"When safety deposit boxes, or receptacles are leased or rented to fiduciaries, including executors, administrators, guardians, trustees, custodians, receivers, and the like, the fiduciary or fiduciaries, as lessee or renter, shall have the right to authorize the entering of the box or receptacle by one or by fewer than all of the fiduciaries or by any other person, without the presence or consent of the fiduciary or other person, and upon the receipt of such written authorization the bank or lessor may authorize access to the box or receptacle in accordance therewith, and without any liability. 

Upon cancellation of the authorization, the bank or lessor may require the presence of all lessees or renters for access.' 

§ 255.-Suits by Representative of Estate.-By Acts 1952, p. 224, the Gen eral Assembly increased considerably the responsibilities of personal representatives both as to the bringing and to the defending of actions. This was done by adding a provision for the survival of causes of action for homicide, personal injury or damage to property to Ga. Code § 3-505. The section had formerly been held to apply only to actions which had been filed and were pending at the death of the decedent. The section now reads: "3-505. (4421) Action for tort not to abate by death of either party. No action for a tort shall abate by the death of either party, where the wrongdoer received any benefit from the tort complained of; nor shall any action, or cause of action, for the recovery of damages for homicide, injury to person, or injury to property abate by the death of either party; but such cause of action, in case of the death of the plaintiff, shall, in the event there is no right of survivorship in any other person, survive to the personal representative of the deceased plaintiff; and in case of the death of the defendant, shall survive against said defendant's personal representative. However, in the event of the death of the wrongdoer before suit shall have been brought against him, the personal representative of such wrongdoer in such capacity shall be subject to suit just as the wrongdoer himself would have been during his life; providing that there shall be no punitive damages. (Acts 1889, p. 73; 1935, pp. 94, 95; 

1952, p. 224.)" "The act of 1952 (Ga. L. 1952, p. 224; Code Ann. § 3-505), provides for the survivorship of causes of action to a decedent's representative only where otherwise there is no right of survivorship, and where a husband and father is killed the surviving children have a cause of action for the negligent homicide of their father, after the death of the widow who after the homicide died without instituting suit for the damages." Keenan Welding Supplies Company v. Bronner (1959), 100 Ga. App. 400 (1), 111 S. E. 2d 140.

The title to realty is immediately vested in the heirs of an intestate upon his or her death. Code Ann. 1131905. § 264.-Federal Estate Tax.-As there is no estate tax on an estate having a net value of less than $60,000.00, this tax is of little concern to a majority of the people in this country. However, the estate tax rises rapidly when the net value of the estate exceeds $60,000.00. Any attorney preparing a will or other instrument involving an estate having a gross value of more than $60,000.00

should take into consideration the advantage which might be obtained from the benefit of a marital deduction. 

The Revenue Act of 1948 was revolutionary in two important respects; in the first place, it permitted a married couple filing a joint return to split their income and thus pay taxes in lower brackets. This is a big tax-saver insofar as income tax is concerned. 

In the second place, the Revenue Act of 1948 permitted what is commonly known as a marital deduction for the estate of a decedent. 

These helpful provisions are carried forward in section 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. 

Marital Deduction.-The Federal Revenue Act enacted in April, 

1948, created the right to a marital deduction for the surviving wife or husband for the purpose of reducing federal estate taxes. 

Among other things this revenue act allowed the deduction for any interest in property "which passes . . . . . from the decedent to his surviving spouse." The marital deduction is allowable for either husband or wife. 1954 IRC, section 2056.

The marital deduction can be any portion of the adjusted gross estate up to fifty per cent (50%), and it may be given outright to or put in trust for the surviving spouse. If it is given in trust, the trust must provide that the surviving spouse for whom it is created shall be entitled to all the income from it for life, payable annually or more often, and such spouse must be given an exclusive, general power of appointment over such marital trust to appoint the trust property to himself or to herself or to his or her estate or to anyone else by deed or by will. The same rule applies to any portion of the marital deduction placed in trust. 

To qualify for the marital deduction, the power must be general, and the surviving spouse must be given the exclusive right to exercise it. If the power of appointment is not general, the trust does not qualify for the marital deduction. 

The will or other trust instrument must provide that the power must be exercised exclusively by the surviving spouse; it may provide that the exercise may be solely by deed or other form of transfer executed during life, or it may provide that the exercise may be solely by will; it may also provide that a portion of the trust assets may be appointed by deed during life and the balance by will; it may also provide that, if the powers are not exercised, the trust assets shall be disposed of as directed by the testator or donor. 

The average testator prefers not to give his wife a power to dispose of the assets of the marital trust during life, as a wife is usually not well versed in business affairs.

The marital deduction can be fixed at any per cent up to fifty per cent of the adjusted gross estate. The gross estate is the whole estate left by the decedent. The adjusted gross estate is the estate which is left after the payment of funeral expenses, debts, costs and expenses of administration. 

The marital deduction applies to intestate estates as well as testate estates. It is allowed only where the interest passing to the surviving spouse is not terminable. A marital deduction can not be taken for dower in those states where dower is a life estate. 

Whenever the assets of a husband and wife are approximately equal, it may be best not to provide for marital deduction in either estate. If assets are unequal, a savings in tax may be made by providing for a marital deduction in the larger estate. 

For an excellent discussion of estate planning, including marital deductions, see "Basic Estate Planning" by Appleman, published in 1956 by The Bobbs-Merrill Company, Inc., 730 North Meridian 

Street, Indianapolis 7, Indiana. 

Note: See Additional Forms, this supplement, post. 

In Love v. Fulton Natl. Bank (1958), 213 Ga. 887, 893, 102 S. E. 2d 488, a trust instrument provided, among other things, that the trustees "shall not have power to use income or corpus of the trust fund or any part thereof for the purpose of discharging any legal obligations or debts of the donor. It was held that while under 26 U. S. C. A. 2502 (d), it is provided that the gift tax shall be paid by the donor, 26 U. S. C. A. 6324 (b) provides that, if the tax is not paid when due, the donee of any gift shall be personally liable for such tax to the extent of his gift. Under this latter section, no matter what the reason and whether or not any attempt has been made to collect the tax from the donor, the tax then becomes an immediate and direct liability of the donee. 

That the gift tax in this case was, therefore, a direct obligation upon the trust fund, and that the Treasury Department was authorized under 26 U. S. C. A. 6324 (b), to collect the tax from the trustees. § 265.-Georgia Estate Taxes.-In making income tax returns fiduciaries are allowed exemptions under an act of 1953, as follows: "(h) The net income of the estate or trust shall be computed in the same manner and on the same basis as in the case of an individual, except that an exemption of $1,000 shall be allowed to an estate and a trust shall be allowed on exemption of $100. (Acts 1941, p. 

213; Acts 1953, p. 297.) Ga. Code Ann., § 92-3106 (h).

Acts 1960, page 835, superseded Code § 92-3401 in regard to the assessment, collection, and returns of estate taxes, which said Code section is now as follows: 

"It shall be the duty of the legal representative of the estate of any person who may die a resident of this State, and whose estate is subject to the payment of a Federal estate tax, to file with the

State Revenue Commissioner a duplicate of the estate tax return which he is required to make to the Federal authorities, and pay to the State of Georgia a tax in an amount equal to the amount allowable as a credit for State death taxes under section 2011 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954: Provided, however, that if the decedent owned at the time of his death either real property in another State or personal property having a business situs in another State which State requires the payment of a tax for which credit is received against Federal estate taxes, any tax due hereunder shall be reduced by an amount which bears the same ratio to the total State tax credit allowable for Federal estate tax purposes as the value of such property taxable in such other State bears to the value of the entire gross estate for Federal estate tax purposes. If, after the filing of a duplicate return and the assessment of the State taxes the Federal authorities shall increase or decrease the amount of the Federal estate tax, an amended return shall be filed with the State Revenue Commissioner showing all changes made in the original return and the amount of increase or decrease in the Federal estate tax, and the State Revenue Commissioner shall assess against said estate the additional amount found to be due hereunder, or in the event of a decrease in the Federal estate tax shall refund to said estate any overpayment of the tax imposed by this section."

§ 266.-Sales by Executors.-In 1955 the legislature enacted the following provisions: "37-616. Power of sale as authorizing private sale and sale by successor donee.-Unless expressly limited in a will, deed or other instrument creating a power of sale or unless specifically otherwise provided in such instrument, a power of sale conferred upon an executor, trustee, guardian or attorney in fact shall authorize a private sale by such executor, trustee, guardian or attorney in fact,

with or without advertisement and on such terms and conditions as the donee of such power may deem advisable, without the necessity of applying for leave to sell or obtaining any order therefor from any court: Provided, however, that the provisions of this section shall not apply to powers of sale in security deeds, mortgages, trust deeds, bills of sale and other instruments conveying property or creating a lien thereon, to secure a debt or debts. 

Unless expressly limited in the instrument creating a power of sale or unless specifically otherwise provided in such instrument, such power of sale conferred upon an executor, trustee or guardian may be exercised and executed by an administrator with the will annexed or by a successor administrator, trustee or guardian; and if such power be conferred upon more than one executor, trustee or guardian the surviving or remaining executor or executors, trustee or trustees, or guardian or guardians, may exercise and execute such power. (Acts 1955, pp. 430, 431.)”

The Act from which this section was codified provides that the section shall not affect any instrument dated prior to the approval date of the Act, which was March 4, 1955.

Acts 1958, pages 670, 671, amended Code § 113-1703, relating to the terms of sales by administrators, to include executors, where the will of testator is silent on the terms may be made by the executor under his will. 

The public policy of this state pertaining to sales by administrators is fixed by Code §§ 113-1706 and 113-1707, and all such sales must be public and in the manner prescribed by law. An agreement by an administratrix to make a conveyance upon stipulated terms is contrary to public policy and unenforceable. 

Cummings v. Johnson (1963), 218 Ga. 557, 562 (5), 129 S. E. 2d 762. "In the absence of any authority for that purpose conferred by a will, the executor nominated therein and subsequently qualified has no authority to enter into a contract granting an option to a certain person to purchase at private sale land belonging to the estate for a specified price.” Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553, 556, 118 S. E. 2d 456. "Where, by the terms of a will creating a trust estate for named beneficiaries, the executor-trustees are empowered and directed to invest, reinvest, sell, lease, or transfer any of the property of the estate upon such terms as to them seem best, at public or private sale, without any order of any court and without reporting to any court, the power granted by the will, not having expressly included the right of the executor-trustees to encumber real property of the estate by a long-term option to purchase, will ordinarily not be enlarged to include such right.'' Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 Ga. 553 (1), 118 S. E. 2d 456.

Such sales may be made at any time after obtaining an order authorizing such sale from the ordinary which order may be issued at any time after application therefor by the administrator or executor, and the administrator and executor shall be accountable in all other respects as is otherwise provided by law."' "A sale by an administrator without order from the ordinary is void and passes no title to the purchaser. Code 1933, §§ 113-1702, 113-1705, 113-1706, 113-1709, 113-1720, 113-1724." Dowling v. Keen (1939), 187 Ga. 394, 200 S. E. 

789 (1); Fisher v. Pair (1943), 69 Ga. App. 492, 26 S. E. 2d 187; Consolidated 

Realty Investments, Inc. v. Gasque (1948), 203 Ga. 790, 48 S. E. 2d 510; Davis v. Auerbach (1949), 78 Ga. App. 575, 51 S. E. 2d 527.

Where a will conferred upon the executors thereof full and complete power to sell any part of testator's estate, not specifically devised, at public or private sale, with or without notice, and without any order of court, as they may deem best, with authority to make good and sufficient conveyances to the purchasers, and to hold the proceeds of any such sale to the same uses and trusts declared in said will, such power of sale contemplates only a bona fide and valid sale upon a sufficient valuable consideration, and does not authorize the executor to make a sale or conveyance of the land as a gift, or upon nominal consideration. Harrison v. Harrison (1958), 214 Ga. 393 (3), 105 S. E. 

2d 214.

§ 268.-Sale of Land.-Porter v. LaGrange Banking & Trust Co. (1939), 187 

Ga. 528, 1 S. E. 2d 441; Zeagler v. Zeagler (1940), 190 Ga. 220, 9 S. E. 2d 263; 

Hortman v. Vissage (1942), 193 Ga. 596, 19 S. E. 2d 523; Sangster v. Toledo 

Mfg. Co. (1942), 193 Ga. 685, 19 S. E. 2d 723. "Under statute providing that an administrator may not sell property held adversely to the estate by a third person, but shall first recover possession, if land is in adverse possession of an heir, administrator must first recover possession before land can be sold. Code 1933, § 113-1714.' Hortman v. 

Vissage (1940), 191 Ga. 446, 12 S. E. 2d 294 (3). "An administrator may not sell property held adversely to the estate by a third person, he shall first recover possession." Moore v. Hartford Accident & 

Indemnity Company (1960), 102 Ga. App. 514, 517, 117 S. E. 2d 206.

It has been held repeatedly that allegations "to the effect that a sale by the executrix should be enjoined because there are in fact no debts of the estate, afford no reason for the grant of an injunction, since . . . the executrix had obtained from the ordinary an order permitting its sale for the purpose of paying the indebtedness claimed by the executrix to be due." Brewton v. 

McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 696, 119 S. E. 2d 105. ''Where, after due notice, leave has been regularly granted by the court of ordinary to an administrator to sell realty of a decedent, equity will not restrain the sale by injunction at the instance of an heir on account of reasons which could have been as readily urged on a caveat to the application for leave to sell.'' Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 696, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

The order by the ordinary's court is not only leave to sell but is an adjudication by a court of competent jurisdiction that it is necessary for the land to be administered for one or the other or both of the purposes indicated in Code §§ 113-901 and 113-1706, that is, for payment of debts and distribution among the heirs and that it is for the benefit of the heirs and creditors. 

Therefore, if either reason for selling the land is found by the court to exist, the sale may be authorized. Warren v. Warren (1961), 104 Ga. App. 184, 185, 121 S. E. 2d 343. "Under the facts of this case the evidence demanded the finding that it was necessary for the administratrix to sell the real property of the estate for the purposes of the payment of debts and distribution among the heirs, and it was not error for the court to direct a verdict for the administratrix and against the caveat." Warren v. Warren (1961), 104 Ga. App. 184, 121 S. E. 2d 343.

The order of the court of ordinary granting leave to sell is the judgment of a court of general jurisdiction; and, when granted according to law, it is binding on all persons interested in the estate. Such an order cannot be collaterally attacked in any court, except in the single instance where the order has been granted without personal notice to an heir from whom the representative of the estate seeks to recover land held adversely. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 696, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

Acts 1958, page 671, again amended Ga. Code § 113-1706, by the addition to the first proviso an administrator with will annexed, and by adding the proviso at the end of the section, "that nothing herein shall limit the powers contained in the will of a decedent." The Code section as amended by the 

1958 Act is as follows: 

"113-1706 (4026) Land, petition to sell; notice; order. If at any time it shall become necessary, for the payment of the debts of the estate or for the purpose of distribution, to sell the land of the decedent, the administrator shall, by written petition, apply to the ordinary for leave to sell, setting forth in the petition the reason for such application; and notice of the same shall be published once a week for four weeks before the hearing, in the newspaper in which the county advertisements are published. If no objection is filed, and the ordinary is satisfied of the truth of the allegation in the petition, an order shall be passed granting the leave to sell, specifying therein the land as definitely as possible. Said order by the ordinary granting permission to an executor, or an administrator with the will annexed, to sell shall be binding, final and conclusive as to all devisees under the will of the testator regardless of any prior assent of the executor to the devise in the will. Provided, however, that nothing herein shall prevent the devisee from entering an appeal from said order in time provided by law, or from filing a claim to said land prior to the actual sale thereof by the executor, or the administrator with will annexed, and Provided further, that nothing in this section shall prevent a bona fide purchaser or mortgagee of said land who purchased prior to said order of the ordinary and who holds under a deed or mortgage duly recorded prior to said order, from asserting his title to said land by showing that the executor had assented expressly or impliedly to the devise in said will prior to the said order to sell, and, Provided further, that nothing herein shall limit the powers contained in the will of a decedent. (Act 1816, Cobb, 319. Act 1826, Cobb, 323. Acts 1851-2, p. 

95; 1869, p. 13; 1951, p. 476; 1958, p. 671.)”

The order by the ordinary's court is not only leave to sell but is an adjudication by a court of competent jurisdiction that it is necessary for the land to be administered for one or the other or both of the purposes indicated in Code §§ 113-901 and 113-1706, that is, for payment of debts and distribution among the heirs and that it is for the benefit of the heirs and creditors. 

Therefore, if either reason for selling the land is found by the court to exist, the sale may be authorized. Warren v. Warren (1961), 104 Ga. App. 184, 185, 121 S. E. 2d 343. "Under the facts of this case the evidence demanded the finding that it was necessary for the administratrix to sell the real property of the estate for the purposes of the payment of debts and distribution among the heirs, and it was not error for the court to direct a verdict for the administratrix and against the caveat." Warren v. Warren (1961), 104 Ga. App. 184, 121 S. E. 

2d 343.

"The court of ordinary, in passing upon the application of an executor to sell a specific tract of land of his testator, has no jurisdiction to determine the rights of a son of the testator under an alleged contract between the son and the testator, wherein the son asserts an agreement whereby the testator agreed to devise the specific property to him in consideration of services rendered and to be rendered." Fambrough v. Fambrough (1952), 209 Ga. 23, 70 S. E. 2d 468. 

Court will not enjoin sale solely because lands were described in the order as being bounded on the south by lands of petitioner, instead of giving the original land lot line. Strickland v. Padgett (1952), 209 Ga. 261, 71 S. E. 2d 545. "It is no ground of caveat to the application of the executor to the ordinary for leave to sell land that the executor has assented to a devise in the will of the testator. The caveator's remedy is a claim.". Salter v. Wetmore (1954), 90 Ga. App. 672, 83 S. E. 2d 852.

An order granting leave to an administrator to sell land is conclusive as to the necessity of such sale by the administrator. City of Griffin v. McKneely (1960), 101 Ga. App. 811, 815, 115 S. E. 2d 463.

The order by the ordinary's court is not only leave to sell but is an adjudication by a court of competent jurisdiction that it is necessary for the land to be administered for one or the other or both of the purposes indicated in Code §§ 113-901 and 113-1706, that is, for payment of debts and distribution among the heirs and that it is for the benefit of the heirs and creditors.

binding on all persons interested in the estate. Such an order cannot be collaterally attacked in any court, except in the single instance where the order has been granted without personal notice to an heir from whom the representative of the estate seeks to recover land held adversely. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 696, 119 S. E. 2d 105. “‘Irregularities,' within statute providing that to divest title of heirs at law, administrator shall have authority to sell, and if there shall be irregularities, or if he shall fail to comply with law as to mode of sale, sale shall be voidable except as to innocent purchaser, refers to such matters as mode of advertising, or other irregularities in the procedure." Guthrie v. Moran (1941), 192 Ga. 607, 15 S. E. 2d 890 (1, 2).

With reference to the sale of contingent interests in land devised, our Code provides: "In all cases where property is left by will providing for the keeping together and holding the real estate named in such will until the beneficiaries shall arrive at the age of 21 years. and in all cases where property has been left by will providing that the property therein designated shall not be sold until the happening of some contingency relating to the future, and when such estate owes debts, whether such indebtedness was owing at the death of the testator or bas been lawfully contracted by the executor, administrator, or trustee of the estate, and there are not sufficient personal belongings of the estate to pay off and discharge the indebtedness, the executor, administrator, or other trustee, may sell at private or public sale a sufficiency of the real estate belonging to such estate to pay off and discharge any such debts or liabilities and make to the purchaser in his official capacity good and sufficient title in fee simple to the property so sold, and shall apply the proceeds of such sale, or so much thereof as is necessary, to the extinguishment of the indebtedness. (Acts 1920, pp. 245, 246.)" 

Ga. Code Ann. 113-1721. "Before any sale shall be finally consummated the executor, administrator, or other trustee shall file in the office of the clerk of the superior court of the county where such administration is being had, a petition in writing addressed to the judge of the superior court of such county, setting forth fully and in detail the amount of such indebtedness, to whom same is due, when and by whom contracted, the rate of interest being paid, when such indebtedness will be due, whether such indebtedness, or any part thereof, is secured by deed, mortgage, or other lien on any property belonging to such estate, stating the amount of secured indebtedness, how secured, date same was contracted, to whom due, when due, rate of interest, and disposition of property so incumbered by security deed, mortgage, or other contractual lien, and if judgment is outstanding against the estate it shall be fully stated in the petition, with the name of the plaintiff, the amount of the judgment or judg-

ments, the date or dates of same, from what court issued, with the full amount due on such judgment or judgments. (Acts 1920, pp. 245, 247.)" Ga. Code Ann. 113-1722. "In all respects other than as provided in the two preceding sections all sales shall be made as provided in sections 49-203 and 49-204, relating to sales for reinvestment by guardians; all such sales to be approved and confirmed by the judge of the superior court by appropriate order, and the entire proceedings to be recorded on the minutes of the superior court, and properly indexed. (Acts 1920, pp. 245, 247.)" Ga. Code Ann. 113-1723.

On November 29, 1939, the Supreme Court of Georgia, in construing these Code sections, held that they provide the exclusive and not a cumulative remedy for the sale of land devised with the requirement that it be held until the beneficiaries reach the age of 21 years. Mutual Benefit Life Ins. Co. v. 

Wilson (1939), 189 Ga. 344, 6 S. E. 2d 716. 

See also section 272 of this supplement. "A sale of land by administrators under an order by the court of ordinary authorizing such sale would not be enjoined where petition for injunction failed to allege facts to negative the availability to petitioner of the statutory remedy afforded under statutes relating to claims and sales by administrators or other trustees. Code 1933, 88 37-120, 37-1211, 113-1801 to 113-1804." 

Hall v. Findley (1939), 188 Ga. 487, 4 S. E. 2d 211 (1). "Where, after due notice, leave has been regularly granted by the court of ordinary to an administrator to sell realty of a decedent, equity will not restrain the sale by injunction at the instance of an heir on account of reasons which could have been as readily urged on a caveat to the application for leave to sell." Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 696, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

Laws 1920, pp. 245247, 88 1, 2; Code 1933, § 113-1706." Mutual Benefit Life Ins. Co. v.
