The public policy of this state pertaining to sales by administrators is fixed by Code §§ 113-1706 and 113-1707, and all such sales must be public and in the manner prescribed by law. An agreement by an administratrix to make a conveyance upon stipulated terms is contrary to public policy and unenforceable. Cummings v. Johnson (1963), 218 Ga. 557, 562 (5), 129 S. E. 2d 762.

While administrator may withdraw property from sale when all bids are grossly inadequate, where auctioneer at such sale actually knocks off property to bidder, the sale is completed, and specific performance will lie to compel conveyance of realty so disposed of. Smith v. Tippins (1950), 207 Ga. 262, 61 S. E. 2d 138. 

See also section 270 of this supplement. 

§ 273. Claims at Administrators' Sales.-"Claim is a cumulative remedy, and a person claiming title to property advertised for sale by an administrator may file a claim with the ordinary or sue in trover." Godwin v. Mitchell (1939), 60 Ga. App. 713, 4 S. E. 2d 678 (4).

An administrator cannot sell property as that of the estate where such property is held adversely to the estate by a third person, but he must first recover possession. However, where, as here, there is a conflict in the material evidence of whether or not the property was held adversely, it is reversible error to direct a verdict. Livingston v. Livingston (1954) 210 Ga. 

607, 82 S. E. 2d 1. § 274 Sales by Attorneys in Fact.-"Where, by the terms of a will creating a trust estate for named beneficiaries, the executor-trustees are empowered and directed to invest, reinvest, sell, lease, or transfer any of the property of the estate upon such terms as to them seem best, at public or private sale, without any order of any court and without reporting to any court, the power granted by the will, not having expressly included the right of the executor-trustees to encumber real property of the estate by a long-term option to purchase, will ordinarily not be enlarged to include such right." Adler v. Adler (1961), 216 

Ga. 553 (1), 118 S. E. 2d 456. 

§ 275.-Completing Sales Where Bonds for Title Given.-Acts 1958, page 

668, amended Code § 113-1601, relating to the application by a holder of a bond to make title to land, by striking said code section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "113-1601. If an intestate, or a testator whose executor is not authorized by the terms of the will, during his life, shall execute a bond to make title to land, or a contract for the sale of land, and die without making title or fulfilling the terms of the contract for the sale of land, the holder of such bond for title, or of the contract for the sale of land, after having complied with the conditions or obligations therein, may apply to the ordinary having jurisdiction over the estate for an order requiring the administrator or the executor to make title according to the terms of the bond for title, or of the contract, and in all cases attaching to his petition for such an order a copy of the bond or of the contract." 

Acts, 1958, pages 668, 669, and Acts 1959, pages 140-141, amended Code § 113-1602, relating to the notice and procedure for obtaining an order requiring an administrator or executor to make title pursuant to the terms of a bond for title, which said code section, as amended, is as follows: "113-1602. Ten days' notice shall be given in writing to the administrator or executor and notices shall be given to the heirs at law of said deceased, unless waived, by publication in the news-

paper publishing the legal advertisements of the county once a week for four (4) weeks. If no objection is filed, and the ordinary is satisfied of the truth of the allegations in the petition, the order shall be granted. When objections in writing are filed in the office of said ordinary, it shall be the duty of the ordinary to hear evidence as to the fact whether the conditions of said bond or contract for the sale of land have been complied with by the payment of the purchase money or not, and to grant an order requiring said title to be made or not, as he may think the principles of justice may require; and either party, being dissatisfied with the decision, may appeal to the superior court upon the same terms as appeals are granted in other cases.'

Acts 1958, page 669, amended Code § 113-1603, relating to applications of heirs at law of a deceased vendee for an order requiring title to be made pursuant to a bond for title, which said code section as amended is as follows: "113-1603. If the vendee shall die, having possession under a bond for title, or under a contract for the purchase and sale of land, or having paid the purchase money for land, the ordinary of the county having jurisdiction of the estate, upon a similar application by any one of the heirs at law of the vendee, and on notice to the vendor, as provided in the foregoing section, may order the title to be made to the heirs at law of the deceased, unless by the terms of a will the title should vest otherwise. The making of such a title, however, shall not prevent such lands from being assets in the hands of the administrator or executor for the payment of debts." 

Acts 1958, pages 669, 670, amended Code § 113-1605, providing for the taxing of costs in an application for an order for the making of title, by making contracts for the sale of land also applicable.

"An administrator, who is an heir at law of his intestate, and as such has an interest in the property sold, may purchase at the sale of the property of the estate, provided he is guilty of no fraud, and the property is exposed for sale in the ordinary mode and under circumstances to command the best price.'

§ 282.-Persons Entitled to Year's Support.-Farmers Bank of Tifton v. 

Williams (1939), 188 Ga. 789, 5 S. E. 2d 195; Chance v. Chance (1939), 60 Ga. 

App. 889, 5 S. E. 2d 399; Clark v. Clark (1940), 62 Ga. App. 738, 9 S. E. 2d 

710; Mashburn v. Mashburn (1941), 64 Ga. App. 388, 13 S. E. 2d 190; Pardue 

Medicine Co. v. Pardue (1942), 194 Ga. 516, 22 S. E. 2d 143; Harris v. Mandeville (1943), 195 Ga. 251, 24 S. E. 2d 23; Pierce v. Harrison (1945), 199 Ga. 

197, 33 S. E. 2d 680; Saxon v. Aycock (1945), 72 Ga. App. 728, 34 S. E. 2d 914; 

McCommons v. Reid (1946), 201 Ga. 500, 40 S. E. 2d 73; Cox v. Stowers (1948), 204 Ga. 595, 50 S. E. 2d 339; Diggs v. Diggs (1955), 91 Ga. App. 634, 86 

S. E. 2d 639.

A year's support is a favorite of the law, and it is the policy of the law to provide an immediate and effectual means of support of the widow and children for such time, and the courts should in all proper ways forward and carry out this policy. The provision for a year's support out of the estate of a decedent is an anomaly dictated solely by a very humanitarian public policy, and its administration this public policy should not be overlooked or disregarded in any instance. Its provisions are highly beneficial. The courts, in passing upon cases involving the rights of the beneficiaries under such statutes, should keep in mind the beneficial and benevolent purposes of the law and should jealously protect rights accruing thereunder. The ends to be obtained under the act

are not to be encumbered with technicalities; and provisions contained therein which, if liberally construed, might seriously impede the purposes of the act should be strictly construed. Wade v. Thompson (1958), 97 Ga. App. 675, 677, 104 S. E. 2d 250.

Widow is entitled to a year's support within three years after the death of her husband and must be filed during her widowhood and lifetime. Ga. Code 

§ 113-1002. See §§ 283 and 289 of this supplement. 

The right of a minor to a year's support is barred by the marriage or death of such minor or by the minor attaining the age of 21 years prior to filing the application. Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1034. See §§ 283, 289 of this supplement. It should also be noted that Code § 113-1002, as amended, provides that all applications for a year's support shall be filed within three years from the date of death of decedent. "Under statute requiring that on death of any person leaving a widow or a widow and minor child or children, or minor child or children only, property or money to support them for a year be set aside, where mother died survived by minor children of herself and deceased first husband, by second husband, and by minor child of herself and second husband, minor children of herself and deceased first husband were entitled to 12 months' support out of her estate. Code 1933, § 113-1002.'' Edwards v. Addison (1939), 187 Ga. 756, 2 S. E. 2d 77 (1). "Where decedent leaves a widow or minor children, or both, the family is entitled to a year's support from his estate, and widow is not deprived of such right because there are no minor children, but title to property set apart to her alone vests absolutely in her. Code 1933, §§ 113-1002, 113-1006. "In proceeding to set apart year's support to widow, the court of ordinary is a court of general jurisdiction as to such matter. Code 1933, §§ 113-1002, 113-1006." Smith v. Smith (1939), 187 Ga. 743, 2 S. E. 2d 417 (1, 2). "The right to a year's support vests in a widow and minor children, if any, immediately upon the death of the husband. Code 1933, § 113-1002. "Where surviving widow was given a life estate under her husband's will, the widow, if she had so desired, would have been entitled to a year's support, notwithstanding that she was given the life estate. Code 1933, § 113-1002. "The right of a surviving widow to a year's support is statutory and did not exist at common law. Code 1933, § 113-1002.'' McDaniel v. Kelley (1939), 61 Ga. App. 105, 5 S. E. 2d 672 (1, 2, 4). "The statute providing for a year's support for widow and minor children of deceased and fixing its priority is to be construed liberally in favor of the defendants. Ga. Code Ann. § 113-1002.'' Rimes v. Graham (1945), 199 Ga. 

406, 34 S. E. 2d 443 (2). "Upon the death of any person, testate or intestate, leaving an estate, solvent or insolvent, his widow and minor children are entitled to a year's support. 

Code, § 113-1002. And, since the provision is made for a class as a whole, and not for the benefit of one or some of the class, any amount set apart under the provision therefore inures to the benefit of the class named in the statute." 

Ennis v. Ennis (1951), 207 Ga. 665, 63 S. E. 2d 887. "When year's support has been set aside from a deceased's estate to his widow only, year's support may be awarded thereafter to a minor child of the deceased.'' Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 125 S. E. 2d 694.

"The Georgia law without doubt permits, and in some cases requires, separate portions of the estate to be set aside as year's support to the widow and to children of the deceased." Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694. "In order for minor children to take an interest in property set apart as a year's support, it should in some manner appear in the application that it is made in their behalf; and where it affirmatively appears that the application was made by the widow, and that the minor children were not referred to therein by name or otherwise, they take no interest in the property set apart." 

Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694.

In every year's support case the question of whether the applicant is the deceased's widow is involved. A caveat filed by parties interested in the estate may raise that issue. When that issue is not raised and in the year's support proceedings all of the property of the estate is set apart to the applicant, no administration of the deceased's estate is necessary. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 25, 120 S. E. 2d 874.

On a caveat to a year's support where the evidence was conflicting as to the marriage of the parties, it was error to direct a verdict for the applicant. 

Hosley v. Ridley (1959), 100 Ga. App. 752, 112 S. E. 2d 304. 

Where divorced parent who has been paying alimony for support of minor child dies, and it is provided that such alimony payments will continue to be paid from his estate, the child is not entitled to year's support. Riggs v. 

Prather (1952), 86 Ga. App. 178, 71 S. E. 2d 109.

Taxes and tax liens inferior to year's support. Acts 1939, page 236; Ga. 

Code Ann. 113-1002. 

See section 288 of this supplement. 

§ 283.-Application for Year's Support.-Acts 1953, page 453 (having been codified as a part of Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1002), provided that all applications for a year's support from the estate of the decedent had to be filed within seven years from the date of the death of such decedent. The amendments of 1958 and 1959 (Acts 1958, pages 665, 666; Acts 1959, pages 138-140) to Code § 113-1002 provide that such application must be filed within three years. However, the Acts of 1958 and 1959, qualified the right of a widow to have a year's support set aside to her. The law, as it now stands, being based upon Acts 1959, pages 138-140, and being the last sentences of Code § 113-1002, is as follows: "All applications for a year's support from the estate of a decedent shall be filed within three years from the date of [the death of] such deceased, and in addition thereto, application for a year's support by a widow, or for the benefit of a widow, must be made and filed during her widowhood and during her lifetime, and not otherwise. Provided, however, that the application for a year's support for any person who was entitled thereto on or before March 3, 1953, or who subsequently became entitled thereto, may be filed at any time within three years from the effective date of this Act." The effective date being March 10, 1959, the date the same was approved by the governor. 

It should be noted that Acts 1958, page 673, repealed Acts 1955, page 626, codified as Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1033, which provided that the right of a widow to a year's support was barred by her death, remarriage, and twelve months from the death of her husband, but added to Code § 113-1002 a similar provisions as above quoted, which provisions was enacted by the 

1959 Act.

The effect of the three-year statute of limitations in making application for a year's support by a widow is to withdraw such applications from the operation of Code § 3-704, relating to the statute of limitations as to statutory rights. And the case of Nixon v. Nixon (1943), 69 Ga. App. 667, 26 S. E. 2d 

722, is apparently no longer applicable insofar as it relates to a 20-year statute of limitations.

It is also apparent that the rule in Smith Sanders (1951), 208 Ga. 405, 67 

S. E. 2d 229; s. c. (1951) 84 Ga. App. 785, 67 S. E. 2d 735, to the effect that the legal representative of a widow can apply for and have set aside a year's support for her after her death is no longer applicable in view of the present law that application by a widow for a year's support, or for the benefit of a widow, must be made and filed during her widowhood and during her lifetime. 

Acts 1958, page 378, amended Acts 1955, page 638, codified as Ga. Code Ann. § 113-1034, relating to when a right to a year's support is barred by a minor, which said as amended is as follows: "The right of a minor to a year's support from the estate of a deceased parent shall be barred by the marriage or death of said minor or by said minor's attaining the age of 21 years, prior to the filing of the application for such year's support.” "A widow's right to a year's support 'accrues' upon the death of the husband and not upon the qualification of the legal representative of the estate." 

Nixon v. Nixon (1943), 69 Ga. App. 667, 26 S. E. 2d 722 (2, 3).

It is immaterial who makes application for a year's support. The notice required to be given to the representative of the estate, if there is one, in Code § 113-1002, is not spelled out as to how the notice is to be given, by whom or the time to be given, but notice of some kind or character must be given. Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524, 526 (1), 123 S. E. 2d 128. "We know of no provisions of law that require service or notice of the widow's application for a year's support to be had on the devisees in the husband's will.' Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 357, 110 S. E. 2d 762. An executor is not only the personal representative of the decedent, but occupies the position of a trustee for the legatees and devisees. The required notice of an application for a year's support and the return of the appraisers is not for the benefit of the widow, but for the benefit of persons whose interest would be affected by the judgment. Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524, 527, 123 S. E. 2d 728. "Where there are two executrices of an estate, notice of an application for a year's support to one executrix who is the applicant in her individual capacity is not notice to the coexecutrix." Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524 (1), 123 S. E. 2d 728. "It is true that, when a widow makes application for the benefit of herself and her minor children, the year's support set aside inures to the benefit of the widow and children, and not the widow alone." Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694.

An agreement by a widow to marshall all the assets of an estate together and use whatever property necessary to support her minor children until they became self-supporting could only be accomplished by setting aside a year's support to such children since after the payment of debts the estate became subject to distribution. White v. Wright (1955), 211 Ga. 556, 87 S. E. 2d 394.

The widow, by filing an application seeking the declaration that no administration was necessary on the estate of the deceased, does not thereby revest title to the property set apart in the estate of the deceased. Strain v. Monk (1956), 212 Ga. 194, 91 S. E. 2d 505. "A court of equity in a direct proceeding has jurisdiction to set aside a judgment of the court of ordinary awarding a year's support on the ground that the judgment is void for want of service or notice on the complaining parties where the necessary parties to the judgment in the court of ordinary are before the court." Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524 (1), 123 

S. E. 2d 728.

Where all of the assets of an estate are set aside to the widow as a year's support, no administration of the deceased's estate is necessary. Taylor v. 

Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 24, 120 S. E. 2d 874. 

§ 284.-Jurisdiction and Procedure.-Hill v. Hill (1938), 58 Ga. App. 179, 

198 S. E. 279; Smith v. Smith (1939), 187 Ga. 743, 2 S. E. 2d 417; Farmers 

Bank of Tifton v. Williams (1939), 188 Ga. 789, 5 S. E. 2d 195; Jones v. 

Federal Land Bank of Columbia, S. C. (1939), 189 Ga. 419, 6 S. E. 2d 52; 

Whitfield v. Maddox (1940), 189 Ga. 870, 8 S. E. 2d 57; Lunsford v. Kersey (1941), 191 Ga. 738, 13 S. E. 2d 803; Matthews v. Matthews (1941), 64 Ga. 

App. 580, 13 S. E. 2d 843; Rogers v. Woods (1941), 66 Ga. App. 195, 17 S. E. 

2d 283; Cannon v. Whiddon (1942), 194 Ga. 417, 21 S. E. 2d 850. "The provision for a plat in statute requiring appraisers to set apart a year's support to surviving spouse is merely directory and if a plat is not essential to full and accurate description, and land is otherwise described completely and accurately, it will be substantial compliance with the statute. 

Code 1933, § 113-1005."' Chapman v. Chapman (1939), 59 Ga. App. 602, 1 S. E. 2d 697 (3). "Appraisers' return, setting apart year's support to decedent's widow, is prima facie correct." Chance v. Chance (1939), 60 Ga. App. 889, 5 S. E. 2d 

399 (11); Touchton v. Mock (1955), 91 Ga. App. 689, 86 S. E. 2d 699.

The necessity of urging an equitable claim to an estate in the superior court rather than the court of ordinary where it is claimed that there has been a virtual adoption does not apply to cases where a minor child makes application for a year's support from the estate of his alleged deceased father on the ground that he is a legitimate offspring of the deceased. Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (a), 100 S. E. 2d 594. "The court of ordinary has no jurisdiction to determine conflicting claims between widow and persons claiming under wills of third persons respecting title to realty, and hence third persons would not be bound by procedure on widow's application for year's support, as respects subsequent claim of title by widow or her assignees.'' Smith v. Pitchford (1939), 189 Ga. 307, 5 S. E. 

2d 766 (3).

A court of ordinary has no jurisdiction to pass upon conflicting claims of title on the hearing of an application for a year's support. Pioneer Investments, Inc. v. Adrine (1958), 97 Ga. App. 520, 524, 103 S. E. 2d 686. "The court of ordinary does not have jurisdiction to try and determine title to property, either real or personal; and, upon appeal to the superior court of a caveat to a year's support, the jurisdiction of that court was no broader or greater than that of the court appealed from. Consequently, the judge of the

superior court did not err in excluding from the jury's consideration the question of whether or not title to funds in a bank account was in the widow or in the estate." Hartsfield v. Hartsfield (1953), 87 Ga. App. 707, 75 S. E. 2d 276. "The court of ordinary had plenary control over the judgment setting apart the year's support during the term at which it was entered and, in the exercise of a sound discretion could vacate such judgment as the ends of justice might require, and the judge of the superior court, on the appeal, was invested with the same authority." Hall v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1952), 87 Ga. App. 

142, 73 S. E. 2d 252. "The statutory requirement that appraisers appointed to set apart a year's support to widow shall file with their return a plat is not 'mandatory.''' 

Wall v. Griffith (1941), 193 Ga. 11, 17 S. E. 2d 57 (3).

The legislature in 1947 provided that appraisers appointed to set apart a year's support may serve in the county where the administration is pending, or where the deceased resided, or in any other county. Acts 1947, page 866; 

Ga. Code Ann. 113-1002.1.

An administrator, though a proper party, is not a necessary party to a proceeding to set aside a year's support. Holland v. Froklis (1954), 89 Ga. App. 

768, 81 S. E. 2d 317. 

See section 289 of this Supplement.

In certiorari proceedings to review an order of the court of ordinary allowing a year's support to a child born out of wedlock, whose parents subsequently married, making the child legitimate, and to correct errors in said order, the issues being ones of law only, the Court of Appeals, and not the Supreme Court, has jurisdiction to review the exception to the order of the trial court dismissing the petition for certiorari. Miller v. Miller (1957), 213 Ga. 435, 99 

S. E. 2d 129. See Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469, 100 S. E. 2d 594. 

§ 285.-Same-Caveat-Judgment.-Howell v. Howell (1940), 190 Ga. 371, 9 

S. E. 2d 149; Montgomery v. Paradise (1940), 62 Ga. App. 655, 9 S. E. 2d 196; 

Rogers v. Woods (1941), 66 Ga. App. 195, 17 S. E. 2d 283; Anderson v. Caldwell (1942), 66 Ga. App. 703, 19 S. E. 2d 202; Tilley v. King (1942), 193 Ga. 

602, 19 S. E. 2d 281; Cannon v. Whiddon (1942), 194 Ga. 417, 21 S. E. 2d 850; 

Madden v. Madden (1945), 72 Ga. App. 300, 33 S. E. 2d 735; Bowen v. Bowen (1946), 200 Ga. 572, 37 S. E. 2d 797; Bowman v. Bowman (1949), 79 Ga. App. 

240, 53 S. E. 2d 244; Daniel v. Daniel (1953), 87 Ga. App. 325, 73 S. E. 2d 591.

Only heirs, their privies, and creditors may contest with a widow and minor children their right to a year's support out of the estate of the deceased husband and father. Gross v. Shankle (1958), 97 Ga. App. 631, 634, 104 S. E. 

2d 145; Wade v. Thompson (1958), 97 Ga. App. 675, 677, 104 S. E. 2d 250.

Such person must be actually concerned in the legal administration of the assets of the estate. Wade v. Thompson (1958), 97 Ga. App. 675, 677, 104 S. E. 

2d 250.

A tort claimant whose suit is not filed on his claim is not entitled to file a caveat to a year's support. Gross v. Shankle (1958), 97 Ga. App. 631, 634, 104 S. E. 2d 145.

Taxes are not debts for which an action at law or equity will lie, and a tax commissioner, not being, with respect to the collection of taxes, a creditor of an estate, concerned in the legal administration of the assets thereof, is not

entitled in law to file a caveat to the return of appraisers in a year's support proceedings. Wade v. Thompson (1958), 97 Ga. App. 675, 104 S. E. 2d 250. 

"A judgment setting apart a year's support for widow and minor children does not generally amount to an adjudication that the property set apart existed and was the property of deceased." Zeagler v. Zeagler (1940), 190 

Ga. 220, 9 S. E. 2d 263 (5).

Where property is set aside to a widow as a year's support, she acquires such title in the property as her deceased husband had, and she acquires no greater title by reason of a judgment of a court of ordinary setting such property apart to her as a year's support. Pioneer Investments, Inc. v. Adrine (1958), 97 Ga. App. 520, 524, 103 S. E. 2d 686. "A year's support for widow and minor children of decedent to be enforceable must be manifest in a judgment, since such year's support is not in existence as such until the entry of a judgment therefor." Howard v. Davis (1941), 192 Ga. 505, 15 S. E. 2d 865 (4). "Widow has burden of proof to show that she is entitled to have property set apart as a year's support out of her deceased husband's estate." McKemie v. McKemie (1947), 76 Ga. App. 212, 45 S. E. 2d 456.

Where sufficient cause is shown, a court of equity may set aside a judgment rendered by the court of ordinary in a year's support proceeding and such a proceeding is not a collateral attack upon the year's support judgment. Hogg v. Hogg (1950), 206 Ga. 691, 58 S. E. 2d 403. "For sufficient cause, and with proper parties, a court of equity has jurisdiction to set aside a judgment rendered by the court of ordinary in a year's support proceeding." Nuckolls v. Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 35, 37, 114 S. E. 

2d 427. "The attack in the present case on the year's support proceeding, upon which it is alleged the defendant relies for her claim of title, is not a collateral, but is a direct attack. If the judgment in the year's support proceeding is void for want of title in the defendant's husband, as alleged, such judgment may be attacked in any court at any time." Nuckolls v. Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 

35, 37, 114 S. E. 2d 427. "A court of equity in a direct proceeding has jurisdiction to set aside a judgment of the court of ordinary awarding a year's support on the ground that the judgment is void for want of service or notice on the complaining parties where the necessary parties to the judgment in the court of ordinary are before the court." Watkins v. Donalson (1962), 217 Ga. 524 (1), 123 

S. E. 2d 728. A judgment of a court of ordinary awarding a year's support cannot be collaterally attacked except for invalidity appearing on its face. Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 531 (1), 109 S. E. 2d 289.

Even though the award of a year's support cannot be collaterally attacked except for invalidity appearing on the face of the record, it may be attacked in a court of equity for fraud. Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 

531, 532, 109 S. E. 2d 289. "While lapse of time between the death of a husband and the application by his widow for a year's support, during which time she lived upon the land and made use of the personalty of her deceased husband, may furnish a good ground to defeat the application before the ordinary, yet when the final judg-

ment of that court has been rendered in the case, it is too late to attack it, especially before another court, except for causes apparent upon the face of the record, showing a want of jurisdiction either of the person or subjectmatter." Raper v. Smith (1960), 216 Ga. 326, 116 S. E. 2d 554, reversing 101 

Ga. App. 557, 115 S. E. 2d 234, conformed to 102 Ga. App. 669, 117 S. E. 2d 261. "A judgment approving the return of commissioners setting aside a year's support, where all the proceedings are regular, cannot be attacked as fraudulent because interested parties could have successfully resisted the judgment had they interposed timely objection." Raper v. Smith (1960), 216 Ga. 326, 116 S. E. 2d 554, reversing 101 Ga. App. 557, 115 S. E. 2d 234, conformed to 

102 Ga. App. 669, 117 S. E. 2d 261.

Where no objections are filed to the return of the appraisers setting aside a year's support for the widow and minor children out of the estate of the testator, and the return is filed and becomes final, the court of ordinary, had no authority to modify the return on motion of a creditor. Raper v. Smith (1960), 216 Ga. 326, 116 S. E. 2d 554, reversing 101 Ga. App. 557, 115 S. E. 2d 

234, conformed to 102 Ga. App. 669, 117 S. E. 2d 261.

A judgment approving the return of commissioners setting aside a year's support, where all the proceedings are regular, cannot be attacked as fraudulent because interested parties could have successfully resisted the judgment had they interposed timely objection. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 25, 120 S. E. 2d 874. 

A tract of land was set apart to a widow by the court of ordinary and the widow later died intestate and there was no administration on her estate, an order having been entered by the court of ordinary that no administration was necessary. A petition to set aside the judgment awarding the year's support was held not to state a cause of action on the ground that to set aside a judgment the party in whose favor it was rendered, or if dead, his legal representative is the necessary party, there being no administration upon the estate of such deceased widow and she having no legal representative to be made a party. Warr v. Miller (1963), 218 Ga. 691, 130 S. E. 2d 132. "It is not alleged that the petitioners did not have actual knowledge of the year's support proceedings, and no reason is set forth why they could not have urged in the court of ordinary any objection that they had to the granting of a year's support." Hubbard v. Hubbard (1963), 218 Ga. 617 (1), 129 S. E. 2d 862. 

Where no fraud is alleged which prevented timely objections in the court of ordinary to year's support proceedings, and the proceedings were regular and in a court having jurisdiction of the subject matter, the proceeding could not be attacked for fraud on grounds that might have been interposed by interested parties prior to the judgment. Hubbard v. Hubbard (1963), 218 Ga. 

617, 618 (1), 129 S. E. 2d 862.

In an action to quiet the plaintiff's title under a year's support award, a plea by the defendant that the widow had elected to accept a provision in her husband's will in lieu of a year's support was a collateral attack on the year's support decree and did not set forth a valid defense. Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 358, 110 S. E. 2d 762.

A demurrer that the plaintiffs' right to attack the year's support set aside to the defendant was debarred by laches, because the petition alleged that approximately six months had elapsed between entry of the judgment in the

year's support proceeding and the filing of the petition, was properly overruled. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20 (4), 120 S. E. 2d 874.

In every year's support case the question of whether the applicant is the deceased's widow is involved. A caveat filed by parties interested in the estate may raise that issue. When that issue is not raised and in the year's support proceedings all of the property of the estate is set apart to the applicant, no administration of the deceased's estate is necessary. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 25, 120 S. E. 2d 874.

On a caveat to a year's support where the evidence was conflicting as to the marriage of the parties, it was error to direct a verdict for the applicant. 

Hosley v. Ridley (1959), 100 Ga. App. 752, 112 S. E. 2d 304. 

In a year's support proceeding the validity of the marriage could have been attacked in the court of ordinary when the application for a year's support was made and may not be collaterally attacked on appeal to the superior court. 

Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 531, 532, 109 S. E. 2d 289.

On appeal from a court of ordinary the superior court has no greater jurisdiction than the court of ordinary. Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 

531 (1b), 109 S. E. 2d 289.

An executor is a proper party to object to year's support. 

Bank of Atlanta (1952), 85 Ga. App. 498, 69 S. E. 2d 679.

Hall v. First Nat. 

"The issue as to whether the property set aside is the property of the deceased's estate cannot be raised in the court of ordinary by a creditor's caveat which is tantamount to a claim to the property. Courts of ordinary do not have jurisdiction to try claims to or title to real property." Trusco Finance 

Co. v. Crowley (1952), 86 Ga. App. 268, 71 S. E. 2d 294.

In an equitable proceeding to vacate and set aside a judgment awarding a year's support to a minor child and her mother, the child is an indispensable party, though the marriage between the mother and the deceased was a bigamous one, so long as it has not been declared void by a court of competent jurisdiction. Flinn v. Flynn (1954), 210 Ga. 280, 79 S. E. 2d 534. "Every presumption is in favor of the judgment of an ordinarily setting apart a year's support, and it cannot be collaterally attacked except where the record shows a want of jurisdictional facts." Strain v. Monk (1956), 212 

Ga. 194, 91 S. E. 2d 505.

A court of ordinary has no jurisdiction to pass upon conflicting claims of title on the hearing of an application for a year's support. Pioneer Investments, Inc. v. Adrine (1958) 97 Ga. App. 520, 524, 103 S. E. 2d 686.

An ordinary cannot try title as between a widow and claimants in a year's support proceeding. Nuckolls v. Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 35, 37, 114 S. E. 2d 427.

The necessity of urging an equitable claim to an estate in the superior court rather than the court of ordinary where it is claimed that there has been a virtual adoption does not apply to cases where a minor child makes application for a year's support from the estate of his alleged deceased father on the ground that he is a legitimate offspring of the deceased. Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (a), 100 S. E. 2d 594.

Where a party alleges he is entitled to share in the deceased's estate because the latter breached a contract to adopt him, he is not an heir or creditor of

the deceased and cannot file a caveat objecting to a year's support being set apart out of the deceased's estate. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20 (3), 120 S. E. 2d 874.

"Where the title to property was not vested in a decedent at the time of his death, it can not be set apart as a year's support for his widow and minor children, so as to vest title in them." Kenner v. Kenner (1958), 214 Ga. 381 (2), 104 S. E. 2d 896. "It is true as a matter of law that a year's support for a widow can be set apart to her only from the estate of her deceased husband; and if property included therein does not as a matter of fact constitute a part of his estate, the judgment of the court of ordinary simply will not attach to such property, but will be void as applied thereto." Nuckolls v. Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 35, 36, 114 S. E. 2d 427. Gilbert v. Fowler (1951), 207 Ga. 720, 64 S. E. 2d 55.

Property in which the grantee had an equity at the time of his death may be set aside for year's support of the grantee's wife, though the estate is insolvent and the purchase price has not been paid. Harry v. Griffin (1953), 210 Ga. 133, 78 S. E. 2d 37.

A widow is not entitled to year's support out of property held by her husband as trustee of an implied trust raised by his fraud in inducing another with whom he entered a bigamous marriage to purchase such property and take a deed out in both their names. Bell v. Bell (1954), 210 Ga. 295, 79 

S. E. 2d 524.

Since widow could acquire no greater title to property set aside to her as a year's support than her deceased husband had, and where deceased husband's title was subject to the paramount title of an assignee of a duly recorded conditional sales contract, claimants who purchased the property from the widow acquired only such title as the widow and her deceased husband had, and the claimants' right to the property was subject to the outstanding conditional sales contract of which they had constructive notice. Pioneer Investments, Inc. (1958), 97 Ga. App. 520, 103 S. E. 2d 686.

When property is set apart to a widow as a year's support, she receives just such title as her deceased husband had, and acquires no greater title by reason of the setting apart to her. Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 358, 110 

S. E. 2d 762.

"The Georgia law without doubt permits, and in some cases requires, separate portions of the estate to be set aside as year's support to the widow and to children of the deceased." Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694.

Wade v. Thompson (1958), 97 Ga. App. 675, 104 S. E. 2d 250. 

Since widow could acquire no greater title to property set aside to her as a year's support than her deceased husband had, and where her deceased husband's title was subject to the paramount title of an assignee of a duly recorded conditional sales contract, claimants who purchased the property from the widow acquired only such title as the widow and her deceased husband had, and the claimants' right to the property was subject to the outstanding conditional sales contract of which they had constructive notice. § 289.-How Right Defeated-Lanier v. Lanier (1939), 61 Ga. App. 123, 5

"Where, during the life of her husband, the wife separates from him and assumes a relationship of separation, she is to all intents and purposes sui juris, and may institute suit for alimony if she so elects; and where permanent alimony is either granted by judgment of a court, or the alimony suit is settled by contract between the parties, whereby she accepts money or property in settlement of the claim for permanent alimony, and such contract is not annulled by subsequent cohabitation and reconciliation, under applicable law it bars her of her rights of dower and year's support from her husband's estate, and she ceases to have any further interest in his estate in her right as wife." McKie v. McKie (1957), 213 Ga. 582 (1), 100 So. 2d 580.

In 1955, the legislature enacted several provisions relative to barring year's support. One of these was Acts 1955, page 626, Ga. 

Code Ann. § 113-1033, which provided: "The right of a widow to a year's support from the estate of her deceased husband shall be barred by the death of said widow, or by the subsequent remarriage of said widow, prior to the setting apart of such year's support. 

The right of a widow to a year's support from the estate of a decedent shall be barred by the death of said widow after 12 months from the date of the death of said decedent and prior to the filing of the application for such year's support." However, Acts 1958, page 673, repealed Acts 1955, page 626, codified as Ga. Code Ann. § 113-1033, which provided that the right of a widow to a year's support was barred by her death, remarriage, and twelve months. from the death of her husband. But Acts 1958, pages 665, 666, in amending Code § 113-1002, added to the end of the section the following: "All applications for a year's support from the estate of a descendant [decedent] shall be filed within three years from the date of the death of such deceased, if application for a year's support by a widow or for the benefit of a widow shall be made and filed during her widowhood and during her lifetime, and not otherwise." Acts 1959, pages 138-140, again amended Code § 113-1002, providing that: "All applications for a year's support from the estate of a decedent shall be filed within three years from the date [of death] of such deceased, and in addition thereto, ap-

plication for a year's support by a widow, or for the benefit of a widow, must be made and filed during her widowhood and during her lifetime, and not otherwise. Provided, however, that the application for a year's support for any person who was entitled thereto on or before March 3, 1953, or who subsequently became entitled thereto, may be filed at any time within three years from the effective date of this Act." (This Act was approved by the governor on March 10, 1959.)

Prior to these acts a widow's right to a year's support survived her death, and as was pointed out in Smith v. Sanders (1951), 208 

Ga. 405, 67 S. E. 2d 229, interpreting the language of Ga. Code Ann. 

113-1002, the widow's legal representative could apply for and have a year's support set apart to her estate in as ample, full, and complete a manner as a widow could if she were in life. Another provision relating to the barring of year's support was that of Acts 1955, p. 638, set forth in the Ga. Code Ann, as follows: "113-1034. Year's support of minor barred by death or majority. 

The right of a minor to a year's support from the estate of a deceased parent shall be barred by the death of said minor, or by said minor's attaining the age of 21 years, prior to the filing of the application for such year's support. (Acts 1955, pp. 638, 639.)" 

Acts 1958, page 378, amended Acts 1955, page 638, codified as Ga. Code Ann. § 113-1034, relating to when a right to a year's support is barred by a minor, which said as amended is as follows: "The right of a minor to a year's support from the estate of a deceased parent shall be barred by the marriage or death of said minor or by said minor's attaining the age of 21 years, prior to the filing of the application for such year's support. 

Further, by Acts 1955, p. 731, the Legislature enacted the following provisions: "113-1035. Year's support of widow or minor barred by sale by administrator or executor.-The right of a widow or minor child to a year's support from the estate of a decedent shall be barred by a sale or conveyance made under authority of a court of competent jurisdiction or under power in a will, by an administrator or executor of such estate prior to the setting apart of such year's support: Provided, however, that such sale or conveyance shall bar the year's support and the rights thereto only as to the property sold or conveyed. (Acts 1955, pp. 

731, 732.)" 

§ 290.-Election in Lieu of Year's Support.-Rogers v. Woods (1940), 63 Ga. 

App. 195, 10 S. E. 2d 404; Matthews v. Matthews (1941), 64 Ga. App. 580, 13 

S. E. 2d 843; Saxon v. Aycock (1945), 72 Ga. App. 728, 34 S. E. 2d 914; 

Walraven v. Walraven (1948), 76 Ga. App. 713, 47 S. E. 2d 148.

"In order to put widow to election between provisions made in her favor in will and her right to year's support under statute, provision in will in her favor must be either expressly made in lieu of year's support, or testator's intention to that effect must be deduced by clear implication from will, founded on fact that claim of year's support would be inconsistent with will or so repugnant to its provisions as necessarily to defeat them. Code 1933, §§ 31110 (2), 113-1002, 113-1007." Clark v. Clark (1940), 62 Ga. App. 738, 9 S. E. 

2d 710 (2). "Testator may make provision by will for his wife in lieu of dower and year's support.

A testator may by his will make provision for his wife in lieu of a year's support and dower. And where, the testator made certain bequests to his wife, but expressly provided that they were in lieu of a year's support and dower and she applied for and received both from his estate, she, by such an election, completely excluded herself from his will. Therefore, the testator's widow by electing not to take under the will was in no position to invoke the provision of Code § 113-107 which prohibits a testator from devising more than one-third of his estate to any charitable use to the exclusion of his wife, child or the descendants of a child; and this is especially true, since an invocation of that section could not possibly result in any benefit to her after she had taken both a year's support and dower from his estate which are expressly declared to be in lieu of any provision his will made for her. Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 

Ga. 180, 184 (2), 127 S. E. 2d 19. "In order for the relinquishment of a widow's right to claim a year's support to be binding on her, it must be made with knowledge of her rights and of the condition of the estate." Hubbard v. Hubbard (1963), 218 Ga. 617 (2), 129 S. E. 2d 862.

An election by the widow to take a legacy in lieu of a year's support, in ignorance of the condition of the estate or of any fact material to her interest, will not bar her right to re-elect and take a year's support where the rights of third persons are not prejudiced. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 52, 129 S. E. 2d 82.

Where a husband makes provision in his will in lieu of a year's support to which his widow is entitled, the election of the widow to take such year's support is governed by the same rules which regulate her election of dower and an election by the widow to take a child's part in realty, in ignorance of the condition of the estate or of any fact material to her interest, does not bar her right to dower, unless the rights of third persons, acting bona fide upon her election, are disturbed or prejudiced. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 

52, 53, 129 S. E. 2d 82.

Where a widow contended that she accepted a legacy under her husband's will thirty-one days after the death of her husband in ignorance of her rights and in ignorance of material facts, particularly as to the condition of the estate and the value of bonds held by the executors along with the estate, did not preclude her from later claiming a year's support by reason of the fact that she had accepted a legacy provided in her husband's will in lieu of dower and year's support. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 52, 129 S. E. 2d 82. "A widow's right to year's support and dower is barred by her acceptance of provision made for her in lieu of dower and such support by her deceased husband's will. Ga. Code Ann. §§ 31-110, 113-1007." Bowen v. Bowen (1946), 200 Ga. 572, 37 S. E. 2d 797 (1, 2).

In an action to quiet the plaintiff's title under a year's support award, a plea by the defendant that the widow had elected to accept a provision in her husband's will in lieu of a year's support was a collateral attack on the year's support decree and did not set forth a valid defense. Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 358, 110 S. E. 2d 762.
