"It is true as a matter of law that a year's support for a widow can be set apart to her only from the estate of her deceased husband; and if property included therein does not as a matter of fact constitute a part of his estate, the judgment of the court of ordinary simply will not attach to such property, but will be void as applied thereto.'' Nuckolls v. Merritt (1960), 216 Ga. 35, 36, 114 S. E. 2d 427.

When the property of the deceased is set apart as a year's support to the applicant, it passes out of the estate, and cannot be recovered by the personal representative. Taylor v. Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 24, 120 S. E. 2d 874. "It is true that, when a widow makes application for the benefit of herself and her minor children, the year's support set aside inures to the benefit of

the widow and children, and not the widow alone." Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694. "In order for minor children to take an interest in property set apart as a year's support, it should in some manner appear in the application that it is made in their behalf; and where it affirmatively appears that the application was made by the widow, and that the minor children were not referred to therein by name or otherwise, they take no interest in the property set apart." 

Gale v. Stewart (1962), 105 Ga. App. 767, 768, 125 S. E. 2d 694. "Where property is set apart as a year's support for the benefit of the widow alone, she shall thereafter own the same in fee, without restriction as to use, incumbrance, or disposition." Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. 

App. 531, 532, 109 S. E. 2d 289. "Where land has been set apart as a statutory year's support for decedent's surviving wife and minor children, title to the land vests in wife and children subject to power of wife alone to convey in fee simple or to mortgage the land for support of herself and the minor children. Code 1933, § 113-1002." 

Powell v. Porter (1939), 189 Ga. 440, 5 S. E. 2d 884 (3).

Where property is set aside to a widow as a year's support, she acquires such title in the property as her deceased husband had, and she acquires no greater title by reason of a judgment of a court of ordinary setting such property apart to her as a year's support. Pioneer Investments, Inc. v. Adrine (1958), 97 Ga. App. 520, 524, 103 S. E. 2d 686.

When property is set apart to a widow as a year's support, she receives just such title as her deceased husband had, and acquires no greater title by reason of the setting apart to her. Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 358, 110 

8. E. 2d 762. "The judgment of a court of ordinary purporting to vest title to the land of a decedent in his widow for a year's support is generally color of title on which prescription can be based.' Wanamaker v. Wanamaker (1959), 215 Ga. 

473, 475 (2), 111 S. E. 2d 94.

Where widow and children attempt to convey land set aside as year's support, conveyance being without the consent of the ordinary, said conveyance is effective only as to the widow's interest in the property. Harnesberger v. 

Davis (1952), 86 Ga. App. 41, 70 S. E. 2d 615. "A widow who obtains a year's support may not only sell, but may execute mortgage or security deed to obtain funds for such support, or for the purpose of building or repairing a dwelling for herself and such children, and irrespective of actual necessity to sell such conveyance is valid and divests children's title as heirs and their claim as beneficiaries of the year's support. 

Code 1933, §§ 113-1002, 113-1005, 113-1006." Jones v. Federal Land Bank of Columbia (1939), 189 Ga. 419, 6 S. E. 2d 52 (4). "The title to property set apart as a year's support to a widow and minor children vests absolutely in the widow and children, subject to the control and management of the widow for the benefit of herself and the minor children, with authority, before the Act of 1937, to convey or encumber not only her title but that of the minors therein, for purpose of obtaining support for herself and the children. Code 1933, § 113-1006; Laws 1937, p. 861."' Whitfield v. Maddox (1940), 189 Ga. 878, 8 S. E. 2d 54 (2).

"Where land belonging to decedent's estate is set apart as a year's support for widow and minor children, the validity of a sale by widow for purpose of such support and maintenance is not dependent upon a necessity to sell." 

Whitfield v. Maddox (1940), 189 Ga. 870, 8 S. E. 2d 57 (4).

Under an act of the legislature in 1943, if the widow to whom a year's support has been set apart for herself and children dies, an application for a conveyance or encumbrance of the property may be made by the guardian of one or more of the children. Acts 1943, page 621 (Ga. Code Ann. § 113-1026). "Where real property has been set apart as a year's support to a widow and her daughter, the daughter alone cannot maintain an action against a third person for trespass upon such property occupied jointly by them, where the only allegation in the petition as to why the action was not brought by the widow is that she 'has failed to take necessary steps to protect' the interest of the daughter. Watts v. Baldwin (1953), 209 Ga. 672, 75 S. E. 2d 1. 

When real and personal property is set apart as a year's support for the widow alone, title vests absolutely in the widow, and she may dispose of any unconsumed portion of it by will. Hiers v. Striplin (1954), 210 Ga. 293, 79 

S. E. 2d 539.

Since widow could acquire no greater title to property set aside to her as a year's support than her deceased husband had, and where her deceased husband's title was subject to the paramount title of an assignee of a duly recorded conditional sales contract, claimants who purchased the property from the widow acquired only such title as the widow and her deceased husband had, and the claimants' right to the property was subject to the outstanding conditional sales contract of which they had constructive notice. Pioneer Investments, Inc. (1958), 97 Ga. App. 520, 103 S. E. 2d 686.

Where all of the assets of an estate are set aside to the widow as a year's support, no administration of the deceased's estate is necessary. Taylor v. 

Taylor (1961), 217 Ga. 20, 24, 120 S. E. 2d 874.

In an action to quiet the plaintiff's title under a year's support award, a plea by the defendant that the widow had elected to accept a provision in her husband's will in lieu of a year's support was a collateral attack on the year's support decree and did not set forth a valid defense. Stephens v. Carter (1959), 215 Ga. 355, 358, 110 S. E. 2d 762. "If a year's support is set apart for the benefit of any person or persons in or with respect to land on which there is a recorded option to purchase or contract to sell outstanding at the time the same is so set apart, such person or persons, and any purchasers or lessees of said land after the same has been set apart, shall take said land, or any interest therein, subject to all of the rights and privileges of the grantee of said option or contract to sell, and of any assignees of said option or contract to sell, if such assignment or assignments are also recorded." Code § 113-1036. 

§ 293.-Payment of Pre-existing Debts.-Griffin v. Wood (1943), 196 Ga. 

510, 26 S. E. 2d 921; Johnson v. City of Blackshear (1943), 196 Ga. 652, 27 

S. E. 2d 316. 

§ 295.-Homestead, Dower, and Year's Support Compared.-Slade v. Barber 

(1946), 200 Ga. 405, 37 S. E. 2d 143; Jones v. Johnson (1949), 80 Ga. App. 340, 55 S. E. 2d 904.

§ 297.-Right to Dower.-Rowland v. Sumner (1946), 201 Ga. 317, 39 S. E. 

2d 655. 

§ 298.-Statutory Modifications.— 

"If a year's support is set apart for the benefit of any person or persons in or with respect to land on which there is a recorded option to purchase or contract to sell outstanding at the time the same is so set apart, such person or persons, and any purchasers or lessees of said land after the same has been set apart, shall take said land, or any interest therein, subject to all of the rights and privileges of the grantee of said option or contract to sell, and of any assignees of said option or contract to sell, if such assignment or assignments are also recorded." Code § 113-1036. 

§ 301.—The Dower Estate.-Scales v. Bellamy (1943), 196 Ga. 412, 26 S. E. 

2d 775; Futch v. Jarrard (1947), 203 Ga. 47, 45 S. E. 2d 420.

The legislature in 1943 amended Ga. Code Ann. 113-1710 by providing that rights of way and easements in dower lands may be sold. Acts 1943, page 239. "If dower is set apart for the benefit of any person in or with respect to land on which there is a recorded option to purchase or contract to sell outstanding at the time the same is so set apart, such person, and any purchasers or lessees of said land after the same has been so set apart, shall take said land, or any interest therein, subject to all of the rights and privileges of the grantee of said option or contract to sell, and of any assignees of said option or contract to sell, if such assignment or assignments are also recorded." Code § 31-111. § 303.—Election by Widow in Lieu of Dower.-"Where a man dies intestate, leaving widow and children, title to his realty vests in the children, subject only to wife's right to take a child's part or have dower assigned, and no presumption will arise that widow ever had any vested estate in fee unless it affirmatively appears that she elected to take a child's part. Code 1933, 

§§ 31-110 (3), 113-903 (3)." Jones v. Federal Land Bank of Columbia (1939), 

189 Ga. 419, 6 8. E. 2d 52 (19).

A testator may by his will make provision for his wife in lieu of a year's support and dower. And where, the testator made certain bequests to his wife, but expressly provided that they were in lieu of a year's support and dower and she applied for and received both from his estate, she, by such an election, completely excluded herself from his will. Therefore, the testator's widow by electing not to take under the will was in no position to invoke the provision of Code § 113-107 which prohibits a testator from devising more than one-third of his estate to any charitable use to the exclusion of his wife, child or the descendants of a child; and this is especially true, since an invocation of that section could not possibly result in any benefit to her after she had taken both a year's support and dower from his estate which are expressly declared to be in lieu of any provision his will made for her. Strother v. Kennedy (1962), 218 Ga. 180, 184 (2), 127 8. E. 2d 19.

"The wife of the testator is not barred by her acceptance of a bequest in the will of $5,000 where the testator neither expressly nor impliedly provides that the bequest is in lieu of dower from obtaining dower as provided by law. 

She is allowed to pay debts secured by deeds to secure debt and then have dower in the property thus freed." Fuller v. Fuller (1961), 217 Ga. 316 (3), 122 S. E. 2d 234. "Testator may make provision by will for his wife in lieu of dower and year's support. "A widow's right to year's support and dower is barred by her acceptance of provision made for her in lieu of dower and such support by her deceased husband's will. Ga. Code Ann. §§ 31-110, 113-1007." Bowen v. Bowen (1946), 200 Ga. 572, 37 S. E. 2d 797 (1, 2).

When a widow elects to take under the will rather than dower she becomes the purchaser only of the interest devised to her, including the burdens placed upon that interest. She cannot elect to take the benefits under the will and reject the burdens." Wells v. Scott (1954), 210 Ga. 756, 82 S. E. 

2d 697.

Where a husband makes provision in his will in lieu of a year's support to which his widow is entitled, the election of the widow to take such year's support is governed by the same rules which regulate her election of dower and an election by the widow to take a child's part in realty, in ignorance of the condition of the estate or of any fact material to her interest, does not bar her right to dower, unless the rights of third persons, acting bona fide upon her election, are disturbed or prejudiced. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 

52, 53, 129 S. E. 2d 82.

Where a widow contended that she accepted a legacy under her husband's will thirty-one days after the death of her husband in ignorance of her rights and in ignorance of material facts, particularly as to the condition of the estate and the value of bonds held by the executors along with the estate, did not preclude her from later claiming a year's support by reason of the fact that she had accepted a legacy provided in her husband's will in lieu of dower and year's support. Brady v. Brady (1962), 107 Ga. App. 52, 129 S. E. 2d 82. § 304.-Same-Method of Election.-Where executor refused to give widow the information she needed to determine whether to take under or against the will, the widow had such an interest in the estate as to be entitled to sue the executor in equity. Jackson v. Jackson (1950), 206 Ga. 470, 57 S. E. 2d 602. § 305.-Bar of Dower.-Anderson v. Caldwell (1942), 66 Ga. App. 703, 19 

S. E. 2d 202; Cheatham v. Sheppard (1944), 198 Ga. 254, 31 S. E. 2d 457.

Section 31-110, subparagraph (6) of the Code of Georgia an notated provides: "31-110. (5249) How barred.-Dower may be barred- 6. By a failure to apply for the dower prior to a sale by an administrator or executor under authority of a court of competent jurisdiction or under power in a will: Provided, however, such administrator or executor shall give the widow 30 days' written notice of such proposed sale personally or by registered mail, at

last known address, and such notice may run concurrently with any application to any court for such sale: and Provided, further, however, that such sale shall bar the dower only as to the land sold. 

The said executor or administrator shall make an affidavit as to the giving of such notice, which said affidavit shall be attached to the deed or deeds executed pursuant to said sale and recorded along with said deed or deeds and shall be evidence of the giving of said notice. (Acts 1937, p. 450; 1955, pp. 615, 617.)"

The 1955 Act removed the provision whereby dower, not applied for, was not barred by sale of the administrator unless made more than 12 months after the death of the husband. The provision for 

30 days written notice was added by the act of 1955, as was the provision that service may run concurrently with any application to any court for the sale. The last sentence was added by the act of 1955. "Where, during the life of her husband, the wife separates from him and assumes a relationship of separation, she is to all intents and purposes sui juris, and may institute suit for alimony if she so elects; and where permanent alimony is either granted by judgment of a court, or the alimony suit is settled by contract between the parties, whereby she accepts money or property in settlement of the claim for permanent alimony, and such contract is not annulled by subsequent cohabitation and reconciliation, under applicable law it bars her of her rights of dower and year's support from her husband's estate, and she ceases to have any further interest in his estate in her right as wife." McKie v. McKie (1957), 213 Ga. 582 (1), 100 So. (2d) 580. § 306.-Assignment of Dower.-Killgo v. Dodson (1943), 69 Ga. App. 673, 26 8. E. 2d 554. 

§ 308-Administration of Reversionary Interest.-Acts 1957, pages 502, 503, amended Code § 113-2305, which section provides that "Whenever an administrator has fully administered the estate except the reversionary interest in land set apart as dower, and it is not necessary to administer the same to pay debts, such administrator shall be entitled to letters of dismission upon complying with the provisions of law regulating the granting of such letters,'' by adding the following: "Provided, that when such dismission letter has been granted, an administrator de bonis non may be appointed to administer any property in which a dower interest was granted, without setting aside said dismission letter. Furthermore, any heir of the original decedent or any creditor of the decedent's estate may be appointed said administrator de bonis non." 

§ 309.-Appeal and Certiorari.-Tilley v. King (1942), 193 Ga. 602, 19 S. E. 

2d 281; Samples v. Samples (1942), 194 Ga. 383, 21 S. E. 2d 601.

In seeking a review of a final judgment of the ordinary in a proceeding brought under Ga. Code Ann. 113-1023 et seq. to obtain leave to convey lands set apart as a year's support, appeal to the superior court and not certiorari is the proper remedy or method. Harnesberger v. Davis (1952), 86 Ga. App. 41, 70 8. E. 2d 615. "Exceptions in writing to the decision of the court of ordinary are necessary as a basis of a certiorari thereto; and where it appears that no such

written exceptions were made, it was proper to dismiss the certiorari.'' Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (3), 100 S. E. 2d 594.

While, under Code § 19-502, where it appears that the judge of the court of ordinary, or the judge of any other inferior judiciary, dies before answering the writ of certiorari, it is the duty of the judge of the superior court who granted the writ to order a new trial as a matter of right, this rule would apply only where the application for certiorari is itself in conformity with law and contains no fatal defect which would render it subject to dismissal. Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (2), 100 S. E. 2d 594. 

§ 310.-How Appeals Are Made.-Wall v. Griffith (1941), 193 Ga. 11, 17 

S. E. 2d 57; Womack v. Williford (1942), 194 Ga. 688, 22 S. E. 2d 510. § 311.-Same-Appeal Bonds.-Appellants in a court of ordinary must give bond, which bond may be amended or new security may be given if necessary. 

However, appellants may not amend by giving bond after a motion to dismiss has been made and sustained. Peppers v. Peppers (1957), 96 Ga. App. 668, 101 

S. E. 2d 105. "The appeal and bond having been executed and signed by the attorney for the appellants by typing the names of the appellants thereto and signing the same in his own handwriting followed by a seal, it was not error to deny the motion to dismiss the appeal." Ganns v. Worrell (1960), 216 Ga. 512, 513 (1), 117 S. E. 2d 533. 

§ 312.-Appeal by Consent and in Forma Pauperis.-Wever v. Miniger 

(1938), 186 Ga. 671, 198 S. E. 671; Roberts v. Carmichael (1942), 68 Ga. App. 

595, 23 S. E. 2d 272.

Appellants in a court of ordinary must give bond, which bond may be amended or new security may be given if necessary. However, appellants may not amend by giving bond after a motion to dismiss has been made and sustained. Peppers v. Peppers (1957), 96 Ga. App. 668, 101 S. E. 2d 105. 

§ 313.-Parties.-Hooks v. Hooks (1944), 197 Ga. 482, 29 S. E. 2d 599. 

A petition filed in the court of ordinary by "A individually and by and through B as his son and next friend" may not be appealed by B in his own name. Stewart v. Stewart (1962), 106 Ga. App. 211, 126 S. E. 2d 716.

The administrator of the estate is not an indispensable party in the court reviewing the judgment denying probate when he was not a party to the probate proceedings in the court below. Beman v. Stembridge (1955), 211 Ga. 

274, 85 S. E. 2d 434. 

315.-Effect of Appeal.-Womack v. Williford (1942), 194 Ga. 688, 22 

8. E. 2d 510; Hooks v. Hooks (1944), 197 Ga. 482, 29 S. E. 2d 599; Wofford v. 

Vandiver (1945), 72 Ga. App. 623, 34 S. E. 2d 579; Jones v. Cannady (1949), 78 Ga. App. 453, 51 S. E. 2d 551.

An appeal from the court of ordinary, like other appeals to the superior court, is a de novo investigation. It brings up the whole record from the lower court and all relevant issues which could have been tried before the original tribunal may be tried on the appeal. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14, 17, 126 S. E. 2d 289.

The case on appeal from the court of ordinary brings the whole case up for a new hearing. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567; Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 517.

An appeal from the court of ordinary to the superior court is a de novo proceeding. Any defense or attack upon the jurisdiction which could have been made in the court of ordinary can be made in the superior court on appeal. 

Cromer v. Chambers (1961), 104 Ga. App. 196, 199, 121 S. E. 2d 397.

The superior court on the trial of an appeal has no broader powers than the court of ordinary itself had. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 

2d 567; Goodman v. Little, (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 517. 

§ 316. Jurisdiction on Appeal.— 

The case on appeal from the court of ordinary brings the whole case up for a new hearing. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567; Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 517.

The superior court on the trial of an appeal has no broader powers than the court of ordinary itself had. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 

2d 567; Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 517.

On appeal from a court of ordinary the superior court has no greater jurisdiction than the court of ordinary. Strickland v. Strickland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 

531 (1b), 109 S. E. 2d 289.

Where a petition is filed in a court of ordinary for a full accounting by the executor, in order to ascertain the rights of the parties and to ascertain whether or not the executor has completed his duties under the will and whether it is his duty to account and to turn over the property bequeathed and devised by the will, a construction of the will is necessary. As the court of ordinary has no power or authority to construe a will, the superior court on an appeal from the court of ordinary likewise has no authority to construe the will. Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

Since the jurisdiction of the court of ordinary to revoke letters of executorship and to require an executor to make an accounting and settlement to the heirs at law is limited to the case as one at law, and the superior court on the trial of an appeal from the court of ordinary having no broader powers than the court of ordinary had, the Court of Appeals and not the Supreme Court has jurisdiction of an appeal from the superior court to decide such questions. 

Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567; Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 517.

In certiorari proceedings to review an order of the court of ordinary allowing a year's support to a child born out of wedlock, whose parents subsequently married, making the child legitimate, and to correct errors in said order, the issues being ones of law only, the Court of Appeals, and not the Supreme Court, has jurisdiction to review the exception to the order of the trial court dismissing the petition for certiorari. Miller v. Miller (1957), 213 

Ga. 435, 99 S. E. 2d 129. See Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469, 100 

S. E. 2d 594.

While, under Code § 19-502, where it appears the judge of the court of ordinary, or the judge of any other inferior judiciary, dies before answering the writ of certiorari, it is the duty of the judge of the superior court who granted the writ to order a new trial as a matter of right, this rule would apply only where the application for certiorari is itself in conformity with law and contains no fatal defect which would render it subject to dismissal. Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (2), 100 S. E. 2d 594. "Those who are named as executors in purported wills of decedents shall be entitled to recover from the estate of the decedent

expenses, including a reasonable attorney's fee if the services of an attorney are employed for offering probate wills in solemn or common form, even though the will is subsequently determined not to be the valid will of the testator: Provided, however, such persons shall not be entitled to recover from the estate the expenses and attorney's fees incurred in the effort to sustain the will in the event of a contest, unless the person so named proceeds in good faith; the court of ordinary shall determine upon the petition of a person so named, the amount of expenses, and the amount to be paid the attorney so employed, and its order shall be subject to appeal to the superior court as is now in other cases provided." Code § 113-619. 

Under the provisions of Code § 113-2008 the administrator may be allowed additional compensation for extraordinary services, and under § 113-2009 he may also be authorized to pay the expenses of employing such agents as he finds necessary to employ for the estate. The allowance of such extra compensation to the administrator and the allowances of expenses for employing agents can only be made after a showing to the ordinary and a finding by him of the necessity therefor. But, where the case is one of appeal from the court of ordinary brought to the superior court to review the ordinary's action in approving or disapproving the administrator's acts in dealing with the estate, and where the proceeding in the superior court takes upon itself the nature of a general accounting and winding up of the estate, that court has jurisdiction to allow or not to allow those items of expense on the same basis as the ordinary would have had. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14, 21, 126 S. E. 2d 289.

In the trial of an appeal from the court of ordinary before a jury in the superior court, the jury has jurisdiction to allow extra compensation to the administrator under Code § 113-2008 or to approve the expense of employing agents to assist in the administration of the estate on the same basis as the ordinary upon a showing that these expenses and charges were reasonably necessary to the prudent and sound administration of the estate. Hartford 

Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 108 Ga. App. 14, 15 (4), 126 S. E. 2d 289. On the trial of an appeal from a judgment of the court of ordinary setting aside the discharge of an administrator, a showing that there were irregularities in the administration of the estate is sufficient to authorize the reopening of the estate. A showing of fraud is not essential. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14 (2), 126 S. E. 2d 289.

Where the ordinary passed an order on a petition brought by heirs against an administrator setting aside a discharge granted the administrator and expressly provided therein that the entire estate would be reopened and the heirs allowed time within which to file objections to the discharge and where the administrator and his surety on the same day filed an appeal to the superior court and invoked the jurisdiction of the superior court to try the issues in the case and such procedure was not objected to by the opposite parties, the surety was thereafter estopped to contend that the superior court did not have jurisdiction to try the case as an appeal and to dispose of all issues respecting the administration of the estate. Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company v. 

Cohran (1962), 106 Ga. App. 14 (1), 126 S. E. 2d 289.

§ 317.-Procedure in Appellate Court.-On appeal to the superior court from the court of ordinary in a proceeding to remove an administrator, or executor, the discretion which by law has been vested in the ordinary is to be exercised by the jury. McLendon v. McLendon (1957), 96 Ga. App. 197 (2), 99 S. E. 

2d 489.

While, under Code § 19-502, where it appears that the judge of the court of ordinary, or the judge of any other inferior judicatory, dies before answering the writ of certiorari, it is the duty of the judge of the superior court who granted the writ to order a new trial as a matter of right, this rule would apply only where the application for certiorari is itself in conformity with law and contains no fatal defect which would render it subject to dismissal. 

Miller v. Miller (1957), 96 Ga. App. 469 (2), 100 S. E. 2d 594. 

§ 318.-Descent. Baldwin v. Atlanta Joint Stock Land Bank (1940), 189 

Ga. 607, 7 S. E. 2d 178; Zeagler v. Zeagler (1940), 190 Ga. 220, 9 S. E. 2d 263; 

McMullen v. Carlton (1941), 192 Ga. 282, 14 S. E. 2d 719; Veal v. Veal (1941), 192 Ga. 503, 15 S. E. 2d 725; Harris v. Mandeville (1943), 195 Ga. 251, 24 

S. E. 2d 23; Strickland v. Jenkins (1944), 198 Ga. 15, 31 S. E. 2d 18; Life &

Casualty Ins. Co. of Tenn. v. Marks (1945), 72 Ga. App. 640, 34 S. E. 2d 633. 

"Under the laws of descent and distribution in this State, upon the death of a husband intestate leaving children and/or descendants of deceased children, title to realty owned by husband at his death vests in such children.' 

Keen v. Thomas (1958), 214 Ga. 362, 364, 104 S. E. 2d 903. 

The widow is not, strictly speaking, an heir at law of her deceased husband, since upon the death of a husband intestate, leaving children and descendants of deceased children, title to realty owned by the husband vests in such children. Kenner v. Kenner (1958), 214 Ga. 381 (1), 104 S. E. 2d 896.

Under Code § 113-801 before title passes to a devisee and before a devisee is entitled to possession of the property devised, there must be assent of the executor. This code section applies with equal force to an administrator cum testamento annexo. Nash v. Williamson (1957), 95 Ga. App. 616, 619, 98 S. E. 

2d 299. "A devisee of land took it subject to easement entitling city to discharge sewage into stream which flowed through the land devised, notwithstanding that devisee had no notice of the easement.' Segars v. City of Cornelia (1939). 60 Ga. App. 457, 4 S. E. 2d 60 (3). 

"The right of an heir or legatee to interest in estate of his decedent is a 'chose in action' and is assignable. Code 1933, § 85-1805." Sanders v. 

Hepp (1940), 190 Ga. 18, 8 S. E. 2d 87 (3). 

See comment in section 267 of this supplement.

In 1943 the legislature amended Ga. Code Ann. 113-901, pertaining to descent, by adding a comma after the word "debts" in line four, by striking from lines four and five the words "and purposes of distribution," and by adding in lieu thereof the words "the purposes of distribution, and other purposes provided for in this Title." Acts 1943, page 237. 

Under Code § 113-909 the right of inheritance is denied any person who kills his decedent with malice. Said Code section is as follows: 

"The right of inheritance is hereby denied any person who shall, with malice aforethought, kill any other person, or who shall conspire with another to kill or who shall procure another to kill any

such person. This denial to inherit shall include any property which the person so killing would otherwise have inherited, whether real, personal or mixed, or any part thereof, belonging to such deceased person at the time of death, or any property which the person so killing would take by deed, will, or otherwise, at the death of the deceased; and all right, interest, and estate in and to said property shall go to such other heirs as may be entitled thereto by the laws of descent and distribution, or by will, deed, or other conveyance duly executed by the deceased in his or her lifetime. For the purpose of determining the descent and distribution through such person so killing, he shall be treated as though he had predeceased the person so killed. No provision of this section shall apply to any such killing as may be done by accident or in self-defense." Code § 113-909. 

The fact that a person was acquitted in a criminal proceeding of the charge that he had with malice aforethought killed his wife would not be a bar to a civil action on the ground that such person by killing his wife with malice aforethought forfeited his right of inheritance under Code § 113-909. Webb v. McDaniel (1962), 218 Ga. 366, 127 S. E. 2d 900. 

§ 319.-Rules of Inheritance.-Blount v. Dean (1939), 187 Ga. 494, 1 S. E. 

2d 653 (12); Hines v. Donaldson (1942), 193 Ga. 783, 20 S. E. 2d 134; Comer v. Comer (1942), 195 Ga. 79, 23 S. E. 2d 420; Morris v. Dilbeck (1944), 71 

Ga. App. 470, 31 S. E. 2d 93; Conner v. Rainwater (1946), 200 Ga. 866, 38 

S. E. 2d 805; Mulligan v. Mulligan (1946), 201 Ga. 444, 39 S. E. 2d 699; 

Morris v. First Nat. Bank of Atlanta (1947), 202 Ga. 51, 42 S. E. 2d 215; 

Driver v. Mott (1947), 75 Ga. App. 667, 44 S. E. 2d 170; Britt v. Fincher (1947), 202 Ga. 661, 44 S. E. 2d 372.

The scheme of the law in cases of intestacy favors the equal distribution of the intestate's property among his heirs. Cassedy v. Bland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 

34, 36, 107 S. E. 2d 697. "There are only two ways by which this scheme of equality among the heirs may be upset. The first, of course, is by the making of a will on the part of the ancestor providing for the distribution of his estate in a manner other than set forth by law; and, the second is by a binding contract executed between the ancestor and the heir, which clearly shows a meeting of minds between them acknowledging on the part of the heir the receipt in full for the heir's prospective share of the ancestors' estate. Such a contract when entered into is binding and enforceable. It matters not what the ancestor thought as to whether the scheme constituted a mere advancement or a settlement of the heir's claim against his estate if the heir did not agree with the ancestor as to the effect of the advancement." Id. "Under the laws of descent and distribution in this State, upon the death of a husband intestate leaving children and/or descendants of deceased children, title to realty owned by husband at his death vests in such children." 

Keen v. Thomas (1958), 214 Ga. 362, 364, 104 S. E. 2d 903.

The widow is not, strictly speaking, an heir at law of her deceased husband, since upon the death of a husband intestate, leaving children and descendants of deceased children, title to realty owned by the husband vests in such children. Kenner v. Kenner (1958), 214 Ga. 381 (1), 104 S. E. 2d 896.

Under the rules of inheritance, brothers and sisters of an intestate shall inherit if there is no widow, child or representative of a child. Therefore, the

caveatrix, a sister, and her brothers or their children or representatives of children inherited the entire estate, the testator leaving neither a wife or children, nor representatives of children. Lawson v. Hurt (1962), 217 Ga. 827, 830, 125 S. E. 2d 480.

Where it appeared that the propounder of a will had been previously married, and there being no evidence that his former wife was dead at the time he entered into the ceremonial marriage with the testatrix, or that a divorce had been obtained by him from his former wife, the evidence did not demand a finding that he was the husband and sole heir at law of the testatrix. Ganns v. Worrell (1960), 216 Ga. 512, 514, 117 S. E. 2d 533.

The right of inheritance is denied as to any person who shall, with malice aforethought, kill, or conspire with another to kill, any other person for the purpose of inheriting the property of the person so killed. Ga. Code Ann. § 113-909 (Acts 1952, pp. 288, 289). For the rule prior to the Act of 1952, see 

Crumley v. Hall (1947), 202 Ga. 588, 43 S. E. 2d 646.

Acts 1959, page 299, amended Acts 1952, pages 288, 289 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-909), by not only providing for the denying of the right of inheritance but also denying the right to receive or take any benefits from any insurance contract or policy issued on the life of a person where such person is killed, with malice aforethought or a conspiracy is entered into with another to kill such person, by a person who is entitled to such inheritance or such insurance. 

The fact that a person was acquitted in a criminal proceeding of the charge that he had with malice aforethought killed his wife would not be a bar to a civil action on the ground that such person by killing his wife with malice aforethought forfeited his right of inheritance under Code § 113-909. Webb v. McDaniel (1962), 218 Ga. 366, 127 S. E. 2d 900.

Apparently this statute makes inoperative the decision in the case of Brookins v. Citizens & Southern Nat. Bank (1949), 205 Ga. 128, 52 S. E. 2d 461.

Code § 74-414 was amended by Acts 1961, page 219, so that now under the present law when a final adoption decree is entered the adopted child may inherit and the adoptive parents may inherit from the child that which he acquires or is vested in him subsequent to the final order of adoption, except that which he has acquired or inherited from blood relatives. Said adopted child shall be considered in all respects as if it were a child of natural bodily issue of the adoptive parents, and shall enjoy every right and privilege of a natural child; and shall be deemed a natural child of the adoptive parents to inherit under the laws of descent and distribution in the absence of a will and to take under the provision of any instrument of testamentary gift, bequest, devise, or legacy, unless expressly excluded therefrom.

Under the principles of common law a child is entitled to inherit from its natural father who dies intestate, and this rule is generally applied even though the child has been adopted by another and is also entitled to inherit from its adoptive parents in the absence of statute expressly prohibiting the right of such adopted child to inherit from its natural parents. Sears v. 

Minchew (1956), 94 Ga. App. 126, 93 S. E. 2d 748.

In the administration of an estate in Georgia, the minor child of the deceased will inherit under Georgia law, regardless of the fact that a child, prior to the death of the natural father, was adopted by another in another state. 

Sears v. Minchew (1955), 94 Ga. App. 126, 93 S. E. 2d 748, conforming to certified questions to Supreme Court in Sears v. Minchew (1956), 212 Ga. 418, 93 S. E. 2d 746.

In administration of estate in Georgia, minor child of deceased will inherit under Georgia law, regardless of fact that she was, prior to death of her natural father, adopted by another in State of Florida. Sears v. Minchew, (1956), 94 Ga. App. 126, 93 S. E. 2d 748.

Under principles of common law child is entitled to inherit from its natural father who dies intestate, and this rule is generally applied even though child has been adopted by another and is also entitled to inherit from its adoptive parents in absence of statute expressly prohibiting right of such adopted child to inherit from its natural parents. Id. 

Since there is no language in Code § 74-414 relating to rights of adoptive children which expressly or by necessary implication forbids adopted child to inherit from natural parents dying intestate, common-law rule prevails and such adopted child will inherit along with other children and spouse of deceased under provisions of Ch. 113-9, regardless of whether or not it also has right of inheritance from its adopted parents. Id. 

An adopted child may inherit from his adoptive parents even though he was adopted in a foreign state. Watson v. Watson (1951), 208 Ga. 512, 67 S. E. 

2d 704.

An adopted child inherits as a natural child from an intestate foster parent; and when the administrator of an estate fails and refuses to account or settle, such adopted child has the same rights as a natural child. Ware v. Martin (1951), 207 Ga. 512, 63 S. E. 2d 335.

A contract by a person to adopt a child of another as his own is not selfoperating; heirship does not grow out of it. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 

Ga. 892, 895 (1), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

A contract or agreement that one shall have a child's part of an estate for services to be performed in taking care of another does not make such person an heir. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 895 (1), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

A parol agreement by a person to adopt the child of another as his own, accompanied by a virtual though not a statutory adoption, and acted upon by all parties concerned for many years during the obligor's life, may be enforced in equity upon the death of the obligor, by decreeing the child entitled as a child to the property of the obligor, undisposed of by will. Banes v. Derricotte (1960), 215 Ga. 892, 895 (2), 114 S. E. 2d 12.

An unfulfilled promise to adopt another does not have the effect of constituting the promisee a child or heir of the promisor. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

The first essential of a contract for the adoption of a child, where no statutory adoption exists, is that it be made between persons competent to contract for the disposition of the child, and be based upon a sufficient legal consideration. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409, 412 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

Where parties agreeing to the adoption of an infant have no authority or legal right to assent to such adoption, the agreement is not a valid and binding contract, nor is it capable of being enforced where it is made upon a condition that, due to no fault of the prospective parents, was never performed by the opposite parties to the agreement. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 

409 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

Where husband and wife enter into a joint agreement to adopt a third person as their child, both are necessary parties to a proceeding to enforce the contract. Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409 (3), 128 S. E. 2d 56.

A petition which alleged a parol contract to adopt certain children, and a relinquishment of the rights of their natural parents, accompanied by a virtual though not a statutory adoption, said adoption being acted upon by all the parties during the obligors' life, a breach of which is alleged, and the refusal of the administratrix of the obligors' estate to recognize the plaintiffs as the children of the deceased, set forth a cause of action to enforce a parol contract to adopt the plaintiffs as the children of the defendant administratrix's intestate. Hollis v. Maxwell (1959), 215 Ga. 483, 111 S. E. 2d 72.

The legislature in 1943 provided that a mother of an illegitimate child, in an action for damages arising out of injuries to or the death of her child, shall not be discriminated against, whether she sues in her own right or in her capacity as guardian, executor, or administrator. Acts 1943, page 538; 

Ga. Code Ann. 74-205.

Under the provisions of Code, § 53-104, the child of a bigamous common-law marriage, born before such marriage was annulled or declared void by a court, is legitimate and is the lawful heir of his deceased father. Campbell v. Allen (1951), 208 Ga. 274, 66 S. E. 2d 226.

The word "child" used in a statute, will, deed, or other conveyance generally means a legitimate child, unless the context shows a different meaning, or the circumstances surrounding the execution of a paper are such as to make the words include an illegitimate child. Pasley v. State (1960), 215 Ga. 768, 769 (2), 113 S. E. 2d 454.

While a person's "status," his legitimacy or paternity, is generally fixed by the law of his domicile, in determining the effect of trust which must be determined what law the trustors intended to control when they executed the trust. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 S. E. 2d 147.

Where a will which incorporated a trust was executed in Pennsylvania and probated both in Pennsylvania and Georgia, the law of Georgia governs trust property located in Georgia but the intestate law of Pennsylvania governs in determining remaindermen and whether certain items of the will were intended to refer to natural or blood relationships to the exclusion of adopted children. 

Carnegie v. First National Bank of Brunswick (1963), 218 Ga. 585, 588 (la), 129 S. E. 2d 780. 

'The trial court correctly decreed that the adopted son of a grandson of the testatrix is a remainderman under her will." Carnegie v. First National Bank of Brunswick (1963), 218 Ga. 585 (1), 129 S. E. 2d 780.

Though statutes conferring legitimacy upon children who would have been bastards at the common law because not born after lawful wedlock are remedial in nature, being intended to prevent the sins of the parents from being visited upon their innocent offspring, leaving the punishment of the parents to the criminal law, the courts of this state having viewed such statutes with circumspection, giving them strict construction, because they disrupt the traditional settled rules of property. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 

534, 542, 129 S. E. 2d 147. "Prior to 1934 it had been determined by this court that a reference in a will to 'children' did not include illegitimate children unless it was manifest from the context that the word was employed in a broader sense. King v. 

King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 540, 129 S. E. 2d 147. 

Where no trust, will or deed is involved, as where the question is one of intestates succession, the status of legitimacy is created by the law of the

domicile of the parent whose relationship to the child is in question; but a trust of movables created by an instrument inter vivos is administered by the trustee according to the law of the state where the instrument creating the trust locates the administration of the trust. King v. King (1962), 218 Ga. 534, 537, 129 S. E. 2d 147.

§ 322a.-Procedure to Establish Heirs.-The General Assembly in 1958 (Acts 

1958, pages 361-364), enacted a procedure by which heirs at law may be established. This Act provides that any executor, administrator, guardian, conservator, committee, trustee, fiduciary, or any other person, who under any instrument it his duty to distribute property, may file an application in either the court of ordinary or the superior court to determine the question of heirship. 

The 1958 Act is codified as Ga. Code Ann., §§ 113-2801 thru 113-2808. 

This Act gives the requirements of the petition, notice, findings, etc. All these requirements will not be discussed herein and the act should be carefully studied before such a proceedings is filed thereunder.

"Where the proceeds of property condemned were claimed by an alleged widow, an alleged heir of the mortgagee, and the administrator of the estate of the deceased holder of the record title to the property, the trial judge properly awarded the funds to the administrator. The conflicting claims of the parties can be asserted against the administrator who may bring an action for determination of heirship." Boswell v. Underwood (1962), 106 Ga. App. 675, 127 S. E. 2d 870. § 323.-Distribution.-Fenn v. Castelanna (1943), 196 Ga. 22, 25 S. E. 2d 

796; Raines v. Shipley (1945), 200 Ga. 180, 36 S. E. 2d 150.

The scheme of the law in cases of intestacy favors equal distribution of the intestate's property among his heirs. Cassedy v. Bland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 34, 36, 107 S. E. 2d 697. "There are only two ways by which this scheme of equality among the heirs may be upset. The first, of course, is by the making of a will on the part of the ancestor providing for a distribution of his estate in a manner

other than that set forth by law; and, the second is by a binding contract executed between the ancestor and the heir, which clearly shows a meeting of minds between them acknowledging on the part of the heir the receipt in full for the heir's prospective share of the ancestor's estate. Such a contract when entered into is binding and enforceable. It matters not what the ancestor thought as to whether the scheme constituted a mere advancement or a settlement of the heir's claim against his estate if the heir did not agree with the ancestor as to the effect of the advancement." Id. "It has long been the policy of the law to approve a family agreement for the settlement of an estate; and where the settlement is between parties having an interest, it is not a voluntary agreement without consideration, but is one that may be enforced in a court of equity." Reynolds v. Bowles (1957), 213 

Ga. 534, 100 S. E. 2d 198. Acts 1958, page 377, amended Code § 49-316, relating to a guardian acting as administrator of the estate of ward, which section as amended is as follows: "49-316. When a ward shall die intestate, the guardian shall proceed to distribute his estate in the same manner as if he had been appointed administrator upon such estate, and the sureties on his bond shall be responsible for the faithful administration and distribution of such estate.' 

This amendment struck from the section "pending his minority."

Therefore, it follows that a guardian of a ward may act as administrator of his ward's estate regardless of the age of the ward when he dies. It would also seem that guardians appointed for any incompetent person may upon such ward's death act as administrator of the ward's estate.

A general demurrer was properly sustained to a petition seeking an injunction to restrain the disbursement of the funds of an estate since plaintiff was never adopted by the deceased and his wife, and an unfulfilled contract to adopt does not operate to constitute plaintiff an heir at law of the deceased. 

Winder v. Winder (1962), 218 Ga. 409, 128 S. E. 2d 56. § 324.-Division in Kind.-Sanders v. Hepp (1940), 190 Ga. 18, 8 S. E. 21

"An administrator cannot recover possession of land from heirs for the purpose of distribution among them where they have in fact divided the property in kind and each has gone into possession of his part. The legislature in 1941 amended the law as to the division of property in kind by adding another sentence at the end of Ga. Code Ann. 113-1018.

This section as amended reads as follows: 

"Whenever it is practicable, the ordinary may order a distribution of the estate in kind; which order may be granted on the application of the representative or any distributee of the estate. 

In all cases the applicant shall give at least 20 days' written notice

to all parties in interest within this State who are of age, and to the guardians, if any, of minor distributees, and shall also give notice to any persons in interest residing out of the State, by publication of the same at least twice a month for two months in the newspaper in which the ordinary's official notices are published. 

Nothing in this section contained shall be construed as limiting or restricting the method of distribution provided for in a will or as requiring the approval of the ordinary to a distribution or division in kind made pursuant to directions in a will; and in all cases where the will directs or authorizes a distribution or division in kind, but fails to specifically direct how, or by whom, such distribution or division in kind be made, it shall be the duty and authority of the executor, or the administrator with will annexed, to make such distribution or division in kind. (Acts 1941, p. 332.)" Ga. Code

In 1947 the legislature provided for the appointment of appraisers to divide property in kind. This act of the legislature repealed Ga. Code Ann. 113-1019 and substituted in lieu thereof a new section, which permits the ordinary to appoint three or more freeholders of the county where the administration is pending whose duty it will be to appraise and divide the property in kind, whether located in the county where the administration is pending or in other counties of the state. Acts 1947, page 1141. 

See section 250.

The heirs of an intestate, when sui juris, may as among themselves settle up the estate as they choose, which will be good as against one another, and when the plaintiff heir alleges full compliance with the agreement of settlement and seeks by her petition to require an heir who agreed to the settlement but who later refused to carry out the agreement, such petition is not subject to general demurrer. Wilson v. Whitmire (1956), 212 Ga. 287, 92 S. E. 2d 20. "It has long been the policy of the law to approve a family agreement for the settlement of an estate; and where the settlement is between parties having an interest, it is not a voluntary agreement without consideration, but is one that may be enforced in a court of equity." Reynolds v. Bowles (1957), 213 

Ga. 534, 100 S. E. 2d 198.

It is well settled that agreements among the heirs at law to distribute or divide property devised under a will, in lieu of that manner provided by the will, are valid and enforceable. Such agreements have as their consideration the termination of family controversies, and are upheld "albeit perhaps resting on grounds which would not have been satisfactory if the transaction had occurred between mere strangers." They partake of the nature of family arrangements and are, in essence, solely contractual and governed by rules applicable to all contracts. West v. Downer (1962), 218 Ga. 235, 241 (5), 127 

S. E. 2d 359.

In order for an advancement to constitute a full and complete settlement of an heir's claim against the estate of the donor, it must have been given by the donor and accepted by the donee with that understanding and agreement between them. Cassedy v. Bland (1959), 99 Ga. App. 34, 107 S. E. 2d 697. "Where money or property is transferred by a parent to his child, and is accepted, the question of whether the transfer is to be treated as an advancement, depends upon the intention of the parent at the time of the transaction, without regard to concurrence on the part of the child." Barron v. Barron, 181 Ga. 505 (2), 182 S. E. 851; Treadwell v. Everett, 185 Ga. 454 (1), 195 S. E. 

762; Kaylor v. Kaylor, 199 Ga. 516 (4), 35 S. E. 2d 1; Berry v. Berry (1951), 208 Ga. 285, 66 S. E. 2d 336. "A memorandum in a will, of advancement to a legatee, is conclusive of the fact, and is not subject to change by parol evidence." Lee v. Boyer (1961), 217 Ga. 27, 31, 120 S. E. 2d 757. 

§ 326.-Interest on Funds of Estate.-Brown v. Parks (1940), 190 Ga. 540, 

9 S. E. 2d 897 (5).

Where a testator gave his estate to his wife for life and provided that on her death his three sons were to receive the net income therefrom and that upon the death of the last surviving son the corpus of the estate was to be divided among his grandchildren, the terms and provisions of the testator's will clearly show that it was his intention that the corpus of his estate be held intact for the ultimate benefit of his grandchildren, and that his wife, during her lifetime and his three sons, should, after her death, personally have and receive annually the entire net income of his estate and that any profit arising from a sale of capital assets of his estate became a part of the corpus of the estate, and that the petitioners have no rights to receive the same as a part of the income of the estate. Also, that it was the intention of the testator that any loss sustained by his estate through the sale of capital assets should be treated as a loss of corpus, and that the petitioners as executors of the estate are not required to deduct a corpus loss from the annual income of the estate before distributing to themselves as life beneficiaries under the will the net income of the estate for any given year. Hirsch v. Hirsch (1960), 216 Ga. 

379, 116 S. E. 2d 318.

At the 1953 Session, the General Assembly liberalized to a considerable extent the laws relating to legal investments by fiduciaries. The law now provides that all fiduciaries may deposit funds held in their fiduciary capacity at interest in a bank or trust company, whether such bank or trust company is chartered by the State or by the United States, provided such deposits are covered by Federal Deposit Insurance. Banks and trust companies holding funds in a fiduciary capacity may deposit such funds with themselves at interest subject to the same provision as to Federal Deposit Insurance. Such deposits may be made without permission, authority, or approval of any court or other regulatory authority and no fiduciary making such deposits shall be liable to account for a greater rate of interest than that received. This law is made specifically applicable to administrators, executors, guardians, trustees, and insurance companies. Code sections 56-224, 108-417, and 113-1518 were revised in accordance with this Act, which is itself to be codified as Ga. Code Ann. 109-512 through 

109-514. Acts 1953, page 108.

In the November session of the Legislature in 1953 a provision was added to Code section 113-1518 which authorizes executors and administrators to invest trust funds in bonds and other securities issued by the Regents of the University System of Georgia. Acts 1953, Nov. Sess., page 178.

§ 327.-Accounting and Settlement.-Lewis v. Grovas (1940), 62 Ga. App. 

624, 9 S. E. 2d 281; Brown v. Parks (1940), 190 Ga. 540, 9 S. E. 2d 897; Quillian v. Tuck (1941), 66 Ga. App. 472, 17 S. E. 2d 921; Cubine v. Cubine (1942), 66 Ga. App. 699, 19 S. E. 2d 174; Ellis v. McWilliams (1943), 70 Ga. App. 

195, 27 S. E. 2d 886; Raines v. Shipley (1944), 197 Ga. 448, 29 S. E. 2d 588; 

Spence v. Brown (144), 198 Ga. 566, 32 S. E. 2d 297; Murphy v. Hunt (1946), 73 Ga. App. 700, 37 S. E. 2d 823; Guest v. Rucker (1948), 77 Ga. App. 696, 49 S. E. 2d 687; Hoffman v. Chester (1948), 204 Ga. 296, 49 S. E. 2d 760.

Though a court of equity has concurrent jurisdiction with the ordinary over the settlement of accounts of executors, it will not assume jurisdiction solely for that purpose unless it be shown that the remedies available in the court of ordinary are inadequate to afford complete relief to the party claiming to be aggrieved. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668, 670, 119 S. E. 2d 28.

An allegation of insolvency of the executor is a substantial factor for consideration where there are specific allegations showing danger of loss to persons interested in the estate, but an allegation of insolvency, standing alone, is insufficient to authorize a court of equity to interfere in the administration of an estate. The ordinary has ample authority to investigate charges that an executor is mismanaging an estate, and to require him to give bond or to remove him as executor. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668, 671, 119 

S. E. 2d 28.

Where the superior court enjoined an executrix in matters such as giving bond, making inventory, procuring an appraisal, filing returns, and prohibiting private sales without court order, that court would be taking over functions which, under our court system, are committed to the court of ordinary, and would be an interference with the regular administration of the estate contrary to Code § 37-402. Fuller v. Fuller (1962), 217 Ga. 691, 696, 124 S. E. 2d 741. 

The mere absence of bond is insufficient to show danger of loss or other injury authorizing equity to assume jurisdiction. Fuller v. Fuller (1962), 217 

Ga. 691, 695, 124 S. E. 2d 741.

The rule that equity gives no relief to those who long delay and renders the ascertainment of the truth difficult and that equity will not aid in the enforcement of stale demands applies to accounts of executors. Welch v. Welch (1959), 215 Ga. 198, 200, 109 S. E. 2d 757.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment under the Declaratory Judgment Act (Code § 110-1101 et seq.), this failure does not affect the right to any other relief to which the plaintiff may be entitled, and the petition is maintainable as one in equity for construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting. Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105. 

In Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105, it was held that even though a petition was insufficient to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, the petition was maintainable as one in equity for the construction of a will and an accounting, with injunction against an executor's sale of property in order to preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting.

Even though a petition fails to allege a situation authorizing a declaratory judgment, in which it was sought a construction of a will and an accounting, with an injunction against an executor's sale of the property in order to

preserve the status quo pending the construction and accounting, relief is not to be denied because of the availability of claim procedure provided by Code §§ 113-1801 and 113-1802; neither is it to be denied because of an order of the court of ordinary authorizing a sale of the property in question; and, nor is it to be denied because of the prior but related litigation in the same case. 

Brewton v. McLeod (1961), 216 Ga. 686, 119 S. E. 2d 105.

The jurisdiction of the court of ordinary to revoke letters of executorship and to require the executor to make an accounting and settlement to the heirs is limited to the case as one at law. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567. See Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 

517. The case was transferred to the Court of Appeals, it being held that such an action was one at law and therefore the Supreme Court did not have jurisdiction of the appellate proceedings. 

Where a petition is filed in a court of ordinary for a full accounting by the executor, in order to ascertain the rights of the parties and to ascertain whether or not the executor has completed his duties under the will and whether it is his duty to account and to turn over the property bequeathed and devised by the will, a construction of the will is necessary. As the court of ordinary has no power or authority to construe a will, the superior court on an appeal from the court of ordinary likewise has no authority to construe the will. Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

Acts 1943, pages 409, 444 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1423), relating to the necessity of construing a will or trust upon an accounting the same shall be transferred to the superior court is as follows: "The court of ordinary upon its own motion, or upon motion of any party at interest whenever it shall appear that a question of construction of a will or trust instrument is involved in said accounting, shall enter an order transferring said accounting to the superior court for the determination of all such questions which shall be presented to, heard and determined by the superior court as appeals from the court of ordinary are presented, heard and determined, and after the determination of such questions of construction by the superior court, the court of ordinary shall proceed with said accounting." See Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 

459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

Until there has been an assent of the executor, or an administrator cum testamento annexo, to a legacy, either express or implied, and until the debts of the estate have been paid, no action can be maintained for an accounting and for a partitioning of property. Nash v. Williamson (1957), 95 Ga. App. 616, 98 S. E. 2d 239. "In a proceeding in the court of ordinary to call executors and administrators to account, a citation is all the pleading that is necessary. Code, § 

113-2201." Cubine v. Cubine (1943), 69 Ga. App. 656, 26 S. E. 2d 462 (4). "A petition to require executors to account and settle testator's estate stated a cause of action." Manry v. Manry (1943), 196 Ga. 365, 26 S. E. 

2d 706 (14). "Generally, heirs are not entitled to equitable accounting for their deceased ancestor's personal property, though there is no administration. Code, §§ 

37-120, 113-901." Robinson v. Murray (1944), 198 Ga. 690, 32 S. E. 2d 496 (15). "While it is true that the will relieved the executor from making an inventory or accounting to the court of ordinary, this does not mean that the executor is unaccountable in any court at the insistence of a legatee or someone interested in the estate." Salter v. Salter (1952), 209 Ga. 90, 70 S. E. 2d 453.

Where the petition sets forth a cause of action for equitable partition of realty owned jointly by two estates, alleges that the funds have been intermingled by the executor, insolvent and not under bond, and who is wasting the estates, and that there should be an accounting and distribution, and where all necessary parties are before the court, a court of equity has jurisdiction and can do complete justice in the premises. Johnson v. Wilson (1956), 212 Ga. 264, 91 S. E. 2d 758. 

§ 328. Jurisdiction and Venue.-Brown v. Parks (1940), 190 Ga. 540, 9 S. E. 

2d 897; McCord v. Walton (1941), 192 Ga. 279, 14 S. E. 2d 723; Peeples v. 

Peeples (1942), 193 Ga. 358, 18 S. E. 2d 629; Morris v. Nicholson (1944), 198 

Ga. 450, 31 S. E. 2d 786.

The jurisdiction of the court of ordinary to revoke letters of executorship and to require the executor to make an accounting and settlement to the heirs is limited to the case as one at law. Goodman v. Little (1957), 213 Ga. 178, 97 S. E. 2d 567. See Goodman v. Little (1957), 96 Ga. App. 110, 99 S. E. 2d 

517. The case was transferred to the Court of Appeals, it being held that such action was one at law and therefore the Supreme Court did not have jurisdiction of the appellate proceedings.

Where a petition is filed in a court of ordinary for a full accounting by the executor, in order to ascertain the rights of the parties and to ascertain whether or not the executor has completed his duties under the will and whether it is his duty to account and to turn over the property bequeathed and divided by the will, a construction of the will is necessary. As the court of ordinary has no power or authority to construe a will, the superior court on an appeal from the court of ordinary likewise has no authority to construe the will. Davis v. Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42. "It has long been the policy of the law to approve a family agreement for the settlement of an estate; and where settlement is between parties having an interest, it is not a voluntary agreement without consideration, but is one that may be enforced in a court of equity." Reynolds v. Bowles (1957), 213 Ga. 534, 100 S. E. 2d 198.

Acts 1943, pages 409, 444 (Ga. Code Ann., § 113-1423), relating to the necessity of construing a will or trust upon an accounting the same shall be transferred to the superior court is as follows: "The court of ordinary upon its own motion, or upon motion of any party at interest whenever it shall appear that a question of construction of a will or trust instrument is involved in said accounting, shall enter an order transferring said accounting to the superior court for the determination of all such questions which shall be presented to, heard and determined by the superior court as appeals from the court of ordinary are presented, heard and determined, and after the determination of such questions of such questions of construction by the superior court, the court of ordinary shall proceed with said accounting." See Davis v. 

Davis (1956), 94 Ga. App. 459, 95 S. E. 2d 42.

In 1947 the legislature provided for the venue of suits and citations for settlement, accounting, or removal against non-resident administrators, execu tors, or guardians appointed by any court of Georgia, or against any resident of Georgia who qualifies as such fiduciary and subsequently removes from Georgia. This act also provides for service, and for an attorney-in-fact for service upon such fiduciaries. Acts 1947, page 1448. 

While equity has concurrent jurisdiction with the ordinary over settlement of the accounts of the administrator, the Constitution vests jurisdiction of

probate in the ordinary, and equity will interfere only where legal relief is inadequate. Hamrick v. Hamrick (1950), 206 Ga. 564, 58 S. E. 2d 145.

While courts of equity have concurrent jurisdiction with the ordinary over settlement of accounts of executors, it will not assume jurisdiction where remedies in the court of ordinary, such as citation for settlement, etc., are available and adequate. Salter v. Salter (1953), 209 Ga. 511, 74 S. E. 2d 241. "A court of equity may bring before it an adjudicate for all parties who have a common interest in a single subject matter, as had the several heirs of the decedent in this case." Deen v. McCorkle (1960), 216 Ga. 20, 114 S. E. 

2d 369.

Where the superior court enjoined an executrix in matters such as giving bond, making inventory, procuring an appraisal, filing returns, and prohibiting private sales without court order, that court would be taking over functions which, under our court system, are committed to the court of ordinary, and would be an interference with the regular administration of the estate contrary to Code § 37-402. Fuller v. Fuller (1962), 217 Ga. 691, 696, 124 S. E. 2d 741.

The mere absence of bond is insufficient to show danger of loss or other injury authorizing equity to assume jurisdiction. Fuller v. Fuller (1962), 217 

Ga. 691, 695, 124 S. E. 2d 741.

Though a court of equity has concurrent jurisdiction with the ordinary over the settlement of accounts of executors, it will not assume jurisdiction solely for that purpose unless it be shown that the remedies available in the court of ordinary are inadequate to afford complete relief to the party claiming to be aggrieved. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668, 670, 119 S. E. 2d 28.

An allegation of insolvency of the executor is a substantial factor for consideration where there are specific allegations showing danger of loss to persons interested in the estate, but an allegation of insolvency, standing alone, is insufficient to authorize a court of equity to interfere in the administration of an estate. The ordinary has ample authority to investigate charges that an executor is mismanaging an estate, and to require him to give bond or to remove him as executor. Gaines v. Johnson (1961), 216 Ga. 668, 671, 119 

S. E. 2d 28. 

§ 330.-Effect of Settlement.-Clair v. Burke (1940), 62 Ga. App. 607, 9 S. E. 

2d 119. "It has long been the policy of the law to approve a family agreement for the settlement of an estate; and where the settlement is between parties having an interest, it is not a voluntary agreement without consideration, but is one that may be enforced in a court of equity." Reynolds v. Bowles (1957), 213 Ga. 534, 100 S. E. 2d 198. § 333.-Kinds of Guardians.-A special guarlian may be appointed for the administration of workmen's compensation benefits. This is stated by the Ga. 

Code Ann. in the following language: "114-421. Appointment of guardian by the Board.-The State 

Board of Workmen's Compensation is authorized to appoint a qualified guardian for any minor claimant who shall be entitled to workmen's compensation benefits, where there is no duly appointed and qualified guardian for such minor, but the authority of any such

guardian so appointed by the board shall be limited to the administration of such workmen's compensation benefits only as such minor might be entitled to receive. (Acts 1952, pp. 271, 272.)" 

When this is construed with other sections pertaining to the Board, the new section permits the appointment of the guardian by a single director; and where an appeal is not entered to the full Board, such appointment is valid, binding, and conclusive. Utica Mutual Insurance Company v. Rolax (1953), 87 Ga. App. 733, 75 S. E. 2d 205.

Although the authority of such a guardian is limited to the administration of the workmen's compensation benefits alone, such guardian must exercise in respect to those benefits the same duties which any other regularly qualified guardian would be required to exercise in his administration of a minor's estate. Id. § 334.-Natural Guardians.—The legislature in 1943 provided that a mother of an illegitimate child, in an action for damages arising out of injuries to or the death of her child, shall not be discriminated against, whether she sues in her own right or in her capacity as guardian, executor, or administrator. 

Acts 1943, page 538; Ga. Code Ann. 74-205; Brown v. Gibson (1948), 203 Ga. 

213, 46 S. E. 2d 68.

Acts 1962, page 97, amended Code § 49-102, and is amended as follows: "The father, if alive, unless otherwise provided herein, is the natural guardian; if the father is dead or if the father is not domiciled with the mother, the parent having custody of the child is the natural guardian. The natural guardian may not demand or receive the property of the child until a guardian's bond shall be filed and accepted by the ordinary of the county. If such natural guardian shall fail or refuse to give bond and surety, the ordinary may appoint another guardian to receive such property." 

Under Code § 49-102 the father, if alive, is the natural guardian of his minor child and as such is entitled to its custody and management. Faith v. Massengill (1961), 104 Ga. App. 348, 354 (3), 121 S. E. 2d 657. 

§ 335.-Testamentary Guardians.-Beavers v. Williams (1945), 199 Ga. 113, 

33 S. E. 2d 343.

In 1943 the legislature amended Ga. Code Ann. 49-103, relating to testamentary guardians, by providing that every parent may, by will, appoint a guardian of the property of his children. Acts 1943, page 396. 

Prior to this amendment this Code section gave the father, but not the mother, this right. This amendment also gives the surviving parent the right to appoint a guardian of the persons of his children. This amendment apparently repeals 

Ga. Code Ann. 49-104 by implication.

Acts 1958, pages 673, 674, again amended Code § 49-103, as amended by Acts 1943, pages 396, 397, which 1958 amended said code section by substituting "parent's will," in lieu of "father's will," in the first sentence of this code section.

S. E. 2d 2 

In Adams v. Lay (1962), 218 Ga. 451, in construing Code § 49-103 as amended by Acts 1943, page 396, which Code section provides for the appointment of a testamentary guardian, pointed out that the law in effect on the effective date of a will providing for the appointment of a testamentary guardian determines whether or not a testatrix had the power to appoint testamentary guardians of both person and property. In further construing the amendatory act of 1943 the court made the following statement: "In 1956, the year of the mother's death, Ga. L. 1943, pp. 396-97 (Code Ann. § 49-103), provided that every parent could by will appoint guardians for the property of his children, and that if one of the parents was dead, the surviving parent could appoint guardians for the person of his or her minor children. The act uses the word 'children' in reference to the appointment of guardians for property and the words 'minor children' in reference to the appointment of guardians for their persons. We do not think, however, that the General 

Assembly by the inclusion of the word 'minor' at one place and its exclusion at the other intended to say that a parent might by his will appoint a guardian for the property of his children who had reached their majority. Therefore, we construe the act as providing for the appointment of guardians for the persons and/or property of minor children.'' Code § 49-103 was again amended by Acts 1958, page 673, but such amendment in all probability did not affect the above ruling as the only change made by the 1958 amendatory act was the substitution of the words "parent's will" for the words "father's will" in the fifth line of the section. "While a mother may by will appoint guardians for property which she devises to her minor child, and if she is the surviving parent may appoint guardians for the person of her minor child, there is no evidence that an effective appointment was made because the record fails to show the age of the child or anything from which it may be calculated and fails to show whether or not the mother was the surviving parent." Adams v. Lay (1962), 218 Ga. 451 (1), 128 S. E. 2d 502. 

§ 336.-Guardians Ad Litem.- 

"The mode of service of writs, petitions, citations, and other legal proceedings in the courts on minors shall be as follows: Service shall be perfected on a minor by delivering a copy of said proceeding, of whatever kind or nature it may be, to said minor personally; and in cases where there is a statutory or testamentary guardian or trustee representing the interest of the minor to be affected by a legal proceeding, service as usual on said guardian or trustee shall be sufficient to bind said minor's interest in his control to be affected by said proceedings. When the returns of such service are made to the proper court, and an order taken to appoint for said minor a guardian ad litem, and such guardian ad litem agrees to serve in writing, all of which shall be shown in proceedings of the court, said minor shall be considered a party to said proceeding." Code § 81-212. "Code § 81-121 provides that a minor between the ages of 14 and 21 years of age must be personally served, after which the court shall appoint a guardian ad litem, and the minor shall then be considered a party to the proceedings." Smith v. Lamb (1961), 103 Ga. App. 157, 158, 118 S. E. 2d 924. "Where an infant is a party defendant in a civil action it is ordinarily necessary to the validity of the judgment that the court appoint a guardian

ad litem to protect his interests. An estoppel in pais to urge the defense, however, may arise where, as here, the fact of infancy is unknown to the court or the opposing parties, no facts are shown which would reasonably cause them to question the defendant's age, and the defendant, with knowledge of his rights and of the ignorance of the court and the parties to the case, appears, pleads, and actively participates in the trial as the leading witness for the defense, being at all times represented by counsel. Silence will constitute deception where there is a duty to speak. Such a duty arises where the machinery of the law would otherwise be subverted to a purpose not intended, that of giving one side two chances for a verdict in his favor where the other side has only one." Smith v. Lamb (1961), 103 Ga. App. 157, 118 S. E. 2d 924.

§ 340.-Jurisdiction.-Harrison v. Tonge (1942), 67 Ga. App. 54, 19 S. E. 

2d 535; Beavers v. Williams (1942), 194 Ga. 875, 23 S. E. 2d 171; Orr v. Orr (1944), 197 Ga. 866, 30 S. E. 2d 900; Turner v. Prigmore (1947), 202 Ga. 377, 43 S. E. 2d 259. "Under Code § 24-1901 (5), courts of ordinary have original, exclusive, and general jurisdiction of the appointment and removal of guardians of unsound mind as well as of minors. In addition the issuance of commissions of lunacy

also comes within the jurisdiction of this court. Code § 24-1901 (9). And the appointment of guardians for insane persons without a trial when in the State mental hospital shall be under the same rules and regulations as govern the appointment for minors. However, the appointment of guardians for persons of unsound mind who are incapable of managing their estates shall occur only after formal examination of such person as required by Code (Ann.) § 49-604. 

For this type of examination inquiring into a person's capacity to manage his own estate the jurisdiction of the ordinary is extremely limited, the proceedings are summary and must be strictly construed, and must show on their face such facts especially as to the giving of notice, the issuance of the commission, and the return thereof, as will authorize the judgment appointing the guardian. 

Milam v. Terrell (1958), 214 Ga. 199, 201, 104 S. E. 2d 219.

The amendment raised the amount that the ordinary could collect from $500.00 to $1,000.00.

Acts 1958, page 675, amended Code § 49-112, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "49-112.
