House Bill Number 500 of the 1963 General Assembly provides that in addition to all other investments which executors, administrators, guardians, trustees, custodians and other like fiduciaries. holding trust funds are authorized by statute to make, they may also invest trust funds held by them in real estate loans (a) which are not default, (b) which are secured by mortgages or deeds to secure debt conveying a first security title to improved realty, (c) which are insured pursuant to the provisions of The National Housing Act, and (d) with respect to which real estate loans, on or after default, pursuant to such insurance, debentures in at least the full amount of unpaid principal are issuable and which debentures are

fully and unconditionally guaranteed both as to principal and interest by the United States. 

§ 346.-Same-Contracts by Guardians.-Turner v. Prigmore (1947), 202 

Ga. 377, 43 S. E. 2d 259.

The legislature in 1945 empowered minors who are eligible for benefits under the Service Men's Readjustment Act of 1944 to make valid and binding contracts or other written obligations for or in connection with a loan guaranteed in part or in full by the United States or any instrumentality thereof. Acts 

1945, page 434; Ga. Code Ann. 78-531.

Acts 1958, page 678, amended Code § 49-213, relating to contracts by guardians for labor and service, by adding to said section the following: "The court of ordinary or the superior court may, upon appropriate application and upon a proper showing by evidence of the need therefor, permit the erection of a dwelling, or an addition, repairs or renovation to an existing dwelling, on property of the ward."

Acts 1958, page 679, amended Code § 49-226, relating to the binding effect of a guardian borrowing money, entering into contract not allowed by law, and creating liens upon his ward's property, by adding the following proviso: "Provided, however, that upon application and showing the need by evidence, the court of ordinary or the superior court may authorize a guardian to borrow money to renovate or to make improvements upon property of his ward, or for the purposes set out in Code sections 49-203 and 49-204."

Acts 1959, page 171, again amended Code § 49-226, but only to change in the body of the section the reference to Code section "42-903" to section "49-203," this error having appeared in Acts 1958, page 679.

Where a will appointing a testamentary guardian of an incompetent to whom a life estate in land is devised only confers upon the guardian authority to manage the lands for the benefit of the ward, the guardian is without authority to create a debt binding upon the ward's estate, for money advanced by another to remodel or renovate houses on the ward's premises without approval of the ordinary or judge of the superior court. Greer v. Greer (1962), 218 Ga. 416 (3), 128 S. E. 2d 51.

Where a will appointing a testamentary guardian of an incompetent to whom a life estate in lands is devised only confers upon the guardian authority to manage the lands for the benefit of the ward, he cannot without the approval of the ordinary contract a debt binding upon the ward's estate for the services of another in caring for the ward. Greer v. Greer (1962), 218 Ga. 416 (2), 128 S. E. 2d 51. 

§ 347.-Same-Compromise of Claims.-"The word 'claims' in statute au thorizing guardians to compromise doubtful claims for or against their wards has a technical meaning and implies that a right is in dispute, including a demand arising out of tort and embraces the assertion of a liability to the party making it to pay a sum of money. Code 1933, § 49-219." Campbell v. Atlanta Coach Co. (1938), 58 Ga. App. 824, 200 S. E. 203 (1).

§ 348.-Same-Sales by Guardians for Reinvestment; Leases.—Turner v. 

Prigmore (1947), 202 Ga. 377, 43 S. E. 2d 259; Hall v. Hall (1948), 203 Ga. 656, 47 S. E. 2d 806.

Acts 1958, pages 676, 677, amended Code § 49-203, as amended by Acts 1953, Jan.-Feb. Sess., page 389, relating to the sale of a ward's estate for reinvestment, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "49-203. By order of the court of ordinary of the county of the guardian's appointment, or in the case of a foreign guardian, the court of ordinary in the county in which all or any part of the property is situated, the real or personal property of a ward, or any part thereof, may be sold, leased, encumbered or exchanged by the guardian upon such terms as the court may order, for the payment of the ward's debts, providing for his care, maintenance, support and education of those who are legally dependent upon the ward, or for the purpose of investing the proceeds in other property, when it is deemed in the best interests of the ward to do so.' 

Acts 1962, page 93, superseded Code § 49-204, which Code section now provides as follows: "When a sale, lease, exchange or encumbrance of the ward's estate, or any part thereof, shall be deemed necessary or in the best interests of the ward, the guardian may file with the ordinary a petition setting forth the facts, terms and reasons for making the proposed sale, lease, exchange or encumbrance. Citation shall be issued thereon and copy of the petition and citation shall be served personally upon the ward, if he is over 14 years of age: Provided, however, it shall not be necessary to serve the ward if he is a patient in a hospital, sanitarium, or other similar institution, operated by the State of Georgia or any other State of these United States; or any agency or political subdivision thereof, or operated by the United States Veterans Administration or any other Federal agency or instrumentality. The citation only shall be published once a week for four weeks in the newspaper in which the sheriff's advertisements for that county appear. On or after the date appointed in the citation the ordinary may consider the petition, hear evidence thereon, and if the proposed transaction is fair and in the best interests of the ward, he shall issue an appropriate order permitting the sale, lease, exchange or encumbrance; however, the ordinary, if he deems it advisable, may require any sale of the ward's property, to be held publicly and subject to the confirmation of the court. 

The provisions hereof are cumulative and not exclusive of other provisions of the law authorizing sales by guardians. Where service is not made upon the ward it shall be the duty of the ordinary to determine the reason therefor and state such reason in his order." 

The property of a minor may be disposed of by his guardian for the payment of a ward's debts, providing for his care, maintenance, support and education

and of those dependent upon the ward, for the purpose of reinvestment when deemed to be in the best interests of the ward. This is accomplished after due hearing and appropriate order by the ordinary, or in the case of sale other than for reinvestment, under his direction. West v. Downer (1962), 218 Ga. 

235, 242, 127 S. E. 2d 359.

Acts 1958, page 685, repealed Code § 49-212, which section required the renting of lands of a minor to be public and to the highest bidder, unless by special order of the ordinary.

The leasing or renting of real or personal property of the ward is now covered by Ga. Code Ann., § 49-203, as amended. See § 348 of this Supplement. 

In 1953, the Legislature set up a procedure for the execution of leases of trust property. Thus it is provided in section 1 of Acts 1953, page 44 et seq. (Ga. Code Ann. § 108-439 thru 108-444) that: "When the assets of a trust include an interest in real property the trustee may apply to the superior court for an order authorizing such trustee to lease such real property or a part thereof for a term of years which may or will continue beyond the termination of the trust and the superior court in the execution of the protective powers of equity over trust estates and the estates of wards in chancery shall have power and jurisdiction to pass an order authorizing the execution of such a lease." 

The word "trust," wherever used in the Act, includes the estate held by an executor, administrator, guardian, or trustee, whether held or in existence at the time of the passage of the Act or later coming into existence. There is provision for action upon the application in vacation and at chambers and for notice to all living beneficiaries as may be ordered by the court. Provision is also made for the appointment of guardians ad litem wherever necessary. A lease so executed is binding upon all beneficiaries in life or born subsequent to its execution during the existence of the lease. It is further provided by section 6 of the Act that: "It shall be the duty of the superior court to hear evidence that may be tendered by the trustee and if the court is satisfied from the proceedings that the lease to be authorized is expedient, the court shall pass an order authorizing the trustee to execute the lease subject, however, to such terms as the court shall deem proper and necessary to protect the value of the trust estate. The granting of such application is not precluded by the fact that the instrument creating the trust only authorizes leases for terms not extending beyond the duration of the trust."

Code Ann. 113-1733. Does "face value" include the premium for which a bond may be selling on the market at the time of the sale? The face value of the bond may be one hundred dollars, and the bond may have a market value of 110, plus interest.

99 The provisions of Code § 81-212 as to service upon minors applies also to insane persons. In an action against such an incompetent, process must be prayed for and also served upon him. Without the required service or waiver thereof, there is no suit, and a judgment in such a case is a mere nullity. 

Accordingly, since it was shown by the record in the case in which the judgment complains of was rendered that there was no service upon the insane ward, the judgment was void. Abner v. Weekes (1955), 91 Ga. App. 682, 683, 96 S. E. 2d 727.

Acts 1958, pages 680-681, amended Code § 49-313, relating to the resignation of guardians, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: 66 49-313. (a) Any guardian who, from age, infirmity, removal from the county, or for other cause, desires to resign his trust as such may apply to the ordinary having jurisdiction of the trust, setting forth the reason therefor, and also the name of some suitable person willing to accept the trust; whereupon the ordinary shall cite such person and the nearest kin of such ward to appear before him at the next term of court, and if the ordinary shall be satisfied that such change of guardians will not be detrimental to the interest of the ward, and no good cause shall be shown against it, he shall grant the prayer of the applicant, discharging him from his trust on condition that he shall forthwith deliver all property and pay all money held by him as such guardian, upon a fair settlement of his accounts to his successor; and upon the filing of the evidence of such settlement and the receipt in full of his successor, the guar- dian shall be discharged from his said trust. The ward shall have the privilege, within five years after he shall have come of age, or

his disabilities have been removed, to reopen such settlement and call for an accounting." "(b) When a guardian desires to resign his trust and the ward has removed to a different county, the resignation of the guardian and the appointment of the successor guardian may be accomplished in the following manner: "1. The guardian may file a petition with the ordinary having jurisdiction of the trust, setting forth the reasons why he desires to resign his trust, and stating whether a petition for appointment of a successor guardian has been or will be filed with the ordinary of the ward's residence. The ordinary shall cite the three nearest adult relatives of the ward residing within the State to appear, or if less than three, upon all, and if the ordinary shall be satisfied that resignation of the guardian will not be detrimental to the interest of the ward and that a petition has been or will be filed for appointment of a successor guardian in the county of the ward's residence, and no good cause shall be shown against it, he shall grant the prayer of the petitioner and enter an order accepting the resignation of the guardian to take effect upon the filing with the court evidence of the appointment of a successor guardian by the ordinary of the county of the ward's residence. Said order shall provide for discharging the guardian from his trust on condition that he shall deliver all property and pay all money held by him as such guardian, upon a fair settlement of his accounts, to his successor; and upon the filing of the evidence of such settlement and the receipt in full of his successor, the guardian shall be discharged from his said trust. The ward shall have the privilege, within five years after he shall have come of age, or his disabilities have been removed, to reopen such settlement and call for an accounting. "2. A petition shall be filed with the ordinary of the county of the ward's residence to have a guardian appointed to succeed the guardian resigning in another county. This petition shall contain a statement of the facts as to the resignation of the guardian in the other county, and notice thereof shall be given as provided by Code section 49-112, as amended, for the appointment of a guardian for a minor under the age of 14 years, other than the child of the applicant. Should the ordinary be satisfied that he has jurisdiction and that necessity for appointment of a guardian exists and no good cause shall be shown against it, he shall appoint the successor guardian upon the filing with him of a certified copy of the order of the ordinary of the other county accepting the resignation of the guardian in that county.'

§ 356.-Accounting and Settlement.-Pettigrew v. Williams (1941), 65 Ga. 

App. 576, 16 S. E. 2d 120; Henson v. Jones (1941), 66 Ga. App. 22, 16 S. E. 

---

2d 886; Harrison v. Tonge (1942), 67 Ga. App. 54, 19 S. E. 2d 535; Pettigrew v. Williams (1942), 68 Ga. App. 435, 23 S. E. 2d 183; Taintor v. Rogers (1944), 197 Ga. 872, 30 S. E. 2d 892; Mitchell v. Mitchell (1946), 201 Ga. 621, 40 S. E. 

2d 738. "When a ward shall die intestate, the guardian shall proceed to distribute his estate in the same manner as if he had been appointed administrator upon such estate, and the sureties on his bond shall be responsible for his faithful administration and distribution of such estate." Code § 49-316. 

While Code § 49-236 provides that, "When any guardian shall fail or refuse to settle and account with his ward upon his coming of age, such ward may institute his suit in the first instance against his guardian and sureties without first suing his guardian," yet, where, as in this case, a duly qualified guardian, under $12,000 bond, had not "filed for approval any annual returns," the ward should have applied to the ordinary, instead of the superior court, for the relief he was seeking, since Code § 49-301 provides that, "A ward, on arriving at majority. . . may apply to the ordinary for an order requiring the guardian to appear and submit to a settlement of his accounts." Moon v. Moon (1959), 215 Ga. 110, 111 (1), 109 S. E. 2d 39.

Where a petition merely sought an accounting of a ward's estate by his guardian, which could have been obtained through the ordinary under Code § 49-301, and by amendment to the petition the plaintiff shows, not only that a final, itemized return had been filed and approved by the ordinary (which, in effect, is the accounting he was seeking), but that the guardian had been discharged, it was not error in sustaining a general demurrer and dismissing the petition. Moon v. Moon (1959), 215 Ga. 110, 112 (3), 109 S. E. 2d 39. "Where an adult ward has had her sanity restored and the sole remaining issue between her and the guardian is one of settlement, and where she dies intestate pending such settlement, the guardian is not vested with authority to administer her estate." Fuller v. Weekes (1962), 105 Ga. App. 790 (1), 125

S. E. 2d 662, reversed on other grounds in Weekes v. Fuller (1962), 218 Ga. 

515, 128 S. E. 2d 715. "Where an adult ward has had her sanity restored and the sole contract between such ward and her guardian relates to an accounting of the ward's estate, the residence of such ward is not necessarily the county of the residence of the guardian." Fuller v. Weekes (1962), 105 Ga. App. 790 (1a), 125 S. E. 

2d 662, reversed on other grounds in Weekes v. Fuller (1962), 218 Ga. 515, 128 S. E. 2d 715. "A receipt signed by a ward, after restoration of sanity but before the approval of a final return by a guardian, stating that the ward has received payment in full of her estate is not an accord and satisfaction because of the fiduciary relationship and because such an acknowledgment, if an accord and satisfaction, would deprive the court of ordinary of examining such final return." Fuller v. Weekes (1962), 105 Ga. App. 790 (2a), 125 S. E. 2d 662, reversed on other grounds in Weekes v. Fuller (1962), 218 Ga. 515, 128 S. E. 

2d 715. "Assuming that the exercise of reasonable care will relieve a guardian of his liability for paying out funds of his ward's estate for a claim not sustainable in law, the failure to make any personal investigation and the acceptance of statements of persons as to facts admittedly not within their personal knowledge does not show an exercise of such care by the guardian." Fuller v. Weekes (1962), 105 Ga. App. 790 (3a), 125 S. E. 2d 662, reversed on other grounds in Weekes v. Fuller (1962), 218 Ga. 515, 128 S. E. 2d 715.

Acts 1958, page 377, amended Code § 49-316, relating to a guardian acting as administrator of his ward's estate, which section as amended is as follows: "49-316. When a ward shall die intestate, the guardian shall proceed to distribute his estate in the same manner as if he had been appointed administrator upon such estate, and the sureties on his bond shall be responsible for the faithful administration and distribution of such estate.'

This amendment struck from this section "Pending his minority." Therefore, it follows that a guardian of a ward may act as administrator of his ward's estate regardless of the age of the ward when he dies. It would also seem that guardians appointed for any incompetent person may upon such ward's death act as the administrator of his ward's estate.

"Under Code § 24-1901 (5), courts of ordinary have original, exclusive, and general jurisdiction of the appointment and removal of guardians of persons of unsound mind as well as of minors. In addition the issuance of commissions of lunacy also comes within the jurisdiction of this court. Code § 24-1901 (9). 

And the appointment of guardians for insane persons without a trial when in the State mental hospital shall be under the same rules and regulations as govern the appointment for minors. However, the appointment of guardians for persons of unsound mind who are incapable of managing their estates shall occur only after formal examination of such person as required by Code (Ann.) § 49-604. For this type of examination inquiring into a person's capacity to manage his own estate the jurisdiction of the ordinary is extremely limited, the proceedings are summary and must be strictly construed, and must show on their face such facts especially as to the giving of notice, the issuance of the commission, and the return thereof, as will authorize the judgment appointing the guardian. Milam v. Terrell (1958), 214 Ga. 199, 201, 104 S. E. 2d 219.

§ 359.-Same-Examination of Capacity to Manage Estate.—Where a peti tion is filed asking for the court of ordinary to appoint a commission to inquire as to the capacity of a person to manage his estate, and only the wife was served with the application, the other nearest of kin can not waive the required 10 days' notice, and where the commission is issued without the requisite notice the judgment appointing the guardian is void. Milam v. Terrell (1958), 214 Ga. 199, 204, 104 S. E. 2d 219. 

§ 360.-Ordinaries as Custodians of Moneys of Minors or Insane Persons.- 

The Legislature, in 1955, page 592, enacted a statute concerned with gifts of securities to minors. Under this act, the method and form of transfer are prescribed, and the powers and duties of the custodian are outlined. The act, which is not to be construed to apply to gifts by bequest or inheritance, is not meant to provide an exclusive method of making gifts of securities to minors. This act is codified in Ga. Code Ann. as Chapter 48-3. 

Acts 1957, page 98, amended Acts 1955, pages 592, 594 (Ga. Code Ann., § 48-301), by providing that any adult person may not only make a gift of securities, but also a gift of money, to persons not yet attained the age of 21 years on the date of the gift. This act also provides the procedure to be followed when the gift is in the form of money. 

Acts 1958, page 650, amended Code § 49-701, which section provides that the ordinaries of the several counties are made and constituted the legal custodians and distributors of all moneys due and owing to any minor or insane person who has no legal and qualified guardian. The amendment raised the amount that the ordinary could collect from $500.00 to $1,000.00. 

§ 361.-Guardians of Incompetent World War Veterans.—Harrison v. Tonge 

(1942), 67 Ga. App. 54, 19 S. E. 2d 535.

Acts 1958, page 683, amended Code § 49-806, relating to notice of a petition for the appointment of a guardian for a incompetent veteran, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "49-806. Upon the application for the appointment of a guardian under Code Chapter 49-8, notice shall be given as provided by Code section 49-112, as amended, for the appointment of guardians for minors under the age of 14 years, other than the child of the applicant."

See § 342 of this Supplement as to the notice required by Code § 49-112, as amended. This is same notice as required in the appointment of guardians for minors under the age of 14 other than the child of the applicant.

Acts 1958, page 683, amended Code § 49-807, by raising the amount of bond required by said section from $500 to $1000, and by adding the following to said section: "Provided, further, however, that the ordinary may, upon a proper showing that the value of the ward's estate has decreased,

permit a decrease in the amount of the bond to an amount equal to the then value, plus the sums estimated to be payable to the ward during the ensuing year, provided, that no such reduction shall affect the liability of the surety for past waste or misconduct of the guardian."

Acts 1958, page 684, amended Code § 49-810, relating to the expenditures of a guardian, by striking said section in its entirety and substituting in lieu thereof the following: "49-810. A guardian shall not apply any portion of the estate of his ward for the support, maintenance and education of any person other than his ward, spouse and the children of the ward who are legally dependent upon the ward, except upon order of the court after a hearing, notice of which has been given the proper office of the bureau in the manner provided in section 49-815. A guardian shall be authorized to make expenditures of funds of his ward for the proper support, maintenance and education of the spouse or dependent child of the ward without a court order, in the same manner as expenditures are made for the support, maintenance and education of the ward.”

Note: It would take many forms to show all variations pertaining to marital deductions, but the two forms shown below give a general idea as to how provisions for marital deductions should be set up. See section 264, this supplement, ante.

FORMS 

213 = 3 Form No. 1 

FORM OF MARITAL DEDUCTION AS A COMPLETE GIFT 

I give, devise, and bequeath to my wife, MARY DOE an amount equal to fifty per cent (50%) of the value of my adjusted gross estate as finally determined for federal estate tax purposes, less the aggregate amount of marital deductions allowed by reason of interests in other property passing, if any, it being my intention to convey to my wife, MARY DOE, the maximum value in assets that may be deducted from my estate as the "marital deduction." 

If my wife does not survive me, such property above bequeathed to her shall be added to the residuum of my estate. 

The executor shall have full power and discretion to satisfy said marital deduction out of the assets of my estate wholly or partly in cash or in kind and to select and designate the cash, securities, or other assets including real estate, which shall constitute said marital deduction assets. The exercise by the executor of the power and discretion hereby conferred shall not be subject to question by any person.

When the marital deduction assets are delivered to my wife, any increase in value thereof and any interest or income earned thereon, between the date selected for the determination of the value of my estate for estate tax purposes and the date of delivery or distribution to her, shall belong to her. Any depreciation in value of said marital deduction assets between said dates shall be borne by the marital deduction assets.¹ 

1. The trust instrument may provide that the wife shall not be entitled to the increase in value but it must provide that she is entitled to all the income from the trust property payable annually or more often from the date of the death of the deceased.

Form No. 2 

FORM OF MARITAL DEDUCTION TRUST 

All the rest, residue, and remainder of my adjusted gross estate, both real and personal wherever situated, I divide into two parts, one to be known as the marital deduction, hereinafter referred to as the "Marital Trust", and the other to be known as the "Residuary Trust." (This portion need not be put in trust but may be devised outright.) 

The "Marital Trust" is for the benefit of my wife, MARY DOE, and it shall consist of an amount equal to fifty per cent (50%)¹ of the value of my adjusted gross estate as finally determined for federal estate tax purposes, less the aggregate amount of marital deductions, if any, allowed for such tax purposes by reason of 1. The marital deduction may be any portion of the adjusted gross estate up to 50%.

other property or interests in other property passing to her under other provisions of this will or which have already passed to her or for her benefit prior to my death or which may pass or which might have already passed to her by operation of law, it being my intention that my wife shall have the maximum value in assets, which may be deducted from my estate as the marital deduction regardless of whether this increases the estate tax on the remainder of the estate or not. When said marital trust assets are delivered to the trustee, hereinafter named, any increase in value thereof accruing between the date of my death and the date of distribution of the marital trust assets to the trustee, shall belong to said "Marital Trust.'' Any depreciation in value of said marital trust assets between said dates, shall be borne by the "Marital Trust. 

Except for that portion of the "Marital Trust" passing by operation of law or by other provisions of this will, as above explained, the executor shall have full authority and discretion to satisfy said "Marital Trust" out of the assets of my estate wholly or partly in cash or in kind, and to select and designate the cash, securities, or other assets, including real estate, which shall constitute said marital trust assets. In no event shall there be included in said "Marital Trust" any assets or proceeds of the sale of any asset with respect to which a marital deduction would not be allowable if so included. I give, bequeath, and devise to my brother, THOMAS R. DOE,* 

2. Examples of the property which may be taxed in the husband's estate and may be subject to the marital deduction, though not passing to the wife either under the will or by operation of law, are the following: (a) Gifts made by the husband to the wife during his lifetime which are held to have been "'in contemplation of death."' (b) Transfers from husband to wife which reserve a life estate in the husband. (IRC 2036). (c) Lifetime transfers from husband to wife which take effect at the husband's death. (IRC 2037). (d) Lifetime transfers from husband to wife which could be revoked or otherwise changed by him up to the time of his death. (IRC 2038). (e) Survivorship annuities. (IRC 2039). (f) Lifetime transfers from husband to wife for an insufficient consideration. (IRC 2043).

All of the foregoing constitute properties "which have already passed to" the wife. They are included in the adjusted gross estate of the husband and should, therefore, be deducted from the assets passing into the "Marital Trust," because each of these assets qualifies for the marital deduction. 

3. This can be modified, if the testator so desires, by providing that the marital deduction shall be valued as of the date selected for the determination of the estate tax-date of death or one year from that date. 

4. It is usually better to name a bank or trust company as trustee or co-trustee as an individual trustee may die or become incapacitated.

In addition to or in support of such powers, I authorize said trustee : (a) to receive, hold, exchange, manage, and control said trust property in his reasonable discretion for the benefit of this trust; (b) To hold the same, or any part thereof, in cash from time to time, and to invest, reinvest, or keep the same invested in such income-bearing securities or other property, real or personal, as the trustee may deem advisable, in his reasonable discretion, and to collect the income therefrom for the benefit of this trust and to dispose of said income as required by the provisions of this will; (c) To have and exercise full power to sell, exchange, lease, or otherwise dispose of, from time to time, in his discretion, for the benefit of this trust, all or any portion of the trust estate in the manner and upon such terms as the trustee may, in the exercise of his judgment and discretion, deem most beneficial to the trust estate. (d) In the exercise of the powers and authority herein conferred for the benefit of this trust, the trustee is empowered, as often as may be necessary in his discretion, to invest, sell, encumber, or exchange, for cash or upon terms, without the order of any court, any part or all of the assets of the trust estate, either publicly or privately, with or without notice by publication or otherwise; no purchaser shall be required to see to the application of the purchase money. (e) I hereby authorize the trustee to invest in securities other than those fixed by the statutes of the state of my domicile at the time of my death for the investment of trust funds, and I expressly relieve the trustee from any liability for depreciation in holding in his discretion any non-legal investments owned by me at the time of my death. (f) After paying all taxes and all costs of administering the "Marital Trust," including reasonable trustee's fees and other charges and expenses incident to the care, operation, and maintenance of said "Marital Trust," the trustee, commencing with the date of his qualification, shall pay all of the net income from said "Marital Trust" to my said wife in quarter-annual installments, or in more frequent installments in the discretion of the trustee, for the duration of this trust. My wife shall also be entitled to all net income earned from said marital trust assets from the date of my death to the date of the qualification of the trustee, and the

same shall be paid to her by the executor or by the trustee in accordance with the law in force at the time of my death. (g) My wife is given the full and exclusive power to appoint the entire assets of the "Marital Trust," free of this trust, to herself or to her estate; she may make such appointment by will or by deed or by other form of transfer to any person, corporation, association, educational institution, church, or charity, jointly or severally including her own creditors or the creditors of her estate, as she may desire. The singular number thus used in describing the possible beneficiaries of such appointment shall be construed to include the plural number also, and the plural number shall also be construed to include the singular number. My wife is also given the exclusive power to appoint from time to time any portion or portions of said marital trust assets by deed or other form of transfer and the remaining portion thereof by will. 

If my said wife fails to make such appointment or appointments, then said marital trust property, or any portion not appointed, at her death, shall become a part of the "Residuary Trust" created by the terms of this will and shall be administered accordingly. (h) If my said wife does not survive me, the assets of the "Marital Trust" above bequeathed shall be added to the residuum of my estate.

Clerk, Court of Ordinary or Notary Public Note: Acts 1958, pages 659, 660, amended Code § 113-601, relating to the probate of a will in common form, which section as amended, provides that the petition to probate a will in common shall also contain all the information as is required of a petition to probate a will in solemn form, which requirements are set form in Code § 113-602, as amended. The requirements to probate a will in common form are as follows: 

1. A will may be probated in common form, proved and admitted to record, upon the testimony of a single subscribing witness, and without notice to anyone. 

2. A petition to probate a will in common form must be verified by the oath of the petitioner. 

3. The petition must set forth the name and post office address of the petitioner. 

4.

The full name, place of domicile, legal residence, and the date of the death of testator. 

5. That testator died owning property in the State of Georgia. 

6. That testator died leaving a will and that the same is offered to the court to be probated in common form. 

7. The names, ages and addresses of the surviving spouse of testator and of all his heirs at law, giving their relationship to the testator. 

8. In the event full particulars are lacking as to the surviving spouse, heirs at law, devisees and legatees, the petition should so state, and should give the reasons for such omissions. 

9. The petition should contain a prayer asking the will be probated in common form, admitted to record upon proper proof, and pray that letters testamentary issue to petitioner.

Objections: See discussion below: 

1. Filed by creditors show debts. 

2. Filed by other interested person showing- (a) Debts, or (b) Heirs at law laboring under disabilities, or (c) Debts owed by estate, or (d) Other legal reason why administration required. 

3. Objection of Creditor must be in writing. 

Duty of Ordinary: 

1. Determine if deceased person was resident of county or if a nonresident owned property in county. 

2. Determine that heir at law filed petition. 

3. Determine (a) who are the heirs at law, (b) if all are of age, (c) if any laboring under disabilities. 4. 

Determine if estate owes debts. 

5. Determine if any legal cause shown why order should not be granted. 

6. Pass order if no such cause shown.

The purpose of this act is to provide a method of judicially determining the question of whether an administration upon an estate is necessary so that where none is necessary, the heirs may sell or encumber the property they inherit without the expense and delay of administration, and the purchaser or lender may be protected.

This act only applies to that class of estates which owes no debts, and where the heirs are sui juris and have agreed upon a division among themselves. Both of these conditions are prerequisite to its application. 

Thus, where one files an objection claiming that the estate owes him a debt, the Ordinary is without jurisdiction to approve the order finding that no administration is necessary. 

It is not proper for the Ordinary to investigate the nature of the debt claimed to be owed to the objector, nor does he have the right to determine whether the objector is a creditor. 

The fact that the objection is filed shows that there is an outstanding claim requiring administration. For it is the prerogative and duty of an administrator to determine, judicially if necessary, the justness of a claim, and this act does not confer any power upon the ordinary to determine such questions under the guise of deciding upon the necessity for administration. 

Section three of the act expressly deprives the Court of Ordinary of the jurisdiction to pass the order, if an objection is filed. 

Section four of the act does not change, and is not in conflict with, § 3 on this question. Section four merely makes it the duty of the Ordinary, even in the absence of the filing of a written objection by creditors, to determine whether there are debts owing by the estate, and if the Ordinary finds that there are debts, he has no jurisdiction to pass the order. 

The act contemplates that other interested persons may file objections. It would seem that, if an objection raises a question making administration necessary, either for the purpose of investigating the question raised or for any other purpose properly falling within the duties of an administrator, the petition should be denied.

The Ordinary is bound by the act to determine if all the heirs are sui juris, and if they are not to deny the order. 

Suppose one should file an objection contending that he is an heir, and that he has not agreed to the division of the estate among the heirs, or that the agreement was procured by misrepresentation or other fraud, or that for some other reason, raising an issue as to the division, he is unwilling to abide by it. 

Would the Ordinary have jurisdiction to pass upon this question and decide the issue raised?

Undoubtedly not, because such a controversy would, upon its face, show the necessity for administration upon the estate, so that such questions would be determined by regular legal investigation with the right to introduce evidence, impeach witnesses, disapprove evidence, cite authority, make arguments, and have the right of appeal.

It would seem that this statute does not apply if debts are owed to the estate because these are collected by the administrator, and for that reason administration is necessary. 

So the Ordinary has jurisdiction to pass an order finding that no administration is necessary under the provisions of this act, only when there are no issues raised, respecting the administration or distribution of the estate. 

This act expressly restricts the jurisdiction of the Court of Ordinary to estates where the deceased died without will. 

The effect of the passage of the order by the court of Ordinary is to free the property in so far as the purchaser or lender in good faith is concerned, from the claim of all creditors of the estate, except such claims, liens, judgments, security deeds, mortgages or incumbrances as have been duly recorded, or filed for record, in the manner required by law, so as to constitute notice thereof, and except the liens for taxes and liens arising from the giving or signing of the bond of a public official. 

The petition is filed by any heir at law, and must be filed in the county where the deceased intestate resided at the time of his death, or if a nonresident of the state at the time of his death, in the county where the property is located. 

If the deceased were a nonresident of the state at the time of his death, and if he had property at the time of his death located in more than one county of the state, the question arises as to whether a petition must be filed in each county where the property is located. 

Another interesting question is whether or not a claimant to a portion of the property, or a person claiming an interest therein, can be heard to object to an order. Georgia, County.

113-1426) changes the law relating to annual returns of administrators, executors, and other fiduciaries such as guardians, trustees, etc. Under the final act of 1943 such fiduciaries are required to file annual returns 60 days after anniversary date of the qualification in each year.

Note: The administrator of the estate may continue the business of the deceased from year to year during administration provided each year he files the application and is granted an order permitting it after a compliance with the 1951 statute.

This statute does not make any special provision for serving minors or persons laboring under disability, nor does it make any provision for the service of guardians of heirs. However, such guardians should be served. 

Nor is any provision made for the service of creditors of the estate. No procedure is prescribed for making and hearing objections. Undoubtedly, the ordinary will be held to have a discretion as to whether or not he will grant the order.

The order denying the application may read: "The above and foregoing application having this day been presented to me, and it appearing that the administrator failed to serve the written notice upon all the heirs at law of the said deceased (or that, it appearing that it is not to the best interest of the estate of the said deceased), said application is hereby denied, etc."

he be allowed as the administrator (or executor) of said estate to borrow a sufficient sum of money to pay the .... taxes due by said estate to and that he be allowed to bind said estate by the execution of a promissory note and other security instruments and pledging the property of said estate therefor, this is to cite all parties interested to be and appear before me on the .... day of ..... 19...., to show cause if any they can, why the prayers of said petition should not be granted. 

Ordinary, County Georgia

Note: The above forms are based on Acts 1959, page 99 (Ga. Code Ann., 

§ 113-1529). The requirements of such a proceeding is as follows: 

1. An executor or administrator by virtue of his appointment, shall have the legal right to borrow money and bind the estate by the execution of a promissory note therefor, and shall have the right to pledge any or all property of the estate for the payment thereof by mortgage, trust deed, deed to secure debt, or other security instrument, for the purpose of paying any gift, estate, inheritance, income, sales or ad valorem taxes due the United States, the state or any municipality or county thereof, which constitute a claim or demand against said estate. 

2. The administrator or executor must petition the ordinary, which petition must set forth all the facts, the amount of money to be borrowed, the purpose thereof, the rate of interest to be paid, the property to be pledged as security, and the period of time over which the money is to be repaid. 

3. Notice of the application shall be published once a week for four weeks before the hearing, in the newspaper in which the sheriff's advertisements are published. 

4. Any person interested may object to such application. 

5. After the hearing, if the ordinary is satisfied of the truth of the allegations and deems it to the best interest of the estate, an order shall be passed granting leave to the administrator or the executor to borrow said money and to encumber the estate, or any part thereof, specifying the portion to be bound as definitely as possible. 

6. The order shall be binding, final and conclusive as to all devisees, legatees, or heirs, and to all creditors of the estate, regardless of any prior assent of the executor or administrator; however, any aggrieved party may appeal said order in the time provided by law. 

7. Nothing in said order shall limit the powers contained in the will of the decedent.

§ 113-2801 ET SEQ. PETITION TO DETERMINE HEIRS AT LAW Note: Acts 1958, pages 361-364 (Ga. Code Ann., §§ 113-2801 thru 

113-2808), provide a procedure for determining the heirs at law entitled to the distribution of property under the laws of descent and distribution, or for determining those who are entitled to the distribution of property under a will, trust, or any other written instrument. The procedure may be filed in either the court of ordinary or the superior court by any executor, administrator, guardian, conservator, committee, trustee, fiduciary, or by any person by whatever named called, having a status which by operation of law, or by any written instrument, such as a will or trust, or any other written instrument, has the duty of distributing property. The proceeding may also be filed by any person who deems himself to be an heir at law of the deceased person involved, or in any way interested as a distributee.

Clerk, Court of Ordinary, or Ordinary if no Clerk.

Note: The above forms are based upon Acts 1958, pages 361-364 (Ga. Code 

Ann., §§ 113-2801 through 113-2808), providing the procedure for determining the heirs at law entitled to the distribution of property under the laws of descent and distributing, or for determining those who are entitled to the distribution of property under a will, trust, or any other written instrument. 

The requirements for such a proceeding, and the effect thereof, are as follows: 

1. Jurisdiction is in the court of ordinary where the administration of an estate is pending, or which would have jurisdiction of such administration if one is filed, or in the superior court of such county as that of the ordinary that has assumed jurisdiction of an administration or would have jurisdiction in the event one is filed. 

2. The petition may be brought by any executor, administrator, guardian, conservator, committee, trustee, fiduciary, or by any other person by whatever named called, having a status which by operation of law, or by any written instrument, such as a will or trust, or any other such written instrument, has the duty of distributing property. The proceeding may also be filed by any person who deems himself to be an heir at law, or in any way interested as a distributee, and his petition must meet the requirements as prescribed for other parties. 

3. The petition should allege the names, addresses, ages and relationships, as far as known, of all parties of such interests, and the nature and character of such interests. 

4. In the event some of the parties are minors or otherwise incompetent, such fact must be alleged, and whether such incompetents have guardians qualified in Georgia.

5. The petition should further allege whether or not the petitioner has reason to apprehend that there might be others who are entitled to participate in the distribution of such property and whose names are unknown. 

6. The petition should be verified by petitioner. 

7. In the event such a proceeding is filed in the superior court, service shall be effected on the parties at interest in the same manner as in equity cases, and the cause shall proceed to judgment in the usual manner as provided for equity cases. 

8. In the event the proceeding is filed in a court of ordinary, a citation shall be issued calling upon all parties at interest to show cause on a day certain, not less than 30 days thereafter, why the court should not proceed to adjudicate the issues involved. All residents shall be served personally with a copy of the petition and citation. All others shall be served by publication, that is, by publishing once a week for four weeks a copy of the citation in the newspaper in which the sheriff's sales are advertised, and a copy of the newspaper, or a copy of the petition and citation, shall be mailed to each nonresident party by registered mail at least 15 days prior to the time set for hearing. After service is effected the ordinary shall appoint a guardian ad litem for minors and those under disabilities. On the date set for the hearing the ordinary shall proceed to determine all the issues involved. 

9. In the event the petition, whether filed in the court of ordinary or in the superior court, discloses an apprehension on the part of the petitioner that there may exist unknown heirs or parties at interest, then the superior court process in addition to naming all parties at interest, or the citation of the court of ordinary, shall be directed to all and singular any other person or person whom it may concern, and the process, if in the superior court, or citation if in the court of ordinary, shall be published once a week for four weeks in the newspaper in which the sheriff's advertisements for the county are published. 

10. Any person who deems himself to be an heir at law or interested in any way as a distributee and who is not named in the petition, may intervene, such petition for intervention to be verified under oath, and setting forth such claim, and shall allege facts showing the basis of such claim. 

11. The findings of the superior court or the court of ordinary shall be res judicata in the absence of fraud. 

12. After the time for appeal has passed the person charged with the distribution of the property shall deliver the same to those entitled in such shares and quantities as the judgment may specify.
